t.cova de gargan@40.2,-0.3:
High in the interior of Castellón, where the coastal orange groves are long forgotten and the land climbs toward the Penyagolosa massif, the shelter known as Cova de Gargán sits in a country of limestone ledges, holm oak and dry-stone terraces. Vistabella del Maestrazgo is the nearest village, a handful of kilometres away on its high plateau, with Villahermosa del Río down in its valley to the other side and Lucena del Cid a little further south. It is quiet up here in a way that the coast never is.

The shelter belongs to the great family of Levantine rock art, the painted overhangs that run down the eastern side of Spain and were listed together by UNESCO in 1998. The figures in these shelters are small, often only a hand's length, painted in reds and blacks by people who hunted and later herded in these hills thousands of years ago: archers in mid-stride, deer and ibex, scenes that feel more like quick sketches than formal art. Many shelters are protected by grilles, and the usual way to see the paintings close up is with a local guide arranged through the village or a visitor centre, so treat the ride as the main event and any viewing as a bonus you plan ahead.

And the riding is the reason to come. The roads that thread between Vistabella, Villahermosa and Lucena are narrow, twisting and lightly used, climbing through pine and oak with the grey bulk of Penyagolosa, the highest summit in the province, never far from view. Surfaces are generally decent but patched in places, with gravel washed onto the inside of bends after storms and the occasional flock of sheep that has absolutely no intention of moving for you. Spring is lovely, with broom flowering yellow on the slopes; high summer is hot in the valleys but fresher on the plateau; winter brings frost and even snow above a thousand metres.

Villages this size have bars and sometimes a small shop, but fuel is another matter. Plan to fill in l'Alcora, about twenty kilometres away toward the coast, or in one of the larger towns on your approach, and carry water on a hot day. As a start and finish point it works well because everything around it is good riding, and the loop back past the same rock walls in a different light can feel like a second route entirely.
t.castell de villafames@40.1,-0.1:
Villafamés announces itself from a long way off: a village of white and ochre houses stacked up a hill of reddish rock, with the remains of a castle crowning the top. It stands a little inland from the coast of Castellón, roughly between Borriol, Cabanes and the beach town of Benicàssim, close enough to the sea that you can smell salt on a westerly breeze turning, yet already in that rumpled hill country that leads up into the Maestrat.

The castle has Islamic origins and was taken during the Christian conquest of the kingdom of Valencia in the thirteenth century, later passing through the hands of military orders. What survives is a round tower and fragments of wall perched on the rock, and the climb up through the old streets is half the pleasure. The village itself has a reputation that is unusual for a place of under two thousand people: since the 1970s it has housed a museum of contemporary art in a Gothic palace, and the narrow lanes are dotted with sculptures and small galleries. It is also one of those places listed among the prettiest villages in Spain, and on a weekend you will not be alone.

For a rider, Villafamés is a compact, satisfying stop rather than a long one. The roads in from Borriol or from the coast are a mix of brisk open bends through almond and olive terraces and tighter work as you climb. Inland from here the CV roads toward Les Useres, Sant Joan de Moró and beyond get properly twisty, and you can stitch together a loop that never touches a main road. Leave the bike at the edge of the old town; the upper streets are steep, cobbled in places and not built for anything wider than a mule.

There are bars and restaurants in the village, and the light in the late afternoon, when the rock and the walls glow orange, is the best reason to time your arrival. For fuel, the bigger towns along the coast are the safe bet: Benicàssim is about thirteen kilometres away and Borriol is closer still. In summer it gets seriously hot by midday, so an early ride up and a long lunch in the shade is the local way of doing things.
t.abrigo de santa eulaliade la pena@42.3,-:
Just north of Huesca, where the flat cereal land of the Hoya suddenly rears up into the first limestone walls of the Pre-Pyrenees, lies the little village of Nueno and, above it, the rock shelter named after Santa Eulalia de la Peña. This is the southern edge of the Sierra de Guara country, a landscape of gorges, conglomerate cliffs and scrub where griffon vultures ride the thermals and the light comes hard off pale stone.

The shelter takes its name from the hermitage and the old hamlet of Santa Eulalia de la Peña, nearly abandoned now, which perches on the slopes above Nueno. Rock paintings in this part of Aragón are mostly of the schematic kind, simplified human and animal figures and abstract marks in red, different in feel from the lively Levantine hunting scenes further south and east. They are part of the same broad Mediterranean rock art inscription, and like most such sites they are small and fragile. Do not expect a gallery; expect a ledge, some faint red marks, and a sense of how long people have looked out over this plain.

The riding around here is better than many people realise. Nueno sits right by the A-23 motorway and the old N-330 that climbs toward the Monrepós pass and on to Sabiñánigo and Jaca, but the interesting stuff is on the small roads. Head east along the foot of the sierra toward Arguis, Bentué de Rasal or round to Loporzano and you get narrow tarmac, tight bends and lovely views back over the plain, with very little traffic. The surface is often coarse and occasionally broken, and in winter the north wind can be bitterly cold coming off the mountains.

Huesca, around fifteen kilometres to the south, is the place for fuel, a proper meal and anything mechanical. It is a pleasant old city with a Romanesque cloister at San Pedro el Viejo and a fine cathedral, and its pastry shops are known for a local almond cake called the trenza. Nueno and the nearby villages are tiny, so take what you need before heading up. Spring and autumn are the sweet spots: green hills, clear air, and none of the furnace heat that summer brings to the plain below.
t.forau del cocho@42.0,-0.4:
South of Huesca the land opens out. The Pyrenees are behind you, a snowy line on a clear day, and ahead stretches the gently rolling cereal country that eventually turns into the dry steppes of Los Monegros. Forau del Cocho lies in this transitional landscape, between Torres de Barbués, Almuniente and the outskirts of Huesca itself, a place where the only relief is the occasional low ridge or gully cut into soft rock.

The name is Aragonese, and forau means a hole or a hollow. Painted and engraved rock sites in this lowland part of Aragón are rarer than in the mountains, which gives them a particular interest: they suggest the plain was used and crossed by prehistoric people who left marks in the few rocky outcrops available. Like the other sites grouped under UNESCO's Mediterranean rock art inscription, it is modest and protected. There is no visitor centre waiting for you; this is very much a quiet, specialist spot.

Riding in this part of Aragón is all about space and sky. The roads south and east of Huesca are long, straight or gently curving, crossing fields of wheat and barley, with irrigation canals and the occasional farm complex. They are good for covering ground and for watching the light change, less so for knee-down entertainment. The wind is the defining feature: the cierzo, the dry northwesterly, can blow hard for days and makes riding on exposed roads tiring. Summer is very hot; winter mornings can bring thick fog in the valleys.

Huesca, around eleven kilometres away, is where to get fuel, food and anything else. If you are using this as a start or finish point, the city makes an easy base with plenty of places to stay. From here you can head north to the Sierra de Guara for proper twisting roads, west to the dramatic red cliffs of the Mallos de Riglos, or east into the Monegros, where the landscape becomes almost desert-like and roads run for kilometres without a village. Each direction has its own personality, and the plain around Forau del Cocho is the hinge between them.
t.abrigo de los gitanos@42.4,-0.8:
The road north-west out of Huesca toward Pamplona runs along the foot of a dramatic wall of rock. To the north are the Pre-Pyrenean sierras, and studded along them are some of Aragón's most striking sights: the Castle of Loarre, a superbly preserved Romanesque fortress on a spur, and the Mallos de Riglos, huge red conglomerate towers rising straight out of the hillside. The rock shelter known as the Abrigo de los Gitanos lies in this country, between Ayerbe, Loarre and Luesia.

The name, shelter of the gypsies, is the kind of label locals gave to places where travelling people might camp, and has nothing to do with the prehistoric paintings found there. The art in this part of Aragón tends to be schematic, simple red figures and symbols, and like all the sites in the Mediterranean rock art group it is small, protected and best appreciated with context from a local guide or interpretation centre.

Loarre Castle is the unmissable stop nearby. Built largely in the eleventh century as a frontier fortress during the Christian advance against the Muslim kingdoms, it is one of the best preserved Romanesque castles in Europe, and its walls appeared in the film Kingdom of Heaven. The road up to it from the village winds through pine and holm oak with a superb view over the plain.

For riding, this area is first-class. The A-132 north from Ayerbe toward Murillo de Gállego and Riglos follows the Gállego river past the Mallos, with good bends and dramatic scenery. From there you can carry on toward the reservoir of La Peña and up toward Jaca, or loop west through the quieter Cinco Villas country toward Luesia and Biel, on narrow roads with almost no traffic. Surfaces are mostly good, but watch out for gravel and for cyclists, as the region is popular with them.

Ayerbe has a petrol station and bars, but the nearest town of any size is Jaca, about thirty kilometres away as the crow flies, or Huesca to the south-east. Ayerbe is also known as the place where the Nobel-winning neuroscientist Santiago Ramón y Cajal spent part of his childhood.
t.raco d en gil@40.4,-0.1:
There is a small triangle of country in the Alt Maestrat, between Benassal, Catí and Albocàsser, where the hills fold into narrow ravines and the stone walls of old terraces climb every slope. Racó d'en Gil, a name meaning something like Gil's corner, lies in this landscape, and it sits within easy reach of the Valltorta gorge, the place that put Levantine rock art on the map.

The Valltorta shelters came to light in the early twentieth century and became famous for their scenes of archers hunting deer, wild goats and boar, painted with extraordinary movement and detail. The museum at Tírig, close by, explains the art and organises guided visits to some shelters. Racó d'en Gil and the many other sites in these ravines fill out a whole prehistoric landscape: dozens of shelters, each with a few figures, scattered along the gorges.

The villages are full of character. Benassal has an old walled centre and a mineral water spring, the Font d'en Segures, whose water is bottled. Catí is a lovely stone village with a Gothic church and a reputation for cheese. Albocàsser and Tírig are small farming communities in the dry hills, and Culla, a little to the south, crowns a hilltop with grand views.

The riding is excellent. The CV roads linking these villages are narrow and wind across the hills with countless bends, mostly gentle but sometimes tight, through olive and almond groves and over little passes. Traffic is light and the surfaces vary from smooth new tarmac to old and patched. The Maestrat sits at between five hundred and over a thousand metres, so it can be surprisingly cold in winter, and summer storms can bring sudden downpours. Late spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers bloom, is ideal.

The villages have bars and small shops, but there are few petrol stations. Alcalà de Xivert, about twenty-eight kilometres away near the coast, is the nearest larger town, but you will also find fuel along the CV-10 corridor. Plan your loop with fuel in mind, and stop at a village bar for a slice of local cured ham and a glass of wine.
t.abric del mas de barbera@41.0,-0.2:
Alcañiz is the capital of the Bajo Aragón, a region of olive groves, cereal fields and dry hills crossed by the Guadalope river in the south-east of Aragón. The town is crowned by a castle built for the Order of Calatrava, now a parador, and its main square, with a Gothic loggia and the town hall, is one of the finest in the region. The shelter of the Mas de Barberà lies in the hills just outside town, toward Castelserás and Calanda.

The Bajo Aragón is rich in rock art, with Levantine paintings scattered in the ravines around Alcañiz, Alcañiz el Viejo and the Val del Charco del Agua Amarga, one of the most important sites in the region, which has a famous scene of archers. These sites belong to the UNESCO-listed group and are protected; some offer guided visits arranged through the local tourist offices. The art here shows hunters and animals, as elsewhere, but also some especially dynamic compositions.

For motorcyclists, Alcañiz is best known for something else entirely: MotorLand Aragón, a modern racing circuit a few kilometres outside the town, which hosts international motorcycle races. The town also has a long history of street racing, with an old urban circuit that was used for decades. Track days at MotorLand are popular, and the town fills with riders on race weekends.

The roads around here are good for riding. The route south toward Calanda, Alcorisa and the Maestrazgo climbs gradually into wilder country, with tight bends and fewer cars. Calanda is the birthplace of the film director Luis Buñuel, and it is famous for its drums: during Holy Week, thousands of people beat drums through the night in the ritual known as the Tamborrada. The area also produces peaches with a protected designation, wrapped in paper bags on the tree to keep them perfect. Alcañiz, about six kilometres away, has all services. Local olive oil is excellent, and the town's restaurants serve hearty Aragonese fare: lamb, ham from Teruel and migas.
t.coveta de la cornisa@40.6,-0.1:
Morella is one of the most dramatic towns in Spain: a walled medieval city wrapped around a conical hill, with a castle on the summit and its walls running unbroken around the base. It stands in the mountains of the Ports in the north of Castellón province, at around a thousand metres, and its silhouette, seen from the roads that climb toward it, is unforgettable. The Coveta de la Cornisa, the little cave of the ledge, lies in the hills about four kilometres away.

The Ports area is part of the heartland of Levantine rock art, and many painted shelters lie in the ravines around Morella, often with scenes of hunters, animals and daily life. The Coveta de la Cornisa is one of them, a small protected site that adds to the picture of a landscape inhabited and painted over thousands of years. The nearby town of Morella has a museum with information on the region's prehistory, and the dinosaur fossils that have been found in the area, which are an unusual bonus.

Morella's history is long and turbulent. It was a Muslim stronghold, then conquered by the Aragonese in the thirteenth century, and in the nineteenth century it was a key bastion in the Carlist wars, besieged and captured several times. The town is also famous for the Sexenni, a festival held every six years in honour of the Virgin of Vallivana, when the streets are decorated with paper and crowds pour in.

The riding around Morella is wonderful. The roads from Morella toward Forcall, Cinctorres, Vilafranca and the Maestrazgo are twisty and scenic, climbing over passes with views over vast expanses of mountains. The route north toward Aragón and the Matarraña is also excellent, as is the road down to the coast through Xert. Traffic is light, surfaces generally good, but the weather at this altitude is unpredictable: cold and windy in winter, with occasional snow, and storms in summer.

Morella has fuel and plenty of restaurants. Local specialities include truffles, croquettes, cured meats and the sweet flaons, pastries filled with almond and cheese. The town's restaurants make a fine lunch stop, and the walls at sunset are magical.
t.barranco de gibert ii@40.4,-0.4:
Up on the roof of the Maestrazgo, where Teruel and Castellón meet, the land rises above fourteen hundred metres into a bleak, beautiful plateau of pasture, pine and limestone. Mosqueruela, on the Aragonese side, is one of the highest villages in the area, and Vilafranca, on the Valencian side, sits in a valley below. The Barranco de Gibert cuts into the hills between them, close also to La Iglesuela del Cid, and its second shelter holds prehistoric paintings.

The painted shelters of this high country are part of the great Levantine tradition, with small figures of hunters and animals in red, and they belong to the UNESCO inscription that covers sites across eastern Spain. Here, at altitude, the shelters suggest seasonal use: hunters following game up to the summer pastures, much as shepherds would later drive their flocks along the drove roads that still cross the plateau.

The most striking thing about this landscape is the dry-stone work. Every field is enclosed by walls of stacked limestone, built without mortar over centuries, and the hills are dotted with stone huts, wells and shelters for livestock. Vilafranca has a museum dedicated to this craft, the pedra en sec, which UNESCO recognises as intangible heritage. La Iglesuela del Cid, a village of noble stone houses, has a Templar past and a fine town hall. Mosqueruela has a well-preserved walled centre with arcaded streets.

The riding is superb but demanding. The roads across the plateau, linking Mosqueruela, Vilafranca, La Iglesuela, Cantavieja and Vistabella, are narrow and wind through pine forest and over passes, with long views and very little traffic. Surfaces can be rough, with gravel and broken edges. The weather is the big factor: at this altitude, winter is long and cold, with snow and ice, and summer storms build quickly in the afternoon. Wind can be strong.

Services are sparse. Vilafranca and Mosqueruela have small shops and bars, and Vilafranca has fuel; otherwise, l'Alcora, about thirty-nine kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. Plan your fuel carefully. Local food is mountain fare: lamb, cured meats, the cheeses of the Maestrazgo, and the hearty olla, a stew of beans and pork. Summer and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.abric del mas blanc@40.4,-0.1:
Benassal is a stone village on a high plateau in the Alt Maestrat, in the interior of Castellón, at around eight hundred metres above sea level, and it is known throughout the region for its spring water, the Font d'en Segures, which is bottled and sold across Spain. The Abric del Mas Blanc, the shelter of the white farmhouse, is one of the many rock-art sites in the area, part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean prehistoric art. The nearby Valltorta gorge, about twenty kilometres to the east, has some of the most famous Levantine paintings, including dramatic hunting scenes, and the Valltorta museum in Tírig is the best place to learn about them.

The Maestrat is a land of high plateaus, deep gorges and stone villages, with dry-stone walls dividing the fields and masías, isolated farmhouses, scattered across the landscape. The name comes from the masters of the military orders who ruled the region after the Christian conquest. Culla, a few kilometres to the south, is a spectacular village perched on a hill, with a castle and views over the surrounding mountains, and Ares del Maestrat sits beneath a huge rock with remains of a castle on top.

The riding here is a delight. The roads from Benassal to Culla, Ares and Catí wind through the mountains with tight bends, climbs and descents, and views over valleys and gorges. Traffic is almost non-existent, and the roads, though narrow, are mostly well surfaced. The CV-15 from the coast up to the Maestrat is a good access road, with long curves. The weather in the mountains can be cold and windy, especially in winter, when snow is possible, and fog can roll in quickly.

Services in the Maestrat are limited. Benassal has a few shops and bars, and fuel can be found in some larger villages like Albocàsser or Vilafranca, but the nearest town over five thousand people, Alcalà de Xivert, is about thirty kilometres away on the coast. Fill up before heading into the mountains. Local food is robust: roast lamb, cecina, cured meats, sheep's cheese and the traditional olla, a stew of beans, meat and vegetables, perfect for cold days.
t.santimamine@43.3,-2.6:
In 1916, a group of boys exploring a hillside in the Basque Country found paintings deep inside a cave, and Santimamiñe became one of the most important prehistoric sites in the region. The cave, near Kortezubi in the Urdaibai valley, contains Magdalenian paintings of bison, horses, goats and deer, made around fourteen thousand years ago, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of cave art of northern Spain. To protect the paintings, the cave itself is closed to the public, but a visitor centre offers a virtual tour that recreates the interior in detail, with guides explaining the art and the people who made it.

The Urdaibai estuary, a biosphere reserve, is a landscape of marshes, sandbanks, oak forests and green hills, home to many birds, especially during migration. Nearby, the painted forest of Oma, a famous art project by Agustín Ibarrola, who painted eyes, figures and geometric shapes on pine trees, became a beloved destination, though the original trees fell ill and a new version has been created nearby. Gernika, about five kilometres away, is a name that resonates around the world: the town's bombing by German and Italian aircraft in 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, inspired Picasso's painting, and the oak tree of Gernika, symbol of Basque liberties, stands beside the Casa de Juntas, the assembly house of Biscay.

The riding in the Basque Country is fantastic: green, hilly, with roads that twist and turn through forests, farms and villages, and spectacular coastal roads. The road from Gernika along the Urdaibai estuary to Mundaka, famous for its surf wave, and Bermeo, a fishing town, is beautiful, as is the coast road east toward Lekeitio and Ondarroa, with cliffs, beaches and sea views. The weather is mild but rainy, so be prepared for wet roads and changing conditions. Summer is the driest season, but also the busiest.

Gernika has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Bilbao, about thirty kilometres away, has everything. Basque food is legendary: pintxos, small bites served on bread in bars, grilled fish, especially hake and bream, and the local cider and txakoli wine. The Monday market in Gernika is one of the best in the region, with farm produce and cheeses.
t.abrigo del arenal de la fonseca o abrigo:
The Guadalope river cuts a deep canyon through the limestone of the Maestrazgo in eastern Teruel, and the Abrigo del Arenal de la Fonseca lies in this wild country near the hamlet of Ladruñán, between the villages of Castellote and Cantavieja. It is one of the important rock-art shelters of Aragon, part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean prehistoric art, with Levantine paintings of animals and human figures in red pigment on the rock. The setting is spectacular: a narrow gorge with towering cliffs, the river flowing below, and pine and holm oak clinging to the slopes. Access involves a walk, and the paintings are protected by a fence.

The Maestrazgo is one of the most sparsely populated areas of Europe, a region of high plateaus, deep gorges and medieval villages, once ruled by the military orders of the Templars and the Hospitallers. Cantavieja, perched on a cliff, has an arcaded main square and Templar origins, and Castellote has a castle and a dramatic rock tunnel. Mirambel and La Iglesuela del Cid are among the most beautiful villages in Spain.

Riding in the Maestrazgo is a dream for those who love mountain roads without traffic. The roads from Castellote to Cantavieja, Mirambel and Morella, across high passes and through gorges, offer endless curves, steep climbs and descents, and spectacular views. Surfaces are mostly good, but expect gravel, potholes and the occasional rock on the road. The altitude is high, often over a thousand metres, so winters are cold and snowy, and summer nights cool. Spring and autumn offer the best conditions, and the colours of autumn are stunning.

Services are scarce. Castellote and Cantavieja have small shops, bars and simple lodging, but the nearest town of over five thousand people, Andorra in Teruel, is about thirty-four kilometres away, and fuel stations are few and far between, so fill up whenever you can. Local food is hearty: Teruel ham, lamb, migas, and sheep's cheese. Dinópolis, a dinosaur theme park in Teruel city with branches across the province, is a reminder that this area is rich in fossils, and several villages have dinosaur museums.
The Roman aqueduct of Segovia strides through the middle of the city on two tiers of granite arches, nearly thirty metres high at its tallest point, built without a drop of mortar, the stones held together by their own weight. It was probably built around the end of the first century or early second century AD, and it carried water to the city until well into modern times. Standing beneath it in the Plaza del Azoguejo, with traffic and people flowing around the base, you can only marvel at the skill of the engineers who built it almost two thousand years ago. The old town and the aqueduct were listed by UNESCO in 1985.

The old town sits on a rocky ridge between two rivers, with the Gothic cathedral, one of the last great Gothic cathedrals built in Spain, in the middle, and the Alcázar, a fairy-tale castle with turrets and a moat, at the western tip, said to have inspired Walt Disney. The streets are lined with Romanesque churches, noble houses and palaces, and the walls still surround much of the town.

Segovia lies at the foot of the Sierra de Guadarrama, and the roads over the mountains toward Madrid are a riders' favourite. The Puerto de Navacerrada, at 1,858 metres, climbs through pine forests with hairpins and views over the plains, and the Puerto de Cotos and the road to the royal palace of La Granja de San Ildefonso, with its fountains and gardens, are equally beautiful. Weekend traffic from Madrid can be heavy, and in winter the passes may be closed or require chains. The plateau north of Segovia is flat and open, with wide views and few curves.

Segovia has fuel, shops and restaurants, and parking in the old town is limited, so leave the bike outside and walk in. The city is famous for its roast suckling pig, cochinillo asado, so tender that it is traditionally cut with the edge of a plate, and for its bean dishes and ponche segoviano, a marzipan-topped sponge cake. Evenings in summer are pleasant, with cool air coming down from the mountains, and the views of the Alcázar at sunset from the valley below are unforgettable.
t.galeria del roure@40.6,-0.1:
Morella rises from the plateau of the Ports like something from a dream: a walled town wrapped around a rocky hill, crowned by a castle, with the Gothic basilica of Santa María la Mayor in the middle, and two kilometres of medieval walls with towers and gates running around the base. It is one of the most impressive historic towns in Spain, and the Galeria del Roure, a rock shelter about four kilometres away, is part of the cluster of prehistoric sites around Morella, including Morella la Vella, one of the important rock-art sites of the Valencian region, all part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The shelters are small and some are protected, so ask at the tourist office in town about visits.

Morella has a long and turbulent history. It was a Moorish stronghold, conquered by the Christians in the thirteenth century, and it played a role in the Carlist wars of the nineteenth century, when the general Ramón Cabrera made it his base. Every six years, the town holds the Sexenni, a festival with elaborate decorations of paper and flowers in the streets, dances and processions, in honour of the Virgin of Vallivana, who is said to have saved the town from a plague.

The riding around Morella is outstanding. The town is at the centre of a network of mountain roads through the Ports and the Maestrat, with endless curves, high passes and spectacular views. The road from Vinaròs on the coast up to Morella, via the Port de Querol, is a classic climb with long sweeping bends, and the roads to Forcall, Cinctorres, Ares del Maestrat and the Tinença de Benifassà are equally good. Traffic is light, but watch for livestock and gravel. The altitude is high, so winters are cold, with snow possible, and fog can roll in quickly; summer evenings are cool.

Morella has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels, and the narrow streets of the old town are full of shops selling local products: cured meats, cheese, truffles in winter, and the traditional woollen blankets. The town is famous for its croquetas morellanas and for flaons, sweet pastries filled with curd cheese and almonds. The views from the castle over the surrounding countryside are unforgettable, especially at sunset.
t.iglesia de santa maria@41.3,-1.4:
Somewhere in the folds of the Sierra de Algairén, south-west of Zaragoza, a bell tower pokes up above a cluster of ochre roofs, and that is your Iglesia de Santa María. Half the villages of Aragon have a church of that name, and this one does the job the others do: it marks the middle of a small place where the shop, the bar and the plaza all orbit the same square of stone. The nearest neighbours on the map are Cosuenda, Almonacid de la Sierra and Alpartir, each a few hundred souls, each about nine kilometres off.

This is the Campo de Cariñena and the edge of Valdejalón, which means wine and fruit. Garnacha vines grow low and gnarled on stony red soil, the kind of bush vine that looks dead in February and drips with grapes by late September. Lower down towards the Jalón river the land turns to orchards of peach, cherry and pear, and in spring the blossom along the valley floor is worth slowing down for. Up in the sierra the scrub smells of thyme and rosemary when the sun has been on it, and you will share the lanes with tractors, the odd shepherd and very little else.

The riding is the reason to come. Narrow local roads wind between the villages with plenty of blind crests and gravel spilled from field entrances, so read the surface and keep something in reserve. The real enemy is the cierzo, the cold north-westerly that funnels down the Ebro valley and can lean a motorbike over without warning. On a calm morning, though, you get empty tarmac, long views back across the plain towards the Moncayo massif and a light that turns the hills copper in the evening.

As a start and finish point it works well because everything practical is close. Fuel is the one thing to plan: the hamlets themselves are hit and miss, so fill up in La Almunia de Doña Godina, about fifteen kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and proper lunch menus. In the villages a bar on the plaza will usually manage a coffee and a bocadillo, and the church square is a calm place to stand, drink some water and work out which way the wind is blowing before you go.
t.subsidiary building la casita del infant:
Most people who come to San Lorenzo de El Escorial only see the monastery, that vast granite grid Philip II raised in the second half of the sixteenth century as palace, basilica, library and royal tomb all at once. A short walk below it, through terraced gardens and woodland, sits something far more human in scale. The Casita del Infante, also called the Casita de Arriba, was designed by Juan de Villanueva in the late eighteenth century for the Infante Gabriel, a son of Carlos III, as a place to retreat, play music and escape the endless etiquette of court. Its sibling, the Casita del Príncipe, lies down the hill near the town of El Escorial and was built for the future Carlos IV.

The town sits on the southern slopes of the Sierra de Guadarrama under Monte Abantos, and the roads around it are why Madrid riders know it so well. The M-505 climbs west over the Puerto de la Cruz Verde towards Ávila with fast, flowing bends and granite boulders scattered through pine and oak. The local speciality worth trying is anything from the Guadarrama mountains in the way of beef or game, and in summer the town is a few degrees cooler than the capital, which is why the royal family came here in the first place. t.la garma@43.4,-3.7:
La Garma is a low limestone hill a few kilometres inland from the Bay of Santander, green with meadows and oak scrub, the sort of rounded Cantabrian hump you might ride past without a second glance. It forms part of the UNESCO site of the Cave of Altamira and Palaeolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain.

For a taste of what lies underground, the caves of Monte Castillo near Puente Viesgo, about an hour inland, are open to visitors and very impressive, and Altamira itself has a full replica and museum near Santillana del Mar.

The area around is coastal Cantabria at its most relaxed. Ribamontán al Monte and the neighbouring villages are farming country, with dairy cows, stone houses with wooden balconies and big tracts of eucalyptus. To the north, the coast breaks into cliffs and long sandy beaches, with Somo a well-known surf spot facing Santander across the bay. The bigger rides lie inland: the passes into the Cordillera Cantábrica, such as the routes up the Pas and Miera valleys, offer steep, tight climbs and remote high pastures.

Paridera is a shepherd's word: a stone pen where ewes give birth, sheltered from the wind. Above Tormón, a tiny village in the southern Sierra de Albarracín, one such overhang has given its name to a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, the Abrigo de la Paridera, part of the Levantine rock art sites the Iberian Peninsula shares under one UNESCO listing. Tormón has only a handful of residents and the feeling of a place at the end of the road. That quiet is the draw. t.moli darrer abric i@40.5,-0.1:
The Alt Maestrat is the high, rugged interior of Castellón province, a country of limestone plateaus, deep ravines and stone villages perched on ridges, and it is crossed by a web of dry-stone walls that farmers have been building and rebuilding for centuries. Near the villages of Benassal, Catí and Villafranca del Cid, under a rock overhang beside an old mill site, the shelter called Molí Darrer holds prehistoric paintings, part of the scattered Levantine rock art that UNESCO inscribed as one site across eastern Spain.

The nearby Valltorta gorge, a short ride south-east, is the best place to see this art properly. Its shelters contain some of the finest scenes of hunters and animals in the whole tradition, and the museum at Tírig runs guided visits. Without a guide, many of the painted overhangs are hard to find and are fenced to protect them.

The Maestrat is beautiful in an austere way. The plateaus are covered in grassland, holm oak and juniper, broken by terraces held up by stone walls, and in winter the wind whistles across them, sometimes bringing snow. Benassal is known for the Font d'en Segures, a mineral water spring whose water is bottled and drunk across the region, and Villafranca del Cid has a long tradition of dry-stone building, with stone huts dotted across the fields. To the north lies Morella, a walled hilltop town crowned by a castle, one of the most striking sights in eastern Spain.

For riders the Maestrat is a paradise. Roads wind across the plateaus and plunge into gorges, with tight bends, long climbs and views that stretch for miles, and traffic is light outside summer weekends. Surfaces are mostly good, but some minor roads are narrow and patched, and gravel and livestock are common. The high country is noticeably colder than the coast, so bring warm layers even in spring, and watch for ice on shaded corners in winter.

Fuel needs planning. The villages here are small, and pumps are few and far between; the nearest large town listed is Alcalà de Xivert near the coast, about thirty-five kilometres away, and Morella is the obvious inland option. Fill up whenever you can. Village bars serve simple, generous food, including local cheeses, cured meats and lamb, and are often the social heart of the place.
t.els covarxos@40.4,-0.2:
Culla stands on a hilltop in the interior of Castellón, a medieval village of stone houses and narrow lanes wrapped around the remains of a castle. In the thirteenth century, after the Christian conquest, the area was granted to the Knights Templar, and later to the Order of Montesa, which explains the old walls and the sense of a place built for defence. Below the village, among the ravines and terraces, the rock shelter of Els Covarxos holds prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Like many such shelters, it is protected and not easy to find on your own; enquire locally before setting off on foot.

The landscape is high and rugged, with limestone plateaus, deep valleys, pine and holm oak woods and stone terraces built over centuries. Culla is one of the most beautiful villages in the region and has been carefully restored, with small museums and views over the surrounding mountains. Nearby Benassal is known for its mineral water spring, and Vilafranca for its tradition of dry-stone walls.

The riding is superb, with twisting roads across plateaus, plunging into valleys and climbing to villages perched on ridges. Bends are tight and frequent, gradients steep and surfaces generally good, though some minor roads are narrow and patched. Traffic is light except on summer weekends, and you will often have the road to yourself. Weather at altitude is changeable, with cold winters, occasional snow and fog, and hot but fresh summers. Village bars offer simple, filling meals, often with local lamb, sausages, cheese and bread, and a glass of wine on a terrace with a view across the valleys is the right way to end the day.
t.covatina del tossalet del mas de a rambl:
This is high Maestrat country, where Castellón's mountains roll into Teruel's, and the small rock shelter called the Covatina del Tossalet del Mas de la Rambla belongs to a family of sites that UNESCO lists together as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Spring, with green fields and wildflowers, and early autumn are the best seasons.

Fill up when you can and do not run the tank low. t.raco de nando@40.4,-0.2:
Racó means corner in Valencian, and this really is a corner: a fold in the limestone hills between Benassal, Culla and Vilafranca, in the interior of Castellón where the coast's crowds feel a continent away. The countryside between them is terraced almond and olive land giving way to holm oak and pine higher up.

The CV roads that link these villages are narrow and full of bends, climbing over cols and dropping into ravines, and you will meet more tractors than tourists. Evening light turns the stone golden, but in winter frost lingers in the shaded corners until late morning, and summer thunderstorms can wash gravel across the road in minutes.

t.covaciella@43.3,-4.9:

The cave is closed to the public to protect the paintings, but the nearby interpretation centre explains what is inside and why it matters.

The road from Cangas de Onís to Panes runs along the Sella, Casaño and Cares rivers through deep valleys, with sharp curves, short straights and the mountains towering above you. It is one of the best motorcycle routes in Spain, though busy with tourists and caravans in summer. The weather in Asturias is changeable, with rain, fog and sunshine all in one day, and the roads can be wet and slippery in the shaded sections. Late spring and early autumn are the best times to ride, with fewer crowds and green landscapes.

t.cueva de pacencia@42.3,-0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is the first big wrinkle of the Pyrenees north of Huesca, a block of limestone sliced into deep canyons by rivers like the Vero, the Alcanadre and the Mascún, and the Cueva de Pacencia sits in that broken country. The area is managed as the Río Vero Cultural Park, with an interpretation centre in Colungo and guided visits to the best-preserved shelters, which is the sensible way to see them.

Alquézar, fifteen kilometres away, is the postcard: a village of ochre houses piled on a cliff above the Vero canyon, crowned by a collegiate church inside the walls of an old Muslim fortress. It has become a hub for canyoning, and in summer the narrow streets fill with people in wetsuits. Look up anywhere in Guara and you will see griffon vultures circling, and with luck the bearded vulture, the great bone-breaker, gliding along the crags. The lower slopes are olive and almond country, part of the Somontano wine region centred on Barbastro, whose reds and whites have earned a good name.

The roads looping around the massif, through villages like Bárcabo, Lecina and Rodellar and over to Boltaña on the Ara, are full of blind bends, short climbs and changing surfaces, with loose stones in places and the odd fallen rock after rain. Distances look short on the map and take twice as long as expected, which is exactly the point. t.cingle de palanques abrigo a@40.7,-0.2:
Els Ports is the high, empty country in the north of Castellón province, a land of stone-walled terraces, deep gorges, juniper and pine, and villages that cling to ridges above the river valleys. Palanques is one of the smallest of them, and above it, in a long cliff band known as the Cingle de Palanques, are shelters with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The Levantine paintings here show human figures and animals in the expressive style typical of this coast's mountainous interior, and like most such sites, they are protected and usually visited with a local guide.

The region is deeply rural and sparsely populated. Forcall, nine kilometres away, sits where three rivers meet and has a fine arcaded square and a Renaissance palace, while Morella, thirteen kilometres off, is the jewel of the region: a walled town piled up around a castle on a rock, with Gothic churches and arcaded streets that feel almost unchanged since the Middle Ages. Morella's cuisine is hearty and mountain-based, with truffles in winter, lamb, cured ham and flaons, sweet cheese pastries.

The riding here is some of the best in eastern Spain. The roads through Els Ports and the Maestrazgo are narrow, winding, often freshly surfaced, and almost empty of traffic outside weekends and holidays. They climb over passes and plunge into gorges, with views over layered ridges that seem endless. Weather can be a factor: winters are cold, with snow on the high ground, summer storms can be violent, and the wind can be strong on exposed ridges.

t.jurisdiction of saint emilion@44.9,-0.2:
Saint-Émilion is a wine village that looks like a stage set, with steep, cobbled lanes tumbling down a limestone hillside, golden stone houses, and a bell tower rising above the rooftops. The village grew around the hermitage of Émilion, a Breton monk who lived in a cave here in the eighth century, and its most remarkable monument is the monolithic church, carved out of the rock beneath the bell tower.

The vineyards surround the village on all sides, with famous châteaux names on every gate. Many estates offer tastings and tours, though the most prestigious ones need booking well in advance. Underneath the village and its surroundings lie miles of quarries from which the stone was extracted, now used as cellars, and some are open to visitors. The cool, damp air smells of wine and stone.

For riders, the lanes through the vineyards are delightful, narrow and winding, rising and falling gently over the low hills of the Libournais. Traffic is light outside harvest time, but in September and October tractors, harvest workers and grape trailers make the lanes slow. The village centre itself is a challenge: cobbles are steep, slippery when wet, and parking is limited, so leave the bike at the edge and walk in.

Libourne, seven kilometres away, is a bastide town on the Dordogne with fuel, markets and plenty of restaurants. Saint-Émilion has cafés and restaurants of its own, along with its famous macarons, made here since the seventeenth century, according to local tradition, by Ursuline nuns. From here, the Dordogne valley leads east toward Bergerac and Périgord, while Bordeaux is just under an hour west. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon to avoid the tour coaches, when the stone glows warm in the low sunlight.
t.chemin de la liebana@43.4,-4.4:
San Vicente de la Barquera is where the Camino Lebaniego begins, the old pilgrim route that leaves the Cantabrian coast and climbs south into the mountains of Liébana to the monastery of Santo Toribio. The town sits on a pair of estuaries, with a long medieval bridge carrying the road across the water, a castle and the Gothic church of Santa María above the harbour, and on clear days the snowy peaks of the Picos de Europa rising behind the marshes like a stage set.

Pilgrims have walked from here for centuries, some breaking off from the coastal Camino de Santiago to venerate the fragment of the True Cross kept at Santo Toribio. The route takes several days on foot through valleys and over hills. On a motorcycle you will cover it in a morning, but it is worth knowing that you are riding a road with very old feet in it, especially when you see a walker with a scallop shell and a staff trudging up the verge.

The riding around San Vicente is a delight. The coast road west to Unquera and east towards Comillas passes beaches, dunes and the Oyambre natural park, with long views across the bay. Heading inland you soon reach the N-621, which follows the Deva river through the Desfiladero de la Hermida, a narrow limestone gorge some twenty kilometres long, before opening into the green bowl of Liébana. The roads are generally well surfaced, but expect wet patches, cattle, slow camper vans in summer and sea fog that rolls in quickly from the Bay of Biscay. Spring and late September are the sweet spots.

San Vicente is a fishing town with fuel, shops and a lot of seafood restaurants along the waterfront. The local specialty is sorropotún, a hearty stew of tuna and potatoes made by fishermen, and anchovies and fresh fish appear on every menu. Comillas, seven kilometres east, is worth a detour for its unusual modernist buildings, including El Capricho, an early work by Antoni Gaudí. At low tide the estuary turns into a mosaic of sandbanks and wading birds, and in the evening the light on the Picos can be extraordinary.
t.collegiale de ziortza@43.2,-2.6:
High on a green hillside above the village of Bolibar, in the Biscayan interior, the collegiate church of Ziortza looks out over a valley of meadows, farmhouses and eucalyptus and pine plantations. It is a tranquil, solid place, a church and cloister built of grey stone with a fortified look, and it stands on the Camino del Norte, the coastal route to Santiago, so you will often see pilgrims resting on the benches outside.

Bolibar is the ancestral home of the family of Simón Bolívar, the liberator of much of South America, whose forebears emigrated from here to Venezuela centuries before he was born. A small museum in the village tells his story and the family's Basque origins. Ziortza itself grew from a medieval church into a collegiate foundation, and today it is cared for by a small monastic community. The Basque countryside around is classic baserri country: big stone farmhouses with wide eaves, apple orchards for cider and sheep on steep pastures.

Getting here involves exactly the kind of riding that makes the Basque Country so addictive. The roads wind through the hills between Markina-Xemein, Bolibar and the coast, narrow but well surfaced, constantly turning and rising, with views opening to the bulk of Mount Oiz to the west. The climb up to the church itself is short and steep. Rain is frequent and leaves the shady corners slick, especially where cattle have crossed, and fog can sit on the tops, so ride with a margin. Weekends bring cyclists and local traffic; weekday mornings are blissfully quiet.

For fuel, Markina-Xemein is the nearest town of any size, and Ermua and Durango lie further west along the main valley. Bolibar itself has a bar or two where you can get a coffee and a pintxo, and the village centre is pleasant for a short walk. In the evening the light catches the church from the west, and the valley below fills with long shadows and the sound of cowbells. It is a good place to stop thinking about the road for a few minutes and simply sit.
t.ekain@43.2,-2.3:
In 1969 two young men exploring a hillside above the Sastarrain valley near Zestoa crawled into a narrow opening and found themselves in a gallery of painted horses. Ekain is one of the finest Palaeolithic painted caves in Europe, its walls covered with images of horses, bison and other animals made some fourteen thousand years ago with remarkable skill. The horses in particular are famous, drawn with shaggy manes and round bellies, so lively that they seem about to move.

You cannot visit the original cave, which has been closed to protect it, and it belongs to the UNESCO group of Palaeolithic caves of northern Spain. Instead, a few kilometres away in Zestoa, Ekainberri reproduces the main chambers with great accuracy, using the same techniques the original artists probably used. The replica is genuinely impressive, with guided tours that explain how the paintings were made and what they might have meant. It is worth booking in advance in summer.

The landscape is the green, folded heart of Gipuzkoa, where steep valleys run down to the coast and every hillside is pasture, forest or apple orchard. The roads between Zestoa, Azpeitia and Zumaia are twisting and well kept, with plenty of tight bends, sudden climbs and views that change around every corner. The main road through the Urola valley is busier, carrying traffic between the coast and the interior. Expect rain at any time of year, and slippery surfaces in the shade under trees. Weekends bring cyclists and families heading to the coast.

Azpeitia, six kilometres away, is a town of fourteen thousand with fuel and shops, and on its outskirts stands the huge baroque basilica of Loyola, built around the birthplace of Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits. Zumaia, on the coast, is famous for the dramatic layered flysch cliffs that featured in Game of Thrones, and a walk along the clifftop path is a fine way to finish a day. Zestoa itself was once a spa town, with an old thermal establishment by the river. A cider house meal in season, with salt cod omelette and steak, completes the Basque experience.
t.cathedrale de vitoria gasteiz@42.9,-2.7:
Vitoria-Gasteiz is the capital of the Basque Country and possibly its most underrated city. It sits on a high plateau, the Llanada Alavesa, surrounded by low mountains and wide farmland, and its medieval old town climbs a small hill in the shape of an almond, with the old cathedral of Santa María at the top. This is the cathedral the label refers to, a Gothic church begun in the thirteenth century as both a temple and part of the town's defences.

For decades Santa María suffered from structural problems, with leaning pillars and cracked walls, and its restoration became famous because the cathedral stayed open to visitors throughout the work. Guided tours take you onto scaffolding, into the foundations and up the walls, showing how a Gothic building actually works. The British writer Ken Follett was so taken with it that it inspired part of one of his novels, and a statue of him now stands outside. There is also a New Cathedral in the city, a huge neo-Gothic building from the twentieth century, so do not confuse the two.

The riding around Vitoria is varied. The plateau roads are open and fast, crossing farmland and passing reservoirs, but within half an hour you can reach the mountain passes of the Basque interior, such as the climb to Urkiola or the roads into the Sierra de Entzia and the Valderejo natural park. Weather on the plateau can be harsh in winter, with cold winds and occasional snow, and pleasant but fresh in summer. In the city itself, traffic is moderate and the centre is largely pedestrian, so park on the edge of the old town and walk up.

Vitoria has fuel, food and everything else you need. The old town is full of bars serving pintxos, and the city is known for its green spaces; it was European Green Capital in 2012 and is ringed by a belt of parks. The Battle of Vitoria in 1813, when Wellington defeated the French, is commemorated by a monument in the Plaza de la Virgen Blanca. Early on a weekday morning, with the city waking up and the light warming the old stone, Santa María is at its best.
t.monastere de santo toribio de liebana@43:
Liébana is a green bowl surrounded by mountains, a valley system in south-west Cantabria with the town of Potes at its centre and the limestone towers of the Picos de Europa rising to the north and west. On a hillside above Potes, among oak and chestnut woods, stands the monastery of Santo Toribio, one of the holy places of Christian Spain. It keeps the Lignum Crucis, said to be the largest surviving fragment of the True Cross, and for that reason it holds a jubilee year whenever the feast of Saint Toribio, the sixteenth of April, falls on a Sunday.

The monastery has a long history. In the eighth century a monk named Beatus lived here and wrote a commentary on the Book of Revelation, which was copied and illuminated in monasteries across Spain for centuries. The surviving Beatus manuscripts, with their vivid, strange images of apocalyptic beasts, are among the treasures of medieval art. Pilgrims come along the Camino Lebaniego from San Vicente de la Barquera, and the monastery church, simple and Gothic, is always open for visitors.

From the coast, the N-621 follows the Deva river through the Desfiladero de la Hermida, a narrow gorge with walls hundreds of metres high, and then opens into the valley. From the south, the passes of San Glorio and Piedrasluengas cross the Cantabrian mountains with wonderful views and quiet roads. To the west, the road continues from Potes to Fuente Dé, where a cable car lifts you onto the high plateau of the Picos. Expect wet surfaces, cattle and slow traffic in summer, and snow on the passes in winter.

Potes, three kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Its old centre, with stone houses and wooden balconies along the river, is charming, and the medieval Torre del Infantado dominates the main square. The local specialties are cocido lebaniego, a hearty chickpea stew, and orujo, a strong spirit distilled from grape pomace, which is celebrated in a festival each autumn. Do not drink it before riding; save it for the evening in Potes.
t.cathedrale de saint jacques apotre@43.3,:
Down in the Casco Viejo of Bilbao, where the old streets run in a tight grid beside the Nervión, the cathedral of Santiago stands at the heart of the Siete Calles, the seven original streets of the medieval town. It is a Gothic church, rebuilt after a fire in the sixteenth century, with a neo-Gothic façade and spire added later, and it sits so snugly among the tall houses that you often see it only when you are standing right in front of it.

Its dedication to Saint James is no accident. Bilbao lies on the Camino del Norte, the coastal route to Santiago de Compostela, and pilgrims have passed through the city for centuries. The cathedral's cloister and its southern porch are quiet refuges from the busy streets. Around it, the old town is a labyrinth of bars, shops and markets, and the nearby Ribera market, on the riverbank, is one of the largest covered markets in Europe.

Riding into Bilbao is a city experience: busy roads, tunnels, steep streets and a lot of traffic, especially at rush hour. The surrounding hills are another matter. Within twenty minutes you can be climbing into the mountains of Biscay, with roads like the climb to Artxanda above the city, the coast road towards Bakio and San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, or the inland routes towards Urkiola and Durango. The Basque roads are generally well surfaced and full of bends, but rain is frequent and can make the corners treacherous.

Bilbao has fuel and services everywhere. The old town is pedestrian, so park on its edge and walk in. The pintxo culture here is legendary: small bites on bread, served at the bar and eaten standing, with a glass of txakoli, the slightly sparkling local white wine. A visit to the Guggenheim Museum, Frank Gehry's titanium building on the riverbank, is almost obligatory, and the walk along the river from the old town to the museum is pleasant. In the evening the streets fill with people, and the city has a warm, lively atmosphere that is hard to resist.
t.la covassa del molinell@40.3,-0.1:
Benassal and Culla are mountain villages in the Alt Maestrat, in the interior of the province of Castelló, a region of limestone plateaus, deep gorges and stone walls that feels a world away from the beaches of the coast. La Covassa del Molinell, a large rock shelter near Benassal, is one of many in the Maestrat with prehistoric paintings. The region is one of the richest areas for Levantine rock art, with the famous shelters of the Valltorta gorge, near Tírig, just to the east.

The Maestrat takes its name from the Maestre, the Grand Master of the military orders, the Templars and later the Order of Montesa, who controlled this area after the Christian reconquest in the thirteenth century. The villages are built of stone, often on hilltops, with churches, castles and arcaded squares. Culla, perched on a hill with its castle ruins, is one of the most beautiful, with views across the mountains. Benassal is known for the Font d'en Segures, a spring whose water is bottled and sold across Spain.

The riding in the Maestrat is superb. The roads wind across high plateaus and through deep valleys, with tight bends, steep climbs and descents, and spectacular views. Traffic is almost non-existent, and the surfaces are generally good. The landscape is wild and empty, with stone walls, farmhouses and sheep. The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and snow is possible on the high ground. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild temperatures and clear skies.

Benassal is a village of thirteen hundred people with basic services, and fuel may be limited in the mountains, so fill up in larger towns on the way. Culla is smaller. The local cuisine is hearty: lamb, cured meats, cheeses and truffles, which grow in the oak forests of the Maestrat and are harvested in winter. The Valltorta museum at Tírig is a good place to learn about the rock art. In the evening, the light on the stone villages and the mountains is golden, and the silence is broken only by the bells of the church.
t.sites of dehua kilns@25.5,118.3:
Dehua, a county in the mountains of Fujian province, in south-eastern China, has been making porcelain for over a thousand years. Its white porcelain, known in the West as blanc de Chine, is famous for its pure, creamy white colour and its fine figures, especially statues of Guanyin, the goddess of mercy, and other Buddhist and Taoist figures. The ancient kiln sites of Dehua, including long dragon kilns built on hillsides, are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China, inscribed in 2021.

In the Song and Yuan dynasties, Quanzhou was one of the greatest ports in the world, and Dehua porcelain was exported from there across Asia, to the Middle East and later to Europe, where it was highly prized. The kilns used the clay from the surrounding mountains, and the dragon kilns, long tunnels climbing the slopes, could fire thousands of pieces at once. Today Dehua is still a centre of porcelain production, with many workshops and factories, and a ceramics museum displays the history of the craft.

Riding in China as a foreigner is complicated. Foreign driving licences are not recognised, and riding a motorcycle requires a Chinese licence and permits, often arranged through specialised tour companies. Many cities restrict motorcycles. The roads in Fujian are generally good, with expressways, though motorcycles are not allowed on them, and national roads that wind through the mountains, with tea plantations, forests and villages. The climate is subtropical, with hot, humid summers and mild winters, and typhoons can strike in summer and autumn.

Dehua town has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Quanzhou, the main city of the region, is about two hours south-east. The Fujian tulou, the round earthen houses of the Hakka people, are another World Heritage Site in the province. Fujian food is light and subtle, with soups, seafood and tea, especially oolong tea from Anxi, a neighbouring county. Visiting a porcelain workshop in Dehua, watching the artisans shape the white clay, is a fascinating experience.
t.pont de brinas sur le fleuve ebro@42.6,-:
Every year on the morning of 29 June, the people of Haro climb a hill outside town and drench each other in red wine, and nobody has ever satisfactorily explained to me why this needs to happen at nine in the morning. The Batalla del Vino is the loudest expression of a town that lives and breathes wine. Haro is the heart of Rioja Alta, and just outside it the old stone bridge at Briñas crosses the Ebro, a medieval structure of solid arches that has carried travellers, mule trains and wine carts across the river for centuries.

The Ebro here is broad and green, flowing between poplars and vineyards, and the bridge leads into the small village of Briñas with its stone houses and manor fronts. A short way upstream the river pushes through the Conchas de Haro, a narrow gap in the rock that marks a natural gateway between the Basque lands of Álava and La Rioja. The route sheets for this ride pair it with places like the Suso monastery at San Millán de la Cogolla, where some of the earliest written words in Castilian were jotted in the margins of a Latin text.

The riding around Haro is a pleasure. Roads wind through vineyards and small villages, with gentle gradients and long views to the Sierra de Cantabria rising like a wall to the north. Cross into Álava toward Labastida and Laguardia and the road climbs along the foot of that range, with tighter curves and wonderful views back over the vines. Surfaces are mostly good, traffic light outside harvest time, when tractors and grape trailers rule the lanes.

Haro has everything you need, from fuel to a long list of bars where a glass of local crianza costs less than a coffee in many European cities. The Barrio de la Estación, by the railway, is home to a cluster of historic bodegas, many of which offer tours. In the old town, the tapas bars around the Plaza de la Paz and the streets nearby are lively in the evening.

Food is serious business: lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings, potatoes stewed with chorizo in the Rioja style, peppers, asparagus and white beans. Come in autumn when the vineyards turn red and gold, or in spring when the vines are budding. And ride carefully if you have been tasting; the local police know exactly what goes on in this valley.
t.abrigo de los arqueros negros@41.1,-1.3:
The prehistoric painters of eastern Spain had a thing for archers. Across hundreds of rock shelters from Catalonia to Andalusia, they painted small, dynamic human figures drawing bows, chasing deer and goats, sometimes fighting each other, and these scenes of the so-called Levantine style are part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Shelters with names like the Abrigo de los Arqueros Negros, the shelter of the black archers, are scattered through the limestone hills of the province of Teruel and its neighbours in Aragon, often in remote ravines and protected by grilles.

These coordinates put you in the high country of the Jiloca valley, between the villages of Báguena and Burbáguena and the old walled town of Daroca. This is open, rolling upland at around eight hundred metres, with cereal fields, almond trees, poplars along the river and bare hills of red and ochre soil. It is a lonely, beautiful landscape, with wide skies and very few people, and the sense of having it to yourself is a big part of its charm.

The riding is relaxed and spacious, with long straight stretches and gentle curves along the valley, and more interesting roads climbing into the surrounding sierras. Traffic is light, but watch for farm vehicles and, at dusk, deer and wild boar. Weather is continental: cold winters with frost and occasional snow, hot dry summers and wind that can be relentless across the high plains.

Daroca, about fourteen kilometres away, has a petrol station, a few restaurants and shops, and its walls, gates and churches make it a fascinating stop, with a long history as a frontier town on the border between Christian and Muslim Spain. Calamocha, to the south, is another service town. West of Daroca the lagoon of Gallocanta attracts tens of thousands of common cranes in autumn and late winter, a sight and sound you will not forget.

Local food is robust: jamón from Teruel, lamb roasted with herbs, migas fried with garlic and grapes, and saffron grown in the Jiloca valley. Come in spring or autumn, and take your time. This is not a place to rush; it is a place to slow down and feel the size and age of the land.
t.eglise santa maria de la asuncion@43.4,-:
Castro-Urdiales has one of the best harbour fronts on the whole Cantabrian coast, and it knows it. The Gothic church of Santa María de la Asunción stands on a rocky headland above the old port, its buttresses and pinnacles silhouetted against the sea, flanked by the remains of a castle that now holds a lighthouse and by a medieval bridge leading to a little chapel on a rock. Built from the thirteenth century onward, the church is one of the finest Gothic buildings in northern Spain, and it lies on the coastal route of the Way of Saint James, which is part of a UNESCO listing that covers the pilgrimage roads of the north.

The town grew from a Roman settlement into a busy fishing and trading port, and the harbour is still full of colourful boats, with seafront promenades and glassed-in balconies on the old houses. Inside the church, look for the strong Gothic columns, the ambulatory and the way the light falls through the high windows. Outside, the view over the harbour is just as rewarding.

Riding to Castro means a choice between the motorway, which is quick and easy, and the old coast road, which is slower but more interesting, passing through villages and offering glimpses of the sea. Head inland and things get much better: the valleys of the Asón and the Cantabrian mountains offer superb twisting roads, with climbs like the Alto de los Tornos, gorges, beech forests and green pastures. Surfaces are generally good, but rain is frequent and the roads can be damp and mossy in the shade.

Castro is a lively town of some thirty thousand, and petrol, beds and lunch are never a problem. The seafront is lined with bars serving pintxos and fresh seafood, and the anchovies of the Cantabrian coast are famous. Try grilled fish, squid in its ink or a bowl of marmitako, the tuna and potato stew of the fishermen.

June and September are the sweet months here, warm enough for the terraces and free of the August crush. In August the town fills with holidaymakers and parking becomes a sport. Walk up to the church in the evening, when the sun lights the stone gold and the fishing boats rock gently below; few town stops on this coast are quite so satisfying.
t.abside@41.4,-1.6:
The apse in question belongs to the collegiate church of Santa María in Calatayud, and it is one of the reasons UNESCO lists the Mudéjar architecture of Aragon as a whole. Mudéjar means the building style of Muslim craftsmen living under Christian rule after the reconquest, and in Calatayud they did wonderful things with humble brick: geometric patterns, lozenges and interlacing arches laid out in relief, glazed tiles catching the sun. Next to the apse rises an octagonal brick tower that is the town's signature, and behind it a cloister, all three named in the listing.

Calatayud itself is a town of about twenty thousand on the Jalón river, on the old road between Madrid and Zaragoza. Its name comes from the Arabic Qal'at Ayyub, Ayyub's castle, and the ridges above the town still carry the ruins of a whole complex of Moorish fortifications. A few kilometres out lie the remains of Bilbilis, the Roman town where the poet Martial was born, a man who wrote sharp, funny epigrams about life in Rome and then came home to grumble about the provinces. The old centre is a mix of fine churches, faded palaces and streets that have seen better centuries, which is part of its charm.

The A-2 motorway makes Calatayud easy to reach and easy to leave too quickly. Better to come in on the smaller roads: south toward Daroca through red clay hills and vineyards of Garnacha, or north into the Moncayo foothills where the land climbs toward the great mountain on the border with Castile. These are open, flowing roads with big skies, and the wind on the plateau can be strong, especially the cierzo, the dry north-westerly that funnels down the Ebro basin. Summer afternoons are hot and bright; winter mornings bring frost.

Fuel, food and beds are no problem here. The region's wine, from the Calatayud appellation, is mostly robust old-vine Garnacha and good value, and the local ham, roasted lamb and migas fried with garlic are made for hungry riders. Spanish folklore knows the town through the song about La Dolores, a girl from Calatayud, which locals will tell you was very unfair to her. Park near the centre, walk up to the collegiate church, and spend a few minutes on the brickwork: the more you look, the more patterns appear.
t.torre de la iglesia del salvador@40.3,-1:
Teruel spent decades as the Spanish joke about forgotten provinces, until its people adopted the slogan Teruel existe, Teruel exists, and turned it into a political movement. Ride into the old centre and you will agree it exists rather vividly. The Torre del Salvador is one of its four great Mudéjar towers, built of brick and glazed ceramic in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries by craftsmen trained in the Islamic tradition. The road, or rather a street, still passes through an archway at its base, and you can climb inside, between the outer and inner shells of the tower, up narrow stairs to the bells.

The town loves a good legend, and the towers have one. The story goes that two Moorish builders, rivals for the same woman, each raised a tower: the Salvador and the San Martín. The San Martín came out slightly crooked, its builder threw himself from the top, and the Salvador's architect won the girl. Teruel's other famous romance is truer to its records, or at least to its tombs: the Lovers of Teruel, Isabel and Diego, whose tragic medieval story is told in a mausoleum next to the church of San Pedro, with their alabaster effigies reaching toward each other.

At around nine hundred metres, Teruel sits high on the plateau where the Turia and Alfambra rivers meet, and its climate is famously extreme: hot dry summers, bitter winter mornings. The riding around it is excellent. The A-23 motorway is fast and empty, but the real joy lies in the small roads into the Sierra de Albarracín or east into the Maestrazgo, with long climbs, open bends and almost no traffic. Distances are big, villages are small, and the colours shift from red clay to grey limestone to dark pine.

Teruel has fuel, mechanics and every service, so it makes a good base. Local ham, cured in the cold dry air, carries its own designation of origin and is worth ordering by the plate; the town also does migas, lamb and a fine selection of pastries. The old centre is compact and best explored on foot, with the Plaza del Torico, a square named after its tiny bull statue, at its heart. Park outside the narrowest streets, walk under the Salvador's arch, and look up at the green and white tiles, still bright after seven centuries.
t.changling porcelain stone mining site@29:
The word kaolin comes from Gaoling, a village in the hills north-east of Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province, where the white clay used in making porcelain was mined for centuries. Porcelain needed two ingredients: kaolin and porcelain stone, a rock that, when crushed and refined, gave the paste its translucency. The hills around Jingdezhen were full of both, and the Changling porcelain stone mining site is one of the places where the stone was quarried, crushed by water-powered hammers and refined into bricks that were carried to the kilns of the porcelain capital of the world.

Jingdezhen made porcelain for the imperial court for centuries, and its blue-and-white wares travelled the world, to the Middle East, Europe and beyond. The city still lives on ceramics, with workshops, studios, markets and museums, and the ancient kiln sites at Hutian, part of the same story, show how production developed. The countryside around is hilly and green, with tea plantations, bamboo forests and villages of white-walled houses with black-tiled roofs, typical of the Huizhou style. Wuyuan, to the north-east, is famous for its villages and the rapeseed fields that turn the valleys yellow in spring.

Riding here is a mix of good roads and complications. Foreign riders need special permits to ride in China, and organised tours are the usual way. The roads in the hills are scenic, winding through valleys and over passes, with villages and tea fields, and the surface is generally good on the main routes. Traffic includes trucks, buses and scooters. Spring is beautiful, with flowers and fresh green tea leaves, but rainy; summer is hot and humid, autumn clear and pleasant. Mount Huangshan, one of China's most famous mountains, and Mount Sanqingshan, with its granite pillars, are both within reach.

Jingdezhen has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. Food in Jiangxi is spicy, with chilli in many dishes, and includes rice noodles, smoked meats and freshwater fish. Tea from the hills is excellent. Visit the mining site and then a workshop in Jingdezhen to see how porcelain is made today; the journey from the stone in the hills to a fine, translucent bowl is still astonishing.
t.cueva de la pena de la moreria@40.3,-1.6:
The Sierra de Albarracín is a high, cold, empty land of pine forests, red sandstone and limestone, at well over a thousand metres, and it hides some of the most interesting prehistoric rock art in Spain. The Pinares de Rodeno, a protected landscape of pine forests and red sandstone outcrops near Albarracín, has shelters with paintings of bulls, deer and human figures, included in UNESCO's inscription of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. The Cueva de la Peña de la Morería is one of the sites in this region, near the villages of Bronchales and Orihuela del Tremedal, at the foot of the mountains.

Albarracín, about seventeen kilometres away, is one of the most beautiful towns in Spain, a medieval town of pink and ochre houses perched on a rock above a bend in the Guadalaviar river, surrounded by walls that climb the hill behind. Its streets are narrow and steep, with wooden balconies and overhanging upper floors. The surrounding mountains, the Montes Universales, are the source of several rivers, including the Tagus, which rises at a spring near Frías de Albarracín and flows across Spain and Portugal to Lisbon.

The riding in the Sierra de Albarracín is a joy. The roads climb through pine forests, over passes and across high plateaus, with curves, views and almost no traffic. Grip is usually reliable, but there are livestock on the roads, and wildlife, including deer and wild boar. The road from Albarracín to Bronchales and Orihuela del Tremedal is particularly enjoyable, with long sweeps and forests. Altitude is high, and the weather is extreme: hot days in summer, freezing nights, and snow and ice in winter. Fog can be dense.

The villages around are small, with shops and bars; Albarracín has restaurants and hotels, and for fuel, Teruel is the safe choice, though there are a few stations in the sierra. Food here is mountain cuisine: migas, lamb, game, and the excellent cured ham of Teruel, as well as local cheeses. Visit the rock art shelters, then ride to Albarracín for a walk through its streets; the combination of prehistoric art and medieval architecture in one of the emptiest regions of Europe is something special.
t.canada de marco@41.0,-1.3:
Calamocha has a reputation in Spain, and it is not for its nightlife. This town in the Jiloca valley of Teruel province is one of the coldest places in the country in winter, a high, open basin where the air pools at night and frost bites hard. In summer that same altitude makes it pleasant when the coast is sweltering. The Cañada de Marco is a site in the hills just outside town, and the name hints at the old drove roads, the cañadas, that once carried flocks of sheep across Aragon between summer and winter pastures.

The Jiloca is a long, gentle valley running from near Monreal del Campo down towards Calatayud, flanked by bare sierras of grey and red rock. It has a quiet history of wool, saffron and mudéjar brick churches. Monreal del Campo, just upstream, has a small museum dedicated to saffron, which was once grown widely here, and the brick towers in villages along the valley are part of the mudéjar heritage that Aragon is so proud of. Calamocha itself has a fine old bridge over the river and a solid parish church.

If you have half an hour spare, ride northwest to the Laguna de Gallocanta, about half an hour away. It is a shallow salt lake on the high plateau, and every autumn and late winter tens of thousands of common cranes stop there on migration. Arrive at dusk and the sound alone is worth the trip. The roads there are straight, quiet and fast, with fields of cereals stretching to the horizon and wind that can be relentless.

The riding in the valley itself is easy cruising: the A-23 motorway carries most traffic, leaving the old N-234 and local roads largely to farmers and the odd lorry. For more interesting curves, head east into the Sierra de Cucalón or south towards the Montes Universales, where the roads climb and twist through pine and oak. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk.

Calamocha has fuel, a couple of supermarkets and several bars serving hearty Aragonese food: lamb, migas, and the cured ham from Teruel, which carries its own designation of origin.
