In winter, wear more than you think; the thermometer here can sit below zero all morning. In summer, it is a fine place for a long lunch in the shade before heading onwards across the plateau.
t.barranco del pajarejo@40.3,-1.4:
Red rock, dark pines and a sky that seems higher than it should be: that is the country south of Albarracín, where the Barranco del Pajarejo cuts into the sandstone. Geologists call this stone rodeno, a coarse red sandstone that weathers into towers, overhangs and smooth shelters, and prehistoric people used those shelters as canvases. The Pinares de Rodeno protected landscape around Albarracín holds a well-known group of painted shelters with bulls, deer and human figures in white and red, and this gully is part of that wider area, quiet and seldom visited.

Albarracín itself is close and stunning. The town clings to a bend in the Guadalaviar river, its houses washed in a pinkish-orange plaster, with a long line of medieval walls climbing the hillside above. For about a century in the Middle Ages it was the seat of a small independent Moorish kingdom ruled by the Banu Razin family, and later an independent lordship before being absorbed into Aragon. Walk the narrow streets early, before the day-trippers arrive, and you will have them almost to yourself.

The riding is excellent in every direction. The road from Gea de Albarracín up the gorge to the town follows the river closely, with rock walls almost brushing your shoulder. Beyond, the climb into the Montes Universales, towards Bronchales, Orihuela del Tremedal or the source of the Tagus, takes you over plateaus above 1,500 metres with long views and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally good but expect gravel and the occasional patch of broken tarmac. In winter, snow and ice are common up here, and even in May mornings can be sharp.

The nearest villages around the pin, Villel, Villastar and Gea, are small and you should not rely on them for fuel. Teruel, about half an hour away, has everything, so fill up there before heading into the high ground rather than gambling on the villages. Food in the area is robust: Teruel ham, lamb, game in season and migas. The air smells of pine resin and wild thyme, and the light on the red rock at sunset is something you will remember long after the ride.
t.hayedos de picos de europa canal de asot:
Valdeón is the valley people forget to mention when they talk about the Picos de Europa, and that is a mistake. On the southern side of the range, in the province of León, it is a deep green bowl ringed by limestone peaks, with the village of Posada de Valdeón at its heart. The beech forests on its slopes, including those in the side valley known as the Canal de Asotín, are part of the UNESCO site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a transnational listing that grew to include several forests in Spain. Walking in them in autumn, when the leaves turn copper and gold and the ground is soft with moss, is unforgettable.

Downstream, the Cares river carves one of the most spectacular gorges in Europe. The famous Cares trail starts at Caín, at the northern end of the valley, and follows a path cut into the cliff face high above the river for about eleven kilometres to Poncebos in Asturias. It is a classic walk, busy in summer, with sheer drops and tunnels through the rock.

The valley is also home to Valdeón cheese, a powerful blue cheese traditionally wrapped in leaves, made from cow and goat milk and aged in natural caves. Try it with bread and a glass of red wine, at a bar in Posada.

The riding is superb. The road into the valley from the south crosses the Puerto de Pandetrave, a high pass with stunning views of the central massif of the Picos, and descends in tight bends to Posada. From there, a narrow road continues north to Caín, a single-lane track with steep gradients and sharp turns, best taken slowly. To the west, the Puerto de Panderruedas leads to the Sajambre valley and on to the Desfiladero de los Beyos, a dramatic gorge road that winds between cliffs towards Cangas de Onís. Surfaces vary, and you will share the roads with cows, sheep and walkers. In winter, snow can close the passes.

Posada de Valdeón has bars, restaurants and accommodation, but fuel is scarce in the mountains; fill up in Riaño or Cangas de Onís before heading in. The weather is unpredictable, with fog, rain and sudden storms, even in summer. Carry warm, waterproof layers.
t.altamira@43.4,-4.1:
In 1879 a nine-year-old girl named María was exploring a cave near Santillana del Mar with her father, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, an amateur archaeologist. While he dug in the floor, she looked up at the ceiling and saw painted animals. The bison of Altamira, painted in red and black on the uneven rock so that their bodies seem to swell and move in the flickering light, are among the greatest works of prehistoric art in the world. When Sautuola published his discovery, most experts refused to believe that cavemen could have produced such sophisticated paintings, and he was accused of fraud. He died before he was vindicated; only after similar paintings were found in France did the leading sceptic, Émile Cartailhac, publish a famous apology. Altamira was listed by UNESCO in 1985.

The original cave is now almost entirely closed to protect the paintings, which were damaged by the breath and body heat of thousands of visitors in the twentieth century. A very small number of people are chosen by lottery to enter each week. For everyone else, the museum next door has a remarkable replica, the Neocueva, which reproduces the cave and its paintings in exact detail. The museum also explains the life of the people who lived here during the last Ice Age.

Santillana del Mar, a short walk away, is one of the best preserved medieval villages in Spain, with cobbled streets, stone houses with wooden balconies and a Romanesque collegiate church. It is sometimes called the town of three lies, because it is not holy, not flat and not on the sea. In summer it is packed with visitors, but in the evening, when the coaches leave, it is lovely.

The riding in Cantabria is excellent. The coast road west towards Comillas, where Gaudí built the colourful villa El Capricho, and San Vicente de la Barquera has views of beaches and cliffs, while the roads inland climb into green valleys and mountains, towards the Picos de Europa. Surfaces are generally good, traffic is moderate, and the scenery is wonderful.

Torrelavega, a few kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try cocido montañés, a hearty bean stew, or quesada, a local cheesecake. The weather is mild and wet, with rain at any time of year; summer is the driest season.
t.barranc del puig abric i@40.4,-0.1:
The Maestrat is the high, rugged interior of the province of Castellón, a land of limestone plateaus, deep ravines and stone villages that seem to grow out of the rock. Near Benassal, the Barranc del Puig cuts into the hills, and its rock shelters contain prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO serial site of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. This area is one of the richest in Spain for Levantine rock art, and the nearby Valltorta gorge, between Albocàsser and Tírig, has some of the most famous paintings, including scenes of hunters chasing deer and wild goats. The Valltorta museum in Tírig explains the art and organises visits to the shelters.

The Maestrat was a frontier land during the Reconquista, and the Knights Templar and later the Order of Montesa held castles here. Villages such as Culla, Ares del Maestrat and Benassal have medieval streets, churches and fortifications, and the landscape is dotted with dry-stone walls and masías, isolated farmhouses. Benassal is known for its spring water, the Font d'en Segures, which is bottled and drunk across the region. The area is sparsely populated, and many villages have lost much of their population in the last century.

The riding in the Maestrat is outstanding. The roads wind across the high plateaus and down into the ravines, with tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular views. Traffic is almost nonexistent on many roads, and the surfaces are generally good, though some minor roads can be rough. The CV-15 and the roads toward Morella and Vilafranca are particularly enjoyable. Watch out for gravel on bends, livestock and the occasional deer or wild boar. The altitude, around a thousand metres on the plateaus, keeps temperatures cooler in summer, but winters can be harsh, with snow and ice.

Benassal, about five kilometres away, is a small village with a few cafés and shops, and fuel can be found in some of the larger villages, though distances between stations are long, so plan ahead. Alcalà de Xivert, on the coast, is the nearest town of more than five thousand people, about thirty kilometres away. Local food includes hearty stews, cured meats, and the famous black truffles of the region in winter. Visit the Valltorta museum, ride the mountain roads, and stop in Culla for the view. It is one of the most beautiful and least known corners of Spain.
t.roca del senallo@40.4,-0.2:
The Maestrat of inland Castellón is a highland of stone: stone villages on hilltops, stone walls running for kilometres across the slopes, stone farmhouses called masos scattered over the plateau. Roca del Senallo is a rock shelter near Culla, Vilafranca and Benassal, one of many painted shelters in this region, and it belongs to the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The Maestrat is one of the richest areas for Levantine art, with famous sites in the Valltorta gorge and around Ares and Albocàsser.

The museum of the Valltorta at Tírig explains the art of the region, with reproductions of the paintings and guided visits to the shelters. The Levantine paintings here include hunting scenes with archers and deer, among the most dynamic images in prehistoric art. Some of the archers are drawn mid-stride, legs flung wide and bows drawn, with a sense of speed that feels startlingly modern for figures a few centimetres tall painted thousands of years ago.

Culla is a medieval village on a hilltop, with views over the surrounding mountains, and Benassal has a famous mineral water spring, the Font d'en Segures. Vilafranca is known for its drystone walls, an art form in itself, and has a museum devoted to the craft. The landscape is high and open, with pine forests, pastures, almond trees and dramatic limestone cliffs.

The riding is excellent: quiet roads with many curves, climbs and descents, and views over the mountains. The roads through the Maestrat are some of the best in eastern Spain, with little traffic and good surfaces. In winter the high plateau can be cold and snowy, and in summer it is cooler than the coast. Watch for livestock, cyclists and occasional gravel.

Vilafranca can usually supply fuel, and l'Alcora, thirty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services. Maestrat cooking is built for cold winters: stews of lamb and beans, game, cured hams hung in cool attics and, from December, truffles.
t.chemin de la cote@43.3,-1.8:
Irun is where the coastal Way of St James, the Camino del Norte, crosses from France into Spain, and pilgrims have been walking over the Bidasoa here for centuries. The river is the border, and in the middle of it sits the Isle of Pheasants, a scrap of land that has been governed jointly by both countries since the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659, changing hands every six months. It is a peculiar, rather charming thing to stand on the bank and look at.

The town itself is a working place, a frontier of warehouses, railway lines and shopping streets, but the coast it opens onto is spectacular. Hondarribia, a few kilometres north on the river mouth, has a walled old town with balconied houses painted in strong Basque colours and a fishermen's quarter full of bars where pintxos line the counters. Across the water, Hendaye looks back with its long beach and French manners.

For a rider, the reason to start or end a day here is Jaizkibel. The mountain road climbs from Hondarribia along a ridge high above the Atlantic, with the Bay of Biscay dropping away on one side and the green Basque hills on the other, and runs on towards Pasaia and San Sebastián. The corners are open and flowing, the surface usually good, and the views are absurd. It is also a favourite with cyclists, and the ridge catches every gust coming off the sea, so ride it with some respect. Sea fog can roll up suddenly and erase the view entirely.

This coast is green for a reason. Rain arrives often and without much warning, and the roads stay greasy in the shaded sections long after a shower. Summer is busy with traffic heading for the beaches; late spring and September are kinder.

Irun has fuel, food and everything else, and prices on the Spanish side tend to make French riders smile. Eat in Hondarribia if you can: grilled fish, txakoli poured from a height, and a slice of Basque cheesecake if the place you sit in makes it. Then follow the pilgrims west, though at a rather higher speed than theirs, along a coast that will keep you busy all the way to Galicia.
t.villaroges@40.4,-0.1:
Villaroges is one of those names that appears on a map of prehistoric sites rather than a road atlas, somewhere in the high country of the Alt Maestrat between Benassal, Culla and Vilafranca. It belongs to the extraordinary concentration of rock art in the mountains of Castellón, where small painted shelters are scattered through the ravines, protected as part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. Exactly where the panel lies, and whether it can be visited, is a question for the local tourist office or the museum at Tírig; treat the name as an invitation into one of the emptiest and most beautiful corners of eastern Spain.

The Maestrat takes its name from the Masters of the military orders, the Templars and later the Order of Montesa, who controlled these mountains after the Christian conquest in the thirteenth century. Their legacy is a landscape of fortified villages on crags, Gothic churches and stone farmsteads, all bound together by tens of thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls. In 2018 UNESCO recognised the art of dry-stone walling as intangible heritage, and nowhere shows why better than the slopes around Vilafranca, where walls and stone huts climb every hill.

Benassal is famous for its water. The Font d'en Segures spring has been bottled for generations, and the village has a pleasant old centre with a fortified gate. Culla, perched on a summit, is a tiny medieval village with views in every direction and a reputation as one of the most beautiful in the region. The ride up to it is short, steep and twisty.

The roads here are the reward for the effort of getting inland. The CV-15 runs through the region, and the minor roads branching off it climb over passes and along ridges at around a thousand metres, with deep valleys below and little traffic. Corners are frequent, the surface is fair to good, and you will often have the road to yourself. Cold is a real factor: snow is common in winter, frost can linger in shaded bends, and even in summer evenings at altitude are fresh.

Fuel needs planning. Benassal and Vilafranca are small but have services; Alcalà de Xivert, on the coast, is the nearest larger town. Eat wherever you find a busy bar: the cooking is mountain fare, lamb, sausages and thick stews.
t.hornos de la pena@43.3,-4.0:
Above the village of San Felices de Buelna, on a limestone hillside in the Besaya valley of Cantabria, a cave called Hornos de la Peña holds engravings made by Palaeolithic hunters. The most famous is the outline of a horse, scratched into the rock thousands of years ago, along with other animals and signs that take time and a good guide to pick out. The cave is one of the seventeen in northern Spain listed by UNESCO alongside Altamira, and visits are limited and guided, so check ahead rather than simply turning up.

This part of Cantabria is a crumpled green landscape of meadows, chestnut woods and limestone crags, with the river Besaya running north to the sea at Torrelavega. Los Corrales de Buelna, the town just below, grew around steel and wire works and is a practical, unpretentious place with fuel, shops and bars. A few kilometres east, at Puente Viesgo, Monte Castillo hides another cluster of decorated caves, including El Castillo itself, where some of the hand stencils on the walls have been dated among the oldest cave art in Europe. Together they make a remarkable half day.

The riding around here is very good and very green. Small roads climb out of the Besaya and the Pas valleys into rolling uplands, with tight bends through villages and longer flowing sections across open pasture. The Pas valley, east of Puente Viesgo, is home to the pasiegos, a pastoral people with a strong identity who moved their cattle between scattered stone cabins on the hillsides. The road up to the passes at the head of the valley is a favourite, steep and twisting, with views over a landscape that looks almost alpine. Expect cows on the road and wet tarmac in shaded corners.

Rain is part of the deal. Cantabria is green because it gets weather from the Atlantic all year, and fog sits in the valleys on many mornings. When the sun comes out, though, the colours are intense, and the light after a shower is beautiful. Summer is the driest season and the busiest.

Do not leave without trying the local sweets. Sobaos pasiegos, dense buttery sponge cakes, and quesada, a baked cheese pudding, are the pride of the Pas valley and are sold in every bakery and petrol station shop. Pair them with coffee in Puente Viesgo before the next climb.
Riding into the centre of Madrid is not anyone's idea of a scenic route, but the Paseo del Prado makes up for the traffic. This broad, tree-lined boulevard, laid out in the eighteenth century under Charles III as a showpiece of the Enlightenment, runs from the Cibeles fountain past Neptune to the Atocha station, and along it stand three of the greatest art museums in the world: the Prado, the Thyssen-Bornemisza and, a short walk away, the Reina Sofía with Picasso's Guernica. Behind the Prado, the Buen Retiro park spreads over more than a hundred hectares of gardens, lakes and avenues, once the grounds of a royal palace. In 2021 UNESCO listed the ensemble as the Landscape of Light, a recognition of the boulevard and the park as a planned urban landscape devoted to science, art and leisure.

The Retiro is where Madrid goes to breathe. On the big lake people row hired boats beneath the colonnaded monument to Alfonso XII; in a quiet corner stands the Palacio de Cristal, a glass and iron pavilion built in 1887 that now hosts contemporary art. On weekend mornings the paths fill with joggers, families and street musicians, and the shade beneath the chestnuts and plane trees is the coolest place in the city in summer.

For a rider, the practical side matters. Madrid has strict low-emission rules, and motorcycles are subject to them too, so check that your bike's environmental label and registration are accepted before you come in. Motorbikes are everywhere in the city, and parking for them is relatively easy compared with cars, but leave nothing on the bike. Traffic around the roundabouts at Cibeles and Atocha is dense and fast, with taxis and buses changing lanes without much ceremony. Sunday mornings are the calmest time to arrive.

The city is also a great base. To the north and west, the Sierra de Guadarrama rises within an hour, with mountain passes like Navacerrada and Morcuera offering proper curves and cool air. To the south, the road leads through La Mancha towards Toledo and Aranjuez.

Fuel, food and rest are everywhere. Eat late, as Madrid does: a plate of calamari in a roll, a cocido madrileño in winter, or a long lunch on a terrace. Then walk the Prado and spend an hour with Velázquez, a surprisingly good way to rest tired legs.
t.aranjuez cultural landscape@40.0,-3.6:
Aranjuez is the green oasis of the dry Madrid plain, a royal town built where the Tagus and the Jarama rivers meet and where Spanish kings came every spring to escape the court. The palace, largely an eighteenth-century Bourbon creation, faces broad avenues and formal gardens, and the riverside parks of the Jardín de la Isla and the Jardín del Príncipe stretch for kilometres along the water, with fountains, statues, an artificial island and tall old trees. In 2001 UNESCO listed the whole thing as a cultural landscape, recognising how the kings shaped nature, agriculture and town planning into a single designed whole.

In the Jardín del Príncipe stands the Casa del Labrador, the labourer's cottage, which turns out to be an exquisitely decorated little palace full of silk, porcelain and clocks, and nearby a museum houses royal barges that once carried the court on the Tagus. Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, perhaps the best-known work ever written for guitar, was inspired by these gardens, and on a warm evening by the river you can hear why.

The town's fields also feed Madrid. The fertile vega around the rivers is famous for its strawberries, the fresones of Aranjuez, sold from stalls along the roads in spring, and for asparagus. In season, a strawberry train runs from Madrid as a tourist attraction, with costumed staff handing out fruit.

Riding here is easy and pleasant rather than thrilling. From Madrid you can take the A-4 motorway, but the old N-IV and the smaller roads through Chinchón and Colmenar de Oreja are much nicer, with gentle curves across olive groves and vineyards. Chinchón is worth the detour for its arcaded main square with wooden balconies, one of the most characterful in Spain, and its anise liqueur. Westward, the road to Toledo follows the Tagus across open country, with wide views and long straights that tempt the right hand.

Summer is very hot, and the gardens are the place to be at midday. Spring, with fruit and blossom, is the best time. Aranjuez has fuel and plenty of restaurants, and if you eat here, try the strawberries with cream and the local asparagus. Park in the shade near the palace and take a long walk; you will have earned it after the Madrid ring roads.
t.hutian ancient kiln site@29.3,117.2:
Jingdezhen has been making porcelain for more than a thousand years, and the Hutian kiln site is one of the places where that story began to turn into an industry. The kilns here produced fine white and bluish-white ware in the Song and Yuan dynasties, and the heaps of broken shards and the remains of long dragon-shaped kilns show how potters adapted slopes of land to fire great quantities of pots at once. Later, in the Ming dynasty, imperial kilns were established in the town itself, and Jingdezhen became the porcelain capital of China, supplying emperors and, via the sea trade, markets from Japan to Europe.

The raw materials came from the hills nearby. The clay called kaolin takes its name from Gaoling, a mountain near Jingdezhen, and the word travelled west with the porcelain trade, eventually becoming a standard term in geology and ceramics. Together with petuntse, a feldspar-rich stone, kaolin gave Chinese potters a white, hard, translucent body that Europe could not copy until the eighteenth century. Wood from the surrounding forests fuelled the kilns, and the rivers carried the finished goods down to the Yangtze.

For a rider, northern Jiangxi is green, hilly, humid country with winding rivers, tea terraces and bamboo thickets. Roads are generally good, with a mixture of expressways and quieter country routes, though motorcycle rules in China are strict: foreign visitors usually cannot ride without a Chinese licence and registration, so check your options before planning, and note that many cities restrict motorbikes. The climate has hot, wet summers and cool, damp winters, so spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons. Rain can come down hard, and the hills fill with mist.

Jingdezhen, only about four kilometres from the site, is a city of over three hundred thousand with plenty of fuel, restaurants and hotels. Visit the porcelain markets and the working potteries, where you can watch painters, throwers and glazers at their trades, and eat a bowl of noodles with local vegetables and chillies. Take time to look closely at the shards on the ground, since each one is a piece of a vanished cargo, and leave them where you found them.
t.abrigo del camino@42.3,-0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is the southern edge of the Pyrenees, a limestone range cut by canyons so deep and narrow that they have made the area a centre for canyoning. The river Vero runs through one of them, a gorge of pale rock and clear green pools, and at its mouth stands the village of Alquézar, whose collegiate church and castle dominate a rocky spur above the water. The Abrigo del Camino is one of the painted shelters in this country, part of the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean arc that UNESCO lists, in a landscape that suits prehistoric hunters well.

Alquézar began as a Moorish fortress, taken by the Christian king of Aragon in the eleventh century, and the canons who later built the church there ruled the surrounding valley. Walkways bolted to the canyon walls now lead visitors above the river, and the village streets are steep, cobbled and photogenic. The cliffs above are home to griffon vultures and, with luck, the bearded vulture, a rare and splendid bird that eats bones, dropping them from a height to crack them open.

The roads to Alquézar are a good ride. From Barbastro, the road climbs through almond and olive country into the foothills, with bends, short climbs and views of bare ridges, and it is quiet outside the high season. Tighter, narrower roads continue up into the sierra, where gravel and broken tarmac are common, and in summer the heat reflects off the rock. Spring has green hills and flowers, autumn is gentle, and winter can bring ice. Take care on the narrow village streets, where cars and walkers share the way.

Barbastro, a bit closer on the plain, has stations and restaurants, and is the market town for the Somontano wine region, whose reds and whites are good. Eat roast lamb or a plate of migas, and try the local ternasco, tender young lamb. Carry water and wear stout shoes if you plan to walk to the shelter, and be careful in the heat.
t.la roca del migdia@40.4,-0.2:
The inland hills of Castellón are some of the emptiest in eastern Spain. Behind the orange groves and resorts of the coast the land rises into the Maestrat, a high, stony country of plateaus, gorges and stone-walled fields, where villages of a few hundred people cluster around fortified churches and the horizon is crowned by the bulk of Penyagolosa, nearly 1,800 metres high. Villafranca del Cid, Culla and Benassal lie in this landscape, and the Roca del Migdia, the Noon Rock, is a shelter in a limestone face that was painted in prehistory.

I cannot tell you in detail what is painted on this one, but the district is well known for the Levantine art of the Mediterranean arc, which UNESCO lists. Not far away, at Tirig, the Cova dels Cavalls shows hunters shooting arrows at galloping deer in a scene of rare movement and economy. The Maestrat also has a medieval past: it was a frontier of the Christian conquest in the thirteenth century, and the military order of Montesa held many of its castles. Culla's castle, on a crag above the village, gives a good idea of how those fortresses dominated the land.

For motorcyclists, this is one of the best places in eastern Spain. Roads climb out of the coastal plain through switchbacks, pine woods and rocky gorges, then run across the plateau with views over ridge after ridge, and the villages along the way are small and silent. The surfaces are mostly good, though patched, and traffic is light even in high summer. Weather can change fast, and snow is possible in winter above a thousand metres. Spring and early autumn are ideal.

The listed distance to l'Alcora is long, since the local villages are small, but Villafranca has a station and a few shops, and Benassal has more bars and restaurants. Try the cured ham and the local lamb, and perhaps a glass of rich red wine from the hills. Carry water if you are going to walk to the shelter, wear sturdy footwear and treat the rock with care, since the paintings are fragile and the paths can be rough.
t.jiuri mountain wind praying inscriptions:
Before the sailing season, officials and merchants climbed a hill above Quanzhou to ask the gods for wind. The Jiuri mountain inscriptions, carved on cliff faces and boulders between the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, record these prayers, and they are among the most unusual documents of China's maritime past. They were written by local officials of the Song dynasty, and they appeal to the sea gods and to the spirits of the mountain to send a favourable monsoon, so that the trade ships bound for Southeast Asia, India and Arabia could set out in safety and return. Standing before a rock face carved with neat columns of characters, you are reading a note that someone left when the world's biggest port was run by hand and weather.

The monsoon pattern was the engine of the whole trade. Winter winds from the north-east carried ships south, and summer winds from the south-west brought them home, and the timing of the voyage determined fortunes. The prayers were an official ritual, and the inscriptions give names, dates and the ceremony, a rare record of how religion and commerce worked together. The group is part of the Quanzhou UNESCO listing of 2021.

Jiuri Mountain lies in the Nan'an district, north-west of the old city, on a low green ridge with views over the Jin river. The nearby village of Fengzhou is small and quiet, and Quanzhou, with around a hundred and eighty thousand people in its core, is a sizeable city with fuel and hotels.

As with other places in China, foreign visitors cannot easily bring their own motorcycles, and local rules about riding are strict, so most people reach the site by taxi or local bus, and then walk the short path to the rock. The path can be steep and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip. The best months are autumn and early spring, when the air is dry and the heat of summer has passed. Bring water, and read the carved characters with a local guide if you can, since the rock gives up its meaning slowly.
t.abrigo de la vacada@40.7,-0.4:
Castellote is a hill town in the Maestrazgo, the high, dry and wonderfully empty country of southern Aragon, and the shelter of La Vacada lies among the limestone gorges nearby. The name suggests a place where cattle were gathered. The area has some of the finest Levantine rock art in Teruel, and the figures here are part of the Mediterranean-arc ensemble UNESCO recognised in 1998: slender red archers, deer and sometimes a hunting scene, painted on the walls of shallow caves. The rock is pale and the cliffs are cut by the river Guadalope, which carves a sequence of narrow canyons through the plateau.

Riding in the Maestrazgo is a pleasure for those who like emptiness. The roads climb from the river valleys onto bare plateaus at around a thousand metres, with wide horizons, thyme and juniper along the verges, and villages built of the same stone as the hills. The tarmac is mostly decent, but there is often a sheen of loose grit, and in winter the plateau can hold snow. Spring is best, when the almond blossom has just gone and the fields are green. In summer, afternoons are scorching.

Castellote itself has less than a thousand people, and the other villages around it are smaller. Mas de las Matas is a little larger, and the nearest real town is Andorra, almost thirty kilometres away, where you will find fuel, supermarkets and workshops. Do not leave it late to fill up. For a coffee or lunch, small bars in the villages serve a plate of local ham, a bowl of stew, or migas, the fried breadcrumb dish that shepherds invented. The Teruel region is famed for its cured ham, and the cold, dry air is the reason.

The landscape holds other stories. Castellote's castle belonged to the military orders after the Reconquista, and the Maestrazgo was a battleground during the Carlist wars in the nineteenth century. Today it has a quiet, almost abandoned feel, and that is why many riders love it.
t.mascun i@42.3,-0.1:
The Mascún gorge is one of the great pieces of rock in the Sierra de Guara, a canyon with walls that rise several hundred metres, and it is the reason the village of Rodellar has become a pilgrimage site for climbers. Mascún I is a small shelter on the high ground above, in a district of cliffs, pines and thin soil, and it belongs to the Mediterranean-arc rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot tell you what is painted there. I can tell you that you will not have to share the view with a crowd. This is one of the emptiest corners of the Pyrenean foothills.

The road to it is slow. From Huesca the main way is long and winding, through oak woods and across ridges, with narrow sections and a few unpaved spurs. Plan on more time than the map suggests. Surfaces are patched, rockfall is possible after heavy rain, and in winter the upper stretches can ice up. The reward is solitude, with griffon vultures turning on the thermals and big skies of the kind you rarely get in northern Europe. A bearded vulture or an eagle is a real possibility.

Do not count on fuel. Alquézar is fifteen kilometres away and has a few hundred inhabitants, Angüés and Boltaña are small, and the nearest big town in the data is Huesca, over thirty kilometres off. Fill up in Huesca or Barbastro, carry water and some food, and tell someone your route if you head onto the unpaved sections. The nearest village bar might be closed on a weekday afternoon.

In summer the canyon has a cool micro-climate, and the cliffs act like a storage heater in the evening, so a night near Rodellar is warm and the sky is full of stars. Spring is the best season, when the hills are green and the stream runs. Autumn is also fine, though the days are short. If you walk to the viewpoint over the gorge, take a hat, because there is no shade, and listen for the sound of rope on rock far below.
t.abrigo del huerto de las tajadas@40.3,-1:
Albarracín is one of the loveliest villages in Spain, a town of pink-ochre houses on a rock bend above the Guadalaviar river, with medieval walls climbing the hill behind. The Sierra de Albarracín around it is high and cold, at about 1,200 metres, a land of pine forest, red sandstone outcrops called rodeno, and wide empty plateaus. The Guadalaviar, which becomes the Turia in Valencia, rises in these hills, and the Tagus and the Júcar are not far from their sources. The rock shelters of this region, including the Huerto de las Tajadas, hold some of the oldest paintings of the Levantine and Schematic styles, and they are part of the Mediterranean-arc group UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot describe this shelter, but the nearby Pinares de Rodeno, with painted walls under pine trees and rust-red cliffs, give a good sense of the setting.

The ride up is the pleasure. From Teruel, the road follows the Guadalaviar to Albarracín, with long bends and big views, and onwards to Gea de Albarracín and the plateau. Traffic is light, apart from weekend visitors to Albarracín itself, and the surface is generally good. Winter brings snow and ice, so check the weather. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, the air cold and clean, and the light low on the stone.

Teruel is the nearest real town, twenty kilometres from the shelter, with fuel, supermarkets and the Mudéjar towers that UNESCO has also listed. The village of Albarracín has a handful of fuel stops nearby, but do not count on them, and Gea de Albarracín is tiny. Fill up in Teruel. For lunch, try the cured ham of Teruel, which has its own designation of origin, or a plate of roast lamb, and finish with a coffee in a square.

Albarracín is crowded on weekends and quiet on midweek mornings. Park below the walls and walk in. The old streets are steep, and the house fronts lean in a way that makes the light curious. A walk along the ramparts at the end of the day is a good way to see the sun on the hills.
t.los estrechos i@41.1,-0.5:
Los Estrechos means the narrows, and the name fits the country around Albalate del Arzobispo, in the Bajo Aragón, where the Martín river squeezes through limestone gorges on its way to the Ebro. The landscape is dry and open, a mixture of olive groves, almond terraces and low scrub, with sudden canyons and cliffs. The Martín valley is protected as a cultural park, because it holds a remarkable series of rock shelters with Levantine and Schematic paintings, some of which belong to the Mediterranean-arc group that UNESCO listed in 1998. Los Estrechos I is one of them, and I cannot say what is on its walls, but its setting in a narrow gorge is dramatic.

Albalate del Arzobispo takes its name from the archbishops of Zaragoza, who owned the town in the Middle Ages and built a castle and palace there. It has a population of about two thousand, with a mixture of Mudéjar and Renaissance buildings. Like several other towns of the Bajo Aragón, it is famous for its Holy Week drumming, in which hundreds of people strike drums together for hours, producing a sound that you feel in your chest. UNESCO recognised the Bajo Aragón drum tradition as intangible heritage in 2018.

The riding is open and relaxed. Roads between Albalate, Ariño and Híjar run across plateaus and along river valleys, with long gentle bends, sun-baked tarmac and large views. Traffic is light. The wind can be strong, and summer heat is intense, so ride in the morning or in spring and autumn. Olive harvest in winter brings tractors and nets across the road. The soil is pale and the sky large.

Fuel is available in Albalate, a few kilometres away, and in the bigger town of Andorra, fifteen kilometres to the south. Ariño, nearby, has a coal-mining past, with a large open-cast pit that shaped the landscape. For lunch, ask for local olive oil with bread, or lamb, and try the peaches in season. A walk to the narrows at dusk, when the cliffs turn amber, is memorable.
t.longhushan guifeng section@28.3,117.4:
Sheer red cliffs rise out of the green hills of Jiangxi, and in some of them, high above a stream, there are dark rectangular holes in the rock. They are the cliff tombs of the Guyue people, who lived in this area about 2,600 years ago and who placed their dead in wooden coffins in caves and ledges on the face of a cliff above the Lushui river. How they hauled the coffins up the cliff is a puzzle that was never fully solved, and when archaeologists excavated some of them in 1979 they found well-preserved cloth, musical instruments and tools, as well as skeletons. Guifeng, the Ghost Peak, is the best-known site, and its name reflects the awe the place has long inspired.

The cliffs belong to a landscape of Danxia, a type of red sandstone and conglomerate that erodes into steep towers, ridges and sheer walls, and Longhushan, the Dragon and Tiger Mountain, is one of the places included in the China Danxia World Heritage listing. The mountain is also the birthplace of organised Taoism, in a sense. Zhang Daoling, the founder of the Celestial Masters school in the second century, is said to have refined his elixir of immortality here, and his descendants, the Celestial Masters, held court at Longhushan for nearly two thousand years, with each generation of the family carrying the title. Temples and a former residence, the Tianshi Mansion, stand in the valley.

I should be straight about riding conditions. Riding a foreign motorcycle in China normally needs a Chinese licence, local registration and plates, and a guide, so most foreign visitors travel by car with a driver, bus or train. The countryside itself is lovely, with a mix of rice fields, bamboo groves, tea terraces and red cliffs above clear rivers, and the villages are quiet, with courtyard houses and local markets. Spring, with mist and fresh green, and autumn are the best seasons. Summers are hot and humid, with heavy rain and sometimes flooding.

Guixi, a city of more than seventy thousand people about twenty kilometres away, has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and it is known for its copper smelting, one of the biggest in the country. Local food is spicy, with river fish, bamboo shoots and sticky rice, and a pot of green tea is the right companion.
t.gaoling porcelain clay mining site@29.5,:
Few words travelled the world quite like kaolin. It comes from Gaoling, which means High Ridge, a hill village in Jiangxi province where a pure white clay was dug for centuries and sent to the porcelain kilns of Jingdezhen. French missionaries in the eighteenth century took samples of this clay back to Europe, and the Chinese place name became the English and French word for the key ingredient in porcelain. So this ordinary-looking hillside is where one of the most famous materials in the world got its name.

Porcelain needs two things: kaolin, which gives the body its whiteness and plasticity, and petuntse, a crushed feldspar-rich stone that fluxes and makes the body glassy when fired. Gaoling supplied the first, and other hills nearby, such as the Changling site on a connected ride, supplied the second. Together they made Jingdezhen the porcelain capital of China for over a thousand years, with imperial kilns producing blue and white wares for the court in the Ming and Qing dynasties. Today the old pits are quiet, and the scenery is a mix of terraced hillsides, small farms, bamboo and tea.

The country is hilly and green, in the northeast of Jiangxi, with winding local roads, village lanes and a fair amount of truck traffic. Jingdezhen lies about 36 km away and has about 300,000 people, with everything you need in terms of fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants. The city itself is a good place to spend time, with a museum of ceramics, old kiln sites and a market where artists sell pieces. Motorbike travel by foreign visitors is difficult in China because of licence rules, so check carefully, and consider a car and driver.

Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, while summers are hot and humid, with heavy rain and sometimes flooding. The climate and the high rainfall are part of why the area produces so much green. The hills smell of wet earth and woodsmoke, and in some villages you can still see families drying clay or firing small kilns. If you buy a piece of porcelain here, ask for its maker, and remember how many hands a single cup passes through.
t.abrigo del torico del pudial@40.7,-0.4:
The Maestrazgo and the Bajo Aragón are among the emptiest parts of Spain, a country of limestone ridges, deep river gorges and villages that look as if they were poured into the hillside. Castellote, Molinos and Mas de las Matas are small stone towns in the Teruel province, with Romanesque and Gothic churches, narrow streets and houses with wooden balconies, set between the Guadalope river and the high ground of the Maestrazgo. The population is small and has been falling for decades, which means traffic is light and the landscape is close to how it has been for centuries.

The rock shelters here, such as the Torico del Pudial, belong to the Levantine rock art tradition that stretches from Catalonia to Andalusia, and the Aragonese examples form part of the UNESCO listing of 1998. They are small, remote and often hard to reach, and the paintings are delicate, so check with the local cultural centre or the Comarca authorities for access. The best-known visitor attraction in the area is not a rock art site but the Grutas de Cristal in Molinos, a show cave full of white crystalline formations that is open to guided visits.

For a rider, this is a joy. The roads twist and turn through the hills with few other vehicles, and the views across limestone crags and pine woods are huge. Surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and some roads are narrow, with livestock and tractors. Winter is cold, and snow and ice can close higher roads, while summers are hot and dry. Spring, with fresh green and flowers, and autumn, with warm light, are the best seasons.

Fuel is a real consideration. Andorra, a town of about 8,000 people some 28 km away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and hotels, while villages like Mas de las Matas have a small station and shops, and others have nothing, so fill up before going deep. Local dishes include ternasco, roast lamb, and the black truffle of Teruel, and the region's olive oil from the Bajo Aragón has its own protected name. The silence and the stars at night are part of the reward.
t.collegiale de santa juliana et son cloit:
The saying goes that Santillana del Mar is the town of three lies, since it is not holy, not flat and has no sea, and the truth is that it is none of those things and one of the prettiest villages in northern Spain. The name comes from Santa Juliana, a martyr whose relics are kept in the collegiate church, and the town grew up around the monastery that held them in the early Middle Ages. Stone houses with carved coats of arms, wooden balconies and cobbled streets line the main road, and cows still wander through the lanes at times.

The collegiate church of Santa Juliana, a Romanesque building of the twelfth century, is the heart of the town, and its cloister is the real treasure. The capitals of the columns are carved with biblical scenes, animals and fantastic creatures, in a rough, lively style that shows the hands of local masons. The church is built of warm, honey-coloured stone, and the interior is simple and cool. The village has been a protected historic site for a long time, and traffic through the centre is limited.

The countryside around is green and soft, with pasture, eucalyptus and oak, and the Cantabrian Sea only a few kilometres north. Close by are the caves of Altamira, where Ice Age bison were painted on the ceiling some fourteen thousand years ago or more, and the original cave is closed to protect the paintings, but a faithful copy, the Neocueva, and a museum are open. A ride through the area passes small coastal villages, meadows and low hills, with rain and mist never far away. The roads are curving and busy in summer, and the weather can change in minutes, so carry a waterproof.

Santillana has about 4,000 people, though it feels smaller, and a few fuel stations on the main road; Reocín and Torrelavega, the larger industrial town, have more. Local specialities include sobaos, small, buttery sponge cakes from the Pas valley, and quesada pasiega, a dense cheese cake. The coastal anchovies from nearby Santoña are some of the best in Spain. Park outside the village and walk, and visit early in the morning, before the coaches arrive.
t.barrio del castillo@40.1,-2.1:
Cuenca is built on a spur of rock between two gorges, and the Barrio del Castillo is its highest quarter, the old castle district at the narrow tip of the ridge. The Huécar river runs along one side and the Júcar along the other, each in a deep cleft with limestone cliffs, and the old town clings to the top between them like a ship's prow. The castle that gave the quarter its name has largely gone, though a gate and a few walls remain, and the Torre de Mangana, a clock tower that was once part of the fortress, stands nearby. The whole walled town is on the UNESCO list as an unusual example of a medieval fortress city that kept its shape.

Tourists come for the Casas Colgadas, the hanging houses, which overhang the Huécar gorge on wooden balconies. One of them holds the Museum of Spanish Abstract Art, started in the 1960s by the painter Fernando Zóbel, which is a surprising and rewarding thing to find in an old stone town. The cathedral, a Gothic building with Anglo-Norman touches, stands in the Plaza Mayor, and the narrow lanes, steps and viewpoints reward slow exploring. The walk across the suspended footbridge, the Puente de San Pablo, gives a famous view back toward the houses.

The ride up from the plain is good. Roads climb through pine forest and open scrub with gentle bends and a few tight sections, and the air is clear and cool at about a thousand metres. The Serranía de Cuenca, to the north-east, is a wild upland of pine, rocks and river canyons, with the strange rock formations of the Ciudad Encantada, an enchanted city of limestone shapes, about 30 km from town. Winter is cold, with snow on the higher roads, and summers are warm in the day but cool at night.

In the old town, the cobbles and steep streets make riding hard and parking is difficult, so leave the bike outside the walls and walk. Cuenca, with about 56,000 people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and many restaurants. The local dish is morteruelo, a rich paste made of game and liver, and the sweet tooth should look for alajú, a cake of almonds and honey from the Moorish tradition. Early morning, when the light is soft and the streets are quiet, is the best time for the old town.
t.san francisco@37.8,-122.4:
San Francisco hits you with its hills first. The city sits on the tip of a peninsula between the Pacific and the bay, and the streets climb and drop at angles that make a fully laden motorcycle feel like a mountain goat. The Golden Gate Bridge, completed in 1937, spans the mouth of the bay in International Orange paint, and when the fog rolls in from the Pacific, as it often does in summer, the towers rise out of the white like something from a dream.

The city has a long and colourful history. It boomed with the Gold Rush of 1849, was nearly destroyed by earthquake and fire in 1906 and rebuilt at speed. In the twentieth century it became a home for the Beat poets, the counterculture of the 1960s, and later the technology industry. The Mission District, named for the Spanish mission founded here in 1776, is known for its murals, taquerias and bars, and has a lively street life. Cable cars still climb Nob Hill, and Chinatown is among the oldest in North America.

The Pacific Coast Highway reaches the city from the south, and from the north the road crosses the Golden Gate. Riding in San Francisco itself is slow, with traffic lights on every block, steep hills and rails to cross, so take care on wet days and watch for cable car tracks. Parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, and many streets have designated motorcycle bays, but be careful to lock the bike and take your valuables with you.

Fuel is easy to find, though a gallon costs more than in much of the country. The best time to visit is autumn, when the fog retreats and the days are warm, and the months from September to November are sometimes called the real summer. Cross the Golden Gate early, before the crowds, and ride up to the Marin Headlands for a view back across the water. The view of the city from there, with the bridge in the foreground, is hard to beat.
t.san luis obispo@35.3,-120.7:
San Luis Obispo is a small city of about forty-seven thousand people, halfway between Los Angeles and San Francisco, and for riders on the coast it is a natural place to rest. It lies in a valley of the Santa Lucia foothills, a short way inland from the Pacific, with hills of oak and grass rising on all sides. Franciscan friar Junipero Serra founded Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa here in 1772, and the mission church still stands on the central plaza, next to a creek that runs through the downtown.

The city has a relaxed, university-town feel, partly because of Cal Poly, the large state university campus on its northern edge. Higuera Street is the heart of the town, with cafes, bookshops and restaurants, and on Thursday evenings it closes to traffic for a farmers' market that brings in food stalls and a barbecue haze. A local speciality is tri-tip, a cut of beef grilled over oak, which you will find at barbecue stands and restaurants across the Central Coast. Bubblegum Alley, a narrow passage plastered with chewed gum, is a weird and slightly gross local landmark.

The riding around the city is some of the best in California. Highway 1 leaves town towards Morro Bay, where a huge volcanic rock rises out of the harbour, and continues north along the coast to Cambria, Hearst Castle and the cliffs of Big Sur. Inland, Highway 46 and the roads through the hills offer curves and quiet. The weather on the coast is often cool and foggy in summer, while the inland valleys are hot, so carry layers and expect to adjust during the day.

Fuel, food and lodging are all easy here, with plenty of petrol stations along the main roads and motels at all price levels. The Madonna Inn, a famously over-the-top hotel with themed rooms, is a local institution, and even if you do not stay it is worth a look at the pink dining room. Spring is lovely, when the hills are bright green and the poppies bloom, and autumn is clear and warm.
t.abric de les dogues@40.4,-0.1:
Benassal sits on a high shelf of the Alt Maestrat, over seven hundred metres up, and the cool, clear air has long made it a summer retreat from the coastal heat. The town has a spa tradition, with springs whose water is bottled and sold across the region, and a medieval centre of stone arcades and Gothic doorways that can stand a slow walk. The Abric de les Dogues, about two and a half kilometres away, is one of the painted shelters scattered through these hills, with Levantine art that UNESCO lists among the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula.

You can see why people came to this country, even long ago. Water is rare but reliable at certain springs, the ravines make natural shelters, and the high ground gives views over game trails. The modern ride adds another layer: Culla, a little to the east, still carries the ruins of its hilltop castle, once a Templar stronghold, and the stone houses of the Maestrat villages show a very long relationship with sheep, olives and almonds.

The wide view from Benassal is dominated by Penyagolosa, the highest summit of the northern Valencian country, above eighteen hundred metres and often snow-dusted in winter. It looks like the master of the district, and on a clear morning you can pick it out for miles. Between you and it lie ridges of pine and holm oak, with the scent of resin and herbs in warm weather.

For riders this is among the most enjoyable parts of the Castellón interior. The roads are quiet and twisty, climbing and dropping through ravines in tight bends, with big views at the crests and the odd well-cambered corner. Surfaces are variable, so watch for gravel at junctions. A short ride away, the road down toward Morella is a favourite of motorcyclists in the region, with long flowing curves in a high, empty landscape.

Benassal has about thirteen hundred people, which is small, so check your tank before you arrive. Villafranca del Cid, a little farther, is a bigger town with more services. If you fancy a long lunch, local restaurants serve robust food, with lamb, sausage and truffle appearing on menus in the right season. Wrap up in winter; this is a cold, high place.
t.royal monastery of santo tomas@40.7,-4.7:
Ávila is the highest provincial capital in Spain, at more than eleven hundred metres, and the cold, clear air gives the whole city a sharp, medieval edge. Its granite walls, about two and a half kilometres around and punctuated by dozens of towers, are among the best preserved in Europe. Just outside them, the Royal Monastery of Santo Tomás is a different sort of monument: a Dominican house founded in the 1480s by the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, who used it as a summer retreat. It is also the burial place of Tomás de Torquemada, the notorious first Inquisitor General, and of Prince Juan, the monarchs' only son, who died young, and whose marble tomb is one of the finest Renaissance sculptures in Spain.

The monastery has three cloisters, and the quiet of them is something to savour after the traffic outside. The mix of Gothic and early Renaissance styles is clear in the stonework, with fine carved choir stalls inside the church.

Arriving by motorbike is straightforward. Ávila stands on a high plateau under the Sierra de Gredos, a granite range whose highest summit, Almanzor, exceeds two and a half thousand metres. The roads over the sierra, such as the old route over the Puerto del Pico, at around thirteen hundred metres, are among the best riding in central Spain, with a Roman road still visible at the pass. Down from the walls, the plain is open, wind-blown and pale gold in summer, with wide skies and few bends, though the weather can turn quickly. Winter brings frost and occasional snow, so check conditions and carry layers.

Fuel and food are easy in a city of nearly fifty-seven thousand people. Try the local chuletón, a huge T-bone steak, if you are hungry, or the yemas de Santa Teresa, sweet egg-yolk confections named after the city's most famous daughter, if you are only peckish. Parking near the walls is easiest outside the main gates, and the old town is pleasantly walkable. Tornadizos de Ávila and Cardeñosa, small villages on the plateau, are quiet but offer little in the way of services.
t.los chaparros@41.1,-0.6:
Albalate del Arzobispo takes its name from its former masters, the archbishops of Zaragoza, and from an Arabic word for a paved road, which suggests the place has been a crossing point for a very long time. It sits in the Bajo Aragón on the Río Martín, a river that has cut a deep, dry gorge through the limestone on its way to the Ebro, and the Los Chaparros shelter, the Holm-Oak Shelter, lies about five and a half kilometres from the town. It belongs to a group of painted shelters, in the Levantine style, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain and managed locally as a cultural park along the river.

For many riders, the draw of the Bajo Aragón is its character: poor, dry, honest and strikingly open. The land is a patchwork of olive, almond and cereal fields, with low hills of red and ochre rock, and small towns whose churches are built of brick in the Mudéjar tradition. It is also drum country. At Easter, towns such as Albalate, Híjar and Alcañiz fill their streets with thousands of drummers in an extraordinary, thundering procession that goes on through the night.

The roads suit a relaxed ride. They are generally good, with long straights and occasional bends where they climb out of the river valley, with views over the cultivated plain. Traffic is light, apart from agricultural vehicles during harvest. In summer the heat is fierce, and winter nights can be bitter, so spring and autumn are best. Fans of motor racing will know that MotorLand Aragón, the circuit at Alcañiz, hosts a Grand Prix, and the area fills with bikes in the right weekend.

Albalate has about two thousand people and a couple of petrol stations, and is the place for petrol. Ariño, a mining town of about nine hundred, lies a few kilometres off with huge open-cast coal pits that make a strange contrast to the old villages. Alloza is smaller still. Take water and food with you, since the countryside is empty.
t.fronton de as capridos@41.1,-0.7:
Look at a map of the Bajo Aragón and you will find a great deal of white space, a country of low ridges, ravines and little villages that have lost most of their inhabitants in a century. Alacón has four hundred people and Oliete not many more, and the Frontón de las Cápridos, a painted rock shelter named for the wild goats, or caprids, that appear among its figures, lies about three and a half kilometres from the former. The paintings are in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO together with the rest of the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula, and they sit within a cultural park that strings several sites together along the Río Martín.

It is easy to see why hunters would have liked this country. Goats and deer need cover and water, and the river gorge offers both. Even now, the scrubby slopes have wild boar and the occasional bird of prey circling. The rock is red and yellow sandstone and pale limestone, cut into pillars and walls by the weather, and the contrast with the green of the river bank and the grey of the olive trees is lovely in low light.

Riding here is different from the usual northern Spain scenery. The roads are quiet and long, with sweeping views over open land, and most corners are gentle, easing through small valleys. Surfaces vary, with smooth tarmac on the main links and rougher lanes between the villages. After rain, mud may wash on to the road near ravines. A tailwind or headwind often decides the speed of the day, since this is open country, and the Cierzo, the cold north-west wind of the Ebro basin, can be fierce.

Alacón and Oliete are too small to bank on for fuel, so fill up before you leave Andorra, the nearest sizeable town, with nearly eight thousand people, or at Albalate. Both have petrol, bakeries and bars. Carry water and a snack, as there is not much between the villages, and enjoy a ride that feels remote, even in the heart of Spain.
t.moli darrer abric ii@40.5,-0.1:
A molí is a mill, and the one that lends its name to this shelter was presumably a water mill on one of the small streams that trickle through the hills around Benassal, in the high interior of Castellón province. Molí Darrer, the Last Mill, was probably the last one before the water ran out or the valley ended, and the shelter here, Abric II, lies about nine kilometres from the town. It carries paintings of the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and is linked to a neighbouring shelter at Mas d'en Badenes and to the Centelles site, which are on the same ride.

Water is the story of this country. At seven hundred metres or more, Benassal and its neighbours sit above the dry coastal plain and catch more rain, and springs and streams are the reason for villages, mills and farms. The water of Benassal is bottled and sold across the region, and the town has been a spa and summer retreat for generations. Walkers will find old irrigation channels, stone washing places and the ruins of mills hidden in the pine woods.

Riding here is a delight. The roads are twisting, empty and well worth taking slowly, with bends that follow the valleys and big views from the crests. The surface varies, from smooth new tarmac to rough, gravelly stretches, and farm vehicles can appear around any corner. A stretch of the main road to Morella is among the better-known motorcycle roads in the region, with long, flowing curves through a high, empty landscape. Winter can be cold and foggy, and snow is occasionally seen on the higher roads, so check conditions.

Benassal has about thirteen hundred people, so do not count on fuel, and Villafranca del Cid, a bit larger, with around twenty-six hundred, is a better bet. Catí, to the east, is smaller. Take water, since there is little between the villages, and linger over a lunch in Benassal, where local restaurants serve hearty stews, lamb and cured meats.
t.covacho de la tia mona@41.1,-0.7:
Aunt Mona's Shelter is the translation of the name, and like most such names, it hides a story nobody can now quite tell. Tía Mona was presumably a woman of Alacón, or of a farm nearby, whose memory stuck to a hollow in the rock long after her family stopped using it. The covacho, a small cave or overhang, lies about three and a half kilometres from the village, in the dry hills of the Bajo Aragón. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO among the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and it belongs to the cultural park of the Río Martín, which links the district's sites together.

What strikes you here is the silence. Alacón has just over four hundred people, Oliete not many more, and between them the hills are empty but for olive terraces, scrub oak and the occasional stone hut where a farmer once sheltered from the sun. Teruel province is among the least populated parts of Europe, and out here you realise why the phrase empty Spain became a political slogan. There is something moving about a painted wall in such a place: people lived in these hills for thousands of years, and then, within a few generations, left.

Riding to the shelter takes you along long, gently rolling roads with excellent views and few cars. The tarmac is generally sound, though rough on the side lanes, and bends are mostly easy, opening occasionally into tighter turns where the road meets a ravine. In spring the fields are green and the almond blossom fades, in autumn the light is low and golden, and in summer midday heat is fierce. The cold Cierzo wind can blow hard through the valleys, so grip the bars on exposed stretches.

Fuel needs planning. Neither Alacón nor Oliete is a safe bet. Andorra, a town of nearly eight thousand people about twenty kilometres away, and Albalate del Arzobispo, with a couple of stations, are both good places to fill up. Ariño, a mining town, lies nearby, and you can eat there simply and well. Bring a bottle of water and wear sturdy shoes.
t.mascun iii@42.3,-0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is among the great limestone landscapes of Spain, and the Mascún gorge, cut deep into its southern flank, is one of the best known. The river has worn a long, narrow canyon, with walls hundreds of metres high, and at its head stands the little village of Rodellar, which has become a pilgrimage place for climbers from across Europe. Mascún III lies about fifteen kilometres from Alquézar and farther still from any big town, and it is one of a series of painted shelters in the canyon. They carry figures in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Another ride connects it to the beech woods of the Hayedos de Navarra, which tells you how far these routes travel.

The land is a mixture of bare crags, holm oak, box and pine, with the Guara's highest point, just over two thousand metres, often with snow in winter. The canyons are full of birds, including griffon vultures, which soar over the rim in the afternoon, and at dusk, bats pour out of the cliffs. In the pools of the Mascún, canyoners in wetsuits drop from ledge to ledge, a sight that gives the place a restless, cheerful energy in summer.

The ride in is a real adventure, narrow, twisty and rewarding. Roads wind through isolated villages in tight bends, with sharp climbs and sudden drops into gullies. They are largely empty, but surfaces can be rough, patched and gravelly, and the last section to the canyon is the sort of road where you slow down without being told. Be careful after rain and in winter, when ice can linger on shaded bends. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and midsummer can be hot, though evenings are cool.

Angüés and Boltaña are small, so plan to fill up in Huesca, which has more than fifty thousand people, or in Barbastro, before you head into the mountains. Rodellar has a small bar and a campsite, but do not count on anything else. Carry water, food, and a warm layer.
t.cova del llepus o particio@40.6,-0.1:
Morella is the sort of town that makes riders stop in the middle of a long day just to look. It sits at about a thousand metres in the high Els Ports country of northern Castellón, ringed by more than two kilometres of medieval walls, with a castle on a crag above and a Gothic basilica below, and the whole mass of golden stone looks as if it grew out of the rock. The Cova del Llepus, about four kilometres away, is one of the painted shelters of the district, a Levantine site protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with another cave, the Escoda, and with a hill the maps call the Peñón de Santo Espíritu.

The cave's second name, Partició, is Valencian for a division, which suggests that a boundary once ran past it. Boundaries matter in a country where villages were fiercely independent and where pastures, springs and stone walls were quarrelled over for centuries. Morella itself was a stronghold in the wars between Christian kings and Muslim rulers, and later in the Carlist wars of the nineteenth century, when its castle changed hands more than once.

The country is sheep country, high, windy and clear, with pastures and holm oak, deep ravines and the bulk of the Ports massif to the north. In winter, snow is not unusual, and Morella can be bitterly cold when the plain below is mild. Black truffles are collected in these hills, and the local pastry, the flaó, a sweet pie of cheese and aniseed, is worth hunting for in the old town.

For riders, this is excellent territory. The main road to the coast, which drops towards Vinaròs through a long run of bends, is one of the classic motorcycle roads of the region, and the lanes around Morella have an agreeable mix of long curves and tight turns. Surfaces are variable, so watch for gravel. Fuel is straightforward in Morella itself, a town of nearly three thousand people with several stations. Forcall and Cinctorres, smaller villages, are good for a coffee. Check the weather in winter, when ice can linger at altitude.
t.torre@40.3,-1.1:
The first thing to know about Teruel is that it is cold. At about nine hundred metres on a high, bare plateau of eastern Spain, it has a reputation as one of the chilliest provincial capitals in the country, and in the winter of 1937 and 1938 the bitter weather turned the battle of Teruel, one of the bloodiest of the Civil War, into a freezing ordeal. The town is also one of the loveliest in Aragón, famous for its Mudéjar towers, brick-and-tile belfries built by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and listed by UNESCO. The ride starts at one of them, the label Torre simply meaning the tower, and then heads out to the Ceja de Piezarrodilla and the Peña del Castellar, where rock art is found in the hills outside the city.

The towers are worth a long look. Their sides are patterned with geometric designs in ceramic tiles, green and white, set into red brick, and their silhouettes dominate the old town. Local legend ties the city to the Lovers of Teruel, Isabel and Diego, whose tragic love story, say the storytellers, ended in the church of San Pedro. Their mummified bodies, according to tradition, lie in a mausoleum next to it, and tourists pay to see them.

Teruel is also known for its cured ham, which has a protected name and a flavour that rivals anything from farther west, and for the plain, hearty food of a cold country. A ham bocadillo and a coffee are all you need.

Riding in is easy. The roads across the plateau are wide and fast, with long views and not many corners, though the wind can be fierce and winter ice is real, so check the forecast between November and March. The city has a good range of fuel stations, and with more than thirty-five thousand people, it has all the services you could need. Villastar and Villel, small villages nearby, offer little but quiet and a bar. Parking is simple around the edge of the old town, and walking its lanes takes an hour well spent.
t.cueva de moncin i@41.9,-1.6:
Borja is a town of four thousand people in the Ebro valley, but its name is known far beyond Spain, because it is the origin of the Borgia family. Rodrigo Borgia, who became Pope Alexander VI, took his surname from this place, and the family's later fame in Italy, for poison, politics and portraits, makes a curious footnote to a quiet farming town. More recently, Borja became famous for a fresco. In 2012, an elderly parishioner's attempt to restore a painting of Christ in the nearby Sanctuary of Mercy turned it into an internet sensation, and visitors have come to see it ever since.

The Cueva de Moncín, about five kilometres from the town, is a different sort of heritage. It is a shelter in the foothills of the Moncayo, the highest mountain of the Iberian System at more than two thousand three hundred metres, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride also links it with a site called Abside, named for its curved, apse-like rock shape.

Wine is the story of the district. Borja lies at the heart of the Campo de Borja, a region that calls itself the Empire of Garnacha, and its hillsides are covered with old vines, some well over a hundred years old, making deep, fruity red wine. Tarazona, thirteen kilometres away, has a Mudéjar cathedral and an octagonal bullring built into the old houses, and is worth a detour.

The Cierzo, the cold north-west wind of the Ebro basin, is the main hazard for riders. It can blow hard for days, and on open stretches it will push a bike across a lane. The roads are otherwise straightforward, with good surfaces, long curves across the vineyards, and a few more interesting twists as they climb towards the mountain. Moncayo itself offers a long and rewarding ride, with views across the plain on a clear day, though snow and ice can close the upper road in winter.

Borja has fuel, food and a pleasant square, and Tarazona has more. Ainzón and Ambel are small, and quiet.
t.los estrechos ii@41.1,-0.5:
The Río Martín is a modest stream that has done something dramatic. Over a very long time, it has cut a deep, narrow gorge through the pale limestone of the Bajo Aragón, with walls that crowd in on either side, and the stretch the locals call Los Estrechos, the Narrows, is where the cleft is tightest. The shelter at Los Estrechos II lies about five kilometres from Albalate del Arzobispo, and is one of the sites along the river protected by a cultural park. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it to the Abrigo de la Higuera, the Fig-Tree Shelter.

It is easy to see why people painted here. The gorge offers shade in summer, shelter from the wind, water and a corridor along which animals move. Red and yellow bands of rock show in the cliffs, and in the right light, the walls glow. Swifts and swallows nest in the cracks, and vultures glide above the rim. In the river itself, reeds and poplars line the banks.

Riding in this area is relaxed. The main roads are fast and straight, crossing the dry plateau, and the lanes along the gorge are narrower, with bends and good views, though some stretches are rough. Traffic is light. The Cierzo, the cold wind of the Ebro basin, blows often and hard, and can make riding on open stretches tiring. In summer, the heat is fierce and shade is rare. Spring and autumn are best.

Albalate has about two thousand people and several stations, so fuel is easy. Híjar, about thirteen kilometres away, is a historic town with a well-preserved old Jewish quarter and a long tradition of drum processions at Easter. Andorra, a larger town of nearly eight thousand people, is another option. Ariño, a mining town, lies close by. Carry water, and give yourself time to look at the gorge from the road.
t.abrigo de los encebros@41.1,-0.7:
Teruel province has some of the darkest skies in Europe. With so few people and so little light, the stars on a clear night over the plateau are astonishing, thick as spilled salt, with the Milky Way arching overhead. The province has taken this seriously: the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory, high in the mountains to the south, is one of the most modern in Spain. If you are staying overnight in this area, go outside after dark and look up. You will remember it.

The Abrigo de los Encebros lies about three and a half kilometres from Alacón, a village of under five hundred people, in the dry hills of the Bajo Aragón. It is one of a string of painted shelters along the Río Martín, part of a cultural park, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it to another site, the Coveta de la Cornisa, the little cave under the ledge.

The land here is open and spare. Low hills of ochre and grey, olive and almond terraces, patches of pine and scrub, and the thin green line of the river. Villages are small and far apart, with brick churches in the Mudéjar style, and many houses stand empty. It is a country of silence, and its emptiness is part of the appeal.

The roads are quiet and gently rolling. Corners are mostly easy, with a few tight bends where the road dips into the gorge, and the surface is mostly good, though patched. A tailwind can make the long straights fly by, and a headwind can make them a slog. In winter, frost forms early and lingers on shaded stretches, and in summer, the sun is relentless.

Alacón and Oliete are too small to be sure of fuel, so fill up in Andorra, a town of nearly eight thousand people about twenty-one kilometres away, or in Albalate del Arzobispo. Both have petrol, bakeries and bars. Carry water, and a warm jacket if you plan to stay out after sunset, since the temperature falls quickly.
t.el cireral@40.4,-0.1:
In Valencian, a cirerer is a cherry tree, and the name of El Cireral suggests an old cherry orchard or a place where wild cherries once grew. That fits the high country around Benassal, where the nights are cool and the fruit trees do well. The shelter lies about five kilometres from the town, in the dry hills of the Alt Maestrat, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with a site called Calçaes del Matá, and with the Arenal de la Fonseca.

Benassal is a nice town to stop in. It sits on a shelf of high land, at over seven hundred metres, and its old centre has stone arcades, Gothic doorways and a pleasant square. The water from its springs is bottled and sold across the region, and in the past the town was a summer retreat for wealthy families from the coast. Culla, to the east, still has the ruins of a Templar castle on its hill, and Villafranca del Cid, to the south-west, is the larger town of the district.

The country around is a mix of pasture, scrub and rock, with long views to the ridges of the Maestrat and the distant hump of Penyagolosa. Spring brings wild flowers and the smell of thyme, and in autumn the oaks turn bronze. The nights are cool even in summer.

The riding is excellent. Roads wind through the valleys and across the plateau in a series of bends, with decent surfaces on the main links and rougher ones on the lanes. Traffic is light, and the views at the crests are worth a stop. A stretch of the main road down towards Morella is a favourite of local motorcyclists. Winter can be cold, with frost and occasional snow.

Benassal, with about thirteen hundred people, may not have fuel to hand, and Villafranca del Cid, with over twenty-five hundred, is the safer choice. Alcalà de Xivert, about thirty-three kilometres away, is the large town on the plain. Pack water and a warm layer.
t.restos mudejares de palacio de la aljafe:
The Aljafería is the one great building in Zaragoza that tells you the city was once Muslim. It was built in the eleventh century as a pleasure palace for the Hudid rulers of the taifa of Zaragoza, a small independent kingdom that emerged when the caliphate of Córdoba collapsed, and its inner courtyard, with slender arches that interlace and curve, is one of the finest examples of Islamic architecture in the north of Spain.
