After the Christian conquest in 1118, it became a royal residence of the kings of Aragón, and the Catholic Monarchs added a sumptuous palace with gilded ceilings in the late fifteenth century. In the nineteenth century, it served as a barracks, and today it is the seat of the Aragonese parliament. The Mudéjar parts, the work of Muslim craftsmen who stayed after the conquest, are part of a UNESCO listing for Mudéjar architecture in Aragón.

Verdi's opera Il trovatore is set partly in the Aljafería, which adds a note of romance to the stone. The building stands on the western edge of the old centre, a short way from the Ebro, and it is a good stopping point if you want to feel the layers of the city's past.

Zaragoza is a big, flat, handsome city of more than six hundred thousand people, strung along the Ebro, with a great baroque basilica to the Virgin of the Pilar on the riverbank and a lively tapas district in the old quarter. The main hazard for a rider is the Cierzo, the dry, cold north-westerly that sweeps the Ebro valley and can blow hard for days, especially in winter and spring.

Riding in the city is not difficult, though trams and one-way systems need attention, and traffic is dense at rush hours. Parking a motorbike near the palace is generally easy. Fuel is no problem anywhere in the city, and you will find plenty of cafes around the old centre. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather, and a long, unhurried lunch is the right way to end a visit.
t.cova del barranquet@40.6,-0.1:
Morella has an unexpected claim to fame. The hills around it, in the high Els Ports country of northern Castellón, are among the most important dinosaur sites in Spain, and the town has a museum, Temps de Dinosaures, devoted to them. Fossil bones and tracks have been found here for decades, from the age when this high plateau was a floodplain. So the area has a double prehistory: the giants of the Cretaceous, and, much later, the small, red-painted hunters who left their pictures on the shelter walls.

The Cova del Barranquet, about four kilometres from Morella, belongs to the second kind. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride ties it to the Cova de l'Escoda, another shelter in the district. The paintings are faint, and the cave is better as an excuse to walk in a remote and beautiful spot.

Morella itself is magnificent. The old town is ringed by more than two kilometres of medieval walls, with a castle on a crag above and a Gothic basilica with an elaborate stone choir inside. Arcaded streets run up and down the slope, and the shops sell local products: honey, cheese, sausages and the flaó, a sweet, aniseed-scented pastry. Black truffles are collected in the hills, and winter menus feature them.

The riding is some of the best in the Valencian Community. The road down to the coast, through a series of long, flowing bends in a high, empty landscape, is a classic of the region. Around Morella, the lanes are narrower and rougher, with gravel on corners and the occasional herd of sheep. In winter, frost and snow are possible, and Morella can be bitterly cold when the plain below is mild.

Morella has nearly three thousand people and fuel, food and lodging in plenty. Forcall and Cinctorres are smaller villages, good for a coffee. Bring a warm layer, even in summer, since the temperature drops quickly after sunset at altitude.
t.mascun iv@42.3,-0.1:
Huesca was the capital of the kingdom of Aragón until the end of the eleventh century, when King Pedro I captured it from the Muslim rulers and made it his base. Today it is a calm provincial city of more than fifty thousand people, with a Gothic cathedral that has a magnificent alabaster altarpiece and the Romanesque monastery church of San Pedro el Viejo. It is the last big town before the mountains, and it is where you will want to fill your tank before heading north into the Sierra de Guara. The shelter at Mascún IV lies about thirty kilometres away, deep in the Mascún valley, about fifteen kilometres from Alquézar. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it with the Cueva de los Moros.

The valley is one of the quietest and most dramatic in the region. The river has cut a deep gorge, and the cliffs rise on either side, hundreds of metres high, in bands of grey, ochre and orange. The hills above are covered with holm oak, box and pine, and the sound of water echoes in the canyon. In summer, the pools are bright green, and canyoners in wetsuits drop from ledge to ledge. The sense of remoteness is powerful, and the villages, with only a handful of residents, add to it.

The road to the valley is narrow, winding and wonderful, with tight bends, steep drops and views that open without warning. It is lightly used, but the surface can be rough, patched and gravelly, and the last section requires care. Take it slowly, and watch for livestock. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter ice can linger on shaded stretches.

Angüés and Boltaña are very small, so fill up in Huesca, or in Barbastro, before you set out. Carry water, food and a warm layer, and tell someone where you are going if you plan to walk.
t.mascun ii@42.3,-0.1:
Boltaña is a small town of nine hundred people in the Sobrarbe, the valley country at the foot of the high Pyrenees, and from its edge the view north is dominated by the great limestone massifs of the Monte Perdido range, often white with snow into early summer. The shelter at Mascún II lies about twenty kilometres away, in the quieter, lower hills of the Sierra de Guara. It carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it with El Remosillo, another site in the canyons.

Between the two lies a whole range of riding. Aínsa, a short way north of Boltaña, has one of the most handsome medieval squares in Aragón, a great arcaded space of stone beneath a castle, and its old town is a lovely place for lunch. Beyond, the road climbs into the Pyrenees, with passes, gorges and a succession of long, flowing curves. The Sobrarbe is also a land of Romanesque churches, small and stone-built, and of bears, vultures and chamois in the mountains.

Mascún itself is the southern, drier part of the story. The canyon is deep and narrow, with warm, golden walls, and the vegetation is holm oak, box and pine. The silence is deep, broken only by the call of a raven or the rush of water in spring.

The roads are narrow, twisty and wonderful, rising and dropping between villages in a series of tight bends, with surfaces that can be patchy and gravelly. Traffic is light, and the main hazards are livestock and fallen rock. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter, ice can linger on shaded corners.

Boltaña has the basics, though fuel is better found at Aínsa or at Huesca, a city of over fifty thousand about thirty-two kilometres away. Angüés and Alquézar are small. Bring water and a warm layer.
t.otros restos levantinos@41.1,-0.7:
Calanda is a modest town in the Bajo Aragón, and it has produced one of the most original film directors of the twentieth century. Luis Buñuel was born there in 1900, and the town's famous Easter drumming, when thousands of people beat their drums through the night, shaped his imagery. He later said that the sound stayed in his head for life. The hills around Alacón, some distance away, are in the same dry, strange country, a landscape of red rock, olive terraces and open sky that feels like a film set.

Otros Restos Levantinos, Other Levantine Remains, is the label here, and it is honest: the shelter lies about three and a half kilometres from Alacón, and is one of a group of painted sites in the Río Martín cultural park, in the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with the Coveta de la Cornisa. I cannot tell you exactly what is painted here, but the label suggests faint traces, and the walk is its own reward.

It is a land of space and silence. Alacón has just over four hundred people, and Oliete not many more, and between them, the hills are crossed by dry gullies and a few dirt tracks. In spring the cereal fields are green, in summer they turn gold, and in autumn the ploughed earth is a deep red. The cold north-westerly wind, the Cierzo, blows often and can be fierce.

The roads are quiet and wide, with long views and easy bends, and a good surface on the main links. Lanes between the villages are narrower, patched and sometimes gravelly. A headwind on a straight can make progress slow, and a tailwind is a gift.

Fuel needs planning. Andorra, a town of nearly eight thousand people about twenty-one kilometres away, is the best bet, and Albalate del Arzobispo is also a good one. Alacón and Oliete have a bar or two, but I would not rely on a pump. Carry water, sun protection and a snack.
t.chaves iii@42.2,-0.1:
The Hoya de Huesca, the plain below the city, is a land of cereal fields and almond trees, and it is guarded to the north by one of the finest Romanesque castles in Spain, the fortress of Loarre, perched on a rocky crest with the Pyrenees behind. A little farther west, the Mallos de Riglos, towers of red conglomerate rock rising hundreds of metres from the valley, are a magnet for climbers and a startling sight from the road. They make a spectacular day out, and a good companion to the quieter shelters of the Sierra de Guara to the east.

Chaves III lies about thirteen kilometres from Angüés, in the hills of the southern Guara, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with Mascún I, in the canyon farther north. It is a modest, remote site in a landscape of low hills, scrub and small villages, many half-empty.

The country here is quiet and rural. Fields of barley and wheat, almond trees, and patches of holm oak and pine cover the slopes. A reservoir in the Guara, Vadiello, lies beneath a spectacular cliff, and its turquoise water is a popular spot in summer. Birds of prey are common, and in the evening, the sound of swifts fills the villages.

Roads are narrow and winding, with plenty of bends, and a mix of good and rough surfaces. Traffic is light, and the main hazards are livestock and loose gravel. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild temperatures. Summer can be very hot.

Huesca, about twenty-four kilometres away, with over fifty thousand people, is the place for fuel and a proper meal. Angüés, Siétamo and Alquézar are small, with a bar or two. Bring water and sun protection, and expect a walk to the shelter.
t.chaves ii@42.2,-0.1:
The village of Chaves lies in the foothills of the Sierra de Guara, in the north of the province of Huesca, in a country of sandstone, scrub oak and long views towards the Pyrenees. The shelter here, listed as Chaves II, belongs to the same family of painted sites that is spread across eastern Spain, with Levantine figures in red among the rocks. The setting is quiet and a little austere, a rocky ravine that glows in the evening light. The nearest towns are tiny: Angüés has fewer than five hundred people, and Alquézar about three hundred, so for fuel you need Huesca, which is a good half hour away at the end of a winding road.

Alquézar is worth the detour on its own. It sits on a rock spur above the Vero river, with a collegiate church and a tangle of medieval alleys, and it has become a base for canyoning in the nearby gorges. The Vero river itself is known for rock art in its valley, and a cultural park has been set up to tell the story.

Riding through this country is enjoyable and a bit demanding. The roads between Huesca, Angüés and Alquézar climb over low passes, drop into river valleys and cross a lot of dry upland where there is hardly a village for kilometres. Corners are plentiful, sometimes tight, and the surface varies from fresh tarmac to patched and worn. Griffon vultures often circle overhead, and the bearded vulture, with its huge wingspan, is sometimes seen in the Guara. Traffic is light apart from weekends when canyoning groups arrive in vans.

Come in spring, when the oak and box are green and the Pyrenees still carry snow on the horizon, or in autumn, when the light is sharper and the air clear. July is hot and the canyons are crowded.

The shelter is reached on foot, and as ever access should be checked before you set off. Take water, sun protection and a map.
t.covacho de eudoviges@41.1,-0.7:
The Bajo Aragón is a country of gypsum cliffs, olive groves and slow rivers, and the Río Martín cuts through it in a series of gorges that shelter some of the finest rock art in Aragon. Covacho de Eudoviges, near the village of Alacón, is one of the painted sites of the Río Martín Cultural Park, and it forms part of the Levantine art that UNESCO recognised in 1998. The paintings are small, red, and sometimes faint, but in the right light the figures stand out sharply from the rock.

The nearest bigger town is Andorra, in the province of Teruel, which has nothing to do with the Pyrenean principality. It grew up around coal mining and a power station, which closed in recent years, and the town has an honest, industrial character. The countryside around it is surprisingly beautiful, with limestone canyons and groves of old olive trees whose oil has a regional protected name. Calanda, to the north, is the birthplace of the film maker Luis Buñuel, and its Holy Week drumming, in which thousands of people beat drums together for hours, is one of the strangest and most impressive sights in Spain.

For a rider the area offers quiet roads, wide landscapes and almost no traffic. The corners are gentle, with the odd tight one where a road drops to cross the river, and long stretches of open plateau where the wind can push the bike. Surfaces are fair, though patchy on the smaller roads. Fuel is available in Andorra. Alacón and Oliete, each with around four hundred and fifty inhabitants, offer bars at best. A ham sandwich, made from the Teruel cured ham with its protected name, is a good lunch.

Summer is hot and dry, and winter is cold and frosty, so the shoulder seasons are best. The poppies in May are a joy, and the October light on the cliffs is tremendous.

Reaching the shelter means a walk on a stony path from the road, and the site is protected, so follow any signs and ask locally if in doubt.
t.mudejar architecture of aragon@40.3,-1.1:
Teruel is one of the coldest and least visited provincial capitals in Spain, and a campaign slogan, Teruel Existe, was coined to remind the rest of the country that it is still there. It stands at around nine hundred metres on a flat-topped hill above the Turia river, in the Aragonese uplands, and its old town holds a group of brick-and-tile towers that UNESCO lists as part of Mudéjar architecture in Aragon. Mudéjar is the style created by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons after the reconquest, and in Teruel it took the form of tall square towers decorated with geometric brickwork and glazed green and white ceramic.

The towers of San Pedro, San Martín, El Salvador and the cathedral of Santa María de Mediavilla are the main ones. The cathedral has a painted wooden ceiling that has been called the Sistine Chapel of Mudéjar art, and a climb up the tower gives a view over the town. Teruel is also known for the story of the Lovers, Diego and Isabel, a medieval tale of love and death that is retold in a mausoleum next to the church of San Pedro, and every February the town stages a festival around it.

Riding here is largely a matter of getting in and out. The surrounding roads run across high plateau and through dry valleys, often at over a thousand metres, with long straights and open bends. In winter, ice and snow are a real risk, and in summer the wind blows hard and the sun is fierce. The Ceja de Piezarrodilla, named in the ride, is a rocky escarpment in the area, and the landscape around it is austere and beautiful. Albarracín, a short way west, is a medieval walled town in rose-coloured stone, and well worth the detour.

Teruel has everything a traveller needs: fuel, hotels, restaurants and shops. The cured ham, with a protected name, is excellent, and is served in thin slices at almost every bar. A good tapas crawl in the old town is a fair way to end the day. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the days are warm and the nights are cool, and pack a warm layer whatever the season.
t.barranco de gibert i@40.4,-0.4:
The Maestrazgo is a name that should be said slowly, because it covers a huge and rugged region in the borderlands of Teruel and Castellón, and Mosqueruela lies in its heart. The village is among the highest in the province, well over a thousand metres up, in a country of pine forest, stone farmhouses and wide grassy valleys. The Barranco de Gibert, a ravine nearby, holds painted shelters with Levantine art, and one of the numbered sites is the subject here. It is part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean basin, and one of the highest and most remote of its kind.

The history of the Maestrazgo is one of fortified villages, shepherds and war. The Knights Templar, and later the Order of Montesa, ran the area in the Middle Ages, and in the nineteenth century it was the stronghold of the Carlist armies, led by the general Cabrera, nicknamed the Tiger of the Maestrazgo. Villages like Villafranca del Cid, in Castellón, still have long, arcaded streets and big stone houses from the time when wool made them rich.

The riding is spectacular but demanding. Roads climb over high passes and wind through forests, with sudden drops into valleys and long views over bare hills. The corners are tight, the surface is variable, and there is a real chance of ice from late autumn to early spring. Wind on the ridges can be fierce. The rewards are a landscape that feels untouched and a silence broken only by sheep bells and the wind in the pines. The black truffle is harvested around here in winter, and the local restaurants serve dishes that make the most of it.

Fuel is a problem. The nearest decent town is l'Alcora, nearly forty kilometres away, with eleven thousand people, and the road there is slow. Fill up before you start, and carry extra if you can. Mosqueruela has a few bars and a shop, but little else.

Come in late spring or early autumn. The shelter is reached on foot, and in this remote area it is best to ask in the village for advice.
t.cueva del garroso@41.1,-0.7:
The Río Martín runs northward through a series of deep gorges before reaching the Ebro, and the villages along it are among the least visited in Aragon. Cueva del Garroso is one of the painted sites in this valley, in the cultural park that protects the rock art of the region, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing of Levantine art in the Mediterranean basin. The cave is a modest opening in a limestone cliff, and the paintings inside are small, in red, and faint in places.

The nearest town of any size is Andorra, in Teruel province, a place built on coal. For decades the open-cast mines and the power station dominated the area, and the town still has a plain industrial feel, though the surrounding country is gentler than that suggests. Olive groves stretch across the terraces, and the oil from the Bajo Aragón has a protected name. Alacón and Oliete are small villages with about four hundred and fifty inhabitants each, and between them they have a few bars and a church or two.

I like the Bajo Aragón for its silence. Roads run along the river and cross high plateaus where the only sounds are the wind and the larks. The bends are open, the surface is mostly good, and the traffic is light. There are long straights where the wind can catch a bike, so keep a firm grip. In the gorge itself the road narrows and the cliffs close in.

Fuel is available in Andorra, about twenty kilometres away, and it is worth filling the tank there. Cafes in the villages open early, and a coffee and a slice of tortilla make a good start to the day.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. The summer sun is harsh, and the winter nights are cold. The walk to the shelter is a short but rough one, and the area is protected, so follow any signs and ask locally.
t.longhushan longhushan section@28.1,117.0:
Longhushan means Dragon and Tiger Mountain, and the name is only slightly more dramatic than the scenery. In northeastern Jiangxi, thirty-odd kilometres from Guixi, the Luxi river winds between red sandstone cliffs and pinnacles that look like animals, towers and, with a little imagination, a dragon and a tiger staring each other down. The rock is Danxia, a reddish landform that China has recognised as a world heritage group of sites, and it glows when the sun is low.

The mountain matters as much for what people did here as for how it looks. In the Han dynasty a Taoist teacher called Zhang Daoling is said to have settled here and founded the Celestial Masters, a school that became the root of the Zhengyi Taoist tradition. His descendants held the title for generations, living in a mansion in the village of Shangqing, and Longhushan stayed the most important centre of Taoism in southern China. In the cliffs above the river there are also ancient wooden coffins, set into high rock niches by people who lived here well over two thousand years ago. How they were lifted up is still debated.

The approach is on regional roads from Guixi and Yingtan, with the usual Chinese mix of lorries, scooters and the occasional farm cart. Surfaces are generally good, but expect heavy stretches of traffic near the park gates in holiday weeks. The best months are spring and autumn, when the humidity eases and the cliffs stand out against clear skies. In summer it is hot, damp and sometimes flooded after heavy rain on the Luxi.

Guixi is the nearest town of any size and has the fuel and the restaurants, so fill up there before heading to the mountain. Local cooking here leans on rice, freshwater fish and chilli. Bamboo rafts drift down the river with visitors, and it is a lovely way to see the cliffs if you have the time. As elsewhere in China, ask about licensing for foreign motorcyclists well in advance.
t.monterey@36.6,-121.9:
Monterey is a town with a layered past, and the best way to read it is to walk from the old adobe buildings of the first capital of Spanish and Mexican California to the shiny aquarium on the water's edge. Spanish explorers anchored in the bay in the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, and Monterey served as the capital under Spain, then Mexico, and briefly under the United States. Colton Hall, where California's first constitution was drafted in 1849, still stands in the middle of town.

For much of the twentieth century Monterey meant sardines. The fish were so plentiful that the waterfront street, Cannery Row, was lined with canneries, and John Steinbeck wrote about its workers, drifters and marine biologists. The sardines collapsed in the 1950s, from overfishing and changing ocean conditions, and the factories closed. Today the old cannery buildings hold restaurants and shops, and the Monterey Bay Aquarium, opened in 1984 in a former cannery, has turned the local underwater world into a world-famous attraction, with kelp forests and sea otters.

The ride along this stretch of the Pacific Coast Highway is a dream and a nuisance, depending on the day. Highway 1 hugs the coast, with cypress trees clinging to rocks and the sea glittering below, but traffic is heavy at weekends and fog can blanket the road in summer. Mornings are cool and the light improves around midday. The famous 17-Mile Drive loops through Pebble Beach, with a gate fee for vehicles, and Pacific Grove nearby is known for the monarch butterflies that cluster in the trees from about October to February. South of Monterey, the Big Sur coast begins, one of the great roads in America, subject to landslides and closures after winter storms.

Monterey and the neighbouring towns have plenty of fuel, lodging and food, though prices are high. Order clam chowder in a sourdough bowl, a local habit, and look out for sea lions barking on the breakwater. Check for road closures on Highway 1 before heading south.
t.town area porcelain production center@29:
Jingdezhen has been making porcelain for over a thousand years, and for most of that time it supplied emperors. The town lies on the Chang river in northern Jiangxi, and its name comes from the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, in the early eleventh century, when the court ordered porcelain from its kilns for the first time. From the Yuan dynasty on, the town made the blue-and-white wares that became world famous, and during the Ming and Qing the imperial kilns here produced porcelain for the court, while merchants shipped export wares to Europe and the Middle East.

The secret was local materials. Kaolin, the fine white clay that gives porcelain its strength and translucency, was mined from the hills around the village of Gaoling, and the word kaolin itself comes from the name Gaoling, travelling into European languages in the eighteenth century. With abundant pine wood for fuel and the river for transport, the town grew into a huge industrial centre, with kilns burning day and night, and in the nineteenth century a visitor described the glow from hundreds of kilns lighting the sky.

Today the old kiln sites and workshops give you a feel for that heritage, and the town still produces porcelain, with studios, markets and a thriving community of young ceramic artists. You can watch craftsmen throw, paint and glaze, and buy pieces at every price from tourist souvenirs to fine art. The surrounding countryside is green and hilly, with tea fields and forests.

Roads in this part of Jiangxi are usually good, with moderate traffic, and the ride across the hills is pleasant. Summers are hot and humid, and spring brings rain, so autumn is best. Jingdezhen has fuel stations, restaurants and hotels, and lies less than a kilometre from the coordinates. Pack your purchases carefully, since porcelain and panniers are an uneasy pair, and check the licensing rules for foreign motorcyclists in China before you plan.
t.mount wuyi@27.7,117.7:
Mount Wuyi is the home of some of the most famous teas in China, and the mountains that grow them are almost as remarkable as the leaves. Straddling the border between Fujian and Jiangxi provinces, the range is made of red sandstone and granite carved into steep cliffs, sharp peaks and deep gorges, with a winding river, the Nine-Bend Stream, flowing between them. The highest point, Huanggang Shan, is about 2,158 metres, the highest peak in south-east China. UNESCO listed the area in 1999 for both its nature and its culture.

Tea grows on the rocky ledges and in crevices, drawing minerals from the stone, and the resulting oolongs are known as rock teas, with a deep, roasted flavour. The most famous is Da Hong Pao, the Big Red Robe, whose original bushes grow on a cliff face and are protected as a national treasure, and the quality of the variety has made it one of the most expensive teas in the world. The region is also the birthplace of black tea, with Lapsang Souchong, the smoky variety, first made here several centuries ago. A visit to a tea farm and a tasting session are an essential part of any trip.

The area is also a cradle of Neo-Confucian thought. The philosopher Zhu Xi, who lived in the twelfth century, taught and wrote near the river, and his ideas shaped education and government across East Asia for centuries. Cliffs along the river hold ancient boat-shaped coffins placed in caves more than three thousand years ago, which show how long people have lived here.

Bamboo rafts drift down the Nine-Bend Stream, and the views are best from the water. The road network is good, with smooth tarmac, mountain bends and the green of bamboo forest. Be aware that China's rules on foreign motorcyclists are strict, so check the licensing situation before you plan to ride yourself. The town of Wuyishan, thirty kilometres away, has fuel, hotels and tea shops.

Spring, when the new leaves are picked, and autumn, when the air is clear, are the best seasons.
t.waypoint 3@35.4,-120.8:
Morro Rock is a volcanic plug, the hard core of a long-extinct volcano, and it rises out of the water at the mouth of Morro Bay like a great grey bell, about 175 metres high. It is the last of a chain of nine such peaks that run inland toward San Luis Obispo, the Nine Sisters, and its slopes are a protected nesting place for peregrine falcons, which means that climbing is forbidden. Rock and town share a name, and the waterfront is dominated by the three tall stacks of the old power station beside it.

Morro Bay is a working fishing town of about ten thousand people on California's Central Coast, and the Embarcadero along the water is lined with seafood restaurants, kayak rentals and gift shops. The estuary behind the sandspit is one of the best places on the coast to see birds, and sea otters float on their backs among the kelp. Fog comes in often, particularly in early summer, and the temperature can fall by ten degrees within an hour.

For riders, the town sits on Highway 1, the Pacific Coast Highway, at the southern entrance to one of the great motorcycle roads in the world. North of town, the road passes Cayucos, Cambria and San Simeon, home to Hearst Castle, and then runs along the Big Sur coast, with cliffs, headlands, redwood canyons and the Pacific stretching out below. The road is narrow and twisting, with sections of steep drop, and traffic can be heavy with tourists and campervans, especially in summer. Landslides and storms have closed parts of Big Sur for months at a time in recent years, so check Caltrans reports before setting out.

Fuel is easy in Morro Bay, with stations on the main road, and the town has plenty of cafés and hotels. Order clam chowder in a bread bowl or fresh fish tacos, and walk along the sand to the base of the rock.

Go in the early morning, before the traffic builds and the fog burns off, and stay clear of the coast road at dusk.
t.skyline boulevard ridge@37.5,-122.3:
Skyline Boulevard runs along the spine of the Santa Cruz Mountains, high above the cities of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its ridge has a character quite unlike the coast or the bay. The road, also known as State Route 35, follows the crest through redwood and Douglas fir forest, with the fog of the Pacific on one side and the sunny, hazy bay on the other. Climbing from Belmont, about four kilometres away, you leave the suburbs behind within minutes and find yourself in cool, shaded woodland that smells of damp bark and bay laurel.

Beneath the ridge lies the San Andreas Fault, which runs through the long valley of the Crystal Springs reservoirs, the lakes that supply much of San Francisco's water. Nearby Sweeney Ridge is where in 1769 the Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá and his party looked down and saw San Francisco Bay for the first time, which they had missed on their march north. Redwoods in the folds of the hills include some of the oldest in the region, and many of the big trees were logged in the nineteenth century to rebuild the city.

For motorcyclists, Skyline is a pilgrimage. The road has long, flowing curves, short climbs and descents, a good surface in most places and light traffic on weekdays. On sunny weekends it is busy with riders, and the crowds gather at the old roadhouse at the junction with Highway 84, a long-time biker stop. Cyclists share the road, so take care, and watch for deer, loose gravel and damp patches under the trees, where the sun rarely reaches. Fog can drop the temperature sharply and cut visibility in a minute.

Fuel is easy in Belmont, a city of twenty-seven thousand, and there is little on the ridge itself, so fill up before you climb. Cafés in Woodside and La Honda serve coffee and sandwiches, and the roadhouse does burgers and pie.

Ride it early on a weekday, when the light comes through the trees and the road is almost empty.
t.point reyes station@38.1,-122.8:
Point Reyes Station is a single street of low wooden buildings in a green valley north of San Francisco, and it has more good food per metre than most cities. It sits on the Pacific side of Marin County, at the southern end of Tomales Bay, beside Highway 1, with dairy farms and cattle ranches stretching away toward the hills. The town has a bakery that draws queues on weekend mornings, a famous creamery that makes cheese from local milk, an old-fashioned feed store and a bookshop, and the pace is slow and friendly.

The land beneath it is anything but calm. The San Andreas Fault runs right through, along the long, straight trough of Tomales Bay, and in the 1906 earthquake the land on the western side moved about six metres north in a few seconds. A short walk at the Earthquake Trail near the park headquarters shows a fence that was pulled apart by the shift. The Point Reyes National Seashore, a wild peninsula of grassland, cliffs and beaches, lies to the west, and it holds a lighthouse built in 1870 on a rocky cliff, where whales can be seen from December to April. Tule elk graze on the grassy headland at Tomales Point, and in autumn the bulls bellow.

For riders, the roads here are among the best in the Bay Area. Highway 1 twists north from Mount Tamalpais through Stinson Beach and along the edge of Bolinas Lagoon, and the back roads over the hills, with redwood groves, fog and tight bends, are a favourite for local riders. Surfaces vary, with some patches that are bumpy or damp, and the fog can roll in without warning, dropping the temperature by ten degrees. Weekends bring heavy traffic from the city, so a weekday is better. Oysters from the farms along Tomales Bay are a local speciality, and several places serve them fresh.

The village has a small fuel station, but check hours, and the nearest larger supply is back in the towns toward San Rafael. Late summer and autumn often bring the clearest weather, while spring is green and flower-filled. Plan on a slow lunch.
t.xidi@29.9,118.0:
Xidi is one of the loveliest villages in China, and it sits in a green basin in southern Anhui, forty kilometres or so from the Yellow Mountains. The houses are built in the Huizhou style, with white-plastered walls, grey tiled roofs and tall horse-head gables that stand up like steps against the sky, and carved wooden screens and brick doorways show the wealth of the merchants who built them. UNESCO lists Xidi together with nearby Hongcun as two villages that preserve the look of rural China in the Ming and Qing dynasties.

The wealth came from trade. Merchants from Huizhou were among the most successful in China, dealing in salt, tea, timber and ink, and they invested their profits in handsome homes back in their home villages, along with schools, ancestral halls and memorial arches. Xidi was largely the home of one family, the Hu, who claimed descent from a Tang dynasty prince, and the village shows how a clan organised itself around ancestry and learning. Streams run through the lanes in stone channels, which provided water for the houses and gave a fire safety system, and in some courtyards a small square of sky is the only roof.

For a rider, southern Anhui is a green and rolling region of bamboo, tea terraces and misty hills. The road up toward the Yellow Mountains twists through forest and past small villages, and in the early morning cloud pools in the valleys, so that the ridges look like islands. The roads are generally good, with tight bends, steep sections and plenty of trucks, and rain is frequent, particularly in early summer. Mist and wet leaves make for slippery surfaces. Tea picking in spring turns the slopes into patterns of green, and the famous Huangshan Maofeng tea comes from this area.

Huangshan city lies thirty-eight kilometres away with services, fuel and hotels, and the village has simple guesthouses where you can eat home cooking, including bamboo shoots, stinky tofu and tea-smoked dishes. Visit early or late, because tour groups crowd the lanes at midday. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences and permits, so check before you plan. Autumn is the best season, with crisp air and golden light, and spring brings rain and blossom.
t.potes@43.2,-4.6:
Potes is the capital of Liébana, a hidden-away valley in Cantabria that is walled in by the Picos de Europa on three sides and so mild and sheltered that it grows fruit and grapes at the foot of mountains that still carry snow in June. The town sits where the rivers Deva and Quiviesca meet, under a square medieval tower, the Torre del Infantado, with stone bridges, arcaded houses and narrow streets climbing away from the water. It has only a little over a thousand residents, which is why everybody on the street seems to know everybody else.

The valley has more history than its size would suggest. Just outside town is the monastery of Santo Toribio de Liébana, said to hold the largest surviving fragment of the True Cross. It makes the valley one of the few places in the world that celebrates a Holy Year, and pilgrims arrive on the Camino Lebaniego from the coast. In the eighth century a monk of Liébana, Beatus, wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse whose lavishly painted copies became some of the great treasures of Spanish medieval art. The cooking is a reward for the effort of getting here: cocido lebaniego, a stew of chickpeas, cabbage and pork, hard to beat in cold weather, along with the local cheeses and the clear, strong orujo, a grape spirit that you will be offered after a meal.

The riding is exceptional but not easy. Coming from the north, the road squeezes through the Desfiladero de la Hermida, a gorge some twenty kilometres long, where limestone walls rise sheer from the river and the road clings to the bank with barely any shoulder. Rockfall is a real risk after rain, and the tunnels and narrow sections need care. South and west, mountain roads climb to passes toward the meseta of Castilla. The best excursion from Potes is the road up to Fuente Dé, which ends beneath a great horseshoe of cliffs, and the cable car there lifts you about eight hundred metres in minutes to the high plateau.

Potes has fuel, supermarkets, and many restaurants, but beyond the valley services are sparse, with Llanes on the coast the nearest larger town. The weather is changeable, with mist and sudden rain, even in summer. Early autumn gives the kindest light, with golden chestnut woods, while market day brings the local farmers down in force.
t.church of san nicolas@40.7,-4.7:
San Nicolás is one of those small Romanesque-era parish churches that Ávila scatters around the walled city like punctuation. It is easy to walk past, and easy to love once you slow down: a granite building with plain walls, a modest tower and the kind of thick doorway that has been touched by centuries of hands. The interest here is not in grand art but in how closely the town is packed with faith. Within a few minutes' walk of each other are churches, convents, a cathedral that doubles as part of the wall and houses dedicated to a woman who reformed a religious order.

Ávila sits high, at around 1,130 metres, on a bare plateau under the Sierra de Gredos, which makes it the highest provincial capital in Spain. That altitude shapes everything. Winters are cold, with frost and the occasional dusting of snow; summer evenings are cool even after hot days, and the light on the granite is thin and clean. Bikers who come in summer find it a relief after the baking plains of the Meseta, though a wind-proof layer is a good idea even in July.

For a stop, the practical side is straightforward. The town has nearly fifty-seven thousand people, so fuel and food are plentiful, and the best place to leave a bike is outside the walls, near one of the gates, then walk in. Parking inside the old town is tight and the streets are cobbled. Eat the local beef, the chuletón de Ávila, a thick grilled cut, and finish with yemas, sweet egg-yolk confections named for Santa Teresa.

The ride that starts from here runs east toward Alcalá de Henares, the old university town of Cervantes, and that shift from a mountain town of stone to a brick and plaster university city makes a good day. Leave early, because the plateau roads are open and fast and the sun comes up with little to block it.
t.recinto intramuros@40.1,-2.1:
Cuenca is a city that looks as though it grew out of a gorge by accident, and it did, more or less. The old town sits on a narrow ridge between two river valleys, the Huécar and the Júcar, and the medieval houses lean over the drop. The walled part, the recinto, is the upper town, a compact knot of steep lanes around the Plaza Mayor, with a cathedral whose Gothic design carries Anglo-Norman echoes thanks to the English-born wife of the king who reconquered the town in 1177.

Walking inside the walls means climbing, and the cobbles are rough, so this is not a place to ride in. Leave the bike in the lower town and use your feet. The reward is views: from the upper lanes you look across the Huécar gorge toward the hanging houses, and the light turns the limestone ochre in the evening. The streets are quiet at night once the day-trippers from Madrid have gone home, and a late stroll is one of the best things to do.

The roads around Cuenca are another matter, and good ones. The Serranía de Cuenca to the north-east is a high, forested limestone country, with pine woods, rock towers and the headwaters of both the Júcar and the Tagus, and the roads that wind through it are quiet and satisfying. A ride that begins here, heading out to a rock shelter on the way to Albarracín country, will pass through that kind of terrain. Check the weather, as at nearly a thousand metres of altitude you can have frost into May.

Cuenca has about fifty-six thousand people, so you will find fuel, supermarkets and many bars with no trouble. Ask for morteruelo, a rich game and liver paté served warm, or ajoarriero, a salt cod and garlic stew, and finish with resolí, the sweet local liqueur flavoured with coffee and spices. A sensible evening starts with a long walk and ends with a long dinner.
t.historic walled town of cuenca@40.1,-2.1:
The postcard view of Cuenca is the Casas Colgadas, the hanging houses, wooden balconies thrust out from the rim of the Huécar gorge, one of which houses a museum of Spanish abstract art. The less photographed truth is that the old town is really an exercise in vertical living. Every building here exists because someone found a way to build on a ledge too small for it, and the result, recognised by UNESCO in 1996, is a medieval city that looks balanced on a blade.

You get the best view from the opposite side, by climbing to the footbridge of San Pablo, a metal span over the gorge which replaced an older stone one, and looking back as the late afternoon sun lights up the cliffs. For riders, the little road beside the Huécar and the loop around the Júcar are pleasant, but the real roads start outside the town, where the plateau opens into a country of juniper, pine and pale rock.

North and east of the city lies the Ciudad Encantada, a natural labyrinth of limestone towers sculpted by wind and water, and beyond it the Serranía, whose roads wind across high ground at over a thousand metres. Mornings can be cold and wet with mist in the gorges, and summer afternoons turn hot and dry, so the best months are May, June and September. Winter brings ice, and some mountain sections are slow when snow has fallen.

Cuenca itself is a working city with fuel on the way in and out, and with food that suits cold weather: stews, roast lamb and gamey flavours that have not changed much in centuries. Be wary of cobbles and tight turns inside the old quarter, and note that some streets are closed to cars at certain times. If you can only manage one thing here, make it the walk across the San Pablo bridge at dusk, with the lights coming on in the houses opposite and swifts screaming overhead in summer.
t.church of san martin@40.7,-4.7:
Ávila has a way of making you feel as though the walls are the only thing holding the past in place, but San Martín reminds you that the neighbourhoods around the churches were once lively parishes of their own. The city had many such parishes in the Middle Ages, each with its own church, its own priest and its own sense of rivalry with the next. Today they mostly sit quietly, built of the same grey-gold granite as the walls, and a walk from one to the next shows how the town's life was once organised.

From here the ride heads north-east toward the beech forests of Ayllón, a long journey across the plateau and over the Sierra de Guadarrama before the land drops toward Segovia and the Ayllón mountains. It is a day of contrasts. Ávila's plateau is open and treeless, with wind that can shove you sideways on exposed stretches, and the beech woods of Montejo and Ayllón are a very different world, dim, mossy and gold in October. That is the best season, when the leaves turn and the fog sits in the hollows.

On the road, expect long, fast stretches and a handful of tighter climbs where the highway crosses the sierra. In winter the passes can ice up, and snow occasionally closes the higher roads, so look at the forecast before you set off. Early starts are rewarded because the Meseta light is flat and bright by midday.

You have all you need in Ávila itself, since it has about fifty-seven thousand people, plenty of fuel and a surprising number of good bakeries. A traditional start to the day is a coffee and a few yemas, which are sweet enough to see you across the plateau. Leave the bike outside the old walls, wander in on foot for a little while, and find the church at the point where the lanes narrow.
t.abrigo del arquero de los callejones cer:
Near Albarracín, the land turns red. The Pinares de Rodeno, a pine forest growing on russet sandstone, stretches along the road below the walled town, and the rocks are so full of paintings that the whole area is a kind of open gallery. The archer shelter is one of many painted overhangs, and the name, Abrigo del Arquero, refers to a small red figure drawing a bow. The art belongs to the Levantine tradition, with slim, active human figures hunting and gathering, and it is the reason this area is protected.

Riding here is a gentle pleasure. The roads around Albarracín are narrow and quiet, climbing through pine woods and then opening onto bare plateau, with the Sierra de Albarracín rising to the west. The headwaters of the Tagus, the Turia and the Júcar all rise in this region, and the countryside has a wild, high character, with juniper, gorse and skylarks. Surfaces are generally fair, and traffic is light except on summer weekends near the town.

Albarracín itself is built of the same rose-coloured stone, with walls climbing a ridge above the Guadalaviar river and a skyline of towers. It is small, with about a thousand people, so fuel is limited; plan ahead, and consider filling up in Teruel, the provincial capital to the east. In town you can find simple restaurants serving roast lamb, ham and local cheeses, and the cold in winter is notable, with real snow possible.

The rock shelters are often marked on small tracks, and some require a short walk. Respect the fencing, because the paintings are fragile and the red pigment is easily damaged. Go on a mild day in late spring or autumn, when the light on the sandstone is warm and the pines smell of resin. Look closely and the whole forest reveals other figures.
t.church of san andres@40.7,-4.7:
San Andrés is among the oldest Romanesque churches in Ávila, and one of the first you meet if you come in from the north side of the walls. It stands near the great basilica of San Vicente, so that a single short walk gives you two good examples of how Ávila's builders handled granite, with thick walls, round arches and a modest scale that seems right for a place so exposed to wind. You can feel the age of it in the stonework without needing any dates.

What I like about this church is its place in the day. Ávila rewards slow wandering, and San Andrés is the sort of building you step into for five quiet minutes in the middle of a longer walk. After the noise of the plateau road, with trucks and wind, it offers cool air and old stone.

The ride that begins here heads east to Alcalá de Henares, the university city east of Madrid, where Cervantes was born. That means the highway across the plateau, then through the hills around Guadarrama, where you can use the mountain roads rather than the motorway if you want something more fun. There are fast open sweeps with views of the Gredos range behind you, and then a dive toward the capital's outskirts, where traffic builds and the day becomes a different one.

Ávila has all the services you need: fuel stations on the main roads, supermarkets, bakeries and bars. Because of the altitude, the climate is harsh in winter, with sharp frosts, and even in June the first hour of the morning can be chilly. Dress in layers and expect a warm afternoon. Park outside the walls, and bring change for the car park meter, which tends to be less forgiving than the weather. If the day turns grey and the wind picks up, as it often does, take it as local colour and keep walking.
t.barrio tiradores@40.1,-2.1:
Tiradores is one of Cuenca's old quarters, a slice of the hillside town where the steep lanes climb between tall, narrow houses and the sound is mostly footsteps and swifts. It is not a sight in the sense of a single monument. It is a neighbourhood, and that is why it is worth the effort: Cuenca's famous gorge-edge silhouette is made of ordinary houses like these, stuck onto the rock with extraordinary stubbornness, and the people who live here still carry their shopping up the hill.

The town as a whole was made a World Heritage Site in 1996, and the old centre has a medieval, almost Moorish density, with a few remaining fragments of the walls. Come on foot and be ready to climb. The reward is views over the Huécar gorge and across to the green hillsides beyond, and a chance to see the town without the crowds that pack the main square.

Riding out of Cuenca in any direction is a pleasure. West and south the land opens into the plains of La Mancha, with long straight roads and distant windmills, but north and east the Serranía de Cuenca offers forest, rock and curves. Spring and early summer are the best time, with flowers and green slopes; autumn brings mist and gold, and winter can bring frost, so check the tarmac before enjoying the corners.

Fuel is not a concern, since Cuenca has fifty-six thousand people and plenty of petrol stations on the approach roads. Food is hearty: lamb, game and cheeses, with the sweet pastry called alajú, made with honey and almonds, a good thing to carry in a tank bag for later. Be careful with the one-way system near the old town, which can trap the unwary, and park in the lower town where it is flatter.
t.church of san pedro@40.7,-4.7:
San Pedro stands outside the walls, on the large open square beside the Puerta del Alcázar, and that position is its character. It is a big, plain Romanesque church with a fine rose window, and the square in front is where Ávila likes to meet, with terraces, a statue of Santa Teresa nearby and the wall looming just across the way. If you want a spot for a coffee in the sun with a view of the best section of the ramparts, this is it.

The walls themselves are among the best-preserved medieval fortifications in Europe. They were begun in the late eleventh century, run for about two and a half kilometres, and carry some eighty-eight towers and nine gates. You can walk along part of the top, and the view over the city and the plateau is a good way to understand why Ávila was built here: the site is high, hard to attack and open to every wind.

Ávila lies on the road from Madrid toward Salamanca and the west, so it gets plenty of traffic, but the old town is calm. If you are riding in, use the main avenues and park near the square, which usually has room. The roads east toward Alcalá cross the sierra and the plateau, with fast sections and a few pretty climbs in the hills where the road crests and the view opens.

Fuel is easy, since this is a provincial capital with about fifty-seven thousand people. Try a pastry or yemas at one of the old shops, and a hearty plate at lunch: judías del Barco de Ávila, big white beans with chorizo, are a regional favourite, especially in cold weather. In winter, frost on the stone steps is real, and in August the nights stay cool, so you can sleep with the window open.
t.old town of avila with its extra muros c:
There is a kind of satisfaction in a city that is exactly what its postcards say, and Ávila is one. The walls are intact, golden at sunset, and the cathedral is built right into them, its apse forming one of the fortress towers, which gives the whole thing the look of a church that has chosen to defend itself. The old town and its churches outside the walls, the extra muros, were recognised by UNESCO in 1985, and most of what makes it special can be seen in a morning.

That morning should include the walk on top of the wall, which is open for much of the length of the eastern side, and a loop around the outside, where the stones seem to change colour with the light. Then add the churches beyond the walls, including the great Romanesque basilica of San Vicente, which holds the tomb of the martyrs it is named for, and the convent where Teresa of Ávila founded the first of her reformed Carmelite houses in 1562.

The surrounding country is just as interesting for a rider. To the south the Sierra de Gredos rises, with high passes and hairpins; to the north and west, the plateau offers long, fast roads through cereal fields, oak and granite boulders. The climate is harsh and dry, with cold winters and hot afternoons in summer, so layering is useful. Spring brings green fields and poppies, while autumn has the clearest air.

Town services are good, with fuel on the ring road and a wide choice of eating places, though many of the good ones inside the walls are small. Eat the local beef and finish with yemas or a cup of hot chocolate. Wind is a constant companion on the plateau, so a good visor and a bit of patience are better than speed.
t.abrigo de las cabras blancas@40.2,-1.3:
Teruel is one of the emptiest provinces in Europe, and it is one of the best for riders who like to be alone. Around the headwaters of the Turia the land is high, dry and broken into long ridges, with pine forests, red clay and wide sky. The white goats of the shelter's name belong to a world of shepherding and rock painting, as the paintings here are in the Levantine style, with figures of animals in red pigment, and this is one of many shelters in the region.

Getting here means small roads, with little traffic and long views. The villages are tiny: Villel and Villastar have a few hundred inhabitants each, and the nearest real town is Teruel, with its Mudéjar towers decorated in green and white ceramic, a short way to the east. That is where to fill the tank and buy food. The land between is Celtiberian country, and before the Romans arrived it was the heartland of a people who left stone forts on many of the hilltops.

Weather matters more than you expect. The plateau is about a thousand metres above the sea, so winter is long, frosty and sometimes snowy, and the wind can be fierce. In summer the middle of the day is hot and dry, and the best hours are early morning and evening, when the light turns the earth pink. Spring brings flowers, and autumn brings stubble fields and clear air.

Teruel's local specialities include cured ham, protected by its own designation, and a simple dish of migas. Take water, because the villages may be shut, and bring a spare layer. The reward for the effort is a landscape that feels untouched, and a chance to stand in a shelter and look out on the same valley that the painters saw.
t.convent of san jose@40.7,-4.7:
In 1562 a Carmelite nun named Teresa de Cepeda opened a small convent in Ávila, dedicated to St Joseph, with a handful of women and a very strict way of life. It was the first house of what became the Discalced Carmelites, and it began a reform that would spread across Spain and well beyond. Teresa is now a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and the town she came from has never quite stopped talking about her, but her writing, humane, funny and extremely practical, is the better way to know her.

The convent is not far from the walls, and is still home to a community of nuns. It is a modest building, brick and stone, in a quiet street, and the atmosphere around it is one of calm rather than spectacle. Visitors can see a chapel and a small museum; check the opening hours, because they vary and the nuns keep their own timetable. The best approach is to arrive without expectations and leave the helmet outside.

The riding from Ávila rewards early starts. The ride that begins here heads north-east toward the beech forests of Ayllón, crossing the Guadarrama. Distances are not large, but the plateau road is exposed, and the wind can be strong. In winter, there may be ice on the passes, and in summer, the heat gathers on the plain by midday. Be prepared for large temperature swings between morning and afternoon.

Ávila has everything for a stop: fuel, supermarkets and many bars. For something to take with you, buy yemas from one of the pastry shops. They were originally made by convents, using the surplus yolks left after egg whites were used for starching and clarifying, and they are very sweet. Then walk to the walls, and follow them for a while as the evening light comes up along the stone.
t.basilica of san vicente@40.7,-4.7:
San Vicente is one of the grandest Romanesque churches in Spain, and it sits just outside the walls of Ávila, near the Puerta de San Vicente, with a broad porch and a pair of towers that never quite match. It is named for Vicente and his sisters Sabina and Cristeta, who according to tradition were martyred here in the early fourth century, and their tomb, an elaborate Gothic canopy, is inside the church. The carvings on the west door are among the finest in Castile.

The church is built of the same golden granite as the walls, and in the late afternoon it seems to hold the sun like a stove. t.pfeiffer coast@36.2,-121.8:

t.perth@-32.0,115.9:
Perth is the most isolated big city on Earth, and you can feel it in the way people talk about the rest of Australia as a different country. The place has always lived by its own rules and its own sunshine, which is claimed to be the most of any Australian capital. t.jianglangshan@28.5,118.6:
Jianglangshan looks as though somebody took a giant knife to a block of red sandstone and left three slices standing. The Three Sisters, tall, narrow slabs of rock rising well over three hundred metres above the valley, are the icon of the site, and the cliffs behind them, steep and layered in warm reds and browns, are typical of the landform called Danxia. The word means rosy clouds, and the landscape is a kind of red-bed desert eroded by wind and rain into peaks, gorges and walls. UNESCO listed a group of Danxia sites in south China in 2010, and Jianglangshan, in Zhejiang, is one of the six.

t.mount sanqingshan national park@28.9,118:
Sanqingshan is a mountain where granite has been carved into figures. Tall pillars and spires of grey rock rise out of a sea of cloud, shaped by wind and water into forms that Chinese visitors have named for centuries: the Goddess, a pillar that looks like a woman with a tall coiffure, the Python, a slender tower that leans out over the valley. Fuel and meals are available in the towns near the park, and the local cooking uses bamboo shoots, mountain vegetables and river fish. t.marin headlands and point reyes high poi:
Here the map puts you in the Santa Cruz Mountains, near the redwood village of La Honda. t.napa silverado trail backroads photo pul:

t.yosemite tioga overnight photo pull off@:
American Canyon is a town of twenty thousand people at the southern end of the Napa Valley, where the vineyards give out and the land flattens toward San Pablo Bay. It is a commuter place of big-box shops, tract houses and wide roads, and the first thing most visitors see of wine country as they drive north from the Bay Area. t.skyline boulevard and alice s photo pull:
