Agoston Haraszthy, a Hungarian émigré, planted the Buena Vista vineyard here in the 1850s and is often called the father of California wine. Further up, Jack London bought a ranch at Glen Ellen in 1905, and his Beauty Ranch is now a state park, with his stone house ruins and his grave on a wooded knoll.

The riding is pleasant rather than thrilling. Highway 12 runs the length of the valley, with vineyards on either side and the hills glowing gold in summer, and side roads such as Bennett Valley Road and Sonoma Mountain Road wind up into the oaks, narrow, rough and beautiful. Traffic on Highway 12 is heavy at weekends and during harvest, and cyclists share the quieter lanes. The morning light, the smell of crushed grapes in autumn and the stillness of the hills make it a delight.

Fuel and food are in Sonoma and Santa Rosa, and the plaza has plenty of cafés, bakeries and a picnic-friendly lawn. Spring is green and full of wildflowers, summer is hot and dry, and autumn brings the vintage and bright yellow vine leaves. Winter is wet but quiet. Pick a weekday if you can, and leave time to wander the plaza, where an old mission building and a few adobe walls give a hint of the valley's past.
A long, narrow arm of the Pacific called Tomales Bay lies along the San Andreas Fault, and the pin falls near its head, close to the village of Inverness and the ranch-and-oyster country of West Marin. Here the fault is not an abstraction but a visible trench: Highway 1 runs along it, and in the 1906 earthquake, the land on the west side lurched about six metres north-west, snapping fences and moving roads. A short trail at Point Reyes shows the offset today.

The peninsula behind the bay, the Point Reyes National Seashore, is a place of fog, wind and open pasture, where tule elk graze on the headland and dairy cattle on the lower slopes. Inverness sits under a ridge of Bishop pine, a funny little village of shingled cottages, a store and a few eateries, looking out over the bay. Oyster farms line the eastern shore, and the briny, fresh oysters, grilled or raw, are a local rite. Point Reyes Station, a few miles south, has a cheese shop, a bakery and a bookshop, and a handful of places for a proper lunch.

The riding here is quiet and beautiful, though slow. Highway 1 curves along the bay, a two-lane road with tight bends and low speed limits, and Sir Francis Drake Boulevard runs west toward the lighthouse, rising and falling over grassy hills. The surface is patched and sometimes rough, cattle wander in some places, and cyclists are everywhere on weekends. Fog is a regular presence, especially in summer, and makes the tarmac slick.

Fuel is the thing to plan: there is little in the villages, and the nearest big towns are Petaluma and San Rafael, so fill up before you come. Weather is cool all year, with wind and fog, and winter brings heavy rain and the occasional storm. Spring and autumn offer the clearest light. For wildlife, the bay is a stop for migrating shorebirds, harbour seals pup on the shore in spring, and elephant seals gather on the beaches in winter. Plan on a long, slow lunch.
t.mount hamilton and mines road high point:
Stanford University occupies a vast, flat campus of sandstone arcades and red-tile roofs at the southern end of the Peninsula, and the pin falls near its edge, among the oaks and eucalyptus of the neighbouring foothills. The university was founded in 1885 by Leland Stanford, a railroad magnate and former governor, and his wife Jane, as a memorial to their only son, who died of typhoid as a teenager. Its tall Hoover Tower, completed in 1941, rises over the campus, and a carillon plays from it. The town of Palo Alto next door, with nearly sixty thousand people, was the cradle of Silicon Valley, and the garage on Addison Avenue where Hewlett and Packard began is marked as a landmark.

From here the land rises quickly into the Santa Cruz Mountains, and several of the finest roads in the Bay Area start within a few kilometres. Page Mill Road climbs steadily from the edge of Palo Alto, with long curves through oak woodland and then redwoods, to meet Skyline Boulevard at the ridge top. Alpine Road, narrower and rougher, winds through the Portola Valley. Both have been favourites of local cyclists and riders for generations, and weekend mornings can be crowded with both.

The Stanford Dish, a giant radio telescope in the hills behind the campus, is a landmark for walkers and runners, and the grassy slopes give wide views over the Bay. The area is dry in summer, with golden grass and dusty oaks, and fog from the coast often drifts over the ridge, cooling the evenings. Rain turns the hills green from late autumn, and the creeks run briefly.

Practicalities are easy, with fuel, coffee and every sort of food nearby in Palo Alto, from taquerias to sushi, though prices are high. Bicycles are everywhere, and drivers are used to them, but the roads are narrow and the shoulders are limited. Climb early, when the air is cool, and enjoy the scent of bay laurel. For a coffee stop at the top, the old roadhouses on Skyline have long been favourites with motorcyclists. Descend carefully, since gravel and leaves collect in the bends.
t.mount hamilton and mines road scenic roa:
East Palo Alto sits on the flat edge of San Francisco Bay, a town of about thirty thousand people with a distinctive history and a rough reputation that it has been quietly shedding for years. It was incorporated only in 1983, after a long history of neglect, and its residents, once largely Black and now increasingly Latino and Pacific Islander, have fought for services and recognition. The pin falls on its eastern fringe, beside the salt marshes and the approach to the Dumbarton Bridge, which carries Highway 84 across the bay to Fremont.

The bridge was first built in 1927 as a toll crossing and replaced by the current span in 1982, a long, low concrete causeway stretching across the shallow water, which is open to motorcycles for a toll. The view from the middle, with salt ponds on both sides, pelicans and egrets overhead and the low hills of the East Bay ahead, is rewarding, though the bridge is exposed to wind and often busy with commuters. A parallel old railway bridge stands rusting beside it.

Nearby, the baylands are an important wildlife refuge. The Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge protects thousands of acres of salt pond and mudflat on the south bay, with large flocks of shorebirds in winter and hundreds of thousands during migration. The Bay Trail runs along the dikes, and the brightly coloured salt ponds, red and green from algae and brine shrimp, make a vivid sight from the air. The marsh smells of mud and salt, and the air has a mineral tang.

For the rider, the roads are urban and flat, with University Avenue and Bayfront Expressway carrying heavy traffic. Fuel is plentiful on the main streets, and there are good taquerias and bakeries in the neighbourhood. Wind blows strongly in the afternoon, so ride the bridge early. Fog can drift in at night. The best light comes in the late afternoon, when the sun slants over the salt ponds and the water glows. Use this as a simple link between the Peninsula and the East Bay, and keep an eye on the toll lanes.
t.half moon bay@37.5,-122.4:
Half Moon Bay is where the Peninsula's mountains finally meet the Pacific. The town sits on a wide coastal plain, backed by the green flank of the Santa Cruz Mountains and fronted by a long crescent of sand, and it feels like a different state from the busy bay side only twenty minutes away over Highway 92. Fog arrives most summer afternoons, so mornings are your best bet for sun.

Riders come through on Highway 1 and use the town as a pause on the coast run. The road here is wide and easy, with long views over fields of artichokes, Brussels sprouts and pumpkins, and it grows tighter and more dramatic south toward Pescadero and Santa Cruz. Highway 92 over the mountains is the classic way in from the east, a tight, tree-lined climb with a few steep switchbacks, and it is worth a ride in either direction. Watch for cyclists, who flock to these roads at weekends, and for the cold, wet patches under the redwoods that never quite dry out.

Half Moon Bay is also a place with some history. It began as a Spanish-era farming spot, and later became known as Spanishtown, and during Prohibition its isolated beaches were used by rum-runners who landed their cargo at night. Today, its biggest annual event is the Art and Pumpkin Festival in October, when the whole coast road clogs with visitors. A few kilometres north, at Pillar Point, huge winter swells break far offshore at a place surfers call Mavericks, and in big storms they are a spectacle even from the cliff.

For practical things, the town has more than twelve thousand people, which means fuel, groceries, bike shops and cafes on the main street are all easy. A bowl of clam chowder and a view of the harbour at Pillar Point is a classic and reliable lunch. Weekend traffic on the coast road can be slow, with long tailbacks heading back over Highway 92 on Sunday afternoons, so plan around it.
t.skyline boulevard and alice s high point:
Newark, California, is not the one in New Jersey, and the difference shows: this is a flat, tidy, quietly prosperous town of about forty-five thousand people on the southeastern shore of San Francisco Bay, where the suburbs run out into salt marsh. The pin falls in the shallows just west of town, near the eastern end of the Dumbarton Bridge, where the road runs out over the water toward the Peninsula. The bay shore here is a patchwork of crystallisation ponds, sloughs and tidal flats.

The ponds are the thing to notice. For more than a century, the south bay has been used to evaporate seawater for salt, and the ponds, tinted red, pink and green by algae and brine shrimp, form a surreal palette from the air. Much of that land is now a national wildlife refuge, named for the congressman Don Edwards, whose headquarters are close by in Fremont. The refuge protects the endangered salt marsh harvest mouse and the Ridgway's rail, and in winter hundreds of thousands of shorebirds and ducks stop here. A trail along the dikes offers close views of avocets, stilts and egrets.

For a rider, the interest lies a little way inland. Fremont, just south of Newark, has the old Mission San José, founded in 1797, and from it Mission Boulevard climbs through the hills past oak and chaparral. Niles Canyon Road, Highway 84, follows a creek east from Fremont through a shaded gorge, a winding, narrow route beside an old railway line, popular with local riders though busy. Mission Peak towers behind, and the East Bay hills lie beyond.

Fuel is easy along the main streets, and the surrounding towns have a rich variety of food, with fine Afghan, Indian and Chinese restaurants. Wind is strong on the bridge in the afternoon, and the bridge itself is exposed. Summer mornings are foggy, and the marsh smells of mud. Winter brings green hills and flocks of birds. Come early, enjoy the quiet over the marsh, and then climb into the hills where the real riding is.
t.skyline boulevard and alice s scenic roa:
Castro Valley sits on the east side of the first range of hills behind Oakland, a large suburban community of about sixty thousand people with a long main boulevard of shops and restaurants. It is a place most people drive through on the way to somewhere else, but its location is useful: the green folds of the East Bay hills begin at its edge, and some of the best narrow roads in the region start nearby. The pin falls on the western side, among the oak-covered ridges.

Lake Chabot, a reservoir created in the 1870s to supply water to Oakland, is the town's best-known feature, a long, winding lake in a wooded valley, with a regional park offering hiking trails, fishing and boating. Beyond it, Anthony Chabot Regional Park rises into the hills with eucalyptus groves and grassy ridges, and from the top there are views over the Bay. The Hayward Fault runs along the foot of the hills, and the geological tilt of the land is part of what makes the ridgelines so steep and sudden.

For riders, there are fine back roads here. Redwood Road climbs from Castro Valley up through the hills, a narrow, curving lane through shaded woodland, to reach Skyline Boulevard, which runs along the ridge toward Oakland. Crow Canyon Road and Palomares Road wind through quiet valleys of horse ranches and old farms. The surface is mixed, with patches and bumps, and the corners are often blind, with cyclists and joggers sharing the way. Deer and wild turkeys are common.

Fuel and food are easy along Castro Valley Boulevard, with a good selection of Mexican, Chinese and Vietnamese restaurants. Weekday mornings are crowded with commuters heading for the freeway, so wait until after nine or go on a weekend. Fog often creeps over the ridge in summer, and the morning air can be cold. In autumn, the hills turn gold and the light is clear. The redwood groves in Redwood Regional Park, a short ride north, are worth a stop on a hot day for their cool shade.
t.riano@43.0,-5.0:
Riaño is a town that was moved. In the 1980s the Spanish government built a large dam on the Esla river, and when the reservoir filled in 1987, it drowned the old town, along with eight other villages in the valley, in the face of years of protest from the people who lived there. The residents were resettled in a new town built on the shore, with modern streets and a church rebuilt on higher ground, and the old stone houses disappeared beneath the water. In dry years, the water drops and the shapes of walls reappear. About five hundred people live in the new town today.

The setting is superb. The reservoir lies in a high valley on the southern side of the Cantabrian Mountains, with the limestone peaks of the Picos de Europa rising to the north and the rounded hills of the Mampodre range to the south. The mountains here are a refuge for wildlife, including brown bears, wolves, chamois and capercaillie, and the forests of oak, beech and holly are rich. The area is known for its cheeses, including the blue cheese of Valdeón, produced in the high valleys nearby, and for hearty mountain cooking, with beans, chorizo and roasted lamb.

For a rider, Riaño is a fine crossroads. The road north climbs to the Puerto del Pontón, over a thousand metres, then descends through the dramatic Desfiladero de los Beyos, a narrow gorge, toward Asturias, a magnificent mountain ride with tight bends and rock walls close to the road. The Puerto de San Glorio, to the northwest, crosses to Cantabria and Potes, with long views of the Picos. Surfaces are generally good, but fog, rain and snow are common, and passes can close in winter. Livestock sometimes stand in the road, so go carefully.

Fuel is the thing to remember. The nearest large town is Guardo, about twenty-four kilometres to the south, and stations in the mountains are scarce, so fill the tank beforehand. Cafés and restaurants in Riaño serve a good menu del día, and the lakeshore is a pleasant place to rest. The best months are May to October, with autumn colours especially beautiful. Carry warm layers, as even summer nights are cold.
t.leggett@39.9,-123.7:
Leggett is where Highway 1 gives up. After hundreds of miles of salt air, fog banks and cliffs that fall straight into the Pacific, the road swings inland through the redwoods of Mendocino County and simply ends at a junction with Highway 101, in a clearing among enormous trees. The village is tiny, a scatter of buildings along the Eel River's south fork, and the nearest towns of any size, Laytonville and Redway, are each almost thirty kilometres away. That tells you most of what you need to know about how empty this corner of California is.

The last stretch into Leggett is the part many riders remember best, and it is not the coast at all. Once Highway 1 leaves the shoreline near Rockport it climbs and twists up a narrow, shaded canyon, tight bends one after another with redwood trunks close enough to touch, patchy asphalt, and a sun that flickers through the canopy so that you keep misjudging the surface. Speeds stay low, and they should. After the long ocean run it feels like entering a different country, cooler, darker and smelling of damp bark and bay laurel.

Leggett itself is a logging story. These hills were cut hard for timber through much of the twentieth century, and the area still lives partly on the memory of it and partly on tourists who stop for the roadside curiosities, among them a drive-through tree that cars can squeeze through for a small fee. It is kitschy, and I found it hard not to enjoy. Behind the novelty are real old-growth groves, some of the tallest living things on earth, and a few minutes walking among them does more for a tired rider than another coffee.

For practical matters, remember that services thin out fast up here. Fuel and a snack are the sensible things to sort out in the village or in the small towns along Highway 101 rather than counting on anything after dark, and if the tank is low, treat the long empty miles on Highway 1 behind you as a lesson learned. Mobile coverage is patchy in the canyon.

If you can choose your day, aim for late morning when the fog has lifted off the coast and the canyon floor has warmed a little. Summer afternoons can be hot inland, while winter brings rain, the odd fallen branch across the road, and wet leaves that make the tight bends slippery. From Leggett the 101 runs north into the heart of the redwood country or south toward Willits and the wine valleys, so you finish here with the choice of two very different ways home.
t.ragged point@35.8,-121.3:
Ragged Point is the last act of the southern approach to Big Sur, or the first, depending on which way you are going. The mountains of the Santa Lucia range come down to meet the Pacific here in a line of steep, grassy cliffs, and Highway 1 follows them in a ribbon cut into the slope, with a long, long drop on one side and rock on the other. The village itself, a cliff-top cluster of an inn, restaurant and viewpoint, serves as a gateway marking the end of the open coastal flats near San Simeon.

The riding on both sides is superb. North of the point the road starts its serious climbing and twisting, dipping into canyons and rising to headlands, with wide ocean views, bridges across creeks, and tight turns that need real attention because a wide-turning camper or a stopped tourist taking photos can appear around any bend. To the south the highway eases and runs along open country toward San Simeon, with ranch land and cattle on the hills. The coastline here is wild and has few buildings, which is part of its character.

A little way south, the elephant seal colony at Piedras Blancas is a surprise even for people who know about it. Thousands of the huge animals haul out on the beach to moult and breed, mostly in winter and spring, and you can watch them from a boardwalk, bellowing, scrapping and sleeping in heaps. Further on, Hearst Castle stands high on the hill above San Simeon, the extravagant creation of a newspaper magnate in the early twentieth century.

Fuel is the practical point. There is a small station at Ragged Point, but prices tend to be steep, and Cambria, about thirty kilometres south, has more choice. North of here there is very little for a long way, and Big Sur has few stations, all expensive, so fill up before committing.

Fog is the main variable. Summer mornings often bring a cold grey blanket along the coast, which lifts around noon, and the best light arrives in the late afternoon. Spring brings green hills and wildflowers, while autumn offers clearer air. Winter storms sometimes close the road with slides, so check conditions first.
t.santa cruz@37.3,-122.3:
The pin falls up in the redwoods of the Peninsula's Skyline ridge, near La Honda and the county parks that surround Pescadero Creek, rather than in Santa Cruz itself. That is the kind of place where the Bay Area's tech wealth seems very far away, even though Woodside and Portola Valley, home to some of the most expensive real estate in the country, are only a few kilometres down the hill.

The roads are the reason riders come. Skyline Boulevard, State Route 35, runs along the crest of the Santa Cruz Mountains, with redwoods and Douglas firs on both sides, and the cross roads, such as Highway 84, plunge down to the coast through shaded canyons. The corners are tight and technical, the surface is variable, patched and sometimes lined with fallen needles, and the light comes through the trees in broken shafts, so judging the road takes concentration. On a weekend you will meet plenty of other riders and cyclists.

Alice's Restaurant, a rustic roadside spot at the crossing of Skyline and Highway 84, has been a biker meeting place for decades and is worth a stop, if only to look at the bikes lined up outside and swap notes. It is a casual place with simple American food and good conversation.

The redwoods here are second growth, since the original giants were cut in the nineteenth century to build San Francisco, but they have recovered into dense, dark groves where fog drips off the needles. Some old stumps are huge. The smell of damp bark and bay laurel is strong.

For fuel, ride down into Woodside or on to Redwood City or Half Moon Bay, because the ridge itself has little. The best weather is spring and autumn, with summer fog often creeping over the crest and chilling things. Watch for deer at dusk and gravel in the tight bends after rain.
t.tomales bay@38.2,-122.9:
Tomales Bay is a long, thin finger of water that points north-west from Point Reyes, and it lies exactly on the San Andreas Fault. The Pacific plate on the western side is moving north, slowly, against the North American plate on the east, and the straight, narrow shape of the bay is the scar left by the rift. In 1906, the fault slipped here with such violence that fences and roads were displaced by several metres, and you can still see where in places near Point Reyes Station.

The water is calm and green, with oyster farms along the eastern shore, tide flats and small boats pulled up on the mud. Inverness, a village of about thirteen hundred people on the western side, is a cluster of wooden houses and a few cafes, while Point Reyes National Seashore stretches beyond it. On the road along the eastern shore, State Route 1, villages like Marshall have fish restaurants and oyster stands where you can eat fresh shellfish at a picnic table with a view.

The ride here is excellent. Highway 1 follows the bay in a series of gentle curves, with the water on one side and rolling hills on the other, and the surface is generally good, though some stretches are rough and narrow. Fog is common, especially in summer, when it rolls in from the Pacific in the afternoon and can drop the temperature by ten degrees in minutes. Bring a layer even on a warm day, and be careful on damp corners. On weekends, cyclists and tourists crowd the road, so go on a weekday if you can.

Fuel is scarce on this stretch. Petaluma, about twenty-four kilometres east, is the nearest large town, and the villages around the bay have limited services, so fill up before you come. Food is easier: the oyster shacks and bakeries along the shore are a Bay Area institution.

Early morning, when the water is flat and pink and the first fishermen are out, is the best time for a photograph. Elk, herons and pelicans may all make an appearance, and in winter the sky is full of migrating birds.
t.placerville@38.7,-120.8:
Placerville has an unforgettable old name. In 1849, during the California Gold Rush, the town was known as Hangtown, after a series of impromptu hangings of thieves, and the name stuck for years until the more respectable citizens managed to change it. A hangman's dummy still swings from a building on Main Street, and the town leans into its rough-and-tumble past.

It sits in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, on Highway 50, about sixty kilometres east of Sacramento, at the point where the Central Valley's flat farmland gives way to oak woodland and rolling hills. James Marshall found gold at nearby Coloma in January 1848, the find that started the rush, and Placerville grew up as a supply town for the diggings. It was also a stop on the route of the Pony Express in 1860 and 1861, and the main street still has old brick buildings and wooden storefronts from the period.

For a rider, Placerville is an ideal fuel stop, with a population of over ten thousand, stations and shops along the highway, and cafes in the old town. Beyond it, Highway 50 climbs into the high Sierra toward Lake Tahoe, passing through pine forest and along the American River, with long curves and big views. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with campers and skiers heading to the mountains, and in winter chains may be required on the higher sections.

Apple Hill, an area of orchards just east of town, is a popular autumn destination, with farm stands selling apples, pies, cider and doughnuts. The smell of baking drifts across the lanes in October. Wineries have taken hold in the foothills as well, and the vineyards produce good zinfandel and other reds.

The best time is spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers are out, or early autumn, when the apples are ripe. In midsummer the grass is golden and the heat can be fierce, with afternoon temperatures above thirty-five degrees. Fill up, stretch, and keep climbing.
t.bilbao@43.3,-2.9:
Bilbao was an industrial city for most of its life, an iron-ore and shipyard town on the Nervión river, and then in 1997 it reinvented itself with a titanium-clad museum that changed how cities think about culture. Frank Gehry's Guggenheim sits right on the riverbank, curved and glittering like a ship that has run aground, and its success gave the whole place a new confidence. You will notice that the older parts of town, the Casco Viejo with its seven original streets, are still very Basque, loud and unpretentious, with bars full of locals at lunchtime and counters stacked with pintxos.

The valley setting matters for riders. Bilbao is squeezed between green hills that rise steeply on every side, so any road you take out of town immediately climbs and bends. Mount Artxanda, reached by a short funicular, gives the best overview, with the whole urban sprawl and the river bend spread underneath, while the Bizkaia Bridge at Portugalete, a hanging ferry from 1893 and a UNESCO site, shows how the old industry linked both banks of the estuary. The climate is mild and often damp, with drizzle common even in summer, which keeps the hills a deep, almost Irish green.

On two wheels, the ride starts best by getting out early. Inside the city, traffic is dense, tunnels and viaducts carry the main roads, and parking is tight, so plan to leave the bike in a garage if you stay overnight. Fuel is easy to find in the surrounding districts, and Santutxu, Basauri and the other neighbourhoods all have stations. The N-634 and the smaller coastal roads that run east toward Gernika, Lekeitio and beyond are twisty and often slow, with fishing harbours and cliffs worth every stop. Allow longer than the map suggests, because the roads follow every inlet and the villages demand attention.

Eat before you leave. A couple of pintxos at the counter and a coffee will carry you through the first hour of bends, and nothing else on the coast will taste quite as good.
t.lekeitio@43.4,-2.5:
Lekeitio is the kind of fishing harbour that makes you slow down whether you meant to or not. It sits on the Bay of Biscay coast of Bizkaia, behind a sheltered cove, and it has a town centre of about seven thousand people packed between the sea and a ring of green hills. The first thing you notice is the island, San Nicolás, which lies just offshore and joins the mainland by a causeway at low tide, when the beach opens up and the whole town seems to walk out over the sand.

The old part is built around the Gothic church of Santa María de la Asunción, a big, buttressed building with a tall bell tower and a finely carved interior, and the stone houses in the narrow streets behind it. The fishing fleet still operates, and the port smells of salt, diesel and grilled fish, which is the best argument for lunch. Anchovies, hake, squid and the local sea bream are the standard orders, and nobody takes offence if you linger.

The town is also known for an odd festival around the first week of September, the Day of the Geese, when a goose is hung over the harbour and young men try to grab its neck from a boat. It is a tradition that divides opinion and has been modified in recent years, but it is part of the identity of the place and gives you something to talk about.

The riding on the coast road is the best of Basque Spain in miniature: short, twisty sections that climb away from the sea through eucalyptus and pine, drop back into little harbours, and offer constant views of surf on dark rock. The surface is good, the corners are close together, and traffic is steady in summer, particularly at weekends. Rain comes without warning, and a wet road under dense trees is slippery, so keep to your own pace.

Lekeitio has fuel and plenty of places to eat, so this is one of the easiest stops on the route. Park near the harbour, and if the tide allows, walk out toward the island, then ride on with the smell of the sea still in your jacket.
t.zumaia@43.3,-2.3:
Zumaia is where you go to look at time. On the cliffs just beside the town, at Itzurun beach, the sea has cut through layer after layer of tilted sedimentary rock known as flysch, thin bands of limestone and shale that stack up like the pages of a book and run into the water in long ridges. The rocks span a huge stretch of geological history, and geologists come from all over the world to study the layer that records the end of the Cretaceous, the period when the dinosaurs disappeared. That makes this one of the great natural clocks in Europe, and it is part of the Basque Coast Geopark.

The town itself, about nine thousand people, sits where the Urola river meets the sea, with a small harbour, a stone bridge and a promenade. It is also where the painter Ignacio Zuloaga had his house, now a museum, and the hermitage of San Telmo perches on the cliffs above the beach in a very cinematic way. The coastal pilgrim route of the Camino de Santiago passes through, so you will meet walkers with scallop shells on their packs.

The riding is classic Basque coast: narrow, wooded, undulating roads that climb out of one valley, drop into another and thread between small farms with their traditional stone houses. The corners are tight and frequent, the tarmac is generally good, and the green slopes around Getaria, a few kilometres up the coast, are planted with vines producing txakoli, a lightly sparkling, very dry white wine that goes beautifully with grilled fish. Getaria is also the birthplace of Juan Sebastián Elcano, who completed the first circumnavigation of the globe after Magellan died.

Zumaia is a proper town, so fuel, cafes and parking are easy. Go for a pintxo and a small glass of txakoli at one of the bars near the harbour, and if the tide is low, take the steps down to the beach and look at the rock layers up close. The weather can turn quickly from sun to drizzle, so carry a waterproof even when the sky looks innocent.
t.laguardia@42.6,-2.6:
Laguardia stands on a ridge above the Ebro valley, a walled hill town with the long blue wall of the Sierra de Cantabria rising behind it like a stage backdrop. It is the main town of the Rioja Alavesa, the part of the Basque Country that lies south of the mountains and produces some of Spain's best-known wine, and it has about fifteen hundred permanent residents, most of whom seem to have a cellar.

That is not a joke. Beneath the old streets runs a network of medieval tunnels and caves, dug to store and age wine, and many of the houses have their own cellar below. The town was founded in 1164 by King Sancho VI of Navarre, known as the Wise, as a frontier fortress against Castile, and its name means roughly the guard. Inside the walls the layout is a tight spine of cobbled lanes, with several gates and a few towers.

The church of Santa María de los Reyes has a remarkable Gothic doorway that was painted in bright colours and survived in unusually fine condition because it was sheltered by a porch. It is worth a look if it is open. A few kilometres away the wine world gets interesting in a different way: at Elciego, the Marqués de Riscal winery has a hotel designed by Frank Gehry, in titanium ribbons of pink and gold, and the Ysios winery near Laguardia, by Santiago Calatrava, has a long wave-shaped roof against the mountain.

The riding is gentle and scenic: smooth roads running through vineyards, which turn deep gold and red in October and look bare and sculptural in winter. There is little traffic outside harvest, when tractors with grape trailers slow everyone down. Winds can be strong on the open ridge, and the temperature swings between hot afternoons and cool evenings.

The old town is largely pedestrian, so park outside the walls and walk up. There are bars and restaurants in plenty, and a glass of local red with roast lamb or grilled vegetables is the obvious choice. For serious fuel, plan on Logroño, about fifteen kilometres away, though smaller stations may be found closer.
t.haro@42.6,-2.8:
Haro is the capital of the Rioja Alta, a mid-sized river town with twelve thousand inhabitants and an astonishing density of wine. It sits where the Tirón river comes down to meet the Ebro, with the Sierra de Cantabria on the north side and the blue ridges of the Sierra de la Demanda far away to the south, and the soil of the surrounding slopes gives the wines their reputation for elegance rather than muscle.

The best of the town lies in the Barrio de la Estación, the district beside the old railway station, where several of the great historic bodegas were built in the late nineteenth century. The reason is simple: the railway arrived in the 1860s, and merchants who had learned winemaking from Bordeaux, where the vine disease phylloxera had devastated the vineyards, suddenly had a way to ship Rioja out to the rest of Spain and abroad. Houses such as López de Heredia, CVNE, Muga and La Rioja Alta still make wine in the same quarter, and the old stone buildings and tall brick chimneys give the neighbourhood an industrial charm that is rare in a wine region.

Haro also likes to claim a first: it was reputedly the first town in Spain to have electric street lighting, switched on in the 1890s. Whether or not you check the detail, the old quarter around the Plaza de la Paz, with its bandstand and handsome balconied town hall, is a pleasant place to sit. The church of Santo Tomás has an elaborate Renaissance doorway worth a look.

On the twenty-ninth of June comes the Batalla del Vino, in which crowds climb up to the Riscos de Bilibio above the town in purple and white and soak each other in red wine. It is deliberately silly and enormously popular, so do not plan to ride through that morning.

The riding to and from Haro is smooth and easy, through vineyards on gentle roads, with little hard braking and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is light except around harvest, when tractors with loaded trailers are common. Haro has fuel, parking and any number of bars; the thing to do in the evening is to follow the crowds to the narrow streets of the Herradura, the old tapas quarter, and eat standing up. If you are still riding afterwards, remember that the Spanish limit for alcohol is low, and a glass of Rioja is not a free pass.
t.alto tajo gorge@40.3,-3.9:
This final point lies on the south-western edge of Madrid, near Arroyomolinos and Navalcarnero, a long way from the Alto Tajo itself. The natural park that gives the ride its name is some hundred and fifty kilometres to the east, in the high limestone country on the borders of Guadalajara and Cuenca provinces, where the Tajo and its tributaries have cut deep, tree-lined gorges through a plateau of pale rock. Here, you are back in the commuter belt, among new housing estates and fields of cereal and olive.

Navalcarnero deserves a stop if you have any energy left, because its Plaza de Segovia is a proper arcaded square, built in brick and timber, with galleries on all sides and the feel of a small Castilian market town. It is also known historically as the place where Charles II married Marie Louise of Orléans in 1679, a royal wedding in the middle of nowhere, and the local wine, a rustic Madrid red, has been drunk here for centuries. Arroyomolinos is mostly modern, but it does have some old cork and holm oak in the surrounding land.

The Alto Tajo you rode in the morning is something else entirely. The river runs a rich turquoise between cliffs, with griffon vultures wheeling overhead, juniper and pine on the slopes, and high plateau roads that feel closer to Aragon than to Madrid. The gorge roads there are often narrow and empty, with the occasional village such as Poveda de la Sierra or Peralejos de las Truchas hidden in the folds of the hills. Fuel stations in that area are scarce, so you will have been glad of a full tank at the start, whereas here, with Navalcarnero's twenty thousand people and Arroyomolinos beside it, you are never far from a pump, a bar or a supermarket.

Traffic is the main hazard at this end of the day. The A-5 and M-50 get sticky in the evening and in summer the tarmac holds heat long after sunset. Take it calmly, let the tired muscles unwind, and think about those turquoise gorges while the brake lights glow ahead.
t.segovia old town@40.9,-4.1:
Segovia announces itself with a Roman aqueduct, and nothing else in Spain quite prepares you for it. Built around the first or second century, the granite blocks are stacked in two tiers of arches without any mortar, and the whole thing strides through the middle of the town like something from a film set. It carried water from the mountains for nearly two thousand years, and in the oldest parts of the city you can still see how it dictated the shape of the streets around it.

The old town stands on a rocky spur between two small rivers, the Eresma and the Clamores, and it is a UNESCO site since 1985. At the western tip, the Alcázar rises like the prow of a ship, with pointed turrets that are said to have inspired Walt Disney, and at the centre the Gothic cathedral, late and magnificent, is nicknamed the lady of cathedrals. The city sits at about a thousand metres, which means cool mornings and sharp winters even when Madrid is baking, and the old stone smells faintly of woodsmoke. Eat here as the locals do: cochinillo asado, roast suckling pig, is the speciality, served in dim cellars where the waiters traditionally cut it with the edge of a plate. For something sweet, ask for ponche segoviano, a sponge-and-custard cake with marzipan.

For riding, think of Segovia as the reward at the end of the mountain section. The roads in from the sierra, over passes like Navacerrada or Cotos, climb through pine forest with sweeping views and cool air, and the descent toward the Castilian plain comes with long, easy bends. In town, the old quarter is difficult for cars and tough on bikes, with steep cobbles and one-way systems, so park below near the aqueduct or in an underground car park and walk up. Segovia has fuel on its outskirts, and you can find coffee in almost any plaza.

Come when the day is cooling. The aqueduct goes honey-gold in late light, the storks arrive on the towers, and you will want to sit with a drink and simply look at it.
t.la granja palace@40.9,-4.0:
Philip V was a homesick king. Born in France and raised at Versailles, he came to the Spanish throne in 1700 and spent much of his reign longing for the gardens of his childhood, so in the early eighteenth century he built himself a retreat at La Granja de San Ildefonso, on the northern slope of the Sierra de Guadarrama, and filled the grounds with French-style avenues, clipped hedges and an extravagant series of fountains and statues. The result is a baroque palace that looks out on a mountain wall rather than a French plain.

The gardens are the draw. Water is fed from the mountains above, and on certain days the fountains are switched on in sequence, a spectacle that draws crowds in summer and is worth timing if you can. The palace itself, a warm pink and cream building, houses a fine collection of tapestries, and Philip V, who abdicated and then returned to the throne, is buried in the collegiate church next door. There was also a royal glass factory in the town, which turned out mirrors and chandeliers, and the glass tradition survives in a museum.

The town sits at an altitude of around twelve hundred metres, which means cool nights even in summer and proper winters, and the pine forests of Valsaín stretch up behind it towards the Puerto de Navacerrada. The riding in and out is a lovely mix of sweeping main roads and narrower forest lanes, with plenty of shade and the scent of pine resin. The surface is good in general, but ice can linger in shaded bends from late autumn to early spring, so check conditions in the colder months.

San Ildefonso itself has about five thousand people and is a convenient stop, with a petrol station, cafes along the main street and several bakeries selling the local speciality of ponche segoviano, a sponge cake layered with custard and marzipan. Segovia, with its Roman aqueduct, lies only a short distance down the hill, so you can pair the two on a single day.

If you are here for pictures, the best light on the palace front comes in the morning, before the tour coaches arrive, and the gardens look their best in autumn when the chestnuts and limes turn gold.
t.rascafria food@40.9,-3.9:
Rascafría is the main village of the upper Lozoya valley, a green, high, glacier-carved trough on the northern side of the Sierra de Guadarrama where the Lozoya river runs down from the peaks. It is a small place, around sixteen hundred people, but it feels bigger than it is because of what surrounds it: the great ridge of Peñalara, the highest summit in the range at a little over two thousand four hundred metres, lies just to the west, and the old pine forests close in on all sides.

On the edge of the village stands the monastery of Santa María de El Paular, founded as a Carthusian house at the end of the fourteenth century by a Castilian king and later used by Benedictine monks. The buildings include a Gothic church with a famous carved altarpiece in alabaster, a cloister, and a quiet, prosperous feeling that suits the setting. A short walk away a wooded path leads past the Lozoya river to the old bridge and the Presillas pools, where Madrileños come in summer to splash about in cold clear water.

This is also a food stop with some character. The valley is known for river trout, for roast lamb and for hearty mountain stews, and the village has plenty of cosy restaurants and bars where you can sit at a big table by a fire in winter. Do not expect an elegant menu; the point is warm, solid food in good quantity, with a plate of cheese and a jug of local wine, and a coffee afterwards on a terrace with the sound of running water.

The riding here is what draws motorcyclists. The road from the Puerto de Cotos down through the pines is a long, flowing run of well-banked bends, and the approach from the Morcuera pass on the other side is equally good, with some tight hairpins and lovely views. In summer the traffic is heavy at weekends, with walkers and cyclists, and in winter the high passes can have snow and ice, so look for any closures before setting out.

For fuel, check your tank before leaving the valley: San Ildefonso, over the pass to the north, is the sensible larger town, and Rascafría itself should have a pump, but do not rely on it late in the evening.
t.sierra de guadarrama sweep@40.6,-3.6:
This is the northern fringe of Madrid, the area around San Sebastián de los Reyes and Alcobendas, two towns that have grown together into a single built-up mass of nearly two hundred thousand people. The land is flat and the architecture is of offices, logistics parks and tidy housing blocks, so the interest here is mostly practical. It is exactly where you want to be on a cold morning with a tank to fill and a long day ahead.

Fuel is not a problem: there are stations on every main road, open early and late, and you will rarely have to queue. Pick up a bottle of water, check your luggage and your route, and then take the A-1 north or one of the smaller roads off the ring toward the Sierra de Guadarrama, which rises in front of you in a long ridge. On a clear day you can see the snow-patched summits from the fuel station forecourt.

San Sebastián de los Reyes has one claim to fame beyond the suburbs, which is its bull-running festival in late August, the Fiestas Populares, when young men run before the bulls through the streets, a tradition rivalling the more famous Pamplona version in local passion if not in global attention. The rest of the year the town is quiet and residential, with a lovely old church and a tree-lined plaza you will rarely have time to see.

The sweep that begins here is an invitation to the mountains. The first section is easy motorway or dual carriageway, and then you leave the plain, the grey of the city giving way to cereal fields and then to holm oak and granite. The ride works best on a weekday, or a very early Sunday: later on the main roads north of Madrid fill with day-trippers heading for the sierra, and the junctions at the foot of the mountains can be slow.

One local tip: the temperature difference between the city and the high ridges can be ten to fifteen degrees in winter, so wear a warm layer even if the pavement feels mild. In summer the opposite problem applies, and the earlier you set off, the cooler the first hour will be.
t.sierra de guadarrama sweep scenic road@4:
There is not much drama in the landscape east of Madrid, and that is exactly what makes it a good place to relax the shoulders. This stretch lies on the flat plain of the Henares river, around Ajalvir, Cobeña and Daganzo de Arriba, three small towns of a few thousand people each, framed by cereal fields, scrubby hedgerows and the odd line of poplars along a stream. The soil is pale and a bit chalky, and the colours change dramatically by season: gold in June, bare ochre in August, a thin green haze after autumn rain.

Aircraft are the main spectacle. Madrid's Barajas airport lies not far to the south-west, and you will often see airliners descending low across the fields, while the military base at Torrejón is a short way south-east. Neither is a nuisance on the road, but they give the place a slightly unreal air, with huge machines gliding overhead above wheat fields and tractors.

The riding is easy: long straights broken by gentle curves, junctions with farm tracks, a decent surface though patched in places, and very little traffic outside commuting hours. It is not a road for a fast ride, because the visibility can be poor at some of the crossroads and the cross-wind in open country is stronger than you expect, but it is relaxing and the farmland light in the early morning is lovely. Spring brings green wheat and poppies, and in September the stubble fields are scorched gold, with the occasional flock of sheep moving across them.

A little history sits under the surface. This is the Corredor del Henares, the old route linking Madrid to Guadalajara and the Alcarria, and the main road along it, the A-2, follows lines of travel that have been used since Roman times. The villages grew along the route and many have old churches with brick towers in the Mudéjar tradition, a style created by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons.

Practical points: Daganzo de Arriba is the biggest of the villages and has the services, including fuel, and the larger towns of Alcalá de Henares and Torrejón are a few kilometres further. Water and a coffee are easy to find in the villages' cafes, though they close early in the evening.
t.sierra de guadarrama sweep high point@40:
Hills in this part of the Madrid region are not mountains but tablelands, the páramos, flat-topped uplands of limestone and gypsum that stand above the river valleys of the Jarama and the Tajuña. This high point lies on that kind of land, close to Campo Real, Loeches and the larger town of Arganda del Rey, and the elevation gain is modest but the views over the valley below are wide and surprisingly good.

Campo Real is known for olive oil, and the groves of grey-green trees around the village produce one of the few oils with a Madrid designation. The town has an old church and a quiet centre, and in November the harvest smell of crushed olives hangs over the lanes. Loeches, a few kilometres on, has a seventeenth-century convent founded by the Count-Duke of Olivares, the powerful minister of Philip IV, who is buried there. The building is a fine piece of Spanish baroque, and it still houses a community of nuns.

Arganda del Rey is a bigger and more industrial place of over fifty thousand people, set on the banks of the Jarama, and it has a long tradition of winemaking too: the Vinos de Madrid designation covers vineyards here, and you can still find small bodegas around the old centre.

The riding is relaxed and pleasant, with long gentle climbs onto the plateau, wide views of vines and olives, and a surface that is generally smooth. The wind is the main factor. On an exposed páramo a gust can push a loaded bike sideways, and in winter the cold is bitter, particularly in the early morning. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the light is clean and the colours are rich.

Practical matters are easy: Arganda has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, and Campo Real and Loeches both have small bars where you can stop for coffee and a tortilla, the Spanish potato omelette that is the default solution to most rides. Check the weather before going, because the plateau can be foggy on winter mornings.
t.sierra de guadarrama sweep photo pull of:
South of Madrid, where the Jarama river meets the Tagus basin, the land flattens into a pale plain of cereal, vineyards and gypsum badlands, and this pull-off sits right in the middle of it. The towns around are Ciempozuelos, Seseña and the tiny village of Titulcia, with the larger city of Aranjuez, famous for its royal palace and gardens, a short distance south.

On a clear day, this is the place to turn and look north. The Sierra de Guadarrama appears as a faint blue line on the far horizon, sometimes capped with white in winter and spring, and it is a reminder of how far the plain stretches between you and the mountains. The air is dry, the sky enormous, and in the early morning the shadows lie long across the fields. The view is subtle rather than dramatic, and you need good light to appreciate it.

The geology is the interesting part. The soil here is rich in gypsum and salt, laid down when this whole basin was a vast inland lake millions of years ago, and where rivers have cut into it you find white and pale-grey cliffs. Titulcia stands on one of these slopes and has a very old history: it was a settlement in Roman times, and archaeologists have found traces of earlier occupation too. Nowadays it is a quiet village with a few hundred inhabitants and an old church.

Seseña is known for a very different reason. Close to the road, a huge residential development begun in the property boom of the 2000s was left half-finished when the market collapsed, and its rows of empty blocks became a national symbol of the crash. It is a strange thing to see from a motorbike, and a reminder that not every wide-open plain is as empty as it looks.

The riding is flat and open, with straight roads, level crossings and the occasional roundabout, but it is the kind of country where you cover ground without effort and the main danger is boredom or a crosswind. Fuel and food are easy at Ciempozuelos, a town of twenty-two thousand people with all the services, and Aranjuez has the best restaurants if you have time. In summer, aim to be off the plain by early afternoon.
t.sierra de guadarrama sweep@40.3,-4.1:
Navalcarnero is the kind of town that surprises you when you stop. It sits west of Madrid at the edge of the plain, with a population of around twenty-one thousand, and its centre is built around the Plaza de Segura, a long arcaded square lined with wooden columns and balconies, like a stage set from the sixteenth century. A short ride from the sprawling suburbs and the motorway, you find yourself in a space that is calm, shaded and entirely human in scale.

The area is wine country. The Vinos de Madrid designation includes a subzone around Navalcarnero, where the garnacha vines grow in sandy soil, and the local bars and bodegas serve robust reds that suit the hearty food of the region. Expect grilled meats, lamb, stews with chickpeas and the sort of rough-and-ready tapas that appear in front of you the moment you order a drink. There are plenty of places around the plaza, and the midday menu is the best deal: a starter, a main and a dessert for a modest set price.

To the west flows the Alberche river, which comes down from the Gredos mountains and gives the country a more varied character, with pines on the sandy ground and scrub along the banks. Villamanta and Valmojado, the smaller villages nearby, have old churches and quiet streets, and from Valmojado the road leads toward Toledo's open landscapes.

The riding here is of a gentle, rolling kind: wide roads through farmland and pine groves, with long sight lines and not much traffic. The surface is usually good, though some of the older roads are worn and patched. It is a pleasant approach to the western mountains, and the evening light, with long shadows and warm tones across the vines, is the best of the day.

Fuel is easy in Navalcarnero, with several stations on the ring road, and the smaller villages have a bar and a shop but not much else. Parking around the plaza is limited on market days and on summer weekends, so be prepared to walk a few minutes. A long lunch here is a good way to let the heat of the day pass, because the plain around can be fiercely hot in July and August.
t.sierra@40.6,-3.6:
On the northern edge of Madrid, where the capital's sprawl begins to thin into open plain, the coordinates fall among San Sebastián de los Reyes, Alcobendas and Tres Cantos. These are tidy, prosperous commuter towns with business parks, wide roads and a lot of roundabouts. Tres Cantos was a planned new town of the 1970s, a bit of an experiment in suburban living, and it has more green space than you might expect, thanks to the surrounding Monte de Viñuelas and woodland.

San Sebastián de los Reyes has the real local colour. At the end of August, the town holds its famous fiestas with bull running through the streets, the encierros, which compete with Pamplona in popularity for those who like their Spanish traditions loud and slightly dangerous. The rest of the year it is calmer, a town of low houses and a small old centre around the parish church, where you can find a good coffee and a decent plate of eggs and potatoes. Alcobendas is bigger and more corporate, home to the offices of many international firms.

The reason this makes a finish for a Sierra de Guadarrama ride is geographic. The A-1 motorway leads north from here toward the Somosierra pass and the mountain wall that separates Madrid from Castile, and on a clear day you can see the snowy ridges from the car parks of the shopping centres. That means when you come back from a day in the hills, the last bit is straightforward and quick, a fast run down off the sierra with lorries in the right lane and plenty of space to settle into. Fuel is no problem here, with several large stations and a reliable supply of cafés.

The only caution is the evening commute. Traffic backs up on the A-1 and the M-607 on weekdays, and weekend returns from the mountains are just as heavy, so a slightly early or late finish pays off. In the quiet of the hour after the rush, the sky over the sierra turns a soft violet, and the last twenty kilometres feel like a gentle wind-down.
t.fuente de@43.1,-4.8:
Fuente Dé is the end of the road, in the best sense. The CA-185 climbs up a narrow glacial valley from Potes, the little capital of the Liébana region, and finishes in a vast amphitheatre of limestone, a cirque of grey cliffs that rise nearly vertically above the meadow and block off the sky. There is nowhere further to ride, so you park, tip your head back, and look up.

What makes the place famous is the cable car. It carries visitors from the valley floor at about a thousand metres to a viewing platform on the cliff edge at around eighteen hundred, a rise of roughly seven hundred and fifty metres in a few minutes, and from the top you can see the central massif of the Picos de Europa, a landscape of peaks, snowfields and deep gorges. Queues build up on summer weekends, and the cable car closes in bad weather or for maintenance, so check ahead if the ride up is the point.

The Picos are the first mountains in Spain to be protected as a national park, and the range supports chamois, golden eagles, griffon vultures and a few Cantabrian brown bears that roam the forests lower down. Fuente Dé itself has a small cluster of buildings, a few restaurants and a shop, and the meadow is full of cattle bells in summer. The light is superb in the late afternoon, when the cliffs turn amber and the shadows fill the valley.

The ride up from Potes follows the Deva river, with a mix of straights and long, flowing bends, and views of the cliffs opening ahead. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow in places and the weekend traffic of coaches and campervans can be slow. The mountain weather changes quickly: you can arrive in sun and be in cloud within twenty minutes, and the temperature at the base is always cooler than in Potes.

Potes is also the place for local food, with a hearty bean-and-cabbage stew called cocido lebaniego and the strong local fruit spirit orujo, and the monastery of Santo Toribio de Liébana, a short drive from the town, claims the largest surviving fragment of the True Cross.
t.santander@43.5,-3.8:
Santander is a seaside capital that happens to have a mountain range at its back. The city wraps around a broad, sheltered bay, with long beaches at El Sardinero on the Atlantic side and a working harbour facing the old town, and on a clear day the Picos de Europa show as a faint white line far to the west. A great fire in 1941 destroyed much of the historic centre, so the architecture is mostly post-war, but the waterfront has been given a bright new face, with the glass and steel Centro Botín by Renzo Piano projecting out over the water. For riders arriving from England, the ferries from Plymouth and Portsmouth land here, which gives it a slightly salty, expectant air.

Eat before you leave. Anchovies from the Cantabrian Sea are the local pride, along with rabas, crisp fried squid rings, and sobaos pasiegos, the soft butter cakes that come from the valleys inland. The Palacio de la Magdalena, a royal summer residence of the early twentieth century, stands on a headland with gardens and a long view across the bay, and is worth a stroll if you are in no hurry.

The day's riding goes inland and south, toward Puente Viesgo and the caves of Monte Castillo, where early humans painted the walls tens of thousands of years ago. The caves of El Castillo and Las Monedas sit within the same limestone hill, part of the UNESCO listing for Cantabrian cave art. The roads between Santander and the Pas valley are generally smooth and quick, with gentle curves through green meadows and eucalyptus, and then narrower and more rural once you leave the main road. Cantabria is famously rainy, so the hills are a rich, damp green and the roads can be slick in the morning. Visits to the caves are limited and usually need advance booking, so check before you arrive and carry something to put over your riding jacket in the cool of the cave.

Fuel is no concern in a city of nearly two hundred thousand, and there are stations on the ring road and around the port. Bring a waterproof layer whatever the forecast says. The weather on this coast rolls in from the sea, and a bright morning can be grey by lunchtime.
t.zaragoza@41.7,-0.9:
Zaragoza is a big, grown-up city on the Ebro, halfway between Madrid and Barcelona, and it has a no-nonsense character that suits a motorcyclist. It is the capital of Aragón, with some six hundred and seventy thousand people, and it sits in a wide, dry basin where the Ebro has laid down a flat plain bordered by low hills. The wind here is famous. The cierzo blows hard from the north-west, sometimes for days, and can push a bike sideways on an open bridge, so check the forecast and keep a firm grip on the bars when crossing the river.

The Basílica del Pilar dominates the waterfront, with its cluster of tiled domes and four towers reflected in the Ebro. According to tradition, the Virgin appeared here to St James and left a pillar behind, which is why the city celebrates its Fiestas del Pilar every October with parades and flowers. Nearby, the Aljafería, an eleventh-century Moorish palace, shows exquisite horseshoe arches and carved plaster, and later became a seat of Aragonese kings. The painter Goya grew up in the region and frescoed parts of the basilica as a young man. The old quarter, known as El Tubo, is a tight tangle of lanes packed with tapas bars, and it is a fine place to eat standing up with a glass of local red.

For the ride, Zaragoza is a convenient start and finish. Fuel stations and workshops are everywhere, and getting out of the city means following the signs toward the hills. The roads around the Ebro valley are generally fast and open, with long straights and gentle curves between fields and vineyards, and the real interest comes once you leave the plain. Summers are very hot and winters can be bitterly cold, with fog on the river. In spring and autumn, the light is fine.

Aragón does not get as many visitors as the coast, but its roads are empty and its food is honest. Try ternasco de Aragón, a tender young lamb, if you stay for dinner. The traffic inside the city can be heavy, so allow time on the way out and avoid the commute.
t.cite fruges@44.8,-0.6:
Pessac is better known for wine than for modern architecture, so it is a surprise to find a small colony of Le Corbusier houses in its southern suburbs. In 1924, the industrialist Henry Frugès, a sugar and timber magnate with a social conscience, commissioned the young architect to build cheap, comfortable homes for his workers, and Le Corbusier designed rows of cubic houses with flat roofs, long ribbon windows and bright colours, inside and out. It was one of his first large housing experiments, an attempt to apply factory methods to building, and it took a few years to finish. The result was a village of around fifty houses.

The place was not an instant success. Residents found the flat roofs leaked, the layouts unconventional and the colours outlandish, and for decades many of the houses were altered or neglected. Gradually, the estate was recognised as a key work of modern architecture, and a restoration brought back the original colour schemes of pale pink, blue, green and ochre. In 2016 it became part of a UNESCO listing of Le Corbusier's architectural works, and one house is kept as a museum, with the original furnishings and fittings to see.

Around it, Pessac is a big suburb of Bordeaux, a university town of nearly fifty-eight thousand with plenty of fuel stations and cafés. Its other claim to fame is Château Haut-Brion, one of the first-growth wines of Bordeaux, whose vineyards lie within the suburb, surrounded by houses, and whose reputation dates back to the seventeenth century, when the English drank it in London. The Graves vineyards of Pessac-Léognan roll away south, and the Saint-Émilion jurisdiction, the other part of the ride, lies on the far side of the city, among limestone plateaus.

Riding around Bordeaux is mostly flat, fast and heavy with traffic, so take the quieter roads, and avoid the ring road at rush hour. Park beside the estate and walk its quiet streets, and you will notice the clean geometry of the houses against the leafy gardens. The estate is quietest in the morning, and on a bright day, the colours seem to hum against the blue of the sky.
t.biarritz@43.5,-1.6:
Biarritz was a fishing and whaling village until the 1850s, when Empress Eugénie, who loved the place from childhood holidays, persuaded Napoleon III to build a villa on the headland. Royalty followed, then the rest of Europe's idle rich, and the town still carries that Second Empire swagger: a palace hotel on the beach, a lighthouse, a casino, and a rock with a statue of the Virgin Mary joined to the shore by a little footbridge. Then, in the late 1950s, a film crew brought a surfboard and the town found a second career. It is now one of the oldest surf towns in Europe, and on a decent swell the Grande Plage is full of black wetsuits.

For a rider it is a very good place to start a day, because the Basque interior is only twenty minutes away and it looks nothing like the coast. Head inland and the villages turn white with red or green shutters, the hills are small and steep and impossibly green, and the roads twist between them in short, tight, slightly bumpy sections that reward patience rather than speed. Ainhoa and Espelette are the obvious targets, the latter hung with strings of drying red peppers in autumn, and the Pyrenean foothills start to rise behind them. Go early. The coast road and the Anglet side are slow with beach traffic in July and August, and the ring of roundabouts around the airport can eat half an hour.

Practically, you are in a built-up area of well over seventy thousand people counting Anglet next door, so fuel, coffee and parking are not a worry. Parking a bike near the old port is possible if you do not mind squeezing between scooters. The Atlantic is the thing to respect here: it changes the weather quickly, and a clear morning can turn to drizzle by the time you reach the hills, with a warm, wet wind from the southwest. Take a layer.

Eat something Basque while you are here. t.big sur pacific coast day scenic road@37:
Behind Berkeley and Oakland the East Bay hills rise in a long green wall, and the roads that cross them are the secret playground of every motorcyclist in the Bay Area. The coordinates here are near Orinda, a leafy, quiet suburb tucked behind the first ridge, with Berkeley and its university a few miles to the west. The name on the stop suggests the Pacific coast, but this is a different kind of beauty: oak woodland, eucalyptus groves, grassy ridges and, in the folds of the hills, groves of coast redwoods that have grown back since the original giants were logged to build San Francisco.

Wildcat Canyon, Tilden Regional Park and Redwood Regional Park form a chain of protected land along the crest, and the roads that run through them, such as Grizzly Peak Boulevard and Skyline Boulevard, are twisty, narrow and rewarding. Between Highway 280 and the Pacific, the San Francisco Peninsula is split by a long, straight valley, and the valley is where the story of the San Andreas Fault begins. It was here, in the 1890s, that the geologist Andrew Lawson, studying the long trough that now holds San Andreas Lake and the Crystal Springs Reservoir, named the fault after the lake, and then learned, after the 1906 earthquake, that it ran for hundreds of miles. Half Moon Bay lies on the far side of the hills, a few miles further west.

The reservoirs were built in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to supply water to San Francisco, and they are still part of the system that brings water from the Hetch Hetchy Valley in the Sierra. The land around them is protected, and the lakes are closed to boats and swimmers, which keeps the water clean and the shores wild. A road runs along the dam, and you can stop at pull-offs to look at the water and hills. Bald eagles and ospreys fish here, and deer graze on the slopes.

Richmond is the East Bay city that built ships for a war. t.dawson creek@55.8,-120.2:

t.avila@40.7,-4.7:

t.huesca@42.1,-0.4:

t.bunbury@-33.3,115.6:
Bunbury sits on the coast of Western Australia about a hundred and seventy kilometres south of Perth, and it is the gateway to the south-west, the corner of the continent famous for tall forests, surf, caves and wine. It is a working port as well as a seaside city, and a place with a straightforward, friendly feel: broad streets, a long beach, and a scattering of big old pubs. Spring brings wildflowers, and from September to November humpback whales pass off the coast, visible from headlands. Summer is hot and dry with a risk of bushfire, so check warnings. t.sonora pass approach@38.3,-120.4:
This is the Highway 4 side of the Sierra, in the pines above Arnold, rather than the Sonora Pass road itself, which crosses the range further south on Highway 108. Arnold is the little mountain town nearby, with a few shops, a gas station and places to eat, and it is the main supply point on this stretch of road. Do not rely on any services on the high passes themselves. Fill up here, carry layers, and start early in the day.
t.tamparuli@6.1,116.3:
Tamparuli is a small town on the road from Kota Kinabalu toward Mount Kinabalu, about thirty kilometres from the coast. Leaving the coast, the highway runs flat and straight for a while, past rice paddies, villages of stilt houses and roadside stalls selling fruit, before it starts to rise. Past Tamparuli the bends begin, the temperature drops, and the Kinabalu massif can appear ahead, a long grey wall above the clouds on the clear mornings that often come before the haze. For fuel you will find stations in and around Tamparuli, but fill the tank before you climb: the road ahead is long, and prices up on the mountain are higher. t.kundasang@6.0,116.6:
Kundasang is a highland town below the huge shoulder of Mount Kinabalu, which at 4,095 metres is the highest mountain in Borneo and one of the most striking in Southeast Asia. The town sits well above a thousand metres, and the climate is a surprise to anyone who has come up from the coast: cool, damp, often wrapped in cloud, with farms of cabbage, carrots and tomatoes on slopes so steep it seems unreasonable. The nearby hot springs at Poring are a good reward after the mountain's cool.
t.kinabalu park@6.1,116.6:
Mount Kinabalu stands 4,095 metres above the north of Borneo, and it dominates the landscape from every angle, a huge granite dome that appears and disappears in cloud. The park at its foot, Kinabalu Park, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the richest places for plants on earth, with thousands of species, including orchids, rhododendrons and pitcher plants. The park headquarters sits at about 1,500 metres, so the air is cool and often damp, and the forest around is moss-covered and dripping. Take a jacket, because evenings are cold. Mornings are clearest, so enjoy the view of the summit before the clouds close in.
t.arnold california@38.3,-120.4:

The reward is a very quiet road, thick with pines, with granite domes, meadows and the gleam of small lakes.

Take fuel in Arnold, since there is none on the pass. Black bears are common in the area, and so are deer, so be careful at dawn and dusk. The best time to ride is from June to October, with wildflowers in July and aspen colour in late September. Pack a warm layer, because the temperature at the top can be freezing even in summer.
t.sonora california@38.0,-120.4:

Cold air and thin atmosphere at the top mean warm clothes are needed, and autumn is a good time to ride, with golden aspen along the streams.
t.dauria reserve@49.9,115.4:
The Daursky Nature Reserve lies in the south of Zabaykalsky Krai, on the border with Mongolia and China, and it is one of the great wild places of the Eurasian steppe. At its heart are the Torey Lakes, shallow salt lakes whose levels swing dramatically over the decades, filling to the brim in wet years and shrinking to stretches of cracked mud in dry ones. When they are full they draw swans, geese, cranes and countless waterbirds that gather on their way between Siberia and Asia, and the whole system is protected jointly with neighbouring reserves across the border.

There are no towns at the coordinates. The nearest real centre is Borzya, around a hundred kilometres to the northeast, and everything you need must come with you: fuel, water, food, a spare tube and the patience to deal with a puncture on your own. The tracks leading here are unsurfaced, with sandy patches, washboard, and sections that become impassable after heavy rain. Distances look short on a map and turn out to be long on the ground, and mobile coverage is patchy. Treat the trip like an expedition, tell someone where you are going, and do not set out in a bad forecast.

Because it is a protected zone, access is regulated. Permits and local rules may apply, especially close to the border and inside the core areas, so ask in Borzya or at the reserve office before you ride the last stretch. This is not mere bureaucracy; the steppe is fragile, and the wildlife is shy. Mongolian gazelles, known locally as dzeren, move across the plain in great herds, and Pallas's cat, a small, round-faced wild cat, hunts in the rocky outcrops, though you are far more likely to see eagles and hares than anything rare.

The best months are May to September, with early summer offering green grass and birdsong. Midsummer is hot and dry, with dust devils twisting across the flats, and autumn brings the migration. Light here is extraordinary, wide and clean, and the horizon is so low that the sky seems to take up most of the world. Take only photographs, keep to existing tracks, and let the silence do the rest.
t.cueva de los moros@42.7,-0.8:
There is a Cueva de los Moros in half the valleys of Spain. Every unexplained cave, ruin or rock shelter used to be credited to the Moors, and this one, in the hills of the western Aragonese Pyrenees between the valleys of Hecho and Ansó, is a rock shelter with ancient traces. You should approach it as an excuse to spend time in two of the most beautiful and least spoiled valleys of the Pyrenees, rather than as a monument.

The Hecho and Ansó valleys run north from the Canal de Berdún toward the French border, and they are full of stone villages with steep roofs, massive chimneys and wooden balconies. Hecho, with about a thousand people, keeps its own dialect, cheso, and Ansó is famous for its traditional costumes, worn at a festival each summer. The upper valleys are wild: the Selva de Oza, a forest of beech and fir at the head of the Hecho valley, and the Boca del Infierno, a narrow gorge where the road squeezes between rock walls above a roaring river.

The roads are narrow, winding and often in good condition, with little traffic outside the summer holidays. The road between Hecho and Ansó crosses a low pass through pine woods, a short and satisfying ride. North, the roads end in the mountains, and there are no passes into France here, so the valleys feel like dead ends in the best sense. Weather in the Pyrenees can change quickly, and snow is common in winter.

For fuel, head south to the Canal de Berdún or east to Jaca, a lively town of over thirteen thousand with a Romanesque cathedral and a pentagonal citadel. Hecho and Ansó have bars, small shops and restaurants serving hearty mountain food like migas, lamb and trout. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the forests are full of colour and the mountains are clear.
t.covalanas@43.2,-3.5:
Covalanas is known as the cave of the red deer. Its walls carry red ochre paintings of hinds, drawn in a distinctive dotted technique, and they are among the finest Palaeolithic paintings in the Cantabrian region. The cave sits on a steep, wooded hillside above Ramales de la Victoria, in eastern Cantabria, and it was one of the first painted caves to be recognised in Spain, in the early twentieth century. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Cave of Altamira and Palaeolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain, and visits are limited to small groups, so booking ahead is advisable.

The walk up to the cave is short but steep, with views over the valley. The landscape here is a karst of limestone hills covered in oak, chestnut and beech woods, with green meadows below, and the caves are numerous. Nearby, the Cullalvera cave in Ramales is open to visitors, showing a huge underground gallery whose entrance is so tall that the morning light reaches deep into it.

The Asón valley is great riding country. The road south from Ramales toward Arredondo and the source of the Asón river, where a waterfall drops from a cliff, climbs through narrow valleys with steep slopes, and the passes over to Burgos province, such as Los Tornos and La Sía, offer twisting roads with views over the mountains. Weather in Cantabria is changeable, with rain and fog common, especially in winter and spring, and the roads can be slippery.

Ramales de la Victoria is a small town of over two thousand people with fuel, bars and restaurants. Colindres and Laredo, on the coast, are larger towns, and Santoña, across the bay, is famous for its anchovies, cured and packed by hand. Try cocido montañés, a hearty bean stew, and sobaos pasiegos, a buttery sponge cake. Summer is the most reliable time for weather, but the crowds are biggest then, so consider late spring or early autumn.
t.friso abierto del pudial@40.7,-0.4:
Deep in the Maestrazgo of Teruel, where the Guadalope river carves its way between limestone walls, the rock shelters around Castellote and Molinos hold painted figures left by prehistoric communities. The Friso Abierto del Pudial is one of them, an open frieze on a sheltered rock face, part of the extraordinary chain of Levantine art sites listed by UNESCO. The figures are faint, and visiting typically means a walk on rough ground, but the setting alone is worth the effort.

This part of Aragón is wild and sparsely peopled. Castellote, with a few hundred residents, perches beneath a crag topped by the ruins of a Templar castle, and the Guadalope here forms a reservoir hemmed in by cliffs. Molinos is known for its Grutas de Cristal, caves with delicate formations and a small museum about cave bears, and the wider area is rich in dinosaur fossils; Teruel province is one of the leading places in Europe for them. Griffon vultures nest on the cliffs, and the scent of thyme and rosemary hangs over the hillsides on warm days.

The roads are the reason many riders come back to the Maestrazgo. They wind along gorges, climb to high plateaus at over a thousand metres and drop into green river valleys, with little traffic and often an excellent surface. Some routes have narrow sections, short tunnels carved into rock and unguarded drops, and wandering sheep or goats can appear round any corner. In winter, snow and ice are possible on the higher passes, and in summer afternoon storms can roll in quickly over the mountains.

Fuel is scarce in this corner. The nearest towns of any size are Andorra de Teruel and Alcañiz, both a fair distance away, so do not pass up a pump when you see one and carry enough range for the gorges.
