Village bars and family restaurants serve hearty food: roast lamb, migas made from fried bread crumbs with sausage and grapes, and the famous Teruel ham, which has its own designation of origin. Bring plenty of water for the walk to the shelters, as shade is limited.
t.chaussee et tunnel de san adrian@42.9,-2:
Imagine a mountain with a hole through it, and a medieval road running straight through the hole. The tunnel of San Adrián is a natural cave passage near the crest of the Aizkorri range, on the border of Gipuzkoa and Álava, and for centuries it carried one of the main routes between the Castilian plateau and the Basque coast. Pilgrims on the inland Camino de Santiago, merchants, armies and kings all passed through it, and a small chapel was built inside the cave. The old paved road leading up to it survives in sections, worn smooth by centuries of hooves and boots.

The tunnel lies within the Aizkorri-Aratz Natural Park, a range of limestone peaks and beech forests that reach well over a thousand metres. Shepherds still bring their sheep to the high pastures in summer, and the cheese made from their milk, Idiazabal, takes its name from a village not far away; Segura, one of the nearby towns, was a key stop on the road. The forests are carpeted with ferns and moss, and in autumn the beeches turn copper and gold. Mist often swirls around the summits, giving the walk up a slightly enchanted feel.

You cannot ride to the tunnel itself. The usual approach is on foot from the car park at the Otzaurte pass on the road between Zegama and Altsasu, a walk of around an hour each way on a good path, or from the Álava side above Zalduondo. The roads around are a pleasure: winding mountain routes through green valleys and small Basque villages, with frequent changes in weather. Rain is common all year, so expect damp patches, moss and cow muck on the road.

Fuel is available in Altsasu and other valley towns, and the villages have bars and asadores serving grilled meat and pintxos. Alavese villages such as Araia and Agurain sit on the plateau side, where the climate is drier and the landscape opens out into wheat fields. Pack a waterproof, good shoes and a torch for the tunnel, which is short but dark, and take your time on the polished stones of the old road.
t.vizcaya bridge@43.3,-3.0:
Few riders get the chance to cross a river hanging from a bridge, but at Portugalete you can. The Vizcaya Bridge, opened in 1893 across the mouth of the Nervión just downstream of Bilbao, is the oldest transporter bridge in the world: a tall iron structure from which a gondola, suspended on cables, glides from one bank to the other carrying cars, motorcycles, bikes and pedestrians in a couple of minutes. It was designed by the Basque architect Alberto de Palacio, often described as a disciple of Gustave Eiffel, to let tall ships pass beneath while still linking the two towns, and UNESCO listed it in 2006.

The bridge connects Portugalete, an old port town with steep streets and a Gothic church, with Getxo, the wealthy suburb where Bilbao's industrialists built grand villas along the shore. The contrast tells the story of the estuary: on one side the working-class towns that grew around the iron mines, steelworks and shipyards, on the other the mansions of the people who owned them. You can also take a lift to the top of the bridge and walk across the high walkway, with views down the estuary to the sea and up towards the city.

Riding in the Bilbao area is urban, busy and hilly. Traffic is dense, roundabouts frequent and parking tight, but drivers are generally disciplined. Once out of the city, the Basque coast and interior are superb for motorcycles, with twisting roads through green hills, fishing villages such as Bermeo and Lekeitio, and the cliffs and hermitage of San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, all within an easy day. The weather changes constantly, and rain is frequent all year, so expect damp patches even on sunny days.

Fuel, food and parking are plentiful in Portugalete and Getxo. Along the riverside promenade, bars serve pintxos, small snacks on bread, and a glass of txakoli, the slightly sparkling local white wine. Try grilled sardines or bacalao al pil-pil, salt cod in an emulsified garlic and olive oil sauce. If you take the gondola, ride on slowly, follow the staff's instructions, and enjoy one of the strangest short crossings in Europe.
t.las rozas i@40.7,-0.3:
The upper valley of the Guadalope in Teruel is a place where limestone has been folded, cut and carved into an extraordinary array of shapes: cliffs, gorges, natural arches and pinnacles, with the river winding between them in places of startling green. Near Castellote, the painted shelter labelled Las Rozas I is one of the sites of Levantine rock art listed by UNESCO. Its figures are faint and fragile, but they speak of people who hunted deer and ibex in these same valleys thousands of years ago.

Castellote itself is a striking village of a few hundred inhabitants, built on the side of a crag beneath the ruins of a Templar castle, with stone houses, arcades and a large church. Below it, the Guadalope has been dammed into a long reservoir held between cliffs, where the water takes on a deep jade colour in summer. The Maestrazgo, the historic region to the south and east, was a stronghold of the military orders in the Middle Ages and later a centre of the Carlist wars in the nineteenth century, and its villages still carry that history in their castles, walls and porticoed squares.

For riders, the roads of the Maestrazgo are a joy, with an abundance of curves, gorges and high plateaus, and often the road to yourself. Routes link Castellote with Molinos, Ejulve and Aliaga, crossing passes at over a thousand metres, while others descend through the Guadalope gorges towards Mas de las Matas and Alcañiz. Expect varying surfaces, occasional gravel, livestock and wildlife, and be aware that winters can be cold and icy, while summer storms can be violent.

Fuel is the main concern, as there are few stations in this sparsely populated region. Fill up in Andorra de Teruel, Alcañiz or one of the larger villages when you can. Castellote has bars and restaurants serving local dishes such as roast lamb, crespillos, fried borage leaves dusted with sugar, and the cured ham of Teruel. Stay overnight if you can, as the night skies here are some of the darkest in Spain.
t.abrigo del barranco hondo@40.8,-0.3:
Castellote is one of those villages in the Teruel Maestrazgo that seems to have been built by people who wanted to be left alone. Its houses pile up beneath a great rock wall topped by the ruins of a castle associated with the Knights Templar, and the Guadalope river winds below on its way into the Santolea reservoir. The Abrigo del Barranco Hondo, a painted rock shelter in a deep ravine outside the village, is part of the extensive collection of Levantine rock art scattered through these mountains, with small figures in red ochre that have survived on the stone for millennia.

The Maestrazgo is quietly one of the finest riding regions in Spain, and the roads around Castellote show why. The terrain is a jumble of limestone ridges, gorges and high plateaus, and the roads follow it faithfully, which means endless changes of direction, short steep climbs and descents into valleys where poplars line the river. Traffic is almost nonexistent outside the weekends, and the surface quality varies from fresh tarmac to patched and bumpy. Livestock and the occasional deer appear without warning, so it pays to ride with something in reserve.

The area is also rich in dinosaur fossils, and Castellote has a small paleontological centre linked to the Dinópolis network based in Teruel. Further along, the village of Molinos has the Grutas de Cristal, a show cave with fine formations that is cool to visit on a summer afternoon. Mas de las Matas, a little to the north, is a pleasant agricultural village with a handful of bars and shops on the main street.

The practical problem in this region is fuel. These are small villages, some of them with only a few hundred residents, and petrol stations are spaced far apart. The town of Andorra, about twenty five kilometres away, is the nearest of any real size, and Alcañiz to the north is the other reliable option. Fill up whenever you get the chance and do not assume the next village will have a pump. Winters are cold and can bring snow to the higher passes, while summer days are hot but the evenings cool down beautifully, which is when the Maestrazgo looks its best, with the rock walls glowing gold above dark pine.
Red sandstone is the first thing you notice. Between Albarracín, Bezas and Gea de Albarracín the ground turns the colour of rust, broken into towers, corridors and rounded boulders under a dense cover of maritime pine. This is the Pinares de Rodeno, a protected landscape in the Sierra de Albarracín, and its overhangs shelter some of the best-known Levantine rock paintings in Aragon, including pale and red bulls that seem far too large for the shallow hollows that hold them. The Abrigo de la Paridera de las Tajadas is one of these shelters, its name borrowed from the shepherds' pens, parideras, where ewes were brought to lamb under the rock.

The riding is a treat. A small road loops through the pine forest from Albarracín towards Bezas and back, narrow, often freshly surfaced, and full of short, flowing bends between the rock formations. The views are not wide, because the trees and boulders hem you in, but the colours shift constantly with the light, from a dull brick at midday to a deep glowing red in the evening. Watch for walkers and climbers parking along the verges on weekends, and for deer at dusk.

Albarracín itself, a dozen kilometres away, is one of the most striking small towns in Spain. Its houses, plastered in a pinkish render that matches the rock, cling to a ridge inside a loop of the Guadalaviar river, and a long line of medieval walls climbs the hillside above. For a few centuries it was the seat of a tiny independent kingdom, first under a Muslim dynasty and later under a family of Navarrese lords who refused to bow to Castile or Aragon. The town is busy at weekends but magical early in the morning before the coaches arrive.

For fuel and the full range of services, Teruel is the place, about twenty kilometres away, with its extraordinary Mudéjar towers and a firm claim to the best cured ham in the region under its own designation. Smaller villages like Gea and Cella have shops and bars but limited options for petrol. The Sierra de Albarracín sits high, and winters are properly cold, with frost and snow on the roads; spring and autumn bring the best riding weather, while summer days are warm but rarely oppressive at this altitude.
t.la covassa@40.3,-0.2:
Culla sits on a narrow rocky crest in the Alt Maestrat, the inland highlands of Castellón, its houses wrapped around the remains of a castle that once controlled a large swathe of these mountains. The Knights Templar held it in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and the village still has the feel of a lookout, with views in every direction over terraced slopes, stone walls and empty ridges. La Covassa, just below the village, is one of the many rock shelters in this part of Valencia that hold prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean rock art group that UNESCO protects across eastern Spain.

The roads in this part of the Maestrat are some of the most rewarding in the region for anyone who likes a constant stream of corners. From Benassal or Vilar de Canes the road to Culla climbs along hillsides in a long sequence of curves, mostly well surfaced but narrow and sometimes bordered by drystone walls with no margin for error. The traffic is light enough that you can settle into a rhythm, though agricultural vehicles and the occasional flock of sheep keep you honest. The light is clear and the air smells of thyme and dry earth.

It is worth knowing that the famous rock art of the Valltorta gorge, near Tírig and Coves de Vinromà, lies not far to the north east, with a museum explaining the paintings and guided visits to the shelters. Combining both makes a good day. Benassal, five kilometres from Culla, is known for its mineral spring water from the Font d'en Segures, bottled and sold well beyond the region.

Practical matters need attention up here. These are small villages, many with fewer than a thousand people, and fuel is scarce. L'Alcora, a ceramics town about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest larger place, and Vilafranca or Albocàsser can also be useful depending on your direction. Food is simple but good, with lamb, hearty stews and local cheeses. The Maestrat sits high and catches the weather from both the sea and the interior, so fog and cool winds are common, and winter can bring snow to the ridges. Above Culla, the massif of Penyagolosa rises to the west, the highest peak in the province and a fine destination for a separate ride.
t.llonin@43.3,-4.6:
The cave of Llonín is not one you can walk into. It sits in the valley of the river Cares in Peñamellera Alta, in the far east of Asturias, and it is one of the decorated Palaeolithic caves of northern Spain listed by UNESCO alongside Altamira. Its walls hold engravings and paintings of deer, goats and other animals, and the cave has been studied by archaeologists for decades, but access is restricted to protect the art. What you get instead is the landscape that sheltered those artists, and that is very much worth the trip.

This is the eastern gate of the Picos de Europa. The limestone walls rise sharply on both sides of the Cares and Deva rivers, green with oak, chestnut and hazel lower down and bare grey rock higher up. The roads around Panes and Alles are narrow and twisting, following the river bends and climbing in places to small villages perched on terraces. The surface is mostly good but can be damp and mossy in the shade, and fallen stones are not unusual after heavy rain. Traffic picks up in summer, especially on the main road through the Hermida gorge towards Potes, a deep, dark canyon where the road and river squeeze between cliffs for kilometres.

The Cares valley is also cheese country. Cabrales, the pungent blue cheese ripened in limestone caves, is made in the villages just to the west, and the local cider is excellent with it. Llanes, on the coast about thirteen kilometres away, is the largest nearby town, with a lively harbour, beaches and every kind of service, while Panes, much closer, has shops, bars and fuel for the immediate needs.

Potes, about twenty kilometres to the south east, is the main town of Liébana and the gateway to the monastery of Santo Toribio, which holds what is said to be the largest surviving fragment of the True Cross. Combining the caves, the gorge and the monastery makes for a classic loop. The weather here is changeable at best, with Atlantic rain and mountain fog arriving quickly, and the high roads into the Picos can be closed by snow in winter. Ride early in summer to beat the crowds and the haze.
t.jingdezhen handicraft porcelain industry:
For a thousand years, the best porcelain in China, and for much of that time the best in the world, came from Jingdezhen. The city, in the north east of Jiangxi province, grew up around imperial kilns that produced fine ceramics for the emperors, and its blue and white porcelain was exported across Asia, the Middle East and Europe. The secret of its success lay partly in the hills around the city, where the white clay known as kaolin was mined. The word kaolin itself comes from Gaoling, a village in the hills north east of Jingdezhen, where the clay was first dug. The point on this ride lies in that countryside, between the city and the old clay mines, in a landscape of wooded hills, tea plantations, rivers and villages.

The traditional porcelain industry involved a complex chain of skills, from mining and refining the clay to throwing, shaping, decorating and firing, and each step was done by specialist workers. The ancient kiln sites, such as Hutian, have yielded vast quantities of shards from different periods, and the old workshops and dragon kilns in the city, some of which have been restored, show how porcelain was made. Today, Jingdezhen is still a centre of ceramics, with thousands of artists and craftsmen working in studios and workshops, and its markets are full of porcelain of every kind.

Riding in China is complicated for foreigners. Foreign-registered vehicles need special permits and, in most cases, an accompanying guide, and foreign driving licences are not generally valid, so riders usually need a Chinese licence or join an organised tour. The roads in this part of Jiangxi are a mix of modern highways and smaller country roads, with traffic that can be heavy and unpredictable, including trucks, scooters, tractors and pedestrians. The countryside is green and hilly, with rice terraces and villages of whitewashed houses with black tiled roofs, in the traditional Huizhou style.

Jingdezhen, a city of several hundred thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the local food is spicy, with Jiangxi cuisine known for its use of chili peppers. The climate is subtropical, with hot, humid summers, heavy rain in spring and early summer, and mild winters. Autumn is the most pleasant season for travel.
t.hayedos de navarra aztaparreta@42.9,-0.8:
Aztaparreta is a beech forest that has been left alone. High in the Pyrenees of Navarre, at the head of the Roncal valley, in the karst massif of Larra-Belagua on the border with France, this forest has never been logged, and its trees, some of them centuries old, grow, die and decay naturally. It is one of the components of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a World Heritage Site that brings together beech forests from across the continent, from the Carpathians to the Pyrenees. Walking through it is like entering a cathedral, with tall grey trunks, a green canopy high above, and a thick carpet of moss and fallen leaves.

The Roncal valley has a strong identity. Its people were famous for their independence, and they have their own traditions, costumes and, until recently, their own dialect of Basque. Every year on 13 July, on the Piedra de San Martín pass on the border, the mayors of the Roncal valley and the neighbouring Barétous valley in France meet for the Tribute of the Three Cows, a ceremony that dates back to a medieval treaty settling disputes over grazing rights, and is said to be one of the oldest treaties in Europe still in force. The valley is also known for its cheese, Roncal, made from sheep's milk, with a protected designation.

The road from Isaba up through Belagua to the Col de la Pierre Saint-Martin, at 1,760 metres, is one of the great rides of the Pyrenees, climbing through beech and pine forests, past meadows full of cows and sheep, and onto the bare limestone of the high karst, with views over the mountains on both sides of the border. The road is well surfaced but narrow in places, with tight bends and steep sections, and livestock wander freely. Snow closes the pass in winter, and fog and storms can be sudden in summer.

Ansó and Echo, in the neighbouring valleys of Aragón, are lovely stone villages with traditional houses and good restaurants, and Isaba and Roncal have fuel and basic services. The nearest larger town is Oloron-Sainte-Marie, on the French side, about thirty six kilometres away. The weather is mountain weather, with cool summers, cold winters and rain at any time of year.
t.hocino de chornas@40.9,-0.7:
The Martín river cuts a deep, winding gorge through the limestone hills of Teruel, and its walls are full of shelters where prehistoric people painted animals, hunters and abstract symbols. The Hocino de Chornas, near Estercuel and Montalbán, is one of these sites, a narrow gorge with rock art on its walls, part of the Río Martín Cultural Park, which protects dozens of painted shelters along the river between Montalbán, Obón, Alacón and Ariño. The sites are part of the Mediterranean rock art group listed by UNESCO, and the cultural park has interpretation centres and guided visits that make the art more accessible than at many other sites.

The landscape is rugged and dry, with steep gorges, rocky hills and patches of pine and holm oak, and the river, lined with poplars, cuts through it like a green ribbon. Vultures soar overhead, and the cliffs are home to eagles and other birds of prey. In spring, the hills are covered in wildflowers, and the smell of thyme and rosemary fills the air.

This was also mining country. The area around Utrillas, Escucha and Andorra, to the south and east, was a centre of coal mining for much of the twentieth century, and the mining heritage is preserved in museums and old installations, while the great power station at Andorra, now closed, once dominated the landscape. Estercuel has a former convent, the Monasterio del Olivar, set in a quiet valley of oaks and olives.

The roads in this part of Teruel are quiet and winding, following the valleys and climbing over the hills, with little traffic and plenty of bends. The surfaces are generally good, but narrow, and there are few barriers. Fuel is scarce in the small villages, so fill up in Montalbán, about nine kilometres away, or in Andorra, a town of almost eight thousand people, about twenty six kilometres away. Services in the villages are limited, with small shops and bars, but the food is hearty, with lamb, migas, a dish of fried breadcrumbs with garlic and sausage, and the excellent hams of Teruel. The weather is continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and the gorges can be very hot in the afternoon, so plan your visit for the morning.
t.mascun v@42.3,-0.1:
The Barranco de Mascún is one of the great canyons of the Sierra de Guara, a limestone range in the pre-Pyrenees of Huesca, where rivers have carved deep, narrow gorges, caves and towers into the rock. The canyon, near the village of Rodellar, is famous among climbers for its overhanging walls and among canyoners for its pools and waterfalls, and it also holds traces of prehistoric painting in its shelters. Mascún V is one of these sites, part of the group of Mediterranean rock art sites listed by UNESCO, and the setting, with sheer orange and grey walls rising above the river, is extraordinary.

The Sierra de Guara is a wild, sparsely populated area, with abandoned villages, ancient bridges and a remarkable population of vultures, including the bearded vulture, which feeds on bones, dropping them from a height to break them. Rodellar, at the end of a long, winding road, is a small village that has become a base for climbers from all over Europe, with a campsite, a refuge and a couple of bars. The views from the village over the canyon and the surrounding peaks are superb.

The road to Rodellar is narrow and twisty, with tight bends, steep drops and rough sections, and it is a ride that demands concentration. The roads around the Sierra de Guara, linking Alquézar, Bierge, Adahuesca and other villages, are quiet and scenic, with views over the mountains and the plain. Alquézar, a stunning village of stone houses perched on a ridge above the gorge of the river Vero, with a collegiate church and castle at its top, is a highlight. To the north, the roads lead towards the high Pyrenees, with Boltaña, Aínsa and the Ordesa valley, offering some of the most spectacular riding in Spain.

Services in the Sierra de Guara are limited, so plan carefully. Alquézar and Boltaña have restaurants and accommodation, but fuel is scarce, and the nearest larger town is Huesca, about thirty two kilometres away, or Barbastro, to the south. The local wines of the Somontano region, around Barbastro, are excellent. The weather is hot in summer, especially in the canyons, and cold in winter, with snow on the higher ground. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, when the rivers are full and the weather is mild.
t.la joquera@40.0,-0.1:
Just behind Castelló de la Plana, where the coastal plain meets the first hills, the ravine of La Joquera cuts into the limestone near the village of Borriol. Its shelters hold prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin, and the area has been studied for its archaeology for decades. It is unusual to find such ancient art so close to a large modern city, and the contrast between the busy plain below, with its orange groves, factories and motorways, and the quiet hills above is striking.

Castelló is the capital of the northern province of the Valencian region, a busy, working city with a long history in ceramics and tiles, and the plain around it is one of the main centres of tile production in Europe. The city celebrates the Festes de la Magdalena every spring, a week of parades, fireworks and bonfires commemorating the founding of the city, when its people moved down from the hill of the Magdalena to the plain in the thirteenth century. Off the coast, the Columbretes islands, a volcanic archipelago, are a protected nature reserve, reachable by boat in summer.

The riding in the hills behind Castelló is a pleasant surprise. The Desert de les Palmes, a range of hills just north of the city, is a natural park with a Carmelite monastery, winding roads, and views over the plain and the sea. The road up to the monastery and the summit of the Bartolo, with its cross and antennas, is steep and twisty, with tight hairpins and spectacular views. Further inland, the roads lead into the Maestrat and the Alcalatén, with quiet mountain roads, small villages and the peak of Penyagolosa. Cyclists are common, especially on weekends, and the roads can be busy close to the city.

Borriol, about a kilometre away, is a small town with fuel and shops, and Castelló has everything you could need. The local food includes rice dishes, seafood from the port of El Grau, and the famous oranges, as well as the sweet pastries made for the Magdalena festival. The climate is mild, with hot summers and warm winters, and the sea breeze keeps the coast cooler in the afternoons. Inland, the hills can be much hotter in summer and colder in winter.
t.hermitage of san segundo@40.7,-4.7:
Outside the great medieval walls of Ávila, down by the river Adaja, a small Romanesque church stands among trees, quiet and often overlooked by the crowds heading for the walls and the cathedral. The Hermitage of San Segundo is dedicated to the first bishop of Ávila, according to tradition one of seven early missionaries sent to Spain, and it holds an alabaster statue of the saint at prayer, carved in the sixteenth century by the sculptor Juan de Juni. The building itself is simple and austere, with a beautiful carved doorway, and it is a lovely, peaceful place to visit. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Old Town of Ávila with its Extra-Muros Churches.

Ávila is best known for its walls, the most complete medieval circuit in Spain, with dozens of towers and nine gates, built from the late eleventh century onwards. Walking along the top of the walls, with views over the rooftops of the city and the plain, is the highlight of any visit. The city is also the birthplace of Saint Teresa of Ávila, the mystic and reformer of the Carmelite order, and the convent built on the site of her birthplace, along with the monastery of the Incarnation where she lived for many years, attracts pilgrims from around the world. The best view of the walls is from the Cuatro Postes, a small monument on a hill across the river, especially at sunset, when the stone glows gold.

The riding around Ávila is varied. The city stands on a high plateau, more than eleven hundred metres above sea level, and the plain around it is open and windswept, with long straight roads and wide views. To the south, the Sierra de Gredos rises steeply, with granite peaks, forests and rivers, and the roads that cross it, such as the Puerto del Pico, are some of the best in central Spain, with tight bends, steep climbs and views over the mountains. Snow can close the passes in winter.

Ávila, a city of over fifty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The local food is hearty, with chuletón de Ávila, huge beef steaks from the local black cattle, and judías del Barco, large white beans from El Barco de Ávila. The yemas de Santa Teresa, small sweets made from egg yolks and sugar, are a local speciality. The weather is continental, with hot summers and cold winters.
t.el pindal@43.4,-4.5:
On the coast of eastern Asturias, near the village of Pimiango, a cave opens in the cliffs above the sea, and inside, Palaeolithic artists painted and engraved animals on the walls: a mammoth, horses, a bison, a fish, and many red dots and signs. El Pindal is one of the caves included in the World Heritage listing of the Cave of Altamira and Paleolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain, and its location, with the sea pounding the rocks below and the Picos de Europa rising inland, is spectacular. Visits are limited and guided, to protect the paintings.

The surrounding area is the Asturian coast at its best, with green meadows running to the edge of cliffs, sandy coves, and the mountains close behind. Nearby Colombres is known for its grand houses built by indianos, emigrants who made their fortunes in the Americas and returned to build mansions in their home villages, often painted in bright colours, and one of them now houses a museum of emigration. San Vicente de la Barquera, just across the border in Cantabria, is a fishing port with a castle and a long bridge.

The riding here is wonderful. The coastal roads, along the cliffs and through villages, offer views of the sea and the mountains, and inland, the roads into the Picos de Europa, through the gorge of La Hermida or up to the lakes of Covadonga, are among the best in Spain, with dramatic scenery and winding roads. The weather is often damp and changeable, and the green landscape is the result of frequent rain. Summer is the best season, though it is also the busiest.

Llanes and San Vicente de la Barquera both have fuel, shops and restaurants, and the seafood is superb. Asturian cider, poured from a height into a wide glass to aerate it, is a local ritual, and the sidrerías are lively places to eat. Try fabada, a rich bean stew with sausages, and the local cheeses, especially Cabrales, a strong blue cheese ripened in caves in the Picos. Visits to the cave are limited and must be booked in advance, and the clifftop path near the entrance offers lovely views over the sea.
t.cueva de dona clotilde@40.4,-1.4:
The rock art in the Cueva de Doña Clotilde, in the pine forests outside Albarracín, is a little different from the typical Levantine scenes. Painted in white or pale colours rather than the usual red, the figures include schematic human shapes and animals, and they sit on the red sandstone of the Rodeno, a landscape of rust-coloured rocks and maritime pines that is now protected as a cultural park. The shelter is part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing, and the Rodeno is full of painted shelters, several of which, like the bulls of the Prado del Navazo, can be visited along marked paths.

Albarracín itself is one of the most beautiful towns in Spain, a medieval settlement of pink and ochre houses clinging to a rocky spur above a loop of the Guadalaviar river, surrounded by walls that climb the hillside above. It was the capital of a small Moorish kingdom in the eleventh century and later an independent lordship, and its narrow streets, wooden balconies and overhanging houses look almost untouched by time. In winter, snow and frost add to its magic; in summer, it fills with visitors.

The roads around Albarracín are superb for riding. The road from Teruel climbs through farmland and then enters the gorge of the Guadalaviar, with the town appearing suddenly on its rock. Beyond, the roads through the Sierra de Albarracín, towards the source of the Tagus and the Montes Universales, are quiet, winding and spectacular, through pine forests, limestone gorges and high meadows. Surfaces are good, traffic is light, and the air is fresh even in summer, though winters are harsh.

Teruel, twenty-five kilometres away, is the provincial capital, famous for its Mudéjar towers and the legend of the Lovers of Teruel, and it has fuel and everything else. Albarracín has restaurants, bars and hotels, and its cooking includes local ham from Teruel, lamb and migas, fried breadcrumbs with sausage. Bring warm clothing even in spring, as the altitude makes the nights cold.
t.chaves i@42.2,-0.1:
The Cueva de Chaves, in the foothills of the Sierra de Guara in Huesca, was one of the most important Neolithic sites in the Iberian Peninsula, with deposits showing some of the earliest farming and herding in north-eastern Spain. In 2007, in an act that caused outrage, the landowner bulldozed the cave's floor deposits, destroying much of the archaeological record, and the case went to court. Rock art shelters in the area, including Chaves I and others in the Vero river valley, survive and are part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing, with paintings ranging from Palaeolithic to schematic art.

The Sierra de Guara is famous for its canyons, deep limestone gorges carved by rivers, which attract canyoning enthusiasts from all over Europe. The village of Alquézar, perched on a rock above the Vero gorge with a castle and collegiate church at the top, is one of the most beautiful in Aragon, and the walkways through the gorge below offer spectacular views. The Somontano, to the south, is a wine region producing excellent reds and whites, and the town of Barbastro is its centre.

The roads around the Sierra de Guara are a joy, narrow and winding, with spectacular views over the canyons and the Pyrenees to the north. The road from Huesca through the foothills to Alquézar and on to Barbastro is a favourite, and the roads north into the Pyrenees, through Aínsa and towards the Ordesa valley, are among the best in Spain. Surfaces are generally good, but watch out for gravel and cyclists, and in summer, the heat can be intense.

Huesca, twenty-four kilometres away, is the provincial capital with fuel and everything else, and Barbastro has services too. Alquézar has restaurants and hotels, and the Somontano wineries welcome visitors. Try the local wines with ternasco, roast lamb, and the pastries of Huesca.
t.ceja de piezarrodilla@40.2,-1.3:
The Ceja de Piezarrodilla is a rock shelter in the mountains of southern Teruel, near the village of Villel and the Rincón de Ademuz, a curious enclave of the Valencian region surrounded by Aragon and Castilla-La Mancha. Its paintings, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing, include human figures and animals in the Levantine style, and they sit on the red sandstone that characterises this area. The landscape is rugged and dry, with pine forests, limestone cliffs and the valley of the Turia river, which flows south towards Valencia.

The Rincón de Ademuz is one of the most isolated parts of the Valencian region, with small villages perched on hills above the Turia, terraced orchards and vineyards, and a slower pace of life. Ademuz itself, the main village, has a church and a ruined castle, and the valley produces apples, walnuts and wine. Villel, on the Aragonese side, sits below a castle on a rock, and the road between Teruel and Ademuz follows the Turia through a series of gorges and valleys.

For riders, this is a quiet and rewarding corner of Spain. The roads along the Turia valley are winding and scenic, with little traffic, and the roads into the mountains, towards the Sierra de Javalambre and the Montes Universales, offer climbs, descents and views. Surfaces are generally good, but watch out for gravel and wildlife, and the winters are cold, with snow in the mountains.

Teruel, twenty-three kilometres away, has fuel and everything else, and Ademuz has a few shops and bars. The villages have bars and restaurants serving local food, including the cured ham of Teruel, lamb and migas. Carry water and fuel, as services are scarce in the mountains. Teruel itself is worth a visit for its Mudéjar towers, decorated with glazed tiles, and for the mausoleum of the Lovers of Teruel, the city's tragic legend.
t.bordeaux@44.8,-0.6:
Bordeaux makes a confident start or finish to a ride, and you feel it the moment you come along the left bank of the Garonne: a curved river front of honey-coloured eighteenth-century facades that runs for kilometres, the Place de la Bourse at its centre, and the shallow Miroir d'eau in front of it reflecting the whole thing back at the sky. The crescent bend of the river gave the city its old nickname, the Port of the Moon.

The money that built all this came from wine and from the port. For three hundred years after Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in 1152, Bordeaux belonged to the English crown, and the trade in claret to London set a pattern that never really ended. Later the port grew rich on Atlantic trade, including, it should be said, the slave trade, which the city now acknowledges in its museum. In the 2000s Bordeaux cleaned its blackened stone, brought back the tram and gave the quays to pedestrians, and the change was startling.

For riders the city is a place to arrive, not to ride. The ring road, the rocade, is busy and often jammed at rush hour; inside it, tram lines, cyclists, narrow one-way streets and a 30 km/h limit across most of the centre make for slow progress. Mind the tram rails in the wet. The best riding starts once you leave: north up the Médoc to the great chateaux of Margaux and Pauillac on the D2, east across the river to Saint-Émilion and the rolling Entre-deux-Mers, or south towards the pine forests of the Landes.

Food is the reason to linger. Canelés, the little caramel-crusted cakes, oysters from the Arcachon basin, entrecôte cooked over vine cuttings, and of course the wine, which is cheaper here by the glass than you would guess. Fuel is everywhere on the outskirts, less so in the centre; the large supermarkets along the rocade are the easy option. Summer afternoons can be properly hot and humid, so a morning arrival and an evening walk along the quays, when the stone glows and the whole city seems to be outside, is the way to do it.
t.landscapes of dauria@49.9,115.4:
Dauria is the great steppe that straddles the border between Russia's Zabaykalsky region and northeastern Mongolia, and it is one of the last places on earth where you can see a grassland ecosystem working on its own terms. UNESCO listed the landscapes of Dauria in 2017 as a joint Russian and Mongolian site, recognising the importance of its steppe, wetlands and wildlife. The scale is vast: rolling grasslands stretching to the horizon, dotted with lakes, under a sky that seems to go on forever.

The most remarkable thing about Dauria is its cycles. The Torey lakes and other lakes of the region fill and dry out over a period of about thirty years, driven by long-term climate rhythms, and the whole ecosystem adapts to these changes, with plants, birds and animals moving in response. Wetlands that are full of birds in one decade may be dry salt flats in another. Mongolian gazelles, the dzeren, migrate across the steppe in herds of thousands, and the area is a vital stopover for migrating birds, including rare cranes such as the white-naped crane and the hooded crane, as well as swan geese and bustards.

Riding here is an expedition, not a day trip. There are few paved roads, and those that exist are long and straight, connecting distant towns across the steppe. Most routes are dirt tracks, often unmarked, that can turn to mud after rain or become dusty and corrugated in dry weather. Fuel stations are very far apart, and towns are small. On the Russian side, Borzya and the villages near the Daursky reserve are the main settlements; on the Mongolian side, distances are even greater. Navigation, spare fuel and water, and self-sufficiency are essential, as is a vehicle suited to rough terrain.

The border itself is a serious matter: crossing points are few, and the frontier zone is controlled, with permits sometimes needed. Weather is extreme, with hot summers, bitterly cold winters, and strong winds at any time. Spring and autumn bring the bird migrations, and early summer the green flush of the steppe and wildflowers. For anyone who loves open spaces and wildlife, Dauria is unforgettable, but it requires careful planning and respect for its remoteness.
t.hayedos de navarra lizardoia@43.0,-1.1:
The Irati forest, straddling the border between Navarre and the French Basque Country, is one of the largest beech and fir forests in Europe, and Lizardoia is its wildest heart. This is a strictly protected reserve of primeval beech forest, where the trees have been left to grow, age and fall without human intervention, and it was inscribed in 2017 among Europe's ancient beech forests. Walking in the forest, you are surrounded by massive grey trunks, moss, ferns and the silence of a cathedral, broken only by birdsong and the rustle of leaves. Woodpeckers, including the rare white-backed woodpecker, live here, along with deer, wild boar and, in the high pastures, griffon vultures soaring overhead.

The forest has been used by people for centuries, for timber, grazing and charcoal. In the eighteenth century, the Spanish crown built an arms factory at Orbaizeta, using the forest's wood and iron from nearby mines to make cannonballs and weapons. The ruins of the factory, with its arches and canals overgrown with vegetation, are a striking sight in the valley below Lizardoia. Shepherds still bring their flocks to the high pastures in summer, and their stone huts dot the hillsides.

The riding here is some of the best in the Pyrenees. The road over the Port de Larrau, at around 1,570 metres, links the French village of Larrau with Ochagavía in Navarre, climbing through forest and over open mountain pastures with spectacular views of the Pic d'Orhy, the first two-thousand-metre peak of the Pyrenees from the west. The road is narrow, steep and twisty, with livestock wandering freely and no barriers in places; it is often closed by snow in winter. The roads to the Chalets d'Irati on the French side and to Orbaizeta on the Spanish side wind through the forest, with dense trees and damp, mossy surfaces.

There are no towns here, only small villages and mountain chalets. For fuel, Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, about twenty kilometres away, Mauléon and Ochagavía are the nearest options, and it is wise to fill up before setting out. Try the Basque cheeses, like Ossau-Iraty, made from sheep's milk, and the local trout, and bring warm clothes: the weather in the mountains changes quickly, with fog, rain and cold even in summer.
t.suso monastery and archaeological sites@:
In a quiet valley in the foothills of the Sierra de la Demanda, in La Rioja, two monasteries stand one above the other, and between them they tell a story that matters to hundreds of millions of people. The upper monastery, Suso, is small and ancient, built partly into caves on the hillside where the hermit Saint Aemilian, San Millán, lived in the sixth century. The lower monastery, Yuso, is a grand complex of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, sometimes called the Escorial of La Rioja. Together they were listed by UNESCO in 1997, recognised as the birthplace of the written Spanish language.

The reason is the Glosas Emilianenses: notes written in the margins of a Latin manuscript by a monk around the tenth or eleventh century, explaining difficult Latin words in the everyday Romance language that would become Spanish, along with a few words in Basque. These are among the earliest written examples of both languages. A little later, Gonzalo de Berceo, born in the nearby village of Berceo, became the first known poet to write in Castilian, composing poems about the saints in a simple, popular style. Visits to Suso are by guided tour, with a shuttle bus from Yuso; the cave tombs and Mozarabic arches are evocative.

The landscape is green and rolling, with vineyards, cereal fields and forests of oak and beech climbing towards the mountains. Rioja wine is everywhere: the area around Nájera and Haro produces some of Spain's most famous wines, and many bodegas offer tours and tastings. Santo Domingo de la Calzada, on the Camino de Santiago, has a cathedral famous for the live hen and rooster kept in a cage inside, in memory of a medieval miracle.

The riding is excellent, with quiet roads through the vineyards and up into the Sierra de la Demanda, where the roads climb through forests to the ski station of Valdezcaray above Ezcaray and over passes into the province of Burgos. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light. Watch for pilgrims on the Camino, cyclists and agricultural traffic during the grape harvest in autumn. San Millán de la Cogolla is a small village with a few restaurants; Santo Domingo de la Calzada, fourteen kilometres away, and Nájera have fuel and full services. Try patatas a la riojana, potatoes stewed with chorizo, and lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings.
t.xiacaopu iron production site of qingyan:
In the green hills of Anxi county, inland from the port city of Quanzhou in Fujian, the Xiacaopu site preserves the remains of an iron industry that flourished during the Song and Yuan dynasties, roughly from the tenth to the fourteenth centuries. Archaeologists found furnaces, slag heaps, ore-roasting pits and workshops on a hillside, evidence of large-scale production. The iron produced here was shipped down the rivers to Quanzhou and exported to Southeast Asia and beyond, and that is why the site is part of the World Heritage listing of Quanzhou, Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China, inscribed in 2021. At that time, Quanzhou was one of the largest ports in the world, visited by Arab, Persian and Indian merchants, and described by Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.

Anxi today is best known for something gentler than iron: tea. It is the home of Tieguanyin, the Iron Goddess of Mercy, one of China's most famous oolong teas, and the hills around are covered with neat rows of tea bushes on terraces. You will see tea farms, processing workshops and shops everywhere, and a cup offered with the traditional ceremony of small cups and repeated infusions is a good excuse for a break. Further inland, Dehua is famous for its white porcelain, the blanc de Chine that was exported to Europe in large quantities, and the ancient kiln sites there are also part of the World Heritage listing.

The roads through the hills of Anxi and Dehua wind through tea terraces, bamboo forests and valleys, with good asphalt on main roads and narrower lanes leading to villages. Traffic is lighter than near the coast, but trucks, scooters and pedestrians share the road, and driving can be unpredictable. Foreign riders should know that China does not recognise international driving permits, so a Chinese licence and proper registration are required, and many cities restrict motorcycles in central areas.

Longmen and the larger towns of Anxi county have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Quanzhou, a short drive away, is a large city with everything you need. Try the local dishes: noodles with seafood, braised duck, and the small pastries and sweets of southern Fujian, and do not leave without trying a proper Tieguanyin.
t.covacho ahumado@41.1,-0.7:
The name means the smoky little shelter, and it fits: a modest overhang darkened by soot, one of the rock art sites around Alacón in the Río Martín Cultural Park in Teruel province. The Martín river has carved canyons through limestone here, and its walls hold dozens of painted panels, from naturalistic Levantine hunting scenes to the later schematic style of stick figures and symbols. Alacón alone has several groups of shelters, and the park has an interpretation centre in the area to explain them.

This is a hard, beautiful land. Villages are small, Alacón has a few hundred inhabitants and Oliete and Muniesa not many more, and the hills around them are covered with almond trees, cereal fields and scrub. Griffon vultures ride thermals over the canyon, and in spring the slopes turn briefly green and yellow with broom. Summers are hot and dry, winters cold and windy, and the light is extraordinary in the evening when the rock glows orange.

The roads that link these villages are narrow, quiet and mostly well paved, with plenty of bends as they wander from plateau to river and back again. Expect gravel on the inside of corners, livestock now and then, and the odd tractor, but very little traffic otherwise. It is the sort of place where you can ride for an hour and see three cars. The way in from Andorra, the mining town to the east, and the road along the Martín toward Ariño and Oliete are especially rewarding.

Andorra de Teruel, the nearest town of size at about twenty four kilometres, grew around lignite mining and a big power station whose chimney once dominated the skyline. It is also one of the towns of the Ruta del Tambor y Bombo, the drum route, where during Holy Week thousands of people beat drums through the night, a tradition made famous by the film maker Luis Buñuel, who was born in nearby Calanda. If you are passing at Easter, the noise is unforgettable.

Fuel, supermarkets and proper restaurants are in Andorra; the small villages may have a bar, but do not count on a filling station. Bring water, especially if you plan to walk to the shelters, which usually involves a short hike on rough paths in full sun. A hat is not optional here in July.
t.torre de la iglesia de san martin@40.3,-:
Teruel is a small provincial capital high on the Aragonese plateau, and its skyline is made of Mudéjar towers, built by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons in brick and glazed ceramic tiles. The tower of San Martín, dating to the early fourteenth century, is one of the finest, a square tower straddling a street, so that traffic passes through an arch at its base. With the other Mudéjar towers of the city and the cathedral, it forms part of the World Heritage listing of Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon.

Local legend says that two Moorish builders, Omar and Abdalá, fell in love with the same girl, Zoraida, and competed to build the most beautiful tower. San Martín was finished first but began to lean, and its builder threw himself from it in despair, while El Salvador, the other tower, won the bride. It is a story, but it gives the towers personality. Teruel is better known for another romance, the Lovers of Teruel, whose mausoleum in the church of San Pedro draws visitors from all over Spain.

Teruel sits at over nine hundred metres, and winters here are among the coldest in Spain, with sharp frosts and snow. Summers are warm by day and cool at night. The air is dry, and the land around is a mosaic of eroded red badlands, ravines and juniper scrub.

For riders the city is a crossroads, not a destination for corners in itself, but what lies around it is excellent. The road to Albarracín, a medieval red stone town clinging to a ridge, is a must. The Sierra de Albarracín and the Montes Universales, south and west, are full of quiet, twisty roads with almost no traffic, and Gúdar-Javalambre to the east offers high mountain roads and ski areas. The A-23 motorway passes the city for quick links to Valencia and Zaragoza.

In the city, try jamón de Teruel, the protected cured ham, in one of the bars of the Plaza del Torico. Dinópolis, a dinosaur theme park, is outside town. Fuel and services are plentiful. Parking near the towers can be tight on old streets; leave the bike on the edge of the historic centre and walk.
t.la coquinera@40.9,-0.7:
You reach La Coquinera through some of the emptiest country in Spain. The rock shelter lies in the hills of the Río Martín Cultural Park, in the triangle between Oliete, Estercuel and Alacón, where the Martín river and its side ravines have sliced the Teruel plateau into terraces, cliffs and narrow gorges. The paintings here belong to the same Mediterranean tradition as the dozens of other panels in the park, figures of animals and people in ochre red, small enough that you have to stand close and let your eyes adjust before they emerge from the stone.

What strikes most visitors is the silence. The villages are tiny, a few hundred people each, many of them older, and the houses are built of the same honey coloured stone as the cliffs. Estercuel has a monastery, El Olivar, set among olive trees a short way outside the village, and Oliete sits on a bend of the river where poplars and vegetable plots make a green thread through the dry hills. The rocks around here are layered like the pages of a book, sediments laid down in ancient seas, and fossils are not rare on the tracks. Griffon vultures nest on the canyon walls, and you will often see a dozen circling at once.

For a rider the joy is the road network itself: narrow, winding, almost traffic free, rising from the river onto bare plateaus where the horizon opens in every direction and then plunging back down in a series of hairpins. Surfaces are mostly fine but patchy, and loose stones gather where farm tracks join. The cierzo wind can push hard on the exposed tops. Spring and autumn are perfect; July and August are blisteringly hot by noon, and in winter the plateau frosts over at night. Access to the shelter is on foot over a rough path, and the panels are usually fenced, with guided visits organised through the park.
t.el pendo@43.4,-3.9:
In 1997, in a cave that people had been visiting for over a century, a group of researchers noticed paintings that everyone had walked past: a frieze of red figures, deer, horses and goats, high on a wall in the main chamber. El Pendo, in the municipality of Camargo just south of Santander, had long been known for its deep layers of Stone Age occupation, but the frieze made it one of the important painted caves of Cantabria, and in 2008 it joined the World Heritage listing of the Paleolithic cave art of northern Spain alongside Altamira.

The cave opens at the foot of a wooded slope in a little valley, surprisingly close to the suburbs of the Santander bay. Visits are guided and limited in number to protect the art, so booking ahead is wise, especially in summer. Inside, the main chamber is huge, cool and damp, and the guides show the paintings with careful lighting.

Cantabria is green because it rains, and the weather turns quickly off the Bay of Biscay. On a bike, that means wet roads under trees, moss in the gutters and cow muck on rural lanes, but it also means lush valleys, limestone peaks and empty mountain roads just behind the coast. From Camargo, you can head south to the valleys of the Pas, home of the pasiegos, the herding families who move their cattle between stone huts on the slopes, and climb roads like the Puerto de la Braguía or the Puerto de las Estacas de Trueba, both twisting and steep with superb views. The sobaos and quesadas pasiegas, buttery sponge cakes and a set cheesecake, are local specialities sold in every village.

Camargo is a busy town of over thirty thousand, effectively part of greater Santander, with all the fuel, food and services you need. Santander itself has a handsome bay, beaches and the Magdalena palace on its peninsula. Peña Cabarga, a mountain topped with a monument east of the bay, has a road to its summit that gives a sweeping view over the whole area on a clear day. Rush hour around Santander is heavy, so time your ride to avoid it.
t.fujian tulou@25.0,117.7:
Picture a giant ring of rammed earth, three or four storeys high, with almost no windows on the outside and a single heavy gate. Inside, galleries of wooden rooms face a courtyard with an ancestral hall at its heart, and up to several hundred members of one extended family once lived within those walls. That is a tulou, and the hills of south-western Fujian are dotted with them, round and square, some centuries old, many still inhabited.

The location here lies in the Hua'an area, where the Dadi group of tulou is listed alongside the better-known clusters in Yongding and Nanjing counties on the World Heritage list. Eryi Lou, one of the most celebrated, is a great double ring of earth and timber with beautifully painted interiors. These buildings were built mainly by Hakka and Minnan clans from the fifteenth to the twentieth centuries, part home, part fortress, in a region where banditry and feuds made defence a family matter. Their walls, made of earth mixed with lime, sand and sometimes sticky rice and sugar, have survived earthquakes that flattened modern buildings.

The landscape is a soft, green tangle of hills, bamboo groves, terraced fields and tea gardens. Anxi, the home of Tieguanyin oolong tea, lies not far to the east, and you will see the neat contour rows of tea bushes on many slopes. The roads are mountain roads in the Chinese sense: long, well-engineered stretches mixed with older, narrower lanes, frequent tunnels on new highways, and switchbacks through the valleys. Rain is frequent, especially in spring and early summer, and typhoons can reach this far inland in late summer.

A practical warning matters more here than anywhere: riding a foreign-registered motorcycle in China requires special permits, a Chinese licence or temporary permit, and usually an organised escort, and many cities restrict motorcycles. Most travellers come through a specialist tour operator or rent locally under supervision.

Small towns in the area have fuel stations, noodle shops and simple guesthouses, and some families rent rooms inside the tulou themselves. Sleeping within those earthen walls, hearing the courtyard wake up at dawn with cooking fires and chatter, is an experience you will not easily forget. Try the local tea, and ask before photographing inside a family's home.
t.mongol daguur spna@49.8,115.1:
Mongol Daguur is a strictly protected area in the far east of Mongolia, in Dornod province, where the steppe rolls away towards the Russian and Chinese borders under a sky that seems twice the size of any other. Together with Russia's Daursky reserve across the border, it forms the Landscapes of Dauria, a World Heritage site covering one of the last great intact steppe ecosystems on Earth. There are no fences, no villages, barely any tracks, just grass, lakes, wind and wildlife.

The landscape is a mosaic of grassland, wetland and scattered lakes, some freshwater, some salty, that swell and shrink in long cycles of wet and dry years. Rivers like the Ulz wander slowly through it. In wet years the lakes fill with birds; in dry years they become cracked white pans. It is a crucial stop for migrating birds between Siberia and China, and home to rare cranes, including the white-naped and the red-crowned, as well as great bustards and swan geese. Huge herds of Mongolian gazelle sweep across the plains, and wolves follow them.

Riding out here is about navigation and self-sufficiency rather than corners. There are no paved roads near the reserve; the routes are dirt and grass tracks that split and rejoin and sometimes vanish altogether. After rain they become muddy and boggy, in dry weather dusty and corrugated. Entry into a strictly protected area normally requires a permit from the authorities, and riding off designated tracks damages the fragile steppe. Summer, from June to August, is the realistic season; winters are long and bitterly cold.

The people of this region are mainly herders, Khalkha and Buryat among them, living in gers and moving with their livestock. If you meet a herding family, you will likely be offered milk tea and dried curd, and a visit to a ger is a lesson in hospitality.

Choibalsan, the provincial capital on the Kherlen river, is the main supply point for this part of Mongolia, and you should carry enough fuel, water, spares and food for days, plus a satellite communicator. The rewards are immense: complete silence, enormous skies and a night sky so dense with stars it seems to press down on the grass.
t.chufin@43.3,-4.5:
The Nansa is one of the shortest and wildest rivers in Cantabria, running from the high mountains on the edge of the Picos de Europa to the Bay of Biscay, and halfway along its course, near the hamlet of Riclones, a cave opens in the limestone above the water. This is the Cueva de Chufín, where Palaeolithic people engraved and painted animals, signs and symbols on the walls thousands of years ago. It is one of the caves of the Cantabrian coast included in the World Heritage site of Altamira and Palaeolithic cave art of northern Spain.

The cave is small and the art is subtle: engravings of deer, horses and bison, and enigmatic signs in red pigment. What makes Chufín special is the setting. The entrance looks out over the river and the steep, forested slopes of the valley, and the approach is beautiful. Visits are limited, so check ahead if you hope to see inside.

The riding in the Nansa valley is superb. The road from San Vicente de la Barquera on the coast climbs up the valley through Puentenansa, following the river through gorges and green meadows, with tight bends and steep climbs. Further up, the road continues towards the Puerto de Piedrasluengas, a mountain pass with views over the Picos de Europa and the high plateau of Palencia. The surface is generally good, but watch for livestock, gravel and wet patches. Cantabria is green for a reason: rain is frequent, even in summer, so bring good gear.

The valley is a classic example of the green Spain of the north, with hay meadows, stone farmhouses, chestnut and oak woods, and cows grazing on steep slopes. Vultures circle overhead, and the river is home to salmon and trout. The villages are small and traditional, with stone houses and wooden balconies, and the people are known for their hospitality.

San Vicente de la Barquera, about eleven kilometres away, is a fishing town with a castle, a Gothic church and a long bridge across the estuary, and it has fuel, restaurants and accommodation. Cabezón de la Sal and Comillas, with its modernist buildings including a villa by Gaudí, are also nearby. Try cocido montañés, a hearty bean and cabbage stew, or sorropotún, a tuna and potato dish from the coast.
t.altxerri@43.3,-2.1:
The Basque coast between Orio and Getaria is a place where steep green hills fall straight into the Bay of Biscay, and Altxerri is a cave in those hills, a few kilometres from Zarautz, one of the great surf and holiday towns of the province. Zarautz has a long beach, a seafront promenade and over twenty thousand people, which means fuel, lunch and everything else you might need.

The cave is the reason people come. Its walls carry Palaeolithic engravings and paintings of bison, deer, horses and some animals that are hard to identify, made around the end of the last Ice Age, and it was added to the list of Franco-Cantabrian caves recognised by UNESCO. It is not a casual stop. Access is tightly controlled to protect the delicate surfaces, so visits are limited to small guided groups and need booking well in advance, and there may be times when no one goes in at all. Check before you set your route around it. If it is closed, the hills themselves are consolation enough.

On two wheels the area is short and twisty. The coast road between Zarautz and Getaria is a lovely bit of tarmac with views over the sea, but it is narrow and busy in summer, and the villages are full of day-trippers. Inland roads lead up through small farms, apple orchards and pine plantations, with plenty of tight bends and the occasional wet leaf on the surface. Rain here is frequent, so expect damp patches even on bright days, and fog on the ridges in autumn.

Getaria, the birthplace of Juan Sebastián Elcano, who completed Magellan's circumnavigation in 1522, and of the couturier Cristóbal Balenciaga, is worth the detour. It is also the home of txakoli, a young, slightly fizzy white wine poured from a height into the glass, and grilled fish is cooked on the pier. Orio, nearer the cave, is a fishing and rowing town with a quiet river harbour. The Camino de Santiago coastal route passes through both Orio and Zarautz, so you will see pilgrims with scallop shells on the verges. The best time is late spring or September, when the weather is mild and the summer crowds have thinned.
t.mas d en badenes@40.4,-0.2:
Mas d'en Badenes is a farmstead name rather than a village, and the coordinates take you into the high country of northern Castellón, in the Maestrat, about five kilometres from Villafranca del Cid, or Vilafranca as it is written locally. This is a thinly populated landscape of limestone plateaus, stone-walled terraces, holm oaks and old farmhouses, a world away from the beach resorts an hour to the east.

People lived here very early. The rock shelters of this region were painted by hunter-gatherers and early farmers several thousand years ago, with small, quick, lively figures of archers, goats and deer. They belong to the Levantine rock art tradition and were collectively recognised by UNESCO as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Several sites in this corner of the Maestrat are open to visitors or lie on marked paths, but many shelters are fragile and access is restricted, so a local information point is a better guide than a guess.

The roads are the real draw. From Vilafranca the N-232 climbs north towards Morella, and the smaller CV roads towards Culla and Benassal wind through ravines and over cols with an easy, flowing rhythm, with the surface mostly good and the traffic almost nil. This is high ground, about a thousand metres in places, so it can be cold and windy. Snow dusts the plateau now and then in winter, and sudden storms roll in on summer afternoons. Wind turbines stand on the ridgelines, and on clear days the sea shows as a thin line far off.

Culla, up a hillside with a castle ruin that once belonged to the Templars, is a lovely small village and well worth a coffee. Vilafranca is the place to look for a bar and a pump, though it is wise to arrive with at least half a tank, since the towns here are small and Sunday opening is thin. Local food is hearty, with lamb, cured meats, truffles from the wooded valleys and cheese, and the region is also known for its olive oil. Spring brings green fields and flowers, autumn mushrooms and golden oak leaves, and both are better than the baking heat of August.
t.monastery and site of the escurial@40.6,:
Philip II began the monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial in 1563 and it was finished in 1584, a short time for a building of its size. It sits on the southern slope of the Sierra de Guadarrama, about fifty kilometres north-west of Madrid, and the two towns beside it, San Lorenzo de El Escorial and El Escorial, are small, tidy and slightly prosperous, living partly off the building that gave them their name.

The king wanted something unusual: a monastery, a royal palace, a basilica, a library and a family tomb in one block. The architect Juan Bautista de Toledo drew up the first plans, and after his death in 1567 Juan de Herrera took over and gave the place its severe, plain, almost military look in grey granite. Nothing is ornamental for its own sake. Tradition links it to the victory over the French at Saint-Quentin in 1557, won on the feast of Saint Lawrence, which is why the monastery carries his name and why the gridiron on which he is said to have been martyred recurs in its imagery. Inside, the Pantheon of the Kings holds the Habsburg and Bourbon monarchs, and the library has a painted ceiling and shelves of manuscripts. The paintings include work by El Greco, Titian and Velázquez.

The ride up from Madrid is easy but not especially exciting, via the A-6 and then the M-505, or you can come by the quieter M-600 from Guadarrama. Better riding starts once you head out of town. The Puerto de la Cruz Verde and the road towards Robledo de Chavela offer fast bends through pine and oak woodland, and the climb up to the Silla de Felipe II, a group of granite blocks where the king reputedly sat to watch the work, gives a view over the whole complex. Autumn is lovely, with golden ash and chestnut trees, but this is high ground, at around a thousand metres, so winter mornings bring frost and sometimes snow. Summer weekends are crowded, and parking near the monastery is awkward.

Fuel and food are no problem. San Lorenzo has about eighteen thousand people, several petrol stations and plenty of restaurants, and the cafes around the square are the place for a long lunch. Go on a weekday, arrive early, and leave time for the gardens, which are free to wander and look over open country.
t.recodo de los chaparros ii@41.1,-0.6:
The Río Martín cuts a deep, narrow canyon through the dry limestone of the Bajo Aragón, in the province of Teruel, and the Recodo de los Chaparros, whose name means roughly the bend of the dwarf oaks, sits on that river a few kilometres from Albalate del Arzobispo. The land is rolling and almost treeless, covered in olive groves, almond trees and pale rocky fields, and it can feel like a different planet from the green north of Spain.

The river valley holds a good deal of Levantine rock art, painted in small shelters on the cliffs of the gorge by prehistoric hunters and herders, with deer and goats and human figures, many of them in red ochre. The Río Martín Cultural Park manages a set of sites and has an interpretation centre in Alacón, and a visit often needs a guide or a booking, because the paintings are delicate. Albalate itself has a former archbishop's palace and a Mudéjar tower, a reminder that this was a frontier land between Christian and Moorish Spain for centuries.

The riding is far better than the map suggests. The A-1402 and the minor roads that follow the river and cross the plateau are lightly used, the surface is usually decent and there are long open curves and a few tight descents into the gorge. Wind can be strong and the temperature swings are large: bitter in winter, with frost and sometimes snow, and hot in July and August, when the best plan is to ride in the early morning. Spring brings almond blossom and fresh green wheat, which turns the whole plateau soft and bright.

Albalate has about two thousand people and a station or two, but the larger town of Andorra, fifteen kilometres to the north and not to be confused with the principality, has nearly eight thousand people and a wider choice of fuel and food. This part of Aragon is famous for its olive oil, and for the Holy Week drumming of the villages, in which hundreds of drummers play together in the streets on Good Friday, a tradition recognised by UNESCO. If you happen to be there at Easter, hearing it in a square is unforgettable, though accommodation fills up and some roads are closed for processions.
t.iglesia parroquial de santa tecla@41.4,-:
Cervera de la Cañada is a village of a few hundred people in the hills south of the Jalón valley, in the province of Zaragoza, with a church of Santa Tecla whose brick apse is one of the finest examples of Mudéjar work in Aragon. The label puts you right in the village, and the town of Calatayud lies twelve kilometres away to the north-east, on the main road between Madrid and Zaragoza.

Mudéjar is the name for the style created by Muslim craftsmen who stayed on under Christian rule after the Reconquista. In Aragon they built churches and towers in brick, using geometric patterns, ceramic tiles and zigzag courses of bricks that look like lace against the sky. Because brick was cheaper than stone and the builders knew it well, the style spread through the region from the twelfth to the sixteenth century, and a group of its monuments is inscribed on the UNESCO list. The apse of Santa Tecla is a good illustration, with blind arcades and decorative panels that seem far too ornate for so small a place. Look at the details for a few minutes, because the village does not offer much else apart from a bar and a cluster of old houses.

The hills around are older still. A cave in this area has been studied for its prehistoric remains and its painted shelters belong to a wider zone of prehistoric art in the interior of Spain. Calatayud itself has Roman origins, in the nearby city of Bilbilis, where the poet Martial was born in the first century AD and to which he longed to return from Rome. The valley produces strong red wines from old Garnacha vines, and the sweet pastries of the town are sold in every bakery.

For riding, the secondary roads here are good fun. They wind between dry, ochre-coloured hills dotted with almond trees and old stone barns, with little traffic and the occasional blind crest, and in spring the almond blossom is lovely. Winters are cold and the plateau gets frost and strong winds, and summer is hot and dry with very little shade. Water is scarce here and the villages are small, so the sensible thing is to fill up in Calatayud, a town of twenty-two thousand people with several stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes. The Monasterio de Piedra, a waterfall park with a Cistercian abbey, lies about forty minutes south-west and makes a good detour.
t.hayedos de picos de europa cuesta fria@4:
The beech forests of Cuesta Fría cling to the north-facing slopes of the Valdeón valley, on the León side of the Picos de Europa, where the limestone mountains rise abruptly above the green of the Cantabrian coast. They are part of a group of old beech woods across Europe that UNESCO recognised for their natural value, because the trees here have grown with little human interference for a very long time. Posada de Valdeón, a village of a few hundred people, lies about five kilometres away.

Walking in them in October is one of the great autumn experiences of northern Spain. The trunks are grey and smooth, the leaves turn copper and gold and carpet the ground, and the light comes down through the canopy in long beams. Wolves, roe deer and the rare brown bear live in these mountains, and the capercaillie, a big woodland grouse, survives in small numbers, though you will be lucky to see any of them. The Cares gorge, the famous trail between Poncebos and Caín, is not far, and its narrow path above the river is one of the most-walked routes in Spain.

Getting there is half the pleasure. From Cangas de Onís the road climbs through the Desfiladero de los Beyos, a narrow gorge of vertical rock with the Sella river far below, and then goes over the Puerto de Pontón, at about 1,280 metres, before dropping to the Valdeón valley. The corners are tight, the surface is good in places and patched in others, and in the gorge the road is cut straight into the rock with little room to spare. The weather is a gamble. Clouds sit low in the valleys in the morning, thunderstorms break in summer, and snow may close the passes from December through March, so check conditions locally.

Fuel is the practical issue, as the villages in Valdeón and Sajambre are tiny and may not have pumps. Cangas de Onís, twenty-four kilometres or more from the forest, has six thousand people and several stations, and you should fill up before entering the mountains. The area is famous for Cabrales, a strong blue cheese ripened in caves, and for cider and fabada, the bean stew, while the village of Posada has simple places for a hot meal. Summer is crowded at the Covadonga lakes, but Valdeón stays quiet, and autumn is the glory.
t.abrigo de la fuente del cabrerizo@40.4,-:
Albarracín is a small walled town of rose-coloured stone, steep and narrow, built on a rocky bend of the Guadalaviar river in the Sierra de Albarracín, in the south of Teruel province. The Abrigo de la Fuente del Cabrerizo is a rock shelter about three kilometres away in the surrounding pine woods, in country of strangely red sandstone outcrops that locals call rodeno.

The sandstone is the reason for the rock art. In the shelters and overhangs of the Sierra, prehistoric people painted small red figures of hunters, goats and bulls, part of the Levantine tradition that UNESCO protects, and the region has one of the best concentrations in Spain. Many of the paintings are in the Pinares de Rodeno protected landscape, where marked paths lead between the rocks, and the walk through the pine woods is pleasant in itself. The shelters themselves may be fenced, and the paintings fade easily in the weather, so keep your distance.

Albarracín was once the capital of a small Muslim kingdom, a taifa ruled by the Banu Razin family in the eleventh century, and it later became an independent Christian lordship before it joined Aragon. The town's walls climb the ridge above, and the houses with their timber balconies lean over narrow lanes that were never meant for anything wider than a donkey. It is lovely in the early morning and very crowded at weekends in summer, and a motorcycle in the old lanes draws more attention than it deserves, so park outside and walk. The mountains around are the source of several great rivers: the Tagus, the Turia and the Júcar all rise within a short distance.

The road from Teruel, the A-1512, is a pleasant ride through pine forest with moderate curves and a decent surface, and the plateau beyond is high and open, around twelve hundred metres, so winters are cold and snow can fall from November through March. Teruel, twenty-seven kilometres away, has thirty-five thousand people and is the sensible place for fuel and a proper meal; Albarracín has several restaurants but I would not rely on a petrol station. The local specialities are the cured ham of Teruel, protected by its designation, and roast lamb, and the town's bakeries sell sweets made with almonds. Spring and September are the best times, and summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms.
t.galeria alta de la masia@40.6,-0.1:
Morella is one of those hill towns that makes you pull over for a photograph before you even know what it is. Its castle crowns a steep crag, its walls run down the slope in a ragged line, and the old streets climb in a spiral to the top. It stands at around a thousand metres in the Els Ports highlands in northern Castellón, near the borders of Aragon and Catalonia, and the surrounding country is wide, cold, windswept and dotted with stone farmhouses. The rock shelters nearby preserve some of the most famous painted scenes of Levantine rock art, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, listed by UNESCO in 1998.

The paintings, in red pigment, show small, lively figures: archers, hunters, animals, groups in motion. They were made by people who lived long before farming spread here, and the style has a delicacy that surprises many visitors. The galleries and shelters near Morella la Vella, a few kilometres from the walled town, are small and fragile, and access is often managed, so ask locally about visiting arrangements before you set off. Never touch the walls, which are far more delicate than they look.

Morella is a small town of under three thousand people, but it has fuel and plenty of places to eat. Try flaó, a local custard tart, and the roasted lamb and truffles of the region. The market and the old convent of Sant Francesc are worth a wander. Further out, villages like Forcall and Cinctorres are tiny, so fill up in Morella before riding the high back roads.

For a motorcyclist, this is excellent country. The roads over the highlands rise and fall in long, open gradients, with curves through pine and oak woods, and the traffic is almost nonexistent.
