Winters are very cold, with snow and frost, and the high roads can be icy, while summers are warm but pleasant, with cool nights. Spring and autumn bring the best light, and the views from the ridges stretch out to the Maestrat hills.
t.archaeological site of atapuerca@42.3,-3:
Atapuerca does not look like much from the road: low, scrubby hills, a railway cutting, oaks and gorse. But the limestone caves here have yielded some of the most important remains in the history of humanity. In the Gran Dolina, archaeologists found bones of Homo antecessor, around 850,000 years old, among the oldest human fossils in Western Europe, and in the Sima de los Huesos, a deep pit, they found the remains of at least twenty-eight individuals about 430,000 years old. UNESCO listed the site in 2000.

It is all deeply odd to stand over. The railway, built in the nineteenth century through a ridge, cut the caves open and led to the first finds, and since the 1970s teams have dug each summer, still finding new bones and tools. Visits to the excavation sites are by guided tour, booked through the foundation that runs them, so reserve ahead. The Museum of Human Evolution in Burgos, a short drive away, is excellent and puts the finds in context.

Ibeas de Juarros, the nearest village, has just a few hundred people, so for fuel, a decent lunch and supplies head into Burgos, about thirteen kilometres west, a city of nearly two hundred thousand with a magnificent Gothic cathedral, also a World Heritage Site. Local food is hearty: morcilla, the rice-filled blood sausage, roast lamb and wheaty bread. The Camino de Santiago passes through Atapuerca village, so you will meet pilgrims on foot in the lanes.

The countryside is high plateau, around a thousand metres, with wide horizons and strong wind, and the roads are straight, empty and smooth. Corners are few, but the long views are striking, with wheat fields turning from green to gold. Winters are very cold, with frost, fog and occasional snow, and summers are hot and dry. Spring and early autumn are comfortable. Take a jacket even in sunshine, because the air at this height cools fast once the sun drops.
t.cova remigia abric l@40.4,-0.1:
Ares del Maestrat hangs on a rocky crest in northern Castellón, one of the highest villages in the region, with a ruined castle above and a grid of narrow, stone-paved streets below. A few kilometres away the Gasulla ravine cuts a deep, wild line through the limestone, and its cliffs hold some of the great shelters of Levantine rock art. Cova Remigia, which has a number of separate shelters, or abrics, is among the best-known, with dozens of figures of archers, deer and ibex, many of them captured in mid-run. The Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula has been on the UNESCO list since 1998.

It is a remarkable place to experience, though it asks for effort. The ravine is rugged, the paths can be rough, and the paintings are small. Many of the shelters are fenced or accessible only with permission, so inquire locally before you set out. The Gasulla also has a rich natural history, with griffon vultures, wild boar and aromatic scrub, and the silence is broken only by wind and the occasional bell.

Benassal, five kilometres away, is a village of around thirteen hundred inhabitants with mineral water springs and some old stone mansions. Services are limited, and the nearest big town on the list, Alcalà de Xivert, is a long way off, so check the fuel gauge before the highlands. Food in this district is old-fashioned and good: lamb, black truffle in winter, and thick stews with local beans.

Riding to the ravine, the roads cross the Maestrat high country, with long, open sweeps, rock outcrops and almond or cherry groves in the folds. Traffic is almost nonexistent. Winter is cold, with snow some years, and July afternoons can be sharply hot, but the evenings are cool. May and October offer the sweetest weather, and mornings in the ravine, when light slants onto the cliffs, are special.
t.university and historic precinct of alca:
Alcalá de Henares has a talent for producing writers. Miguel de Cervantes was born here in 1547, and a house museum in the old town commemorates him. The university, founded by Cardinal Cisneros in 1499, was one of the earliest planned university towns in Europe and a model for institutions in the Americas, and its Renaissance and Baroque buildings, with their stone façades and courtyards, are the core of the UNESCO listing that Alcalá received in 1998 for its university and historic precinct. The Paraninfo, the ceremonial hall, is where the Cervantes Prize is presented each year.

Walk the Calle Mayor, a long, arcaded street, and you pass cafés, bookshops and the Corral de Comedias, a seventeenth-century theatre that is among the oldest in Europe. Storks nest on the church towers and the belfries, and in spring the rooftops are crowned with big, untidy nests. Alcalá is a city of about two hundred thousand, so fuel, food and parking are straightforward, though the centre is largely pedestrianised. The local custom is to go bar-hopping for tapas, with a small plate coming free with each drink.

Alcalá lies about thirty-five kilometres east of Madrid on the Henares river, a flat, open valley with fields and industrial estates, so the approach is by motorway and the immediate surroundings are busy. Madrid's own Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro, listed by UNESCO in 2021, are a short ride away on the same trip, and for riders the pleasure is to combine the old university city with the capital's great boulevards.

For a quiet ride, head north or east into the Alcarria, a land of olive groves, lavender and honey, where the roads are empty and the villages sleepy. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summers are hot and dry, with the town emptying in August. In early morning the light on the golden stone of the university is warm, and the sound of church bells carries across the square.
t.abrigo de los trepadores@41.1,-0.7:
The Río Martín runs through the dry hills of Teruel province in northern Spain, and the villages along its banks, Alacón, Oliete and Muniesa among them, are tiny places that seem to belong to a calmer century. The Abrigo de los Trepadores is one of the rock shelters of the area, part of a cultural park that protects the paintings found in the cliffs and gorges of the valley. Many belong to the Levantine tradition, small red figures of hunters and animals, and others are schematic, simple signs and stick-like human forms, painted by later peoples. The paintings can be hard to find without a guide, and access is regulated, so plan ahead.

The land is hard and beautiful. Low limestone hills covered with scrub, juniper and a few pines rise from a plain of almond and olive terraces, and in the evenings the cliffs turn orange. The Río Martín cuts gorges that are green at the bottom and bare above. This is the Bajo Aragón, a region of few people and long distances. The smell, especially in spring, is of thyme and rosemary, and the silence is real. Griffon vultures circle the cliffs, and in summer the heat is dry and extreme.

The riding is spare but pleasing. Narrow roads wind among the hills, crossing the river on old bridges, with long straights and a few good bends where they climb out of the gorge. Traffic is almost nonexistent, which means you can enjoy the road without anxiety but should also remember that help can be a long way off. The surface can be rough in places, with loose gravel on the edges and the occasional farm vehicle.

Facilities are scarce. Alacón, Oliete and Muniesa have a few hundred inhabitants each, and while you may find a bar for a coffee, fuel is not guaranteed, so fill up in a larger town such as Alcañiz or Andorra before you head into the hills. Carry water and food, and tell someone where you are going. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summer can be fiercely hot, and winter nights are cold with frost on the higher ground.
t.abrigo de los toros del barranco de las:
The Sierra de Albarracín is one of the highest and emptiest corners of eastern Spain, a limestone and sandstone country at the headwaters of the Tagus and the Turia, and it holds an exceptional concentration of rock art. The Barranco de las Olivanas shelter is one of many painted sites in these hills, and it is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO. The pictures of bulls and hunters belong to a tradition of red paintings made thousands of years ago, though the exact age is still debated, and the shelter is far from the nearest village, so reaching it takes planning and a walk.

The land here is wide, rolling and lonely, with pine forests, dry meadows and outcrops of red sandstone known as rodeno, which gives the region its warm colour. Just to the north is Albarracín itself, a medieval town of pink-washed walls, steep lanes and ramparts climbing a rocky spur above the Guadalaviar river, which is one of the loveliest towns in Spain and well worth a detour. Villel, Villastar and Gea de Albarracín are small farming villages, each only a few hundred people, quiet and often shuttered at midday.

For a rider the area offers open, beautiful roads. The highway climbs and rolls across the high plateau, with long views and few other vehicles, and side roads wind into forested valleys with a pleasing mix of bends and straights. At altitude, the weather can be cold and changeable, and frost or snow is possible from late autumn to spring. The surface is usually decent, though rough on minor roads, and wildlife such as deer and wild boar can wander across at dusk.

There is little fuel in the villages themselves, and the nearest real services are in Teruel, Albarracín or Cuenca, so fill up before heading deep into the sierra. Albarracín has plenty of cafés and restaurants serving the local roast lamb and cured ham. Summer is warm during the day and cool at night, and the best months are May, June and September, when the light is clear and the hills are quiet.
t.abrigo de arilla@42.3,-0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is the southern edge of the Pyrenees, a rough range of sandstone and limestone where rivers have cut deep, dark canyons that are among the best in Europe for canyoning. The Abrigo de Arilla lies in that country, well off the main roads, in the lonely hills between Alquézar and the Sierra, and is one of the rock shelters of the Río Vero cultural park. The paintings are mostly Levantine and schematic, thousands of years old, and are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. Reaching the shelters generally requires a walk, and regulations apply.

Alquézar is the village to know in the area, a medieval hill town built around a collegiate church on a rocky spur above the Vero river, with arcaded streets and a long walkway along the canyon walls. It is deservedly popular, so go early or late. The region is also the home of the Somontano wine area, around Barbastro, whose reds and whites are good enough to deserve a place at lunch. In the Sierra the great bearded vulture, the lammergeier, nests on the cliffs and can sometimes be seen cruising the thermals with its wings held straight.

The riding is first class. Roads wind through the foothills with a series of long, flowing curves, climb in tight turns to viewpoints over the sierra, and plunge into gorges with sudden changes of light. Traffic is light outside August, and the surface is mostly good, though minor roads can be narrow and rough. The weather can change quickly in the mountains, and storms in summer can be violent, so check the sky in the afternoon.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Alquézar and the villages nearby have a few hundred people each, so fill up in Barbastro, which is a much larger town, before heading up into the hills. Bars in the villages serve coffee and good sandwiches, and in Alquézar a dinner of local lamb with Somontano wine is worth the effort. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and warm days, while the high roads are cold in winter.
t.abrigo del arquero@40.7,-0.4:
Castellote is a small, grey village in the Maestrazgo, the high, dry upland of eastern Teruel, built round a ruined castle that once belonged to the Templars. The Abrigo del Arquero, the Archer's Shelter, is one of the rock shelters in the cliffs of the area, with painted figures in the Levantine style, including archers, from which it takes its name. It belongs to the Mediterranean Basin rock art group that UNESCO listed in 1998. The shelter lies in the hills several kilometres from Castellote, and the walk in takes some effort.

The country of the Guadalope river is a land of cliffs and gorges, with pine woods, scrub and stony fields in between. The Maestrazgo is thinly populated, and the villages are old, with stone houses and arcaded squares. Molinos, to the south-west, is known for its caves, the Grutas de Cristal, a lovely cavern of white crystalline formations. The sky is large, the air clear and the nights dark, and the smell in summer is of thyme and hot stone.

For a rider the Maestrazgo is a fine area. The roads are quiet, with a good succession of curves, climbs to passes with long views and descents into gorges. Traffic is minimal, and the surface is generally fair, though winter frost damages minor roads and the heat in summer can be fierce. The weather at altitude is changeable, and storms in late summer can be violent, so check forecasts. Wildlife, including deer and boar, can cross the road at dusk.

Castellote and Molinos are small, with limited facilities, and Mas de las Matas, a larger village with a population of nearly fifteen hundred, has fuel and shops. Alcañiz, a good distance north, is much larger, so fill up there if in doubt. Local specialities include cured ham, lamb, and a rich dessert of almonds and honey. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and summer is hot by day but cool by night.
t.abrigo de la higuera del barranco de est:
The Río Martín country of Teruel is a place of deep gorges and bare, honey-coloured hills, and Oliete and Estercuel are two of its tiny villages. The Abrigo de la Higuera del Barranco de Ester is a small shelter in a side ravine, named for the fig tree that grows at its mouth, and it holds paintings that belong to the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, as protected by UNESCO. The pictures include the small red figures of the Levantine tradition, and the setting, under an overhang of golden rock, is a good place to sit and think about how few things have changed in the landscape.

The land has a stark beauty. Limestone cliffs rise from the river, with juniper, rosemary and pine on the slopes, and the fields of almond and olive are laid in terraces in the valleys. Oliete is a place of quarries, and a pale stone from the area has been worked for centuries. The sky is huge, and at night the stars are among the brightest in Spain, since there is almost no light pollution. Griffon vultures and eagles circle the cliffs by day.

The riding is quiet and pleasing, with narrow roads that wind through the gorges and across the plateau, a good rhythm of bends and short straights, and views that open without warning. Traffic is almost absent, and the surface is generally fair, though minor roads may be rough or washed out after rain. The summer heat is intense, and the best riding is in spring and autumn. In winter, frost and ice are possible on the high ground.

There is little fuel in the villages, and it is best to fill up in Andorra, which is larger, or in Alcañiz, before heading out. Oliete and Estercuel have a few bars, and in a good one you will find strong coffee and a plate of cured ham. Carry water, and let someone know your route. The paths to the shelters are rough, so wear proper shoes.
t.cingle de palanques abrigo b@40.7,-0.2:
Morella is one of the great walled towns of eastern Spain, a stack of grey stone houses wound round a conical hill in the high country where Castellón meets Teruel, and the whole thing is crowned by a castle that looks like it was carved from the summit. The medieval walls run for more than two kilometres, the main street is lined with arcades, and a Gothic basilica dedicated to Santa María holds a remarkable choir in the middle of the nave. Every six years the town holds a festival called the Sexenni, with processions and dancing in honour of the Virgin of Vallivana. Outside the festival years, the place keeps a quiet, mountain dignity, and the cheese, truffles and lamb are all good.

The Cingle de Palanques is a rock band in the hills a few kilometres away, in the Ports region, and the shelters in it are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO protects. The paintings are in the Levantine tradition, red figures of archers and animals, and the setting is dramatic, with cliffs above a dry ravine and views across oak woods. Access is on foot and usually needs local guidance, and the paintings are fragile, so touching is out of the question.

Riders know this area as some of the best in the whole Spanish east. The roads out of Morella climb over passes among rolling pastures, with long, open bends and the occasional steep hairpin, and the villages are sparse, so the road feels empty and generous. At more than a thousand metres, it is cooler than the coast by many degrees, and spring brings snow on the tops while the valleys are green. Autumn gives clear light and gold in the oak leaves. Winter can be icy, and mist is common.

Morella is the nearest place for fuel, with petrol stations, supermarkets and several restaurants serving local specialities such as flaó, a sweet cheese tart, and the town's hearty stews. Forcall and Aguaviva are smaller, with a bar or two. Fill the tank in Morella before heading into the hills, and if you stay overnight, stand on the walls at dusk, when the lights come on and the wind drops.
t.jiaotan firewood production area@29.6,11:
Jiaotan is a name that points back to fire. The area lies in the hills of northern Jiangxi, not far from Jingdezhen, and its role in history was to supply fuel, firewood and charcoal for the great kilns of the porcelain capital of China. Jingdezhen has made porcelain for more than a thousand years, and from the Ming dynasty it supplied the imperial court with blue-and-white ware, exported around the world. Making porcelain needs three things: fine clay, water and a huge amount of heat, and the kilns consumed whole forests of pine, which had to be cut in the hills and floated down the rivers to the town.

The stone half of the story belongs to the Changling mining site on the other ride, and the word kaolin itself comes from Gaoling, a village in the hills near Jingdezhen where the white clay was mined, and it is one of the few Chinese words to have entered English through the porcelain trade. Together these places, with the kilns, the clay mines and the fuel zones, form a landscape of production that scholars are working to record and protect, as part of the old ceramic system. I cannot say what stands at this precise point, but the surroundings of forested hills, tea terraces and clear streams tell the story well.

The countryside is green and humid, with bamboo groves, pines and small villages, and the air in the early morning can be misty and fragrant. Summer is hot, sticky and thundery, spring is damp and the best time is October and November, when the air is clear and the leaves turn. Winters are cold and wet.

A practical word: riding in China as a foreign visitor is a bureaucratic project, as foreign motorbikes need special permits and registration, and independent touring is difficult, so most people reach the area by train or car with a guide. Jingdezhen, about thirty kilometres away, is a city of several hundred thousand people with fuel, hotels and restaurants, and its ceramic quarter, with working studios and the old kiln museum, is the real attraction. Buy a small bowl or cup straight from the kiln, and have a plate of local noodles with meat and vegetables.
t.monte castillo el castillo@43.3,-4.0:
Some of the oldest paintings in Europe sit in a hill above a village best known for its hot springs. The cave of El Castillo opens in the flank of Monte Castillo, right above Puente Viesgo in the Pas valley of Cantabria, and inside it are hand stencils and a red disc that scientists dated, in 2012, to more than forty thousand years ago. That makes them contenders for the oldest cave art known on the continent, and possibly older than any made by modern humans, since Neanderthals were around at the time. UNESCO lists the Cantabrian caves, and a visit means a guided group entering in small numbers, so book ahead and expect limits on the day.

The Pas valley is green all year, and the roads show it. From Torrelavega the main road climbs gently through meadows, eucalyptus plantations and stone villages, with the river beside you and mist hanging on the slopes. Beyond Puente Viesgo the road continues toward the Pas passes, where the bends tighten and the views open onto steep grassy ridges dotted with cattle. Rain is frequent here, so a waterproof is not optional, and in wet conditions the surface can be greasy under the trees. The best riding is in late spring and early autumn, when the air is fresh and the mountains clear.

Puente Viesgo has about two and a half thousand people and a long history as a spa, with warm mineral water that has drawn visitors since the nineteenth century. There is a petrol station within reach and a handful of places to eat, and Torrelavega, nine kilometres away, offers everything else. Try the local dairy, such as quesada or sobaos pasiegos, light sponge cakes baked in the valley.

Monte Castillo has several caves, and they differ in what they offer, so ask at the visitor centre which are open. After your visit, walk down to the river and listen. The place feels private and strangely patient, as if the mountain had been keeping its secret long enough to forget it was one.
t.abrigo contiguo a la paridera de las taj:
Albarracín is the town every Spaniard has a photograph of, and with good reason. Its pink-ochre walls climb a rocky spur above a bend in the Guadalaviar river, a medieval fortress-town whose streets are so narrow and steep that cars were long ago banished from the old quarter. Not far off, the Pinares de Rodeno, a forest of pines growing on red sandstone, hides dozens of shelters with prehistoric paintings, also on the World Heritage list. The paridera of the label is a shepherd's stone pen, a humble relic of a pastoral world that endured in these hills for centuries.

The riding is simply excellent. The road from Teruel to Albarracín crosses a high, open plateau and then drops into the river valley through a landscape of red rock, juniper and pine, with views at every bend. Beyond the town, roads climb into the Montes Universales, a high, cold range where the Tagus, the longest river in Iberia, has its source, along with the Guadalaviar and the Júcar. Winters are severe, with snow and ice, and summer nights can be chilly, so pack a layer. Spring and autumn offer the clearest light and the best colour.

Teruel, twenty kilometres away, is a city of about thirty-five thousand people and the reliable place for fuel and food. Its Mudéjar towers, built by Moorish craftsmen under Christian rulers in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries, are listed by UNESCO, and the tower of San Martín, one of the best, is covered in ceramic and brickwork. The city is also famous for its cured ham, protected by a designation of origin, and for the legend of the Lovers of Teruel, a medieval tragedy that is celebrated in a festival each February.

Gea de Albarracín and Albarracín are small, so do not rely on them for fuel late in the day. In the town itself, leave the bike at the car park and walk, because the lanes are steep and cobbled. At sunset, when the walls glow rosy, you will understand why people come here.
t.cerrada del tio jorge@40.2,-1.3:
A cerrada, in the dry uplands of Teruel and Cuenca, is a place where the land closes in: a narrow gorge, a pinch in the valley wall, the sort of spot where a shepherd could shut a flock in for the night and be done. Tío Jorge, Uncle George, is one of those anonymous local names that outlast any record of who he was. The coordinates sit on the high limestone country south-west of Teruel, in the broad uplands between the Albarracín hills and the headwaters of the Turia, a landscape of pine, juniper, red soil and big skies. I cannot tell you what is marked on the ground at this exact point, but I can tell you what surrounds it.

The villages are tiny. Villel and Villastar each hold a few hundred people, and Teruel, the only real town in reach, is some twenty-four kilometres off. That distance matters, because the places in between are quiet in a way coastal Spain forgot long ago. Fill the tank in Teruel before you come. The roads are narrow and often empty, running along river terraces and over low passes in easy curves, with a gravelly surface in places and the occasional flock of sheep that will take its time. Winter is hard on this plateau, with deep frost and snow, so spring and early autumn are the sensible months.

Villastar has one real surprise. On a rock outcrop above the village, the Romans and the local Celtiberians left an inscription at a sanctuary, a long Celtiberian text carved into the rock, one of the longest of its kind. It is a reminder that this thinly peopled country was a crossroads of languages and gods long before it was emptied. The river Turia, which gathers here from the Montes Universales, runs on toward Valencia, and by the time it reaches the sea it has watered some of the richest orchards in Spain.

Back in Teruel, the old Mudéjar towers, with their glazed green ceramic and patterned brick, are worth an hour, and the city celebrates the Vaquilla del Ángel in July with a good deal of noise and wine. After a day among juniper and silence, a table of local ham, bread and strong red wine feels about right.
t.fronton de la tia chula@41.0,-0.7:
The frontón of a Spanish village is a plain wall with a flat court in front of it, where the pelota ball is hit against stone, and in tiny places like Oliete it is still the centre of summer evenings. The Tía Chula in the name was presumably someone local, and the frontón is the label's starting point, but the real attraction nearby is the land: a dry, hilly part of Teruel province where the Martín river cuts its way through limestone. Oliete is part of the Río Martín Cultural Park, a protected district that brings together rock shelters, old mining villages and gorges in a single trail of heritage sites.

The village is small, with fewer than five hundred people, and the Sierra de Arcos rises above it with a skirt of pine and scrub. Roads in this part of Teruel are quiet and empty, winding between hills with long views and a good surface, though patched in places. Spring and autumn are best, as summer heat bakes the stone, and winter nights can be bitter. A short ride brings you to Alacón, another village of a few hundred, with a church tower and a reputation for the best rock art in the district.

Fuel is a point to plan. Andorra, the Aragonese one, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest real town with nearly eight thousand people and several petrol stations, and it is the place to eat as well. Andorra grew up around coal mining, and the old pits and the old power station tell the story of a region that once produced much of Aragón's energy. Oliete is also remembered for its pottery tradition, though I would not promise you an open workshop.

The gorge of the Río Martín, called the Estrechos, is a short drive away and worth the detour, with a narrow channel, steep walls and a strong sense of enclosure. Look up and you may see vultures circling on the thermals. In the evening, as the light drops, the village square fills with the sound of children and the thud of a ball against the wall, the oldest form of entertainment in the place.
t.covacho esquematico@41.1,-0.7:
Some shelters hide in plain sight, and the covacho esquemático is one of them, a shallow overhang in the limestone above the Río Martín, with a few schematic figures painted in red. Schematic art is the shorthand of prehistory, stripped to essentials: a stick-like human, a dot, a zigzag, a sun disc. It belongs to a later phase than the more naturalistic hunting scenes of the Levantine tradition, and it is found across the Iberian peninsula, here in the district around Alacón and Oliete in Teruel province, which forms part of the Río Martín Cultural Park.

The ride is a pleasure in its own right. This is the Spain that city people call empty, a district of small villages, old stone terraces and wide, quiet landscapes, where it is possible to ride for an hour without meeting another vehicle. The roads curve with the contours of the land and the surface is mostly sound, with patches of gravel and the odd pothole. Distances are longer than they look, and signal is patchy, so carry water and a charged phone. Late spring, when the broom is yellow and the fields are green, is a lovely season, and early autumn brings clear light and cool mornings.

Alacón has only a few hundred inhabitants and Oliete a few more, so do not expect more than a bar or a village shop. Andorra, over twenty kilometres away, is the town for fuel, a meal and a bed, and a good base for exploring the cultural park. Ariño, nearby, has a former opencast mine whose scale is striking, a reminder of how much coal came out of the ground here. The contrast between the delicate painted shelters and the vast industrial pit is part of what makes this corner of Aragón interesting.

When you stop at the shelter, take a few minutes simply to look. The paint has survived because the rock is dry and the site is sheltered, but it is fragile, so keep to the path and do not touch. From the overhang, the view over the valley is calm and wide, with just a hawk in the sky and a faint smell of rosemary on the wind.
t.luoyang bridge@25.0,118.7:
The Luoyang Bridge, also called the Wanan Bridge, spans the Luoyang River in Quanzhou prefecture, Fujian, a few kilometres from where the river meets the sea. It was built in the eleventh century, in the Northern Song dynasty, under the direction of Cai Xiang, the local governor and a noted calligrapher. It is a long stone beam bridge, with huge granite slabs laid across stone piers shaped like boat prows, so that the current is split rather than resisted. It was a real engineering achievement, because the estuary has strong tides, and the builders used an unusual technique: oysters were encouraged to grow on the piers and cement them to the foundation, a living mortar that strengthened the structure over the years.

Today the bridge is a quiet monument, with stone guardian figures, pavilions, and ancient inscriptions, and with views over the tidal flats, where fishermen and oyster farmers work at low water. Quanzhou itself was the great port of Song and Yuan China, visited by Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, and its history of Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants adds a cosmopolitan flavour to the whole area, visible in old mosques and temples.

Riding here is coastal-plain riding, with flat roads, junctions, scooters and lorries, and a great deal of local activity. It is not a spirited ride, but the contrast of old stone and modern factory belts is interesting. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summer is hot and humid with typhoon risk in late season, and winter is mild. Mornings are best for the soft light over the water, and for catching the low tide when the mudflats shine.

The town of Luoyang, practically next door, has fuel stations, small restaurants and local seafood, and Quanzhou, about half an hour away, offers every service you could need. Try the oyster omelette or the thin-skinned local noodles if you see them. Foreign riders in China need to consider licence and permit rules in advance, and a local guide or arranged vehicle is common for travellers. Visit the bridge slowly, since the stone slabs are slippery in the wet, and take time to read the inscriptions even if you cannot decipher them.
t.ancient villages in southern anhui xidi@:
Xidi is a village that seems to have been left alone by the twentieth century. It lies in Yi county, on the southern side of the Yellow Mountains in Anhui, a landscape of green hills and rice fields where merchants of the Huizhou region made fortunes in salt, tea, timber and ink, and spent them at home on houses. The Hu clan, who founded the village, built lanes of whitewashed, black-tiled houses with high walls, carved wooden screens, small courtyards, and stone-framed doors, and in the sixteenth century they put up a great stone memorial arch in honour of an official of the clan. The name means west stream, after the water that runs through the village in channels beside the lanes.

Xidi and nearby Hongcun are listed together by UNESCO as the Ancient Villages of Southern Anhui, and the result is a living museum. People still live in the houses, hang out washing, cook on the street and sell tea, bamboo shoots and souvenir paper umbrellas. Ang Lee used the area for scenes in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, and since then visitors have arrived in numbers. Rise early, or arrive in the late afternoon, and you will see the lanes without a crowd, with mist in the fields and chimneys smoking.

Riding in Anhui is lovely in principle, with roads that wind through bamboo forest and tea terraces to villages with ink-wash views, but the practical position is that foreign riders need Chinese licences and plates, which are hard to arrange. Visitors usually go with a driver or by bus from the town of Huangshan, about thirty-eight kilometres away. Spring brings rapeseed flowers, golden yellow, and mist, and autumn is clear and cool. Summer is hot and rainy, and winter can be cold and damp.

Huangshan is a city of about seventy-seven thousand, and has fuel, hotels, a railway station and the full range of food. In the villages, you can eat Huizhou dishes, such as stinky mandarin fish, bamboo shoots and tofu cooked on a stone griddle. A ticket for Xidi usually includes entry for a number of days, and the same ticket may cover Hongcun, so keep it. Wear shoes with grip for the worn stone, and carry some cash for stalls and small guesthouses.
t.monte castillo la pasiega@43.3,-4.0:
Puente Viesgo has the strange distinction of being a Cantabrian village of about two and a half thousand people that sits under one of the most important prehistoric hills in Europe. Monte Castillo is a steep, cone-shaped limestone mountain beside the River Pas, and it is riddled with caves. La Pasiega is one of four that have been explored and painted on a grand scale, the others being El Castillo, Las Chimeneas and Las Monedas. Together they form a small campus of Ice Age art, and people travel from across the world to look at them.

La Pasiega takes its name from the Pas valley and its cattle-herding pasiegos, the mountain people who have kept cows on these hills for centuries. Inside, the cave is a series of galleries and side passages decorated with red and black paintings of horses, deer, bison and ibex, along with signs, grids and dots whose meaning is still debated. It is one of the Cantabrian caves where the old question of Neanderthal art keeps coming up, as new dating work has been attempted on some of the red marks in this part of Spain. Treat any firm claim with a pinch of salt; it is a lively argument.

Visits are by guided group only, with strictly limited numbers to protect the air and the paintings, so book ahead online or by phone, especially in summer and around Easter. There is a modern visitor centre at the foot of the hill, where you can learn about the caves before going up.

The ride itself is classic Cantabria. The N-623 climbs from Santander country through Puente Viesgo and Santiurde de Toranzo toward the Puerto del Escudo, with green meadows, small stone villages, and a mountain pass that sweeps over into Burgos. Expect cooler weather and mist in the morning; Cantabria is a wet corner of Spain and the road can be damp even when the sky looks clear.

Fuel and food are straightforward. Puente Viesgo has bars and a few small restaurants, and Los Corrales de Buelna, nine kilometres away, is the larger town for pumps. Try a cocido montañés or a sobao, the local butter sponge, if you want something local.
t.abric del mas del moli de la cova@40.4,-:
The Maestrat is the old Valencian highland, a country of bare limestone, stone-walled fields and farmhouses called masos, and the name of this shelter refers to one of them: the mas of the mill at the cave. It is a very long way from the beaches that most people associate with Castellón. The shelter lies a few kilometres from Villafranca del Cid, known in Valencian as Vilafranca, which sits at roughly a thousand metres on a plateau where the winters are cold and the summers are mercifully fresh.

Painted shelters like this one are part of the Levantine rock art of eastern Spain, in which tiny red figures of archers, deer and wild goats are drawn under rocky overhangs. The tradition stretches across the Mediterranean side of the peninsula, and the Maestrat holds some of its most important sites. UNESCO recognised the group in 1998. It is easy to imagine why prehistoric hunters would have loved this region: the valleys hold water, the ridges give a view, and the game would have been plentiful.

Culla and Benassal are the villages to know. Culla crowns a rocky hill with the remains of a medieval castle and has a beautiful old centre of narrow lanes, while Benassal is known across Spain for its spring water and for the quiet, handsome stone houses in its streets. The area also makes good sausages, cured ham and truffles in the colder months, which any local bar will happily put in front of you.

The riding up here is excellent, which is not the usual reputation of Castellón. The roads rise from the coast through gorges, then open onto an undulating plateau with long views and open bends. Traffic is light, the surface is mostly good, and there is the sensation of being in a proper mountain region. Pick a spring or autumn day, because snow and fog are real possibilities in winter and the sun can feel fierce in August.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The villages here are small, and the nearest large town is l'Alcora, well over thirty kilometres away. Villafranca del Cid, with a couple of thousand people, is your best local bet, but fill up beforehand if you can.
t.hayedos de ayllon montejo@41.1,-3.5:
Beech trees at the southern edge of their range look different from the northern kind, and anyone who has stood in the Hayedo de Montejo in October will tell you why. This is a small forest on the northern slopes of the Sierra del Rincón, in the far north of the Madrid region, above the village of Montejo de la Sierra, and it is the southernmost beech wood in Europe of its type. It survives in a cool, damp pocket left over from the last Ice Age, and in 2017 it was added to the UNESCO list of ancient and primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and other regions of Europe.

The forest itself is protected, and walking in it needs advance booking and a guide or a permit, with limited numbers allowed each day. That is worth knowing before you ride up, because turning up on a whim in autumn, when everyone wants to see the leaves, will probably end in disappointment. Check the official arrangements first.

The ride makes up for any red tape. The roads that climb from the A-1 corridor into the Sierra del Rincón are narrow, quiet and rural, with stone villages, hay meadows and views toward the Guadarrama range to the south. Corners are friendly, the road surface is mostly good, and there are long stretches where you meet only a tractor. In autumn the hillsides turn gold and copper, in winter there may be snow or ice at this altitude, and in spring the meadows fill with flowers. Summer is warm in the day and cool at night, a relief from Madrid.

The region was once sheep country, part of the network of cañadas along which flocks walked between summer and winter pastures, and there are still shepherds' huts and stone enclosures if you look. Wildlife includes roe deer, wild boar and a good many birds of prey.

Montejo and the nearby villages are small, and fuel is not guaranteed, so fill up along the A-1 or in larger towns on the way. Bars serve hearty food, and a plate of roast lamb or a stew of beans is just the thing after a cool day in the hills.
t.abrigo de los dos caballos@40.4,-1.4:
Red rock and green pine make an unusual pair in Spain, and Albarracín has built a landscape out of it. The hills west of the town are the Pinares de Rodeno, a protected area where rodeno sandstone, a rusty red, has weathered into rounded boulders and little overhangs under a cover of pines. Those overhangs, sheltered from rain and wind, are where prehistoric painters did their work, and the Abrigo de los Dos Caballos is one of the shelters the Albarracín area is known for. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition, part of the group inscribed by UNESCO in 1998, and they show animals, hunters and humans in rust-red pigment on the sandstone.

Albarracín is the sort of town that gets under your skin. It sits in a loop of the Guadalaviar river, which later becomes the Turia that reaches Valencia, with its pink-ochre houses stacked up the hillside and a long run of defensive wall climbing the ridge above. In the eleventh century it was the seat of a small Muslim kingdom ruled by the Banu Razin, and after the Christian conquest it remained a semi-independent lordship for a while. The wooden balconies and narrow, stepped lanes feel like a film set, though people really do live here, and the best time to walk them is early morning before the day trippers arrive.

The ride is the Sierra de Albarracín, a high plateau of juniper, pine and bare rock, often over a thousand metres. Roads are quiet, with long open bends and good views, and the air is cool even in summer. Winter brings snow and ice, and the area is among the coldest in Spain, so check conditions before travelling in the colder months. Spring and autumn are lovely, with clear light and wild herbs scenting the verges.

Teruel, twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest large town and the place for fuel in quantity, although Albarracín is a small place and may have services. Eat well when you get there: cured Teruel ham is famous, and the local bars also serve roasted lamb and migas.

Walk the shelters carefully, since the sandstone is soft and the paint is thin.
t.monte castillo las chimeneas@43.3,-4.0:
Everyone talks about Altamira, but Monte Castillo has a better claim to the title of Europe's oldest gallery. El Castillo, the cave that gives the hill its name, contains a red disc that was dated in 2012 to more than forty thousand years ago, which makes it among the oldest known cave paintings anywhere. Las Chimeneas, the cave marked here, is one of its neighbours inside the same hill, and the whole mountain is a kind of honeycomb of Ice Age art.

The Chimeneas cave takes its name from the vertical shafts, the chimneys, that connect its galleries, and its walls hold animal drawings and a good number of the tangled finger lines that archaeologists call macaronis, made by dragging fingers through soft clay. It is a dark, narrow place, and the guides who take small groups through it do so with a care that tells you how fragile it is. Bookings are essential, and the number of visitors per day is deliberately small, so look up the arrangements before you set out.

Monte Castillo is a limestone cone rising straight out of the Pas valley, and the village of Puente Viesgo sits at its foot, famous since the eighteenth century for its warm mineral springs, which still feed a spa. The river here runs clear over round stones, and the oaks and chestnuts on the slopes shade the road. In the morning mist drifts down the valley and lies in the meadows like milk.

Riders will want to continue up the valley. The road climbs from Puente Viesgo toward the Puerto del Escudo, one of the classic Cantabrian passes, with a long series of curves, steep green slopes, and views that open out once you clear the forest. The surface is mostly good, though wet and slippery in the damp weather the region is known for. Early autumn gives the best compromise of dry days and quiet roads.

Fuel is available in Torrelavega, a town of fifty-five thousand, about nine kilometres from the cave, and Puente Viesgo itself has bars and a few restaurants.
t.monte castillo las monedas@43.3,-4.0:
Las Monedas is the cave that took its name from a handful of small coins, and the story says a lot about the place. Monte Castillo, at Puente Viesgo in Cantabria, has been known as a prehistoric hill since the early twentieth century, and visitors have been coming here for centuries, leaving behind bits of themselves. The coins were found in the cave, and the name stuck.

Las Monedas is different from its neighbours. Most of the paintings here are black, drawn in charcoal or manganese, and they show horses, bison and deer in lively, confident outline, including a reindeer, which is a rarity among Spanish cave art and a reminder of how cold this region once was. The cave has a series of chambers decorated with great skill, and the guides who take small groups through are used to being asked how it was done. The answer, as best anyone can tell, is simply by hand, with torches or lamps and a lot of patience.

The valley below is the land of the pasiegos, the cattle-herding people of the Pas valley, whose summer huts dot the hillsides and whose butter-rich sobaos and quesada pastries are sold in every bakery. The cows grazing the steep meadows are a main feature of the landscape, and the green of the grass is almost startling. It rains here a lot, and the mist often clings to the ridges well into the morning.

The roads of the Pas valley rank among the best in northern Spain. They wind up from Puente Viesgo through oak woods and villages of stone houses with wooden balconies, climbing toward the Puerto del Escudo and the high pastures. Gradients are steady, bends are open, and traffic is usually light. Wet roads are the rule rather than the exception, so tyres and caution matter more than speed.

Los Corrales de Buelna, about nine kilometres away, has fuel and larger shops, and Puente Viesgo has a small selection of cafés and places to eat. Reserve your cave visit well ahead, particularly at weekends.
t.torre e iglesia de san pedro@40.3,-1.1:
Teruel has a legend, and the legend has a tomb, and the tomb stands next to the church marked here. The tower of San Pedro was built in the Mudéjar style, the art of Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Brick, glazed ceramic and geometric patterns that look like woven cloth cover its surface. Together with the other towers of Teruel and a handful of buildings across Aragon, it is part of the Mudéjar Architecture group that UNESCO inscribed in 1986 and extended later.

The legend is that of the Lovers of Teruel, a young man and a woman who loved each other against the wishes of her family and died of grief. Their mummified bodies lie in a mausoleum beside the church, and the story has been retold in poems, plays and music for centuries. Whatever the truth, it has made the city a minor place of pilgrimage for romantics, and the mausoleum, with its alabaster sculpture of the two figures reaching toward each other, is worth the small admission.

Teruel is a handsome city, with arcaded streets, ceramic towers and a lovely main square, the Plaza del Torico, named for the small bull on its column. It also has a strong sense of humour about its position: the province is one of the least populated in Spain, and local people long ago adopted the slogan Teruel existe, Teruel exists, to remind the rest of the country they were there. Teruel's cured ham has a protected name, and so does its cold winter weather, since this is one of the coldest cities in Spain.

For riders it is a base rather than a destination. The old town is compact, with narrow one-way streets, so park outside and walk in. From the city, roads fan out to the Sierra de Albarracín to the west, the Maestrazgo to the east and the Javalambre mountain to the south, all with quiet, rewarding riding. Summer is dry and hot by day, and winter can bring snow and ice.

With thirty-five thousand people, Teruel has all the fuel, food and rooms you could want.
t.el cerrao@40.9,-0.7:
The Río Martín is a modest river by Spanish standards, but it has carved one of the most interesting canyons in Aragon, and the Cultural Park that takes its name protects an extraordinary collection of rock art. El Cerrao is one of the shelters in that park, in the district of Montalbán in the province of Teruel, among cliffs of pale limestone above a dry valley. The paintings here belong to the Levantine tradition and are part of the group UNESCO inscribed in 1998.

Montalbán is a handsome small town of fewer than fifteen hundred people, with a medieval church and the ruins of a castle that once belonged to the Order of Santiago. The country around is called the Bajo Aragón, a landscape of olive terraces, almond trees, cereals and sparse pine, scattered with villages whose names, like Alcaine, Ariño and Albalate del Arzobispo, tell you something of the region's Moorish and ecclesiastical history. Coal mining shaped Ariño and nearby Andorra, and the old workings still scar the hills.

Further east is Calanda, the birthplace of the film director Luis Buñuel, and the home of a Holy Week tradition in which thousands of drummers fill the streets at the same moment, a sound that is exciting and a little overwhelming. If you are in the region at Easter, you will hear it for miles.

On the road the pleasure is solitude. Routes through the Río Martín valley are lightly used, with open bends, long views and good surfaces on the main roads. In summer the heat is fierce and the shade scarce, and in winter the cold can be sharp, with fog collecting in the valleys. Spring and autumn are the easy seasons, and the light on the limestone is beautiful.

Fuel is available in Andorra, a town of nearly eight thousand people about twenty-six kilometres away, and Montalbán may have a pump, though it is wise not to rely on it. Carry water, because the shelters are dry and exposed.
t.barrio del san anton@40.1,-2.1:
Cuenca stands on a spur of rock between two gorges, and the Barrio de San Antón is the part of the old city that most visitors miss. The upper town has the cathedral and the famous Casas Colgadas, the hanging houses that overhang the Huécar gorge, and it gets all the attention. San Antón lies lower, near the junction where the Huécar meets the Júcar, and its streets are quieter and more residential. The whole walled town was inscribed by UNESCO in 1996 as an outstanding example of a medieval fortified city adapted to a difficult site.

The label here connects the barrio to the Marmalo painted shelters, which lie to the south-east in the hills of the Cuenca Serranía. That link is a reminder that the province has some of the best-preserved prehistoric art in inland Spain, and that Cuenca makes an excellent base for visiting it. The city is also known for its museum of abstract art, housed in the hanging houses, which shows the paintings of a group of artists who settled here in the 1960s.

Food in Cuenca has a mountain heartiness. Look for morteruelo, a rich pâté-like dish of game and liver, or zarajos, which are lamb intestines wound around vine shoots and grilled, an acquired taste that many people love. For something sweet, alajú is a traditional cake of honey and almond, made with Moorish methods. Whatever you order, the bread will be good.

For the rider, the route to Cuenca is a pleasure in itself. Roads from Valencia and Madrid run across the high, empty plateau of La Mancha and its borders, then plunge into the deep gorges of the Júcar and Huécar. A short ride north takes you to the Ciudad Encantada, a natural labyrinth of limestone pillars shaped by water and wind. The roads here are well maintained, with long curves and scenic stretches. In winter ice and snow are possible, and summer is hot but dry.

Cuenca has fifty-five thousand people, so fuel and rooms are no trouble. The old town is steep and cobbled, and traffic is restricted, so park on the lower edge and walk up.
t.cova remigia abric ii@40.4,-0.1:
The Gasulla ravine near Ares del Maestrat is among the best places in Spain to understand why Levantine rock art matters. Cova Remigia sits on the rim of that gorge, a cliff-lined cut through the limestone of the Maestrat, and it is where Juan Bautista Porcar, a local priest and amateur archaeologist, recognised the paintings in the 1930s that made the area famous. The panels show archers, hunters and animals in a lively dark red, in scenes of movement that do not look like anything else from the period.

On a motorcycle the approach is part of the draw. The roads here run between Ares, Benassal and Culla over high country, farmed in terraces and fenced with dry-stone walls. Corners are frequent and well-judged, if sometimes tight, the climbing is gradual, and you come over each crest to find another wide view of grey rock and green pines. Culla, with its ruined castle that once belonged to the Templars, is only a short ride on and is a lovely place for coffee, on a ridge that feels remote even in August.

Benassal, five kilometres away, is the sensible base. It has a handful of places to eat, a reputation for spring water and truffles from the surrounding oak woods, and a sleepy main street of old stone houses. It is a small town, though, so do not expect to find fuel at midnight. Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres off towards the sea, is the sure thing; Vilafranca, about twelve kilometres away, is a smaller alternative.

Be ready for fencing and, in places, for restricted access, because the paintings are fragile. The Parc Cultural of Valltorta-Gasulla manages the area, and the Valltorta museum is the right place to ask which shelters can be visited. Do not touch the rock, and do not sprinkle water on the paintings to see them better, which, regrettably, people have done and which ruins them. A morning start gives the best light on the ravine wall and spares you the worst of the summer heat.
t.church of santa maria de la cabeza@40.7,:
Ávila is the highest provincial capital in Spain, at about 1,130 metres, and you feel it in the air even in summer. Its walls, begun in the late eleventh century and finished in the twelfth, run for around two and a half kilometres with 88 towers and nine gates, and they are among the best-preserved medieval city walls in Europe. The Church of Santa María de la Cabeza stands just outside the old town, close enough to the ramparts that a rider can park and walk in a few minutes, and it belongs to the group of Romanesque churches that UNESCO added to the old town's listing.

The ride to Ávila from the Madrid side is a pleasure in its own right. The road climbs through the pine forests of the Sierra de Guadarrama and the granite country of the Meseta, with the Sierra de Gredos filling the southern skyline, and though traffic can be heavy on weekends it thins quickly if you head out on the minor roads. The winters here are cold, with real snow, and the summers are dry and bright, so spring and autumn are lovely. In the early morning the walls glow gold against a very clear sky.

Ávila is a city of saints. Teresa, the sixteenth-century mystic and reformer, was born here, and the town has a way of keeping her story close at hand. Local specialities reflect its past, with yemas, a sweet made of egg yolk and sugar, in every confectioner's window, and the grilled chuletón de Ávila, a huge beef chop from the local breed, in every restaurant. Eating well here is easy, though a plate of beans from nearby El Barco is the dish I would choose after a cold ride.

Fuel is no issue, since Ávila has stations on all its main approaches. The small villages like Tornadizos de Ávila and Cardeñosa are quiet, with a few bars. If you are staying a while, walk the top of the ramparts at dusk, when the swifts are screaming around the towers, and leave your jacket with the bike, since in Ávila even a warm day can end quickly once the sun goes behind the granite.
t.abrigo de lazaro@40.4,-1.4:
Albarracín is built of the colour of the land. The village stands above a loop of the Guadalaviar river in a bowl of rust-red sandstone, with houses of pinkish plaster and timber balconies stepping up the slope and a long line of medieval walls climbing the ridge behind. It has a population of about a thousand and the look of a place preserved by being slightly out of the way, and it was declared a national monument as a whole. The Abrigo de Lázaro is under four kilometres off, in the pine woods of the Rodeno, the red rock that surrounds the town and has been painted by human hands for thousands of years.

The approach by road is splendid. The Sierra de Albarracín runs between Teruel and the Cuenca highlands, a high, cold, dry country of pines and juniper on the divide between the Tagus, the Turia and the Jiloca, and the routes through it are quiet and winding, with long views and few cars. The bends are moderate and the surface good, and in autumn the woods turn colours that are unexpected in Aragon. Be wary of winter, when snow and ice can close the higher roads, and the nights are very cold.

The town has a history that is easy to read. It was an independent Muslim taifa and then a Christian lordship, the Señorío de Albarracín, which stayed practically independent until the late thirteenth century, and its walls and towers recall those turbulent years. The streets are narrow and steep, so leave the bike at the car park at the edge and walk in. Local food, such as roast lamb, cured ham from Teruel and migas, goes well with a cold day.

Teruel, twenty-six kilometres off by the straight line though longer by road, is the sensible fuel stop, and its Mudéjar towers are a World Heritage Site worth seeing. Gea de Albarracín, with its small shops, and Cella, with about 2,800 people, give you closer options. The rock shelters in the Rodeno are among the Levantine sites on the list, with paintings in red among the red rocks, so look carefully, as they can disappear into the stone.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric vi@40.4,:
At the Cingle de la Mola Remigia the limestone does something theatrical. A cingle is a long band of cliff that runs along the flank of a hill, and this one forms a pale wall above the Gasulla ravine, with shelters scooped out of its face like rooms with no fourth wall. Benassal lies a little over five kilometres to the east and the village of Ares del Maestrat perches on its own rock crest not far away, so the whole area has a feeling of scale that is rare in this part of Spain.

The significance of the Gasulla ravine is hard to overstate. In the early twentieth century local people began to talk of painted caves in the barranc, and by the 1930s scholars had realised that it held a remarkable concentration of Levantine art, with scenes of archers, running figures and animals that seemed to move across the stone. The paintings were not made as a single work, but over a long span of time, and there is still debate on which are older. Today the whole zone is protected as a cultural park and is part of the UNESCO listing.

Riding here means high plateau country. Roads around Ares and Benassal climb through terraced slopes of almond and olive, then cross open land with oak and pine, and the corners are generally smooth and easy. The N-232 between Vinaròs and Morella, a short ride to the north, is a favourite with riders for its long runs of bends. In winter the high ground can be cold and icy, so go in spring, when the air is fresh, or autumn, when the colours deepen.

On practical matters, Benassal is the nearest village with food and a few rooms, and the springs of the area are well regarded. Fuel is further away, with Alcalà de Xivert at thirty-three kilometres the nearest town of any real size, though Vilafranca is nearer and larger. You will probably have to pre-book to visit the painted shelters, so ask at the information office in the village or at the museum in Tírig. Carry water, wear boots and expect a modest walk.
t.rillo i@40.9,-1.9:
The Señorío de Molina is a high, cold, sparsely populated tableland on the boundary of Guadalajara and Aragon, and it feels like it, with big skies, wheat and sheep, wide valleys and villages of stone. Rillo, five or six kilometres from Molina de Aragón, sits at about a thousand metres on this plateau, where winters are among the harshest in Spain and snow can lie for weeks. Molina has a reputation as one of the coldest towns in the country, but a rider in June finds only a dry, bright warmth.

Molina itself is worth seeing. A large medieval castle overlooks the town, with a tall tower called the Torre de Aragón, and the old centre has narrow streets, arcaded squares and an old stone bridge over the Gallo. The lordship of Molina was practically independent for a long time in the Middle Ages, and the town has a proud sense of its own history. About thirty kilometres to the west the Alto Tajo natural park cuts deep gorges into the plateau and has some of the best river scenery in central Spain.

The riding is in the big, uncomplicated style of the Meseta. Long straights, rolling gradients and wide bends, with views for tens of kilometres, little traffic and a good surface, though the wind can be fierce. The roads that lead to Alto Tajo are narrower and more interesting, descending in a series of curves into forested canyons. This is a place for a day of easy cruising rather than aggressive riding.

Fuel is easy at Molina de Aragón, which has about three and a half thousand people and several stations. Corduente is smaller, with a few services, and Jaraba, in Aragon to the east, is known for its spas. Local food is hearty, with lamb, cured meats, and migas, and a coffee at Molina's main square is a good break. Painted rock shelters are recorded in the ravines around the plateau, a reminder that this high land has been inhabited for a very long time.
t.cingle del puig@40.4,-0.1:
Puig is the Valencian word for a hill, and it is slightly funny to find it attached to a cliff, because the Cingle del Puig is not so much a hill as the sheer lip of a limestone terrace over a ravine. It lies above the Barranc de la Gasulla, less than six kilometres from Benassal and not far from Ares del Maestrat, a village that sits on a crag at more than a thousand metres and looks across the plateau like a ship on a rock. The high Maestrat has a stark, mineral beauty, with grey stone, dark green juniper and enormous skies.

Riding to Ares is one of the better small adventures in Castellón. The road from Benassal rises across open ground, passes through a belt of oak woods and then runs along the plateau with views to the south over the Plana toward the sea on clear days. The bends are medium and clean, the tarmac usually good, and the traffic mainly local. Ares itself is a steep tangle of lanes with a church and a few bars, and you park at the edge and walk. In winter, ice and fog are real hazards at this height, and even in May the wind can be cold.

The Gasulla ravine is the reason Ares appears in books on prehistory. Its painted shelters have scenes of hunting and of people in motion, and they stand in a long gorge where goats still climb the ledges. The area is managed as a cultural park, and the museum in Tírig, in the next valley to the south-east, explains the images. Some shelters are open only with a guide, and the cliffs are fragile, so check before you set out and stay on paths.

For fuel, Benassal has only village-scale services, so the safe choice is Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away on the way to the coast, or Vilafranca, closer and larger than the villages on the plateau. Culla is nearby and has the ruins of a medieval castle on a ridge, a good excuse for a coffee stop. Bring water, because the plateau has little shade, and a warm layer, because it has little shelter either.
t.cova remigia abric vi@40.4,-0.1:
When Juan Bautista Porcar, a priest from Castellón with a passion for archaeology, found the paintings of Cova Remigia in the 1930s, the news travelled fast through the small world of Spanish prehistory. The shelter sits in the Gasulla ravine, five kilometres from Benassal, and the rock overhang that protects the paintings is a wide, shallow cave in a limestone cliff. What the visitors found were red figures of archers in what seems to be a lively conflict, and animals shown in a few swift lines.

There is a lot of argument about what these scenes mean. Some researchers see hunting, others see ritual, and a more adventurous school reads some of the archer groups as scenes of conflict between people. Dating is no easier, and the best you can say is that the tradition lasted a very long time, from the end of the ice age into the age of early farming, and perhaps beyond. It is perhaps better to stand in front of it and notice the economy of line, the way a few strokes give a running man his balance.

The road to this corner of the Maestrat is a ride you will remember. From Benassal you climb on good tarmac across open plateau, among fields enclosed by dry-stone walls, and the bends are open and flowing with plenty of space to enjoy them. The landscape is austere in winter, golden in summer and a clean green after spring rain. The cold can be real, and fog sits in the hollows on winter mornings, so choose your day with care.

Practicalities are simple but must be observed. The site is protected and visits are controlled through the cultural park, so enquire in Benassal or at the museum in Tírig, and do not expect to walk in unannounced. Fuel is at Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres off, and Culla and Villafranca del Cid are the nearest villages with a bar and a bakery. Bring water and sturdy shoes.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric i@40.4,-:
A mola, in Catalan, is a flat-topped mass of rock, and the one that gives this site its name is a block of Cretaceous limestone that has been sliced out of the plateau by the Gasulla ravine, leaving a cingle, a long band of cliff, along its flank. If you like geology, this is a place for you: the layers are clear, the cliffs are weathered into pockets and overhangs, and the shelters that hold the paintings are simply the places where the rock fell away in the right shape. Benassal is a little over five kilometres to the east.

A ride to the Gasulla is a ride across the high Maestrat, a land of pale rock and dark juniper that stands well above the coastal plain, where everything is sparser and colder than the Valencian stereotype. Roads run in easy sweeps over the plateau and down into the folds, the surface generally good and the traffic light. Gravel does collect where farm tracks join, and sheep or cattle can be on the road, so watch ahead. If you can, come in late spring when the broom is in flower and the wheat still green, or in October when the air is clear and hot is a memory.

The paintings of the Gasulla are among the most important in the Levantine tradition, and the ravine is a protected cultural park. The shelters often hold scenes of archers, hunters pursuing animals, and sometimes figures in what looks like a dance, but the rock surface has been damaged by flaking, and the paint is faint. Bring a sense of patience, and recognise that archaeologists who have been looking at these walls for ninety years still disagree about the details.

Benassal, with about thirteen hundred people, has bars and bakeries and a couple of places to stay, and it is known for the springs that rise around the village. Fuel is more distant, with Alcalà de Xivert thirty-three kilometres off the best choice. Culla, ten kilometres on, has a castle ruin and a fine view, and Villafranca del Cid, twelve kilometres away, is a bigger and busier place if you need supplies.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric ii@40.4,:
By the second or third visit to the Gasulla you stop expecting the big painting and start seeing the small things: the way the cliff catches the early sun, the swifts shooting along the face, the rust-coloured drip stains that streak the grey. The Cingle de la Mola Remigia keeps its shelters in a limestone wall a little over five kilometres from Benassal, and the rock holds as many natural marks as painted ones, so your eye learns to sort one from the other.

The name Maestrat goes back to the military orders that ruled this country in the Middle Ages: first the Templars, who held castles at Culla and elsewhere, and after their dissolution the Order of Montesa, whose master gave the region its name. The villages here still carry the look of fortified places, with houses packed tight around a church on a rock and walls that were once real defences. Culla is the best example, a hill village with a castle ruin that you can reach by a short walk.

Riding on the plateau demands little skill and rewards in feeling. The roads are good, the bends are well judged, and the traffic is almost nonexistent, so you can slow to a crawl and watch the land open out. You may see kites and vultures overhead and perhaps a fox crossing a field at dusk. Winters can be icy and foggy, so aim for the months between April and October, with an early start in the hottest weeks.

Fuel is at Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away, or at Villafranca del Cid, twelve kilometres away, which is small but larger than the hamlets on the plateau. Benassal can supply a meal and a bed. Make sure you book any visit to the shelters in advance, as access is controlled to protect the paintings.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric iv@40.4,:
Weather behaves differently on the Maestrat plateau. At a thousand metres and more, only thirty or forty kilometres from the Mediterranean, the climate has a double character: a sea breeze that brings moisture and cloud, and a continental winter that brings frost and sometimes snow. On a spring morning you may ride up through sunshine and find yourself in a drifting bank of cloud, with the cliffs of the Cingle de la Mola Remigia appearing and disappearing like a stage set.

The road conditions follow the weather. On the plateau they are mostly good, with long, flowing bends, but in damp weather the limestone surface can be slick, and after heavy rain the barrancos shed gravel onto the asphalt. Come prepared with layers, as a clear day on the coast can be cold and windy at Benassal. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, when the air is calm and clear and the light is sharp, and the stone of the cliffs shifts from grey to honey in the course of a morning.

Morella, an hour or so to the north, is the great medieval town of the region, with walls, a castle on a rock and a main street of arcades, and its pastries called flaons are the thing to try. The N-232 that runs there has long been a favourite of riders, and a day that links the Gasulla with Morella and back through the high villages is among the finest rides in the province. Distances are modest, but the corners eat time, so allow longer than the map suggests.

Benassal, five kilometres away, is the nearest village, with a few bars and a bakery, and Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres off, is the reliable place for fuel. The paintings here are part of the Gasulla group, and the shelter walls hold small red figures of the Levantine tradition. Respect the fences, bring water and never touch the rock. If you want to understand what you are seeing, spend an hour in the museum at Tírig before you ride out, and you will walk up to the cliff with a far better eye.
t.cave of altamira and paleolithic cave ar:
In 1879 a little girl lost interest in her father's digging and wandered further into a cave in Cantabria. She looked up and saw bulls on the ceiling. The father, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, a local landowner and amateur archaeologist, was digging in the floor of Altamira, a cave a hunter had stumbled on some years earlier. When he announced that the paintings were of the Ice Age, the experts of Europe laughed at him, and it was not until 1902, after similar paintings turned up in France, that the leading sceptic published a famous apology. Sautuola died long before that.

What those experts missed is still astonishing. The great ceiling at Altamira is a herd of bison painted in red, black and a warm ochre, using the natural bulges of the rock to give the animals a sense of volume, and it was made by people who lived here many thousands of years ago, in the Upper Palaeolithic. The date is a matter of continuing research, and the cave seems to have been used over a very long period. The original cave is now closed to ordinary visitors to protect it, but the neighbouring museum has an excellent full-size replica, the Neocave, and a good exhibition, and it is well worth the time. Check the booking rules for the museum before you ride out.

Santillana del Mar, less than a kilometre away, is a village of stone mansions and cobbled lanes where the writer Jean-Paul Sartre is said to have called it the town of three lies, since it is neither holy, nor flat, nor on the sea. It is one of the most handsome villages in Spain and, in summer, one of the busiest. Park at the edge, walk in early, and look at the Romanesque cloister of the collegiate church of Santa Juliana.

The riding in Cantabria is a different thing from the dry south. From Torrelavega, six kilometres away and the source of fuel, you can head west to the coast at Comillas, with its Gaudí villa, or south-east towards the green valleys of Cabuérniga and into the mountains. Roads are twisting and damp, the bends are tight and often covered in leaves, and rain is likely at any time of year. The Desfiladero de la Hermida, a deep gorge on the way to the Picos de Europa, is a rewarding day's ride, though it lies a good way to the west.
t.cova remigia abric v@40.4,-0.1:
Imagine a visit to a museum where the curator has not turned on the lights and the exhibits are painted on the walls of a cliff. That is Cova Remigia in the Gasulla ravine, where the shelter is a wide hollow in the limestone, a rock-roof high enough to stand under and deep enough to keep out most of the rain. Five kilometres from Benassal, on a plateau that is cold in winter and bright in summer, it lies on one of the great hunting grounds of the prehistoric past, and the paintings are among the clearest in Spain.

Shelter V is one of several in the Remigia complex, which shows how the rock was used again and again, with painted scenes added at different times. The first thing you notice is how small the figures are, often no more than a hand's length, and how much movement is drawn into them. Archers lean forward, run or turn, goats and deer escape in a few lines. It is easy to stand there and wonder what the scene was for, and the honest answer is that nobody knows for certain.

The road up is a pleasure. Leaving Benassal, you cross the plateau on a good surface, with open bends that bring you again and again to wide views across wheat fields and juniper, and a skyline that rarely has a house on it. The cold arrives early in autumn, so take a layer and gloves. Fuel is the question to settle before you set out: Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres from here, is the sure answer, and Culla and Villafranca del Cid have only village services.

Access to the shelters is controlled through the cultural park, so find out in advance what is open. The Valltorta museum in Tírig is the best place to begin. Try not to arrive at midday, when the sun flattens everything; mornings and late afternoons bring the light across the rock at an angle that makes the pigment stand out.
t.cova remigia abric iv@40.4,-0.1:
Red paint in these shelters is mostly iron oxide, ground from ochre and mixed with something that has not been identified for certain, perhaps animal fat, blood, egg or plant sap, and some figures were drawn in black from charcoal or manganese. That is more or less the entire chemistry of Levantine art, and the fact that a handful of earth pigments have survived thousands of years in open air under an overhang is one of the minor miracles of Spanish archaeology. Cova Remigia, in the Gasulla ravine near Ares del Maestrat, is the place where you can see how well it has worked.

Look closely at a panel and you will find that figures overlap. A later artist painted over an earlier scene, and in a few cases repainted the same figure, which is how specialists build a sequence of styles and tell older from younger. It is a slow, patient discipline, closer to reading a palimpsest than admiring a picture. The Gasulla shelters are rich in this kind of evidence, and that is one reason why scholars have studied them for ninety years.

For a rider the interest is in the setting. Benassal is five kilometres off, and the roads that lead into the Gasulla cross a high plateau with oak and pine, easy bends and almost no traffic. They are at their best between April and October, though early autumn mornings can be foggy and the surface slick. The Culla road, to the north-east, is well worth taking for the castle ruin on a ridge. Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away, has the fuel.

You may find that access is arranged through the park management, which asks that visitors go with a guide or at specified times. It is a sensible rule, because every curious hand leaves a mark. Bring water, wear boots, and give yourself time to stand and look for a full five minutes before you take a photograph. Often the second look finds figures the first one missed.
t.cova remigia abric iii@40.4,-0.1:
Benassal makes a good base for a day among the shelters, because it is a living village, not a museum. It stands on a hillside at the edge of the Gasulla plateau, five kilometres from the shelter, and its streets are lined with old stone houses with carved doorways. Locals will tell you with pride about the spring water that rises around the village, and in the surrounding oak woods truffles are gathered in season. It is a place for a quiet coffee and a talk in the plaza.

Food in the Maestrat is a hill farmer's cuisine, built around lamb, cured pork, stews, olive oil and local cheeses. A lunch at a village bar can be remarkably good, and there is none of the fuss of the coast. If you are lucky, someone will bring out the local honey, thyme and rosemary flavoured, and the almonds that grow in every terrace. Alcohol is simple and local, and the Valencian taste for a small glass of sweet liquor after the meal has not died out here.

The road to Cova Remigia from Benassal is easy and open, and the bends are generous. It runs over the plateau among dry-stone walls, with the vast sky overhead, and in clear weather you can see Penyagolosa to the north-west. Winters are cold and sometimes snowy, so check conditions before setting out. The best months are May, June, September and October.

Culla and Villafranca del Cid, a little further, have shops and bars. Respect the fences at the shelter and ask for advice in the village about visiting hours.

If the day goes well, you will want to end it back in Benassal with something cold.
