The village fountains are old and numerous, and the water that comes out of them is cold even in August, which tells you how much altitude you have gained since the coast. Sit on a bench with your jacket over your knees, watch the swifts and let your ears recover from the helmet. Spain's inland villages are best enjoyed at exactly this pace, with no plan beyond the next coffee.
t.abrigo de los recolectores@41.1,-0.7:
Alacón is a village of about four hundred people in the province of Teruel, in a dry country of pale hills, almond trees and scrubby pine, and for most of the last century it did not appear on anyone's list of places to visit. Then it became known that the barrancos around it hold some of the most important rock-art shelters in Aragon, the work of Levantine painters, and the whole area of the Río Martín was declared a cultural park. The Abrigo de los Recolectores, near the village, takes its name from a scene of figures who appear to be gathering something from plants or hives.

The riding is quiet, honest country riding. The roads in the district run along the Martín valley, climb over low ridges and cross a dry plateau, and the bends are gentle, the surface variable, the traffic almost none. It can be hard going in July, when the sun is fierce and shade is scarce, and bitterly cold in January, but April, May and October are excellent. Make sure your tank is full, because the villages are small and fuel is far apart.

Andorra, twenty-four kilometres away, is the real town of the district, with nearly eight thousand people and several stations, and a long industrial history tied to coal and electricity. Oliete and Muniesa, nearer, are small and attractive. None of these has a sure supply of fuel, so use Andorra.

As always with rock art, expect something modest, and be ready for fencing and guided visits. The cultural park provides information in the villages, and it is best to ask there about access and conditions. Keep off the rock, carry water, and remember that the best light is in the morning.

One more thing about this part of Teruel: it is a country that has lost people for a century, and you feel the space it leaves. Farmhouses stand empty, terraces have gone back to scrub, and a village bar may be the only open door for twenty kilometres. Spend a little in it, say good morning to whoever is behind the counter, and ask about the paintings. In places like Alacón, the people who live there are the best guides, and the shelters were first noticed by farmers and shepherds long before archaeologists arrived.
t.caseta de irene@40.4,-0.2:
The wind is the first thing you notice on the plateau between Culla and Villafranca del Cid. It comes in over the Maestrat from the sea or down from the mountains, depending on the day, and it has been put to work: lines of wind turbines stand along the ridges, turning slowly against a sky that seems to start at your shoulder. Caseta de Irene, a hut-sized name on a map, lies in this upland between the two villages, a little under seven kilometres from each, and the shelter belongs to the wider cluster of Gasulla and Valltorta sites that make this district special.

On a motorcycle the wind is a real factor. Gusts across the open ridge can lean you off line, particularly when you are passing a lorry or crossing a gap in a wall, so ride relaxed and give yourself room. The roads themselves are good, with a clean surface and unhurried bends, and traffic is rare. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, since the plateau can be raw in winter and the summer heat is dry and fierce. Penyagolosa stands on the horizon, a pyramid of limestone that is the highest summit in Castellón.

Both villages are worth a visit. Culla has the ruins of a castle that belonged to the Templars and later to the Order of Montesa, and a labyrinth of narrow lanes that climb to the ridge. Villafranca del Cid, a larger place of about twenty-five hundred people, is the district's market town, with shops and bars, and a long history as a centre of sheep and wool. Benassal is not far away either.

Fuel needs planning. Neither Culla nor the hut has a pump, and Villafranca's services are modest, while the nearest real town is L'Alcora, thirty-five kilometres away, which is known for its ceramics, made there since the eighteenth century. Fill up before you leave the lowlands. At the shelter, as elsewhere, keep to the paths and leave the paintings alone.
t.rillo ii@40.9,-1.9:
Rillo lies close to the river Gallo, and the Gallo has cut the Barranco de la Hoz, one of the great surprises of the Señorío de Molina. A flat, windswept plateau suddenly splits open into a canyon of pale rock, and tucked into the cleft is the sanctuary of the Virgen de la Hoz, a small shrine with a long tradition of pilgrimage. The Rillo II shelter lies on the plateau above, a little under seven kilometres from Molina de Aragón and a short distance from Corduente, which is the village closest to the gorge.

The riding on this plateau has a particular quality. The roads are long and mostly straight, rising and falling across the dry landscape, with views that run to the horizon, and then they dive into the valleys and wind through woodland. Traffic is almost nonexistent. Winter is fierce, with snow and hard frost, and the nights are cold even in late spring. July and August are dry and clear, though evening temperatures can be fresh, so pack a layer. Early autumn is the best time, when the light is golden and the trees along the river are turning.

Molina de Aragón is the obvious base, a town of about three and a half thousand people that was once the centre of a semi-independent medieval lordship. Its castle, long walls and towers dominate the skyline, and its arcaded square and old bridge give the town a character that outweighs its size. It has fuel, restaurants and shops, and the surrounding villages offer very little in comparison, so fill up here.

The painted shelters of this high country are among the less-known sites of the Spanish Levant, and the details of access change, so ask at the tourist office in Molina. The Alto Tajo natural park, with its deep canyons and clear rivers, lies to the west and is one of the finest areas for walking in central Spain. Carry water, and keep an eye on the weather, because afternoon storms can arrive fast in summer.
t.abrigo de los borriquitos@41.1,-0.7:
Borriquitos means little donkeys, and whoever named this shelter presumably saw something long-eared and four-legged in the red paint, though Levantine painters drew deer and goats far more often than donkeys. The name is a reminder that these places were named by farmers, long before they were studied by archaeologists, and that what a shepherd sees on a wall may not be what a professor sees. The shelter is near Alacón, in the Martín valley in Teruel, and belongs to the Parque Cultural del Río Martín.

The river Martín runs north through a landscape of low limestone gorges, almond groves and dry hills, and the villages along it include Alacón, Oliete and Albalate del Arzobispo, which belonged to the archbishops of Zaragoza, as its name still says. The roads here are good, quiet and winding, and make for a pleasant day of unhurried riding. April and October are the best months, as summers are hot and winters cold and sometimes foggy in the valleys.

Andorra, twenty-four kilometres away, is the main town of the district and the place for fuel and supplies. It grew with coal mining and the power station, and it is not pretty, but it is useful and friendly. Alacón, a small village of four hundred people, has a bar and is a good place to ask about the paintings.

Visiting the shelter may require a guide, and it is wise to ask at the village or the park office first. Keep to the track, do not touch the paintings, and bring water, since the walk can be dry.

There is something fitting about a shelter named by farmers. Nobody who first saw these walls in the nineteenth or early twentieth century had a theory about Levantine art, but they had eyes, and they passed what they saw on to the next shepherd, until it reached someone with a notebook. Most of Spain's rock art came to light that way, through ordinary people noticing, which is a good reason to be kind to the next person you meet in a village bar who says that they know of a cave.
t.burgos cathedral@42.3,-3.7:
Burgos Cathedral took its time. Work began in 1221 under Bishop Mauricio and King Fernando III, and the building grew in stages for three centuries, which is why it contains a French-inspired Gothic nave, a Renaissance golden staircase by Diego de Siloé, a Constable's chapel of astonishing complexity and, above the crossing, an octagonal lantern whose star-vault, rebuilt in the sixteenth century, is a masterpiece of Renaissance ornament. The two openwork spires of the façade were added in the fifteenth century by a craftsman from Cologne, Johann, and they give the building its unmistakable outline. UNESCO listed the cathedral in 1984, one of the first Spanish sites to be added.

Under the crossing lie the remains of El Cid, Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the eleventh-century warlord whose life turned into a legend of the Reconquista, and of his wife Jimena. Inside the cathedral there is also a mechanical figure called the Papamoscas, the fly-catcher, who opens his mouth when the bell strikes the hour, and children and adults alike wait for it. The city is on the Camino de Santiago, and in the streets near the cathedral you can pick out pilgrims by their scallop shells and tired steps.

Riding into Burgos from the plains of Castile, you pass through a country of wheat fields, pale villages and big skies, and the roads are straight and fast, with good surface and long views. The city lies at about 860 metres, so winters are cold and spring mornings can be frosty. Park the bike in one of the public car parks and walk to the cathedral square, since the old centre is often restricted.

Fuel is no problem, since Burgos has stations all round the ring road. Eating here is a pleasure: morcilla, the rich black pudding made with rice, roast lamb from the wood oven, and the fresh white cheese of Burgos are the staples. A short ride to the east, the Sierra de la Demanda and the monasteries of La Rioja are an obvious excursion, and the great prehistoric site of Atapuerca lies just outside the city.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric v@40.4,-:
Ibex are back. After years of decline, the Spanish ibex, the cabra montés with its swept-back horns, has recovered across the mountains of eastern Spain, and in the Maestrat you may see them on a rocky ledge at dawn or dusk, picking their way along terrain that no human would attempt. They are the descendants of the animals that the Levantine painters drew, and the shelters of the Gasulla ravine hold goats that look much like them: the same curve of horn, the same stance on a slope.

The Cingle de la Mola Remigia, a long limestone cliff over the ravine, is a good place to think about this continuity. The painters hunted ibex and deer, and their pictures show how closely they watched. Today the same cliffs hold griffon vultures, eagle owls and the occasional golden eagle, and wild boar roam the oak woods below. It is a landscape in which life has been constant, with changes at the edges.

Riding up from Benassal, five kilometres away, you cross a plateau with long views, small fields and stone walls, and the bends are easy to read. Take care at dawn and dusk, when animals are on the move and may cross the road, particularly wild boar, which do not look both ways. The roads are good, but fog and ice can appear on winter mornings.

Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away, is the town for fuel, and Culla and Villafranca del Cid have a few shops. The shelter is part of a protected zone, and visits are managed, so enquire first. Carry water and binoculars if you have them, because the cliffs are best scanned slowly.

Dawn is the hour for it. Before the sun is on the rock, the ledges are quiet and the animals that spent the night there are still moving, and a rider who has parked at the lip of the plateau with a flask of coffee has a good chance of seeing something. By nine the thermals have started, the vultures lift off in slow spirals, and the ibex retreat into the shade. If you prefer your wildlife with a bit less effort, a clear evening gives the same show in reverse, with the cliff glowing orange and the first bats appearing.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric iii@40.4:
A farmhouse in the Maestrat is called a mas, and the plateau around the Gasulla used to be dotted with them: low, thick-walled stone buildings with a threshing floor, a sheepfold, a cistern and a few fields of cereal, each one a small self-sufficient world. Many are now roofless, with trees growing through the floors, and the shell of an abandoned mas at the end of a farm track is a typical sight here. Depopulation has been the story of the interior of eastern Spain for a century, and the Cingle de la Mola Remigia lies in the middle of its effects.

It matters to a rider because it shapes the roads. Tracks that once linked farms to villages are now grassy ruts, and the paved roads that survive are the ones that connected the larger places, so you get quiet, well-surfaced tarmac running through country that has almost no buildings on it. You will see a few shepherds, a farmer on a tractor and perhaps a hunter in his orange vest in the season, but mostly you will see the land. Take care with sheep on the road, and remember that fog on a spring morning can drop visibility to a few metres.

Benassal, five kilometres from the shelter, is one of the villages that have held on, with a few hundred families and the services that go with them: a bar, a bakery, a small shop. Culla and Villafranca del Cid are the same. The shelter itself, one of many in the Gasulla, belongs to a past in which these hills were populated by hunters who moved with the seasons, and who left their marks in the places where they sheltered.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The nearest sizeable town is Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away, and Villafranca has a more limited supply. Bring water and expect to walk. The access is regulated to protect the paintings, so check with the information office before you go, and never touch the rock.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric x@40.4,-:
Ramón Cabrera, known to his enemies and his admirers as the Tiger of the Maestrazgo, made this country famous in the 1830s. A Carlist general in the civil war that followed the death of King Ferdinand VII, he turned the high plateaus and fortified villages of the Maestrat into a stronghold, and from his capital at Morella he held much of the countryside for years, to the despair of the government armies sent against him. The war ended in 1840 with a defeat, but the Carlists rose again in the 1870s, and the memory of these campaigns still colours the way people in the Maestrat see their history.

You can see why the plateau suited a guerrilla. The country is a maze of limestone gorges, stone walls and ruined farms, with high villages built for defence, and anyone who knows it can disappear in an afternoon. Today the same terrain makes good riding, with roads that curl along ridges, drop into ravines and climb out again. The surface is mostly fine, the traffic light, and the Cingle de la Mola Remigia, a cliff over the Gasulla ravine, is five kilometres from Benassal.

Morella, an hour to the north, is the best-preserved medieval town in the region, with an almost complete circuit of walls and a castle on a rock. Its main street is lined with arcades, and its sweet flaons, pastries of cheese and almond, are sold everywhere. The ride there along the N-232 is a fine one, with long runs of bends and views over wild country.

For fuel, Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres away, is the sure answer, though Villafranca del Cid has some services. Remember that the shelters are protected and visits are controlled, so ask before you go and keep your hands off the walls. If you have time, the old walls of Morella are worth walking at dusk, when the stone turns amber and the swifts come out; the town is a good place to understand why a guerrilla army could hold a region for years, with its single steep street, its great gate towers and the castle looking down over everything.
t.cingle de la mola remigia abric ix@40.4,:
Rock art is a matter of light. A painting that is invisible at noon can appear at eight in the morning, when the sun rakes across the cliff and the faint orange line of a figure throws a shadow of a fraction of a millimetre. The Cingle de la Mola Remigia faces a direction that gives good morning light on some sections and good afternoon light on others, and a photographer or a patient visitor will learn to follow the shadows along the cliff as the day moves.

The ninth shelter along the cingle is one among many, and it has its own character, which depends on how the overhang catches the sun. Anyone who has stood in front of rock art for long enough knows that the first minute is disappointing. The eyes need time, and then, gradually, the shapes resolve: a bow, the curve of a back, the legs of a running animal. Some people use a torch held at a low angle, but in many protected sites this is forbidden, so ask first.

Benassal, five kilometres from the shelter, is the base. The road from the village to the cliffs crosses a high plateau with a good surface and mostly easy bends, and in the early morning, with mist in the hollows and the first sunlight on the stone walls, it is a lovely ride. Rainy days are best avoided, as the limestone can be slippery and the paths muddy. Wear boots and carry water. A small notebook helps: sketching what you think you can see, then comparing it with what a second visitor sees, is the best way to learn how subjective the whole business of reading these walls can be.

Fuel is at Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-three kilometres off, or at Villafranca del Cid, a smaller place. The shelters are protected and visits are managed, so ask at Benassal or at the museum in Tírig before you set out, and never touch the paintings.
t.convent of la encarnacion@40.7,-4.7:
Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada entered the Convent of the Incarnation in Ávila in 1535, when she was about twenty, and she stayed for twenty-seven years. The convent was large, comfortable and rather sociable, with visitors in the parlour and a lively social life among the nuns, and it was only after decades of illness, prayer and unease that she left in 1562 to found a small, strict house of her own, San José, the first of her reformed Carmelite convents. She became Saint Teresa of Jesus, one of the great writers of the Spanish language, and her cell and the rooms where she lived are still shown in the convent, a short distance outside the old walls.

Ávila is the place to understand how a mystic lived: not in a desert but in the middle of a town, among people who gossiped, quarrelled and gave her trouble. The town itself, with its granite walls and Romanesque churches, is only a few minutes away on foot. Teresa's name is on the pastries, the yemas de Santa Teresa, sweet egg-yolk confections sold in every shop, and on the souvenirs, the street names and the hotels.

For riders the great reward is the road south. The N-502 climbs from Ávila through pine and oak towards the Sierra de Gredos, crosses the Puerto del Pico, a pass of about 1,350 metres, and drops down a ribbon of bends to the warm valley of the Tiétar. Near the top you can walk a stretch of the old Roman road, a paved causeway of granite blocks. The surface is good, the bends are open and well banked, and the views, with the high peaks to the west, are superb. Snow can close the pass in winter, and the descent in rain can be slippery.

Fuel is easy in Ávila, with stations on the main roads, and the villages nearby, Tornadizos and Cardeñosa, are small and quiet. In autumn the oaks and chestnuts on the southern slopes turn copper and gold, and the descent into the Tiétar valley is at its best. Park the bike near the walls and visit the convent, which has its own museum, in the morning, when the town is quiet.
t.recodo de los chaparros i@41.1,-0.6:
There is a moment on the road to Albalate del Arzobispo when the plateau seems to open and a river gorge appears below, and that is the valley of the Martín, one of the hidden corners of Teruel. The river has cut a deep, winding canyon through the limestone of the Bajo Aragón, and the villages that line it, Albalate, Ariño, Alloza, have been farming and mining here for centuries. The Recodo de los Chaparros, the bend of the holm oaks, is a shelter in this country, and it belongs to the group that makes the Río Martín one of Aragon's cultural parks.

The riding around here is easy, quiet and rewarding. The roads follow the valley, climb over low ridges and cross the plateau, passing through fields of cereals and almond groves, with the occasional oak wood. The surface is mostly good, the bends are gentle and the traffic light. In summer the heat in the valley is fierce, and in winter fog can settle in the bottoms, so April, May, September and October are best.

Albalate del Arzobispo has a long history, and the name tells it: the town was once an estate of the archbishops of Zaragoza, who built a palace there. Ariño is known for its coal mines, open-cast pits that scarred the landscape and gave work to generations, though mining there has stopped. Alloza, smaller, holds a church and a few houses. Andorra, fifteen kilometres away, is the largest town in the area, with nearly eight thousand people, and has fuel and supplies.

As in every Levantine site, the paintings are small, faded and fragile, and visits are managed by the park. Ask at the information point in Albalate or at one of the villages, and wear sturdy shoes. The best light is in the morning. Take water, as the walk can be hot and dry, and do not touch the walls.
t.raco molero@40.4,-0.1:
Truffles grow under the oaks of the Maestrat. The black truffle, Tuber melanosporum, favours the cool, limestone soils of the high plateaus of Castellón, Teruel and Tarragona, and in recent decades farmers have planted oak plantations to cultivate it, hoping for a crop that sells for a high price in winter. Dogs are trained to find it, . The Racó Molero, a ravine corner four or five kilometres from Benassal, is in the oak country, and the woods around it hold a mixture of holm oak, pine and juniper.

Benassal is one of the villages where the truffle has become part of local life, and in winter you may find it on the menu in bars and restaurants, grated over eggs or potatoes. The village also has a reputation for its springs, and its old streets, with houses of carved stone, are worth a stroll. Culla, ten kilometres away, and Villafranca del Cid, twelve kilometres off, offer more of the same, with a pleasant view over the plateau.

The ride up is exhilarating. The road crosses open plateau, with bends that curve gently between stone walls, and the surface is generally good. Fog and frost are possible in winter, and in spring the broom and rock rose bloom along the verges. Take care at dawn and dusk, when wild boar and deer may cross the road.

For fuel, go to Alcalà de Xivert, thirty-two kilometres away, as the villages on the plateau cannot be relied upon. The shelter is one of several in the Gasulla area, and visits are controlled, so ask in Benassal or at the museum in Tírig. Take water and walk gently.

Winter is the season to come for the food, and the price is the cold. From December to March the plateau can be raw, with frost on the verges and fog lying in the hollows, and the road above Benassal deserves a careful hand. A rider who is happy in the cold will find the villages warm and welcoming, with a fire in the bar and the smell of woodsmoke in the street, and a plate of something local waiting at the end of the day. In a quiet January the whole district feels like it belongs to the people who live there, which is a good way to see it.
t.moli darrer abric iii@40.5,-0.1:
High up in the interior of Castellón, where the Maestrat hills fold into the mountains of Els Ports, there is a country of limestone ravines and old farms that few foreign riders ever see. The shelter called Molí Darrer, Abric III, lies in that country, about nine kilometres from Benassal. The name means last mill, a reminder that these ravines once powered small mills on seasonal streams, and that the people who farmed here worked hard with little water.

The shelter belongs to the group of Levantine rock art sites listed by UNESCO in 1998, in the Mediterranean Basin. These paintings, mostly in red, show hunters, animals and small human figures and are thought to be thousands of years old, though I cannot tell you what this one shelter holds. Most of these sites are small and delicate, and local museums, such as the one at Tírig in the Valltorta gorge, organise visits and explain what you will see, so start there rather than hunting alone.

The riding in the area is among the best in the Valencian interior. Roads wind over high, open plateaux dotted with holm oak and pine, drop into deep valleys and climb again, and the corners are frequent without being tiring. Surfaces are generally good on the main routes, rougher on the side lanes, and there is very little traffic. Villages such as Benassal, Culla and Catí, with their stone houses and old gateways, appear on the hilltops, and the air is cool and clear. Peñagolosa, the highest summit of Castellón at about 1,800 metres, rises in the north-west.

Benassal, a village of some thirteen hundred people, is the nearest place for a bite and a bed, and Villafranca del Cid, a little farther, is larger, with fuel. Catí is known for its goat's cheese, which is excellent with local honey, and a plate of cured ham, black pudding and bread with olive oil is a fair description of mountain cooking here.

Spring and autumn are lovely, with green slopes and cool temperatures, while summer is hot and winter can bring frost and snow on the higher roads. Take water and a full tank, because distances are longer than they look.
Albarracín looks as though it were poured onto its rock. The old town winds along a loop of the Guadalaviar river, in the hills of Teruel, and its houses, the colour of dusty roses, climb the hillside under a line of medieval walls that follow the ridge. In the eleventh century it was the seat of a small independent Muslim state under the Banu Razin family, and it later became a Christian lordship before joining Aragon. Its wooden balconies, narrow lanes and tilting houses are a national monument, and it is regularly named among the most beautiful villages in Spain.

Four and a half kilometres from the town, the Pinares de Rodeno protected landscape is a forest of pines growing on red sandstone, which weathers into odd pillars and hollows. The rodeno, as the stone is called, gave the town its warm colour, and in many of its overhangs are prehistoric paintings, some in red, and the shelter's name, the Shelter of the Yellow Figures, hints at a different colour. The group of Levantine rock art sites in the Albarracín area is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot describe what is painted at this particular spot, and there are marked trails and guides to help.

Riding here is a joy. The roads cross a high plateau, at over a thousand metres, with open views, juniper and pine woods, and rivers cutting small gorges. Several great Spanish rivers rise within a short distance, including the Tagus, the Turia and the Júcar, in the Montes Universales to the north-west. The bends are open and fast, the surface mostly good, and traffic is light. Winters are cold and snow can close roads, while summer nights are cool.

Albarracín has a thousand inhabitants and a modest range of services, while Gea de Albarracín and Cella, a larger town, offer more, including fuel. Teruel, the provincial capital, is about forty kilometres away. Local food is mountain food, with cured ham from Teruel, lamb, migas and truffles from the forests, and the bakeries sell good almond pastries.

The ride links this shelter with the Balma de la Fabriqueta. Go early or late in the day, when the light on the pink walls is warm and the day-trip crowds have gone.
t.abside@41.7,-0.9:
Zaragoza is a city of brick. In the centuries after the Christian conquest of 1118, the Muslim craftsmen who remained and their descendants, the Mudéjars, built churches and towers across Aragon using brick, glazed tile and decorative patterns of geometric inlay, and the result is a style found nowhere else. In Zaragoza the brick apses and towers of the old churches, with their blind arcades and zigzag courses, are the best examples, and the Mudéjar architecture of Aragon is a World Heritage listing, first awarded in 1986 and extended in 2001. The apse at this stop is a piece of that heritage.

The city lies on the Ebro, in a wide, dry basin between the Pyrenees and the Iberian mountains, and it was Roman Caesaraugusta before it was a Moorish capital. The great Basilica of the Pilar, with its tiled domes, stands beside the river and draws pilgrims from all over Spain, and the Aljafería, an eleventh-century Moorish palace, has some of the most beautiful stuccowork in the country. Goya, born in a village not far to the south, is the city's artistic hero, and the museum named after him is worth a visit.

Riding in Zaragoza means contending with the cierzo, a cold, dry wind that blows from the north-west down the Ebro valley and can reach gale force, especially in winter and spring. On a motorcycle it is a presence to respect, pushing the bike sideways on bridges and open stretches. The surrounding country is flat and steppe-like, and the roads are straight and fast, so the real pleasure is the contrast with the mountains a couple of hours north or south. The old centre is a maze of one-way streets, with trams and cobbles in places.

With over six hundred and seventy thousand people, Zaragoza has fuel, parking and every service. The tapas district around El Tubo is the best place to eat, with small bars specialising in fried mushrooms, garlic prawns, and local ham and sausage. Try a slice of fruta de Aragón, candied fruit covered in chocolate, as a sweet souvenir.

The ride links the Mudéjar apse with the painted shelter known as Arqueros Negros, the Black Archers, which belongs to a very different, much older Aragon.
t.abrigo del ciervo@40.4,-1.4:
The Sierra de Albarracín is big sky country. At over a thousand metres, the plateau is cold in winter and bright in summer, with pine forest, juniper and limestone outcrops, and a population so thin that you can drive for half an hour without meeting a house. Abrigo del Ciervo, the Shelter of the Deer, lies four kilometres from the town of Albarracín, in the sandstone landscape of the Rodeno, and its name suggests that the animal was an important one for those who painted here. The group of Levantine rock art sites in this area is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what the shelter shows, and the marked paths and local guides are the best way to find out.

Deer still live in these woods, and so do wild boar, foxes and, on the high cliffs, the Spanish ibex, which has returned to many of its old haunts. Golden eagles and griffon vultures work the ridges, and in the early morning or at dusk you have a decent chance of seeing deer at the edge of a clearing, especially from a quiet road. The pine forest smells of resin in the heat, and the red earth lights up in the evening.

The roads of the sierra are some of the best in Teruel for riding. They are open and quick, climbing in long, easy bends over the plateau and dropping into river gorges, with a good surface and very little traffic. Winters are hard, with snow and ice, and some roads can close, so check before you set out in the cold months. In summer the heat is dry but the nights are cool. Mornings in spring and autumn are clear and sharp.

Albarracín is a small place of about a thousand people, with a modest range of shops and restaurants, and the nearest place with more choice, including fuel, is Cella, a town of nearly three thousand. Teruel is farther, about forty kilometres. Local food includes cured ham, lamb, truffles in season and almond cakes. The ride links this shelter with the Balma de la Fabriqueta, so you can spend a long day among the pines.

Take water on any walk, and keep to the marked trails to protect the fragile paintings and the vegetation.
t.raco gasparo@40.4,-0.1:
Racó means corner in Valencian, and Racó Gasparo is a corner of the hills, a little fold of land tucked away from the road, about five kilometres from Benassal. The country here is the high interior of Castellón, near the borders of Aragon, where the land lifts toward Els Ports de Morella and the whole region feels more like the Pyrenees foothills than the Mediterranean coast. Villages with a few hundred people, stone houses and a medieval castle on a rock are the norm, and Culla, a small village nearby, is crowned by one of the most dramatic of them.

The shelter at Racó Gasparo is one of the painted shelters of the district, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot describe the paintings, and as at other sites in the area, the best way to find out what you can see is to visit the museum at Tírig or ask at a local tourist office. The ride also visits the Abrigo del Plano del Pulido, which is another shelter in the district.

Benassal sits well inland and high, and the climate is cooler than on the coast, with cold winters and fresh summers. The village has a historic centre of old stone houses, a few noble mansions and an air of quiet pride, and there are springs in the hills around. In the hills around, the oaks, pines and juniper make good cover for deer and boar, and the clear night sky is excellent for stars.

For riders, the roads here are among the best in the Valencian interior. They cross high plateaus and drop into ravines in sequences of fast, open bends, with a good surface on the main routes, little traffic and big views. The wind can be strong on the ridges, and in winter ice and snow may close the highest passes. Distances between towns are long, so keep the tank full. Villafranca del Cid, about eleven kilometres away, is a larger town with fuel and services.

Spring and autumn are the finest seasons. Pack a warm layer, even in summer, and aim to be at the shelters in the morning, when the light is soft.
A cingle is a long band of cliff, the kind of cliff that runs along the side of a hill like a belt, and the Cingle de la Mola Remigia is one of the great ones of the Maestrat. A mola is a table mountain, a flat-topped hill with sheer sides, and this one rises above a ravine near Benassal, about five kilometres from the village. The cliff face is a wall of pale limestone, stained with orange and grey, with ledges, overhangs and hollows that are as good for shelter today as they were when people began to paint on their walls.

Abric VIII is one of a group of shelters in the cingle, listed as part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO included in 1998. I cannot say what it holds, but the group is known to specialists, and the ride goes on to Los Estrechos I, a site in a narrow gorge, which fits its name. Visits are often organised by guides in the district, and the museum at Tírig is a good source of advice, since many shelters are fragile and some are closed.

The landscape around is open and airy. Holm oak, pine and juniper cover the slopes, and the farmland on the plateau is a mix of almond, olive and cereal, with stone huts and old farmhouses at intervals. In spring the ground is green with wildflowers, and in autumn the oaks turn a deep brown. Deer and wild boar are common, and griffon vultures and eagles circle over the cliffs in the heat of the afternoon. The silence is the thing you remember.

The riding is a pleasure in the cooler months. Roads wind over passes and along ridges in easy bends, with a decent surface and very little traffic, though the lanes close to the cliffs may be rough and narrow. In summer, the heat on the exposed plateau is fierce, so start early. Benassal, with a bit over thirteen hundred people, has basic services, and Villafranca del Cid, which is larger, is the place to look for fuel.

Local food is mountain food: cured ham, black pudding, lamb and a good cheese from nearby Catí, with olive oil from the surrounding groves. Try to be at the cliff in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun picks out the colours in the rock.
t.abrigo de los toros del prado del navazo:
Near the high plateau of the Sierra de Albarracín, a few kilometres from the red-walled town of Albarracín itself, there is a patch of pine woodland on a very particular rock. It is called rodeno, a russet sandstone that glows orange when the sun is low and has been carved by wind and water into tall fins, mushrooms and overhangs. The Abrigo de los Toros del Prado del Navazo is one of the painted shelters in these Pinares de Rodeno, and its bulls, cattle depicted in red, are part of the same body of Levantine and schematic art that UNESCO listed in 1998.

Albarracín deserves a long look before or after. The town is a medieval walled settlement strung along a loop of the Guadalaviar, the river that further downstream becomes the Turia and reaches the sea at Valencia. Its houses have rose-coloured plaster, wooden balconies and uneven roofs, and the old walls climb a ridge behind it. For several decades in the Middle Ages it was an independent lordship under the Azagra family, a little state tucked between Aragon and Castile. Today it is protected, quiet in the early morning and crowded by noon at weekends.

The riding is higher and cooler than most of Spain, with Albarracín at about 1,200 metres. Winters are cold and snow is possible from November to March. Summer is the best time, with clear skies and a thin, dry air, and the road from Teruel is a good, mostly fast route that climbs through wide pine-covered hills and farmland. Closer to town the road narrows and gets bendier, and the bends near the rodeno forest are among the nicest you will find in the area.

Albarracín has about a thousand people, so it is small. Fuel is easiest in Teruel, twenty-six kilometres away, which is also where to find the Mudéjar towers and the cured ham that Teruel is known for. In the town you can eat roast lamb or migas, a humble dish of fried breadcrumbs, and wash it down with a cold beer. If you want to walk to the shelters, a path through the forest is marked, but sun and cliffs can be harsh, so bring a hat and a bottle of water.
t.abriga de las figuras diversas@40.4,-1.4:
If you stand in the Pinares de Rodeno on a late afternoon, the rock turns the colour of a brick oven and the pine trunks seem to glow against it. The shelter marked here, the Abrigo de las Figuras Diversas, lies in that sandstone forest less than five kilometres from Albarracín, and the name is an archaeologist's one: it simply says that the wall carries a mixed bag of painted figures. Humans, animals and abstract signs share the rock in the manner of the rock art of the Spanish Levant, which UNESCO listed together in 1998.

Rodeno is the key to the whole area. It is a soft red sandstone, a relic of ancient rivers and deserts, which weathers into hollows and sheltered ledges, and for prehistoric people it provided ready-made walls. The Sierra de Albarracín is also one of the few places in Spain where you find them at such height, with the town at around 1,200 metres. That altitude means cool nights even in July, and it means that in the cold months the pinewoods are quiet and white with frost.

Riding in is a pleasure. From Teruel the road climbs through bare steppe farmland, then into forest and finally into the rocky gorge of the Guadalaviar, with the town appearing suddenly above the river like a stage set. The surface is generally good, the bends are medium, and the real hazards are livestock on the road at dawn and tourist cars at noon. A day trip from Teruel in May or September is hard to beat.

Take a little time to wander Albarracín itself. Its alleys are steep and narrow, so leave the bike at the lower car park by the river and walk up past the cathedral and the pink houses to the old wall. Fuel and a full supermarket are twenty-five kilometres away in Teruel, which also has a wonderful set of brick towers built by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons, in what is called the Mudéjar style. In Albarracín itself, look for roast lamb, local cheese and cured ham, and drink plenty of water if you walk to the shelters.
t.las balsillas@40.4,-1.4:
Las Balsillas means the little pools, and in a sandstone forest where rain drains away fast, a hollow that holds water is worth naming. The pin lies four and a half kilometres from Albarracín, inside the protected pine landscape of the Pinares de Rodeno, and it is one of those places where the guidebooks and the local people seem to disagree about exactly where the line between a place name and a patch of forest falls. What matters is the setting: red rock under dark pine, with a floor of needles that muffles every sound.

The rodeno here is the same stone that colours Albarracín's walls, a sandstone laid down by rivers some two hundred and fifty million years ago, in the Triassic, and it still has the look of dried mud and ripple marks. Wind and rain have sculpted it into rounded boulders that sit on narrow stems, and into low overhangs that sheltered the painters whose small red bulls, goats and hunters are scattered over this district. They are a small part of the Levantine art that UNESCO recognised in 1998, and the area around Albarracín has one of the largest concentrations.

If you ride in from the Teruel direction you will find that the plateau feels strangely like northern Europe. At 1,200 metres the air is thin and clear, the pines resemble those of the Scottish Highlands, and in autumn mushroom pickers fill the forest tracks. A quiet minor road threads through the trees on the way to Bezas and Orihuela del Tremedal, and it offers gentle bends and a surface that is fine in the main with frost damage in a few spots. Snow can close the high roads between December and March.

Albarracín has a handful of rooms, a few bars and restaurants and a very small supermarket, and since the town has barely a thousand residents, fuel is something you want to have sorted out before you arrive. Teruel, twenty-five kilometres off, has everything, from pumps to the famous ham. Keep your bike on the paved areas by the forest, because the sandstone sand is soft and the forest is protected.
t.abrigo del medio caballo@40.4,-1.4:
A horse cut in half is a strange name for a hollow in a cliff, but Abrigo del Medio Caballo is what the shelter is called, and the likely reason is that the painted figure on its wall is partial, or that the rock itself makes a profile. Here the pin lies four and a half kilometres from Albarracín, in the red sandstone woods of the Rodeno, and the shelter is one of dozens in this area carrying small paintings of animals, hunters and abstract marks. They belong to the body of rock art that UNESCO protects as the Mediterranean arc of the Iberian Peninsula.

Albarracín has a long past. Before the Christians arrived it was a Muslim stronghold, and then for much of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries an independent lordship belonging to the Azagra family, who sat between the kingdoms of Aragon and Castile and played one against the other until Aragon absorbed it. Its walls, which crawl up the ridge like a stone dragon, date from various periods, and if you walk up to the tower at the top you can see the whole sandstone landscape spread out below.

On a bike the plateau is a joy in early summer. The road up from Teruel climbs gradually, with gentle bends and long views, and the temperature falls as you rise. Forest tracks leave the main road at several points, but most are unpaved and best left to walkers, and the paved lane from town to the rodeno woods is narrow with the occasional sand drift. Autumn brings cold mornings and the bright yellow of aspen leaves, and from November the chance of snow and ice rises sharply.

Albarracín's population is barely above a thousand, so the services are limited. There is no major fuel station nearby, which makes Teruel, twenty-five kilometres off, your stop. On the other hand there is excellent food, from cured ham to the local lamb stews. A bottle of water and sun cream are sensible for any forest walk, because the exposed sandstone gives off a great deal of heat from midday.
t.barranc del puig abric ii@40.4,-0.1:
Benassal lies in the interior of Castellón province, up in the highlands of the Maestrat where Valencian country turns to rock and pine, and the Barranc del Puig is a ravine close by. The shelter listed here, Abric II, is a bit under five kilometres from the village, which has about thirteen hundred people and a good stone-built centre of arcaded houses. It belongs to the painted rocks of the Maestrat, the northern part of the Valencian region's Levantine art zone, and shares the UNESCO listing of 1998 with sites in Aragon, Catalonia, Murcia and Andalusia.

The Maestrat is a high, windswept land of terraced slopes, stone walls and farmsteads called masos, many of them abandoned. The name comes from the medieval order of Montesa and before it the Templars, who controlled this country after the Christian conquest in the thirteenth century. Castles stand on isolated hills, the most famous at Morella to the north, and many villages preserve medieval bridges and market arcades. It is a place for those who like silence and long views.

Riders consider it a hidden playground, with mile after mile of empty, narrow roads that climb over passes of a thousand metres and more. The tarmac is generally fine, bends come in rhythm and the curves open to wide vistas over bare hills. The weather is changeable, with fog and cold in winter, and a dry, bright summer that is surprisingly mild at night. Late spring, when the broom is yellow and the stone is warm, is the best moment.

Services are limited. Benassal has a couple of bars and shops, and the nearest big town is Alcalà de Xivert, a long twenty-nine kilometres away down towards the coast. It is better to fill up before climbing into the hills and to allow for the distance. Benassal itself is known for its mineral springs, and spa visitors once came here to take the waters. If you walk to the shelter, bring more water than you think you need.
t.hayedos de ayllon tejera negra@41.2,-3.4:
Beech forests are rare in the Spanish interior, and the Hayedo de la Tejera Negra, in the Sierra de Ayllón, is one of the southernmost in Europe, a relic of a colder age that has survived on the shaded north slopes of the range. It lies in the province of Guadalajara, about eight kilometres from Riaza and just across the border from Segovia, at an altitude of well over a thousand metres, and is protected as a natural park. In October the leaves turn gold and copper, and the forest becomes one of the best autumn spectacles in central Spain, so popular that the park limits visitors and asks you to book.

The Sierra de Ayllón is a high, rounded range of slate and quartzite, the north-eastern extension of the Sistema Central, with its highest summit, Pico del Lobo, a little over 2,200 metres. The slopes are covered with oak, pine and heather, and the valleys hold villages of dark stone that look as if they were built to blend in with the rock. Wolves, deer and wild boar live in the woods, and golden eagles and griffon vultures patrol the ridges.

For riders, the approach from Riaza is a delight. The road from Segovia climbs over the Sierra de Guadarrama and drops into the wide, windswept plain around Riaza, then turns up into the mountains in a series of fine bends. Surfaces are generally good, traffic is light, and the villages are little visited. Winters are hard, with snow and ice on the high roads, and the best seasons are late spring and early autumn. Note that the park itself is for walkers and its track is not open to motorbikes.

Fuel and food are easiest in Riaza, a town of about two thousand people with an arcaded main square used as a bullring, and Ayllón, a medieval town farther west, is another useful stop. Riaza has bars where you can have roast lamb or the local sausages. Book your visit to the beech wood in advance if you are going in October, bring warm clothing, and expect cold mornings even in late spring.
t.abrigo del tio campano@40.4,-1.4:
Pine resin has a smell you notice before you see the forest, warm and sweet and a little medicinal, and it is the first thing that greets you in the rodeno woods outside Albarracín. The Abrigo del Tío Campano lies four kilometres from the town, among the red sandstone outcrops of the Pinares de Rodeno, and the name, which means something like Uncle Bellringer's shelter, suggests a local character whose story is lost. The painted figures on the rock belong to the body of rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998 as the Mediterranean arc of the Iberian Peninsula, and in this district they are mostly small animals and people in red.

The pines are maritime pines, grown for their timber and for resin, which for generations was tapped by local families in the summer months. Cut a diagonal scar in the bark, hang a pot under it, and the tree weeps for the rest of the season. The resin went to make turpentine and rosin, and the industry has all but vanished, but you still see old scars on the trunks. Under the trees, wild rosemary, thyme and rock rose cover the sandy ground, and in spring the scent of the thyme is strong enough to cut through the resin.

The road from Teruel to Albarracín is a good way to arrive, rising from the dry basin of the Alfambra and Turia rivers onto the high ground of the sierra, and then dropping into the gorge. At the end of the day the light on the rock is the colour of a ripe apricot. The final approach to the town has some tight bends and a narrow stretch where the road runs between the cliff and the river, with the walls of the old town above. Be careful with sand on the road after rain, and with tourist cars that stop without warning.

Albarracín has about a thousand people and no big fuel station nearby, so plan to fill up in Teruel, twenty-five kilometres off. In the town, lamb, local ham and a hearty soup called sopa de ajo are on offer, and cafés open early. For a walk in the forest, take water and a hat, and avoid the paths in thunderstorms, because the sandstone is slippery when wet.
t.la cocinilla del obispo@40.4,-1.4:
Cocinilla del Obispo, the Bishop's Little Kitchen, is a fine name for a hollow in a sandstone cliff, and it tells you a story that I cannot verify, most likely a legend about a churchman who picnicked or sheltered there. The shelter lies a little over four kilometres from Albarracín, among the red rock and pines of the Rodeno, and it holds paintings of the Levantine type in the same tradition as the rest of the region, protected by UNESCO since 1998. The bishops in question are real enough, because Albarracín was an episcopal see for centuries, and it is still linked to Segorbe in the diocese's name.

The cathedral, in the old town, is a modest building for a bishop's seat, a sixteenth-century church with a tapestry collection, and its position at the top of a flight of steps tells you much about the town's pride. Albarracín was once an independent Muslim taifa kingdom ruled by the Banu Razin family, and its name comes from them. Later it passed to a Christian lordship, and then to the crown of Aragon in the thirteenth century. The result is a tight, sloping town in which each wall and balcony has its own story.

Riding in the area is a reminder that Spain is not all sun and heat. At that altitude the nights are cold even in summer, and a morning start in June can mean a visible breath. The roads are quiet and well kept, but bends come quickly as the gorge narrows, and you should pay attention to livestock, especially in the evening. Autumn is a favourite time for locals, who come to hunt mushrooms, and the forest road is lined with parked cars on good weekends.

Services in the town are limited, so fill the tank in Teruel, twenty-five kilometres away, before you set off. In Albarracín the cafés on the Plaza Mayor are fine for a coffee and a slice of tortilla, but the real feast is the view from the wall at dusk. If you go to the shelter on foot, bring water, because the forest is dry and the sun reflects off the sandstone.
t.torre e iglesia parroquial de san pablo@:
The leaning towers of Aragon are a familiar sight in Teruel, but in Zaragoza the Mudéjar masterpiece is the tower of San Pablo, an octagonal brick shaft rising above the roofs of the Gancho district, west of the old centre. It is part of the Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon, a UNESCO listing that groups together churches, towers and ceilings built by Muslim craftsmen working for Christian patrons between the twelfth and the seventeenth centuries. The brick is the point. Aragon has little good building stone, and the masons made a virtue of necessity by laying bricks in patterns of lozenges and arches that look like lace.

Zaragoza itself is a big, flat, practical city on the Ebro, and approaching it by motorbike you cross dry steppe and irrigated fields, with a skyline of towers and cranes. The wind is the thing to know about. The cierzo, a cold, dry north-westerly, blows down the Ebro valley on many days of the year with enough force to move a parked bike and to make a ride across an exposed bridge an exercise in concentration. Locals say it makes people in Zaragoza a little stubborn.

The city's heart is the Basilica del Pilar, a baroque giant on the riverbank where, according to tradition, the Virgin appeared to the apostle James. Goya, who was born in a village nearby, painted frescoes in its dome. A short walk away is the Aljafería, an eleventh-century Muslim palace that is now the seat of Aragon's parliament. The narrow lanes of El Tubo, between the Pilar and the Plaza de España, are where Zaragozanos go for tapas, and a little glass of wine with a plate of fried mushrooms or a skewer of grilled prawn is a worthwhile pause.

Riding in the city is manageable. Fuel stations are everywhere, traffic is orderly by Spanish standards, and the grid layout is easy to follow. The old centre has some pedestrian streets, and motorbike parking is usually possible on the pavement in designated bays. Take care on tram tracks and on the polished stone of the plazas, which is slippery after rain. In July and August the heat is extreme, and the best time to explore on foot is in the early morning or late evening.
The Spanish language did not spring up all at once, and if you want to see a place where it first stepped on to the page, you come to San Millán de la Cogolla. In two monasteries, Suso above and Yuso below, in a green valley of the Sierra de la Demanda, monks of the tenth and eleventh centuries made notes in the margins of a Latin manuscript, translating hard words into the speech of ordinary people, in a form that has been identified as one of the earliest written Castilian and, in a few lines, Basque. Those notes are known as the Glosas Emilianenses, and the monasteries were listed by UNESCO in 1997.

Suso, the old monastery, is a small stone complex built into the rock of the hillside, with horseshoe arches that show Visigothic and Mozarabic influence, and caves where the hermit Emilian is said to have lived in the sixth century. Yuso, the newer monastery, lies in the valley below, a large Renaissance and baroque building with a fine church, a library and a famous collection of ivory reliquaries. The poet Gonzalo de Berceo, who wrote in the vernacular in the thirteenth century, was educated here and is regarded as the first named poet in Castilian.

For riders, the valley of the Najerilla is a pleasant, calm place. The approach from Nájera, on the Camino de Santiago, is a quiet road through vineyards and poplars, and beyond San Millán the mountain road climbs through oak and beech toward the Sierra de la Demanda, with views of snowy peaks in winter. Bends are gentle, traffic is light and the surface is good. Spring is green and cool, and in autumn the vines turn red.

San Millán de la Cogolla is a village of about three hundred people, so fuel is in Santo Domingo de la Calzada, fifteen kilometres away, a town of about six thousand with a cathedral famous for a live rooster and hen kept in a Gothic coop in memory of a pilgrim miracle. Visits to the monasteries are by timed tour, so check the schedule before you arrive. The best meal in the valley is the local lamb or a dish of potatoes with chorizo, and a glass of Rioja.
t.abrigo del toro negro@40.4,-1.4:
Climbers have made Albarracín famous as well as painters. The Pinares de Rodeno, the red sandstone forest around the town, hold one of the best bouldering areas in Europe, and every year thousands of climbers come to scramble over the rounded blocks with their foam crash pads on their backs. The Abrigo del Toro Negro, the Black Bull shelter, lies four and a half kilometres from the town in the same stone, and its name probably comes from a painted bull, one of the animals that the prehistoric artists liked best. It belongs to the body of Mediterranean rock art protected by UNESCO since 1998.

The climbing tells you something about the rock. Rodeno is a sandstone that is hard enough to grip and soft enough to be worn into pockets, with a rough texture that offers friction. The forest has been protected since 1995 as a landscape reserve, and the rules ask you to keep to marked paths, not to light fires and not to use chalk near the painted shelters, since chalk dust can damage the pigments. The mix of art and sport in one patch of forest makes for some tension, which regulators try to manage.

On a bike, the point is the approach. The road from Teruel is a good one, climbing into the sierra through a landscape of bare hills and pine, and then dropping to the gorge. At the final stretch, where the road follows the river and passes under the town walls, the scenery is almost theatrical. In summer evenings it is cool at this altitude, and many riders stay overnight in town to have the streets to themselves at dawn.

Fuel is not available in Albarracín, so you will need to fill up in Teruel, twenty-five kilometres off. On the way back, the Mudéjar towers of Teruel, decorated in green and white ceramic, are a good reward. If you go to the shelter, take water and a hat, and do not leave your bike unattended with luggage on it, because the forest car parks are busy at weekends.
t.yuso monastery and monastic kitchen gard:
What does a monastery eat? That is a question that visitors rarely ask, but at Yuso, in the valley of San Millán de la Cogolla, the answer lies in the kitchen garden, the huerta, that stretches beside the walls. The monastery, rebuilt from the sixteenth century, is a large, plain-faced building of stone and brick, run today by Augustinian Recollects, and it was listed as a World Heritage site by UNESCO in 1997 together with the older monastery of Suso above. The garden is a reminder that monasteries were also farms, and that the monks' discipline included hoeing and watering as much as chanting.

La Rioja is the vegetable garden of Spain in a way that wine fans sometimes forget. The fertile valley of the Ebro and its tributaries produces asparagus, artichokes, peppers, borage and green beans, and a famous dish called menestra de verduras, a mixed vegetable stew, is a source of regional pride. The Najerilla river waters the soil of this side valley, and its terraces carry fruit trees, vines and vegetables. In spring and early summer the kitchen gardens of the villages are neat rectangles of green, and many families still grow their own food.

The valley is a delightful place to ride, because the roads are quiet and the scenery is varied. From Nájera, on the Camino de Santiago, you follow the river upstream through vineyards, then climb gently to San Millán, passing small villages with stone churches. Beyond it the road continues toward the Sierra de la Demanda, where beech and oak forests clothe the slopes and the air is cooler. Surfaces are good, bends are moderate, and the best seasons are May and October.

The village itself has only about three hundred people, and fuel is in Santo Domingo de la Calzada, fifteen kilometres away, or in Nájera, a bit farther. Visits to the monastery are by guided tour, and there is a limit to numbers, so book ahead if you can. t.rocas del mas de molero@40.4,-0.1:
Mas is the Catalan and Valencian word for a farmhouse, and the Rocas del Mas de Molero take their name from one such farm, which sits among the limestone outcrops of the Maestrat five kilometres from Benassal. t.morro bay@35.4,-120.8:

t.big sur bixby bridge@36.4,-121.9:
Bixby Creek Bridge is the best-known single structure on California's coast, a pale concrete arch spanning a deep canyon where the road crosses from one cliff to another. Big Sur village, further along, has a few stations, restaurants and lodges, but they are busy and costly. Carry water, warm layers and a little patience. The scenery, however, deserves it, with sea mist, the smell of eucalyptus and sage, and the Pacific stretching out to the horizon.
t.santa cruz mountains flow photo pull off:
The Sonoma coast is one of the wildest and most beautiful pieces of the California shore, and the pin sits near Bodega Bay, a small fishing town that sprawls around a sheltered harbour. The whole coast here is a mix of grassy headlands, rocky coves and long beaches, with huge waves rolling in from the Pacific and a cold, persistent fog that creeps in on summer afternoons. Bodega Head, a rocky promontory to the west, is a good place to watch for whales: grey whales pass on their migration between December and April, and humpbacks and sea lions are often seen.

Alfred Hitchcock shot The Birds here in 1963, using the town, the harbour and the little schoolhouse in the nearby village of Bodega, and the schoolhouse still stands and draws visitors. The road follows the cliffs, rising and falling over headlands, with tight bends, sudden views and the surf crashing below, and the surface is mostly good, but patched and sometimes sandy. Fog is the main hazard, and it can reduce visibility to a few metres, while wind and cold are constant. Dress in layers even in summer. The road north to Jenner, where the Russian River meets the sea, is one of the best stretches of coast road in the country, and the road inland through Occidental and the redwood groves of Camp Meeker is a charming alternative.

The label mentions Santa Cruz Mountains, which are far to the south near San Francisco Bay, so the pin is a different stretch of coast. Bodega Bay has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants serving fresh fish and chips, clam chowder and crab, and Sebastopol, twenty-seven kilometres inland, has more. Check fuel before heading north, as stations thin out.

Stop at the headland and watch the waves for a while. The sea air is cold, fresh and salty, and the sky is wide.
t.marin headlands and point reyes@38.4,-12:
Kenwood is a small village in the Sonoma Valley, tucked beneath Sugarloaf Ridge, and the coordinates put you in the heart of California wine country rather than on the Marin coast the ride is named for. Robert Louis Stevenson honeymooned on the slopes of nearby Mount Saint Helena in 1880 and wrote about it in The Silverado Squatters, a charming account of a summer spent in an abandoned mining camp.

Look at these coordinates on a map and you will see open water, well out in the Pacific, roughly fifty kilometres west of the Golden Gate. Mount Tamalpais is the hill every San Francisco rider eventually points a front wheel at. Kentfield, Mill Valley and Larkspur lie at its foot, and any of them will sell you petrol and coffee before you climb.

t.stinson beach@37.9,-122.6:

t.gredos mountain weekend photo pull off@4:
The pin for this stop lands on the high plain of Old Castile, in the province of Segovia, at the edge of the pine woods and wheat fields that stretch north of the Sierra de Guadarrama. The nearest villages are Sangarcía and Marugán, small settlements of a few hundred people, and Segovia lies about twenty-six kilometres to the east. The landscape is wide and open, with big skies and a horizon of low hills, and the Sierra de Gredos, from which the ride takes its name, rises far to the south-west, a long, jagged line on clear days.

The plateau here lies at about nine hundred metres, so even in summer the mornings can be cool and the air crisp. Roads run straight between fields of cereal and sunflowers, with occasional stands of umbrella pines, and the surface is generally good, though some minor roads are patched. Traffic is light, and the best hazards are tractors and the odd flock of sheep. The light in the evening is outstanding, with a golden glow over the stubble fields, and the sky is often a deep, clean blue.

The Alcázar, a fairy-tale castle on a rocky spur, is said to have inspired Walt Disney, and the cathedral is one of the last great Gothic churches in Spain. A few simple bars serve coffee and a bocadillo, and the area is known for its good bread. The rural quiet is part of the pleasure, along with the smell of dry grass and pine resin in the warm air. Spring, when the fields are green and poppies bloom, and autumn, with its soft light, are the best times to ride.
t.alto tajo gorge ride photo pull off@40.8:
The Alto Tajo is a long way east of here, a limestone country of deep river gorges on the Guadalajara and Cuenca borders, but the pin for this stop lies on the other side of Madrid, in the first rumpled foothills of the Sierra Norte, a few kilometres from Venturada and El Vellón. The ground here is granite and slate, scattered with holm oaks and the odd pine, and the horizon to the north is the pale blue line of the Sierra de Guadarrama. It is a quiet, unpretentious corner, close enough to the capital that you can smell the traffic, yet far enough to hear sheep bells.

Madrid's water comes from this country. The Canal de Isabel II, begun in the mid-nineteenth century to supply the growing city, still gathers its water from the reservoirs of the Sierra Norte, and the little lakes here, like Pedrezuela, are blue, clear and pleasantly empty in the middle of the week. Fishermen sit on the banks, kingfishers flash over the reeds, and the smell of warm rockrose and rosemary rises from the slopes in summer. The A-1 motorway runs close by, and its distant hum is the price of the view.

For a rider, this is the staging post. The roads leaving the foothills run north and east through farmland and holm oak dehesa, with moderate bends and a surface that varies from good to coarse. Traffic is light apart from the early Sunday exodus, when city drivers head for the mountains. In summer the heat is fierce by midday, so start early, and in winter frost and fog can linger on the lower roads. Fuel is easy in El Molar and along the A-1, but less so on the byways, so fill up before leaving the main road.

The ride that begins here heads for the Alto Tajo Natural Park, where the Tagus and its tributaries have cut gorges through the limestone, with sheer walls, pine forests, and griffon vultures circling above. The roads there are quiet, narrow and winding, and the villages are tiny, with a bar and a church and little else. It is a long day from Madrid, but an unforgettable one. t.jaca@42.6,-0.5:
Jaca is the old capital of the Pyrenees, a mountain town of thirteen thousand people at the foot of the Peña Oroel, with a cathedral, a fortress and a long history. In the eleventh century it was the first capital of the Kingdom of Aragon, and its cathedral, begun at that time, is one of the earliest Romanesque cathedrals in Spain, with a graceful apse and a cloister, and carved capitals that influenced churches along the pilgrim road. Jaca lies on the Camino de Santiago, the Aragonese branch that crosses the Pyrenees by the Somport pass and heads west towards Pamplona, and in summer the streets are full of walkers with scallop shells. The pentagonal Ciudadela, a huge star-shaped fortress built in the late sixteenth century, stands at the edge of town, and its moat is now a pleasant park, home to a herd of deer. A museum of miniature soldiers is housed inside. The town is lively in winter, as a gateway to ski resorts, and its ice palace was a venue for sporting events.

For riders, Jaca is an excellent base. The N-260 runs east through the foothills of the Pyrenees, a long switchback of passes and valleys, while the road north climbs to the Somport and the French border, through the valley of the Aragón river. Bends are good, the surface is mostly smooth, and the views of the high peaks are impressive. The weather can change quickly, and winter snow can close mountain passes, so check road conditions. In summer, the days are warm, and the nights are cool. Evening is a pleasant time to walk in the old town and listen to the cathedral bells.
t.navacerrada pass@40.8,-4.0:

t.mendocino@39.3,-123.8:
Mendocino looks like a New England fishing village that was picked up and dropped on a California headland, and that is more or less what happened. t.san francisco bay area@38.4,-121.7:
Central California's valley floor is flat in a way that has to be seen to be believed. t.santa cruz mountains flow@38.1,-121.4:

t.salinas@36.7,-121.7:
John Steinbeck was born in Salinas in 1902, and the town has never quite decided whether to be proud or embarrassed about it. This part of the story lives on the southern shore of San Francisco Bay, in Mountain View, a city that has become one of the world's best-known centres of technology. It sits at the bottom of the peninsula, where the Santa Cruz Mountains slope down to a flat, sunny plain and the salt ponds and marshes of the bay. t.fort nelson@58.8,-122.7:

This start is on the western shore of the San Francisco Bay, between Menlo Park and East Palo Alto, near the end of the Dumbarton Bridge. t.napa silverado trail backroads scenic ro:
At this point the map is entirely blue: the pin lies some forty kilometres out in the Pacific, beyond the continental shelf, in water where the California Current sweeps cold south and the fog is born. Cold water, rising from the deep along the shore, chills the air above it, and when that air drifts over the warmer land it condenses into the grey bank of fog that blankets San Francisco on summer afternoons. Fog can fill the valleys on summer mornings, and the temperature changes sharply between the coast and the ridge. Spring and autumn offer the clearest days, and weekdays are quieter. Ride carefully, because the road has a high accident rate and the local police are active. The smell of redwood and damp earth is one of the pleasures of the ride.
Alamo is a quiet, wealthy suburb on the east side of the Berkeley hills, in Contra Costa County, tucked beneath the shoulder of Mount Diablo. The mountain is the dominant feature, rising to nearly twelve hundred metres from the flat plain of the valley, and its twin summits are visible from all over the Bay Area. Everybody on a bike in the Bay Area knows Alice's, the roadhouse at the crossing of Skyline Boulevard and Highway 84 above Woodside. t.pescadero coast@37.3,-122.4:

Alice's has a second life as a rider stop, and it is worth saying a bit about the culture that has grown up around it rather than just the road. In the nineteenth century these hills were logged heavily to feed the growth of San Francisco, and the old skid roads and mill sites are still hidden in the trees. Many of today's roads follow those lumber routes, which explains why they bend and climb so naturally along the ridges. t.pescadero coast view@37.3,-122.4:
On the coast south of Half Moon Bay, the Pacific shows a rougher, more private face than around San Francisco, and the viewpoints here are among the best on the entire Highway 1 run. The land is a narrow marine terrace of grassland and farm fields cut by steep gullies, with sea cliffs of crumbling sandstone and long, empty beaches below. The breeding season runs from December to March, when the big males fight and the pups are born, and the reserve needs a booked guided walk at that time of year. Even from the highway, the huge shapes of the seals can sometimes be made out on distant sand. The road is mostly smooth, with long gentle curves along the bluffs, but the cold wind off the sea can be fierce, and on a foggy day it gets damp and cold fast. t.sonoma coast and russian river@37.6,-122:
Pacifica is where the city lets go of you and the Pacific takes over. t.sonoma coast and russian river scenic ro:
Muir Woods lies in a fold of Mount Tamalpais just above this pin, and the whole area tastes of redwood and wet earth. The old-growth forest in Redwood Canyon was saved in 1905 by the Kent family, who bought the land and gave it to the federal government. President Theodore Roosevelt declared it a national monument in 1908, and at Kent's request it was named for the naturalist John Muir. Coast redwoods here stand more than two hundred and fifty feet tall, and their trunks are thick with centuries of fog drip.

The road to the woods and on to the coast is the Panoramic Highway and Highway 1, a narrow, curving route that falls steeply from the mountain's flank to Stinson Beach. It is a joyful, technical descent through eucalyptus and bay laurel, with sudden views of the Pacific, and it can be crowded with tour buses and cyclists at weekends. The shaded sections stay damp, and the surface can be rough. Muir Woods requires advance booking for parking and entry in many seasons, so check the national park website before you go.

The swim label points to Stinson Beach, a long, broad stretch of sand beyond the little village, with lifeguards in summer. The water is cold and the currents can be strong, so most visitors paddle and walk. Next door lies Bolinas Lagoon, a tidal bay that attracts egrets, herons and harbour seals, and a short way south the Marin Headlands glow in the afternoon sun. Fog often hangs over the coast in the morning and clears by noon, and the best light comes in late afternoon.

Kentfield and the towns of the Ross Valley have fuel and food, and Mill Valley, closer to the mountain, has cafés and bakeries. Stinson has a few places for lunch and a general store. Bring a jacket, since the temperature can drop ten degrees between the village and the beach.
t.sonoma coast and russian river photo pul:
The north shore of San Pablo Bay is a quiet corner of Marin County, a patchwork of marsh, hills and old ranch land, and the pull-off here looks out across the water toward Vallejo and the Carquinez Strait. t.sonoma coast and russian river@37.7,-122:
Fairview is a hillside community above Hayward, in the Alameda County hills, and it stands on the wrong side of the shop window for most visitors, being mostly houses and winding streets with a few small shops. t.mount tamalpais road@37.9,-122.6:
Mount Tamalpais is the hill that every Bay Area rider eventually climbs, a long dark ridge across the Golden Gate that from the city looks like a sleeping woman on her back. t.point reyes station food@38.1,-122.8:
Point Reyes Station is a small, slightly rumpled ranch town at the head of Tomales Bay, and it serves as the pantry for one of the most beautiful parts of the California coast. Taylor State Park, a redwood canyon, and then opens into the grassland of the valley, a lovely, tight and tree-shaded road that rewards a calm pace. Coming from the north on Highway 1, the road follows the bay's edge, with views over the water, oyster shacks and a strong smell of mud and salt.

t.tomales bay view@38.2,-122.9:
Tomales Bay is a long, narrow finger of water that lies in a straight line for fifteen miles along the San Andreas Fault, so straight that it looks as if it has been ruled on the map. Pull over at the signed turn-outs only, because the shoulders are narrow.
t.lagos de covadonga@43.3,-5.0:
The Lagos de Covadonga are two glacial lakes, Enol and Ercina, set in a high pasture of the Picos de Europa, and the road that climbs to them is one of the great climbs of Spain. t.puerto de san glorio@43.0,-4.7:
San Glorio is a high pass on the border between Cantabria and Castile and León, a quiet, grassy saddle at 1,609 metres, and it gives access to the Liébana, the sheltered valley on the southern side of the Picos de Europa. t.san juan de gaztelugatxe@43.4,-2.8:

The chapel has been burned and rebuilt more than once, once by raiders led by Francis Drake according to tradition, and the present building dates mostly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Modern fame came differently: the island appeared in the television series Game of Thrones as Dragonstone, and visitor numbers rose so sharply that the authorities now regulate access. Booking a slot in advance has been required in recent seasons, so check before you ride out, and expect a fee for parking.

The wind off the sea is strong, and a sudden shower is always possible, so pack waterproofs.

t.briones@42.5,-2.8:
Briones sits on a hill above the Ebro, a village of fewer than nine hundred people with a ring of old walls, a big baroque church and more wine in its cellars than anyone could drink in a lifetime. It belongs to La Rioja Alta, the western and highest part of the Rioja wine region, where the river turns the landscape green and the vines run in long lines up toward the grey limestone wall of the Sierra de Cantabria. The surface is generally good, and the traffic is light outside the harvest, when tractors and grape trailers take over in September and October. t.lakes of covadonga@43.3,-5.0:
The climb from the basilica to the lakes is a short road with a long reputation. Over about a dozen kilometres you rise from valley meadows to a high, rolling limestone shelf, and the road threads between steep grassy slopes with cow bells clanking somewhere in the mist. t.arenas de cabrales@43.3,-4.8:
Arenas de Cabrales is the capital, if that is the word, of one of Europe's most pungent cheeses. A late-summer cheese fair in the village celebrates it. You can buy a wedge here to take home, though think about where it will ride.

t.big sur@36.3,-121.8:
Big Sur is not a town but a stretch of coast, about ninety miles of steep mountains dropping into the Pacific between Carmel and San Simeon, with a few clusters of buildings in between.
