t.waypoint 2@36.3,-121.8:
Big Sur is where California's coast shows its teeth. Between Carmel and San Simeon, the Santa Lucia range rises almost directly from the Pacific, with slopes that climb more than a thousand metres in a few kilometres, and Highway 1 is bolted to the cliff like a ledge. The area gets few services, no big towns and a lot of fog, and because the mountains cut the coast off from the interior, it stayed wild long after the rest of California was settled. In 1937 the highway opened, after many years of work, and made the coast accessible by car for the first time.

The drive is famously slow, and for good reasons. The road twists over every headland and into each creek canyon, with sharp bends, narrow shoulders and sudden drops, and speed limits drop to thirty-five or lower in places. Rockfalls and landslides are common, particularly after winter storms, and the road has been closed for months at a time, as it was after slides in 2017 that took out whole sections, so it is wise to check the state of the highway before you set out. Even in good conditions, a long line of cars can follow a camper at twenty-five, and a pull-out is the only escape.

The scenery repays the patience. Waves crash on rocks far below, sea otters lie in the kelp offshore, and in winter grey whales pass close to the cliffs on their way south. Coast redwoods fill the damp canyons, and the smell of salt, sage and eucalyptus fills the air. Pfeiffer Beach, with its purple sand, and McWay Falls, which drops onto the beach, are the best-known sights, though small pullouts hide others. Carmel, to the north, and Cambria, to the south, are the sensible places to fill the tank. Mobile signal comes and goes.

Autumn tends to bring the clearest days and the lightest traffic. Take a layer and a camera, and do not try to cover this road quickly.
t.madrid@40.4,-3.7:

t.dadi tulou cluster@25.0,117.7:
Dadi lies farther east and north than most of the tulou villages, in Hua'an County, where the hills are steeper and the valley floors are smaller, and its cluster has a rather different look from its neighbours. Instead of one grand circle, Dadi has a group of buildings in different shapes, round, square and oval, set in a narrow valley beside a stream. Some have beautiful carved doorways and painted beams, while others are plain, and in places walls have been patched with newer earth where rain had eroded them. No town is listed near the coordinates, so food and fuel need planning, and county towns will have the stations. Foreigners should check the rules before planning to ride, since a Chinese licence and registration are normally required for riding a motorcycle, and many visitors travel by car with a driver. Local tea, grown on the hillsides, is the natural thing to taste on a visit.
t.biescas@42.6,-0.3:

Safety measures have since been added, but summer thunderstorms in these valleys can still be sudden and fierce.

t.logrono@42.5,-2.4:
Logroño sits on the south bank of the Ebro, in the centre of La Rioja, and for a wine lover it is as close as it comes to a capital. t.mount hamilton@37.8,-122.1:
The coordinates fall in the Diablo valley, near Alamo and Moraga, and the dominant presence here is Mount Diablo, a lone peak that rises to about 1,200 metres east of the town and can be seen from much of the Bay Area. t.skyline boulevard@37.9,-122.2:

t.margaret river@-34.0,115.1:

t.gredos mountain@40.0,-3.6:

The setting is exceptional: after miles of dry plain, the green of the river valley is a shock.

The town is famous for strawberries and asparagus, grown in the fertile riverside fields, and in spring the restaurants fill with people eating them, often with a glass of cold white wine. The composer Joaquín Rodrigo wrote his famous guitar concerto, the Concierto de Aranjuez, in 1939, and the slow movement is one of the most loved pieces of Spanish music. If you hear it in your head while crossing the river, you will not be the first.

The point lies seven kilometres from the town, near the little villages of Ciruelos and Ontígola. Ontígola has an old reservoir, the Mar de Ontígola, a lake created in the sixteenth century to supply the royal gardens, and a pleasant spot for birds. The ride back from the Gredos mountains passes through a landscape of dry plains and low hills, which seems quite empty after the peaks and forests of the sierra, and the road runs long and straight under a huge sky.

Aranjuez has about fifty-four thousand people, with plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and is the natural place to stop. Ciruelos, with a few hundred inhabitants, has little. Aim to arrive in the evening, when the stone of the palace turns rose-gold and the gardens are cool. A walk under the trees, with the sound of water, is a gentle end to a long day on the road. In high summer, the heat in the valley can be intense.
t.kota kinabalu@6.0,116.1:
Kota Kinabalu sits on the north-west tip of Borneo, with the South China Sea on one side and the jungle-covered Crocker Range on the other, and on a clear morning the peak of Mount Kinabalu, at 4,095 metres, floats above the clouds to the east. The city, the capital of Sabah, has about four hundred and fifty thousand people, a waterfront lined with seafood restaurants, a lively Filipino market selling dried fish and handicrafts, and a string of islands just offshore that make up the Tunku Abdul Rahman Marine Park. The sunsets over the sea are famously good.

The city was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt in a modern, practical style, so its charm lies less in the architecture than in its position and its people. Sabah is home to more than thirty ethnic groups, with the Kadazan-Dusun, the Bajau and the Murut among the largest, and the cultures are on display at the state museum and the cultural village. Food is a highlight: grilled fish, sour fish soup, the raw fish salad hinava, and the layered tea that is sold in every cafe.

The road to Kundasang, which this ride follows, is the best in the state. It leaves the city, runs through the town of Tamparuli, with its long suspension bridge, and then climbs into the Crocker Range, with a series of bends through forest, with cool mist and a drop in temperature. At the top, the road runs close to Kinabalu Park, a UNESCO site, and the hills of Kundasang are lined with vegetable farms, tea plantations and a dairy farm that looks like a corner of New Zealand. In the afternoon, rain often falls, so start early and carry waterproofs.

Malaysia drives on the left, and the road is well surfaced but busy with trucks and local traffic, so overtaking needs care. Fuel is plentiful in Kota Kinabalu and in the towns on the way, and there are stations at Ranau, but the stretch over the range has few, so fill at Tamparuli. The best months are March to May, when the skies are clearer. Bring a warm layer for the highlands, where it can be cold at dawn.
t.sonoma coast@37.6,-122.5:
Pacifica is the last proper coastal town before San Francisco, a long strip of fog, surf and low houses squeezed between the Pacific and the steep ridge of the Coast Range. It is a place that feels slightly overlooked, which is part of its appeal. The beach at Linda Mar is one of the Bay Area's best-known surf spots, and on a gray winter morning you can watch wetsuited figures bobbing in the breaks while commuters stream by on Highway 1.

For riders, the real story here is the road. For decades, Highway 1 south of Pacifica crossed the cliffs at Devil's Slide, a notorious stretch where winter storms sent the pavement into the sea and traffic closed for weeks. A pair of tunnels opened in 2013 and now carry the highway through Montara Mountain, with a tidy view of the sea at either end. The old road was kept as a quiet bike and walking path, and you can still stand where the cliffs fall away beneath you. The result is a much calmer ride, though the tunnel exits expose you to crosswinds and fog.

North toward San Francisco, the Great Highway and Skyline Boulevard offer long, fast curves above the surf, and in the opposite direction the coast road to Half Moon Bay is a classic. Come early on a weekday if you can, because summer weekends bring a slow line of cars, and the fog tends to hold on until midday. Wear a warm layer even when the Bay is hot.

Pacifica has everything a rider wants after a long day: gas stations along the highway, taquerias, a pier for fishing and a handful of coffee shops that open early for the surfers. Sharp Park's golf course, designed by Alister MacKenzie, sits right on the waterfront, and the wetlands behind it shelter a rare snake and a rare frog that have tangled the course in local politics for years.

If you are riding north from here, the road eventually rises over Fort Funston's dunes, and the city's hills come into view. It is a fine end to a coastal day, even with the traffic.
t.mount@37.9,-122.6:
Mount Tamalpais rises above the northern side of the Golden Gate like a sleeping giant, and the old story goes that its outline looks like a reclining woman, which gave local people the name of the Sleeping Lady. At 2,571 feet it is not a huge mountain, but it springs straight up from the bay and gives a sweeping view over the whole region, from the Farallon Islands to the Sierra on a clear day. For riders, it is one of the best short climbs in the Bay Area.

The nearest towns, Mill Valley, Kentfield and Larkspur, give a hint of the setting. They are leafy, wealthy communities tucked into the creek valleys on the mountain's skirts, with redwoods in the gardens and cafes where cyclists meet. Mill Valley has a good small main street, and the old Mountain Home Inn serves as a landmark on the way up. The mountain was once reached by a famous crooked railway, with a hundred-odd curves, which ran until the 1930s and helped build the area's outdoor culture.

The riding itself is tight and constantly changing. Panoramic Highway climbs out of Mill Valley in a series of narrow bends, with redwood shade and the occasional glimpse of the bay below, then runs along the ridge toward Stinson Beach and the ocean. The East Peak road is a short, steep spur to the top, where a fire lookout and a few trails offer a short stretch of walking. The surface is patchy, the road is narrow and cyclists are everywhere, so a relaxed pace is the right one. Fog can sit on the ridge even when the lower areas are clear, and it often brings damp, cool air.

Fuel and food are best found in Mill Valley and Larkspur before the climb, because there is nothing on the mountain beyond a few small cafes and trailhead parking areas. Weekends are busy and the best time for a quiet climb is a weekday morning.

If you arrive late, the sunset is the real reward. The light turns the fog gold and pink, and the city lights begin to flicker across the water, a view that makes the narrow road worthwhile.
t.desfiladero de los beyos@43.2,-5.0:
The Desfiladero de los Beyos is the gorge the Sella river cut through the limestone heart of the Picos de Europa, and the road that follows it is one of the great short rides in northern Spain. The walls rise sheer on both sides, grey and cream and streaked with orange, so close in places that the sky narrows to a slit, while the river runs green and fast far below. Oseja de Sajambre, a mountain village of a few hundred people, lies near the upper end, and Posada de Valdeon, another small settlement, is farther south in a neighbouring valley. Fuel is in Cangas de Onis, to the north, or Riano to the south.

The riding is exhilarating. The road follows the gorge for several kilometres, cut into the rock face and passing through short tunnels, with tight curves, a surface that is generally good and the occasional patch of fallen stones. There is little room for error, with a drop on one side and a wall on the other, and it is best taken at an unhurried pace, especially in wet weather, when the rock sweats and the road can be slick. Traffic is light for most of the year, though weekends and August bring more cars and campervans. Early morning is atmospheric, with mist rising from the river, and autumn colours in the beech woods are beautiful.

The Picos de Europa carry a lot of history for a small range. At Covadonga, a short ride from Cangas de Onis, a Christian force led by Pelayo is said to have defeated a Muslim army in the early eighth century, an event traditionally taken as the beginning of the Reconquista, and the sanctuary in the mountains is still a place of pilgrimage. The surrounding villages made their living from herding and cheese, and Cabrales, a strong blue cheese ripened in mountain caves, is the region's pride. A slice with a glass of cider is the best lunch you can find.

Nature is dramatic. The limestone massifs rise to well over two thousand metres within a short distance of the coast, and they are a haven for chamois, wolves, brown bears and griffon vultures, which circle on thermals above the gorge. Beech and oak forest clothes the lower slopes, and the air smells of wet stone and moss. The river holds trout and salmon, and anglers stand in the shallows in season.

Carry a rain jacket and a warm layer, since the weather in the Picos changes fast, and fill the tank before you start.
t.najera@42.4,-2.7:
Nájera has been a capital, and the town remembers it. In the eleventh century, it was the seat of the kings of Nájera-Pamplona, and the great monastery of Santa María la Real, founded in 1032 by King García Sánchez III, still stands at the foot of a red sandstone cliff. The legend says the king, chasing a dove while hunting, followed it into a cave and found a statue of the Virgin inside, and he built the monastery on the spot. The church holds the royal pantheon, with carved tombs of the kings and queens of Navarre, and a cloister of delicate stone tracery. The cliff above, the colour of rust, gives the whole town a warm tone.

The Najerilla river runs through the middle, and the town is a stage on the Camino de Santiago, so pilgrims in boots and sunhats pass through every day in season. There is a battlefield nearby too: in 1367 the English Black Prince, allied with Pedro of Castile, won a battle here against his half-brother Enrique, which says something about the town's importance in medieval politics. About eight thousand people live here, so fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of restaurants are all easy.

Nájera is in the Rioja Alta, the upper part of the wine region, and the vineyards of tempranillo run down the valleys in neat rows, with the Sierra de la Demanda on the horizon. A short ride to the southwest, the monasteries of Suso and Yuso at San Millán de la Cogolla are listed by UNESCO, and the earliest known written words in Spanish were scribbled in the margins of a manuscript there, which is why the village claims to be the cradle of the language. Wineries throughout the area offer tastings, though a motorcyclist should treat these with caution.

The riding in the area is relaxed, a gentle mix of country roads between vineyards, with soft curves, wide views and very little traffic outside harvest season. Summer is hot and dry, with temperatures well above thirty degrees in the afternoon, so ride early. Autumn is the best season, when the vineyards turn and the harvest brings a festive mood. Local food is excellent: roast lamb, patatas a la riojana with chorizo, and grilled vegetables. After a day on the road, a glass of Rioja and a plate of local cheese is the right way to finish.
t.emerald bay@39.0,-120.1:
Emerald Bay is the most photographed corner of Lake Tahoe, and it earns the attention. On the southwest shore, a narrow glacial inlet of green and blue water cuts into the granite, with a tiny rocky island, Fannette, sitting in the middle like a lid. Lake Tahoe itself is enormous and cold, sitting at roughly 1,900 metres in the Sierra Nevada and among the deepest and clearest lakes in North America. In calm weather the water is a startling shade of turquoise near the shore and deep indigo further out.

Down at the water's edge stands Vikingsholm, a mansion built in the late 1920s by a wealthy woman who wanted a Scandinavian castle on the lake, inspired by medieval Norse architecture, with sod roofs and carved timber. It is open for tours in summer, reached by a steep path from the highway car park, about a mile each way, which is a long climb back up in riding boots. Nearby, Eagle Falls tumbles down the rock, and the bay has been recognised as a National Natural Landmark.

The road is the famous California 89, which climbs and winds around the bay on a ledge cut into the cliff. Corners are fun, with views of the water at nearly every bend, but the road is narrow, traffic is heavy in summer, and cars and tourists stop suddenly at the viewpoints. Rockfall and snow can close the highway in winter and spring, so check conditions before you ride. Go early in the morning, in late September or on a weekday to have a more peaceful time, and watch out for cyclists.

Parking at the main viewpoint is limited and fills quickly in summer, so patience is required. A few cafes near the viewpoints sell coffee and snacks. Weather can change quickly at this altitude, with cold evenings even in July, so bring a jacket. If the light is right, a few minutes at the rail will explain why people keep coming back.
t.tahoe city@39.2,-120.1:
Tahoe City is the unofficial capital of the lake's north shore, a small town that has the shops, bars and bike racks of a resort without ever feeling too big. It sits at the point where the Truckee River leaves Lake Tahoe, the lake's only outlet, flowing north and east to the Nevada desert. A small dam controls the outflow, and the nearby Fanny Bridge, named for the view people have when they lean over the rail to watch the trout, is a good place to see how a river is born.

The town's history is tied to logging, railroads and tourism. In the nineteenth century, the surrounding forests were cut to supply timber and fuel for the mines of Nevada's Comstock Lode, and the area later became a summer retreat for people escaping the heat of the cities. Just up the valley is Palisades Tahoe, formerly Squaw Valley, which hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics and put the region on the world map. A small local museum covers the story, and the wide bike trail along the river is a pleasant stroll if you want to get off the bike.

The riding along the north shore is excellent. Highway 28 and the road to the north follow the shore in an easy rhythm of long bends, with glimpses of blue water through the pines and the odd bigger view of the Sierra. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the speed limit is low in town, so it is more of a cruise than a charge. Early morning, before the beaches fill, is lovely, with soft light and cool air that smells of pine and warm dust.

Tahoe City has everything a rider needs: fuel, groceries, outdoor shops, cafes and restaurants, mostly along the lakefront and the main street. A coffee on a deck in the morning sun, or a burger and a beer at the end of the day, is easy to find. It is also a good place to refill before the long southern leg of the lake loop. Be ready for variable weather in the mountains, and remember that snow can linger into late spring and return early in autumn.
t.cabrales@43.3,-4.8:
Cabrales is a place most people know by taste before they know it by sight. The municipality lies in the foothills of the Picos de Europa in eastern Asturias, northern Spain, a steep, green country of narrow valleys, stone barns and limestone walls. It is the home of Cabrales cheese, a strong, crumbly blue made from cow's milk, sometimes mixed with sheep or goat, and traditionally matured in natural mountain caves where cool, damp air encourages the blue veins to spread. The cheese has protected status and a flavour that is unmistakable: salty, sharp, earthy and long on the tongue.

Much of life here still revolves around livestock and high summer pastures. Herders take cattle, sheep and goats up to the high meadows each spring, and cheese is made in small huts during the warmer months. Villages like Carreña have a handful of small bars, craft shops and cheese sellers, and it is easy to taste before buying. Cider, poured from a height into a wide glass, is the usual accompaniment, along with fabada, the white bean and sausage stew that fuels anyone who has been out in the hills.

The ride is spectacular. The roads through the valley of the Cares river twist between steep limestone walls, with the grey, jagged ridges of the Picos towering above, sometimes with cloud draped across the tops. Bends are tight and frequent, the road is narrow, and rain is a fact of life in Asturias, so surfaces can be damp even in summer. Nearby, the gorge walk of the Cares starts at Poncebos, and a mountain road climbs to viewpoints from which the Naranjo de Bulnes, the iconic orange-tinted limestone tower of the range, can be seen on a clear day.

Fuel is available in the bigger villages, but for a reliable choice, Llanes, a coastal town about fourteen kilometres away, has everything. Morning is the best time for the road, when mist hangs in the valley and traffic is light. Spring brings wildflowers and green slopes, while autumn is quiet and golden. Take your time, look up often and buy a small wedge of cheese from a local producer, which keeps well in a pannier if you wrap it carefully and do not mind a strong smell in your luggage.

t.near boyes hot springs on the way back@3:
The Sonoma Valley runs north from the bay in a long, narrow trough between the Sonoma and Mayacamas mountains, and the pin falls in its heart, around Glen Ellen and Boyes Hot Springs. This is wine country in its quieter, older form, with small family vineyards on the lower slopes, oak savanna on the hills and old stone wineries, and it is far less crowded than neighbouring Napa. Sonoma itself, the historic town at the southern end, has a Spanish plaza, an old mission and an easy, unhurried feel.

The valley has a rich history. The Sonoma Mission, founded in 1823, was the last and northernmost of California's Spanish missions, and in 1846 a band of American settlers raised the Bear Flag at the plaza and declared a short-lived republic, a rebellion that became part of the story of California's annexation. Agoston Haraszthy, a Hungarian émigré, planted the Buena Vista vineyard here in the 1850s and is often called the father of California wine. Further up, Jack London bought a ranch at Glen Ellen in 1905, and his Beauty Ranch is now a state park, with his stone house ruins and his grave on a wooded knoll.

The riding is pleasant rather than thrilling. Highway 12 runs the length of the valley, with vineyards on either side and the hills glowing gold in summer, and side roads such as Bennett Valley Road and Sonoma Mountain Road wind up into the oaks, narrow, rough and beautiful. Traffic on Highway 12 is heavy at weekends and during harvest, and cyclists share the quieter lanes. The morning light, the smell of crushed grapes in autumn and the stillness of the hills make it a delight.

Fuel and food are in Sonoma and Santa Rosa, and the plaza has plenty of cafés, bakeries and a picnic-friendly lawn. Spring is green and full of wildflowers, summer is hot and dry, and autumn brings the vintage and bright yellow vine leaves. Winter is wet but quiet. Pick a weekday if you can, and leave time to wander the plaza, where an old mission building and a few adobe walls give a hint of the valley's past.
t.near dixon on the way back@38.4,-121.7:
Central California's valley floor is flat in a way that has to be seen to be believed. The land around Dixon and Davis, in the Sacramento Valley, is a table of irrigated fields stretching in all directions, with rice, tomatoes, sunflowers, almonds and sugar beets laid out in squares, and the Vaca Mountains rising to the west. A rider coming from the Bay Area crosses the Carquinez Strait, then drops onto this plain, and the change is abrupt: the fog and the redwoods give way to dry air, big skies and long straight roads.

Davis is the dominant town of the area, a university community of nearly seventy thousand that is proud of its bicycles. It has more bike paths per head than almost anywhere in the United States, and the university's agricultural and veterinary schools help to make the surrounding countryside a laboratory for crops and cattle. Dixon, a smaller farm town, is known for its dairy and for its annual May Fair. A drive through the area in spring, with almond blossom in the orchards, is a sight.

The pin sits in the middle of the plain, and the riding here is a test of patience. The roads follow a section grid, running dead straight between irrigation ditches and fields, with sudden corners at the section lines. The surface is usually good, though truck traffic is heavy on the main routes, and tule fog can reduce visibility to a few metres on winter mornings. Summer afternoons are hot, often above thirty-five degrees, and the wind can be strong. Early starts are wise.

Fuel and services are easy, with stations at every junction along the interstate and in both towns, as well as plenty of cafes and fast food. For a better meal, Davis has a good farmers' market and a range of restaurants. The Yolo Bypass, a flood-control channel to the east, becomes a shallow lake in wet winters, and thousands of waterfowl gather there, including snow geese and sandhill cranes.

This is the gateway to the wine country of Napa and Sonoma to the west, and the Silverado Trail is a short ride through the hills. The contrast between the dull valley and the beautiful vine-covered slopes is a delight, and an early start in the cool of the morning makes the transition a pleasure.
